### [1] [STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00003)
*Animesh Varma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STATERA addresses center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from monocular videos by adapting a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with frozen weights and a temporal tubelet mixer. The method introduces the HiddenMass Benchmark (50K simulation + 63 real-world sequences) and demonstrates significant improvements in CoM prediction, achieving 25.2% normalized error in simulation and 41.0% physics capture in zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion because surface cues and point tracking become unreliable under self-occlusion. This limits the ability to localize center of mass for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos.

Method: STATERA adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. The approach uses a unique phase-aware training objective (Crescent) that handles the trade-off between bimodal predictions and centroid collapse.

Result: In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only method demonstrating consistent movement toward the true hidden offset, improving physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%, despite a monocular vector overshoot artifact.

Conclusion: Frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation. There exists a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids.

Abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.

</details>


### [2] [Emergent Object Binding Has a Finite Spatial Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00006)
*Mayank Singal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper reveals that pretrained Vision Transformers encode an "IsSameObject" signal in patch embeddings, but this signal exhibits a spatial structure: binding probability decays exponentially with patch distance, reaching a nonzero floor. This local spatial coherence explains behaviors that aggregate accuracy metrics miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers noticed that the single accuracy number for decoding whether two patches belong to the same object hides important structural information about the binding signal. They wanted to understand the spatial properties of this object binding in Vision Transformer representations.

Method: The authors decoded the IsSameObject signal from frozen patch embeddings across different backbones (DINO, CLIP, DINOv2, DINOv3), datasets (ADE20K, COCO), and probe families. They analyzed how binding probability varies with patch distance, object size, class relationships, and occlusion, controlling for confounds.

Result: Binding is local: probability of decoding two patches as belonging to the same object decays exponentially with distance, leveling off at a nonzero floor. This pattern holds across architectures, datasets, and probe types. This local spatial coherence explains why binding weakens on large objects, separates same-class objects less reliably than different-class objects, groups parts with wholes, and is unaffected by occlusion when controlling for object size.

Conclusion: Object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining as local spatial coherence with a finite range, rather than as a global object-level signal. This explains various behaviors that aggregate accuracy metrics obscure, indicating that the representation encodes object structure through local patch relationships.

Abstract: Pretrained Vision Transformers encode whether two image patches belong to the same object. This IsSameObject signal is decodable from frozen patch embeddings at high accuracy, which suggests that object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone. We show that this single accuracy number hides the structure of the signal. Binding is local: the probability that two patches of the same object are decoded as bound falls off monotonically with the distance between them and levels off at a nonzero floor, a falloff well described by an exponential with a finite length scale. This decay holds across object sizes, across three families of probe, on both ADE20K and COCO, and across DINO and CLIP backbones, which indicates that it is a property of the representation rather than of the decoder. Reading binding as local spatial coherence with a finite range accounts for a set of behaviors that the aggregate score leaves unexplained: binding weakens on large objects, separates distinct objects of the same class less reliably than objects of different classes, and groups object parts with their wholes. It is, by contrast, unaffected by occlusion once object size is controlled. We map each behavior with confounds controlled. As a preliminary observation, the horizon and its floor are organized at different depths in DINOv2 and DINOv3, which we report as suggestive given the small number of layers probed and the confound between the two models.

</details>


### [3] [Soundwich: Video Generation with Layered and Controllable Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00691)
*Zhuo Ning,AmirHossein Naghi Razlighi,Sagi Polaczek,Daniel Cohen-Or,Ali Mahdavi-Amiri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Soundwich is a training-free framework that transforms a joint audio-video generation model into a multi-track audio stem generator, enabling separate control over speech, music, sound effects, and ambient sounds while maintaining synchronization with the video.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current audio-video generative models produce audio as a single mixed track, limiting source-level control. This differs from practical workflows where different sound types are represented as separate editable tracks (speech, music, sound effects, ambient sounds).

Method: 1) Transform a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into multi-stem generator
2) Generate separate audio stems with explicit temporal activity control
3) Use shared scene representation to maintain global audiovisual context across stems while preserving source separation
4) Route cross-modal interactions between each audio stem and its corresponding visual source

Result: Stems remain synchronized with video and can be independently retimed, muted, replaced, or remixed. Experiments and human evaluations show improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness.

Conclusion: Soundwich enables flexible source-level editing within coherent audiovisual generation, bridging the gap between generative models and practical audiovisual workflows.

Abstract: Recent joint audio-video generative models can synthesize realistic videos with synchronized sound, but typically generate audio as a single mixed track. This limits source-level control and differs from practical audiovisual workflows, where speech, music, sound effects, and ambient sounds are represented as separate editable tracks. We introduce Soundwich, a training-free framework that transforms a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into a generator of multiple synchronized, independently editable audio stems coupled to a shared video. Soundwich generates separate audio stems with explicit control over their temporal activity. To keep separately generated sounds coherent, we introduce a shared scene representation that communicates global audiovisual context across stems while preserving their source-level separation. We further route cross-modal interactions between each audio stem and its corresponding visual source, improving audiovisual consistency. The resulting stems remain synchronized with the video and can be independently retimed, muted, replaced, or remixed. Experiments and human evaluations show improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness, while enabling flexible source-level editing within coherent audiovisual generation. Code is available at https://github.com/CodyNing/Soundwich.

</details>


### [4] [Spatial Lifting for Dense Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00017)
*Mingzhi Xu,Tao Zhou,Yong Li,Yizhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spatial Lifting (SL) is a novel methodology that lifts standard inputs like 2D images into higher-dimensional spaces (e.g., 3D) and processes them with corresponding networks (e.g., 3D U-Net), achieving competitive performance on dense prediction tasks while significantly reducing model parameters and inference costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop a more efficient approach for dense prediction tasks in vision that reduces computational costs and model parameters while maintaining or improving performance. The key insight is that counterintuitively, lifting dimensionality can actually simplify the problem and enable new capabilities.

Method: The method involves: (1) Lifting standard inputs (e.g., 2D images) into higher-dimensional spaces (e.g., 2D→3D); (2) Processing the lifted inputs using networks designed for that higher dimension (e.g., 3D U-Net); (3) Leveraging intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension for dense supervision during training; (4) Using single-forward-pass self-consistency for quality and uncertainty estimation at test time.

Result: The approach achieves good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and drastically lowering the number of model parameters. The structured outputs along the lifted dimension enable dense supervision and self-consistency-based quality/uncertainty estimation.

Conclusion: Spatial Lifting offers a simple and general modeling strategy that provides a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision. The key advantages are: (1) significantly fewer parameters; (2) lower inference costs; (3) intrinsic structured outputs enabling dense supervision; (4) built-in quality and uncertainty estimation capabilities.

Abstract: We present Spatial Lifting (SL), a novel methodology for dense prediction tasks. SL operates by lifting standard inputs, such as 2D images, into a higher-dimensional space and subsequently processing them using networks designed for that higher dimension, such as a 3D U-Net. Counterintuitively, this dimensionality lifting allows us to achieve good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and \textbf{drastically lowering the number of model parameters}. The SL framework produces intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension. This emergent structure facilitates dense supervision during training and enables single-forward-pass self-consistency-based quality and uncertainty estimation at test time. Spatial Lifting introduces a simple and general modeling strategy that offers a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision.

</details>


### [5] [Supervising Sound Localization by In-the-wild Egomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01388)
*Anna Min,Ziyang Chen,Hang Zhao,Andrew Owens*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion (camera motion) as a supervisory signal, where the audio model is trained to predict sound directions consistent with visual estimates of camera motion derived from multi-view geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key challenge in sound localization is obtaining labeled training data. The authors propose using egomotion as a weak but plentiful form of supervision - as the camera moves, the direction to a sound source changes, providing a natural supervisory signal without requiring manual annotations.

Method: 1) Use traditional multi-view geometry methods to estimate camera motion (egomotion) from visual frames
2) Train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with these visual estimates of camera motion
3) Combine this egomotion-based supervision with traditional binaural cues (interaural time differences, level differences)
4) Evaluate on a proposed real-world dataset of audio-visual videos with egomotion

Result: The model can successfully learn from real-world data and performs well on sound localization tasks.

Conclusion: Egomotion can serve as an effective supervisory signal for learning binaural sound localization, providing a way to leverage unlabeled real-world data. This approach combines the weak supervision from visual motion with traditional binaural cues to achieve sound localization.

Abstract: We present a method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as a supervisory signal. Over the course of a video, the cameras direction to a sound source will change as the camera moves. We train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with visual estimates of camera motion, which we obtain using traditional methods from multi-view geometry. This provides a weak but plentiful form of supervision that we combine with traditional binaural cues. To evaluate this method, we propose a dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion. We show that our model can successfully learn from real-world data and that it performs well on sound localization tasks

</details>


### [6] [Encoded but Disconnected: Decomposing Vision-Language Model Failures under a Patching Null](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00024)
*Genpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a negative finding: despite mid-layers of vision-language models encoding ground-truth answers in 68-91% of errors, this encoded information is not causally active for final predictions. Patching interventions fail to flip predictions across three different model architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether mid-layer representations in vision-language models are causally relevant to final predictions, testing the hypothesis that encoded information in middle layers actively contributes to model outputs.

Method: Residual-stream patching experiments across three VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B) on POPE benchmark, testing both layer-level and per-head interventions. Error modes are classified and learned via classifier.

Result: 0% non-trivial flip rate at layer level across all architectures; only one exception (InternVL3 layer-20 head-2) with localized effect. Three failure modes (Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override) learnable above 60% accuracy.

Conclusion: Mid-layer representations encode but do not causally contribute to predictions. The encoded signal is "disconnected" from output. Three operationally distinct failure modes exist and are learnable, suggesting mechanistic reality of these categories.

Abstract: Across three vision-language model architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B), we report a universal negative finding for mid-layer interpretability. On POPE -- the benchmark common to all three -- the mid layers encode the ground-truth answer in 68-91% of errors, yet this signal is not causally active for the final prediction: residual-stream patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at the layer level on all three architectures, and on two of three at the per-head level (Qwen: 0/12,600 patched forwards). The lone exception, InternVL3 layer-20 head-2, is a non-vocab, self-attending head whose effect is localized to that specific head (p < 1e-4). Despite the null, the errors separate operationally into three failure modes -- Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override -- learnable above 60% on all three architectures, and the architecture's prior direction predicts which of two interventions elicits a category-specific response. We report these mitigation effects under oracle labels as evidence the categories are mechanistically real, not as a deployable method.

</details>


### [7] [Exploring Weaknesses of Generative Image Watermarks against Latent Frequency Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02010)
*Kirill Aistov,Khaled Abud,Irina Serzhenko,Egor Kovalev,Aleksey Yakushev,Aleksandr Akimenkov,Dmitry Obydenkov,Yury Markin,Sergey Lavrushkin,Dmitriy Vatolin,Anastasia Antsiferova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Latent Frequency Masking (LFM), an attack that removes invisible watermarks from AI-generated images by manipulating Fourier coefficients in the latent representation. The attack has two variants—one using Gaussian noise for efficiency and another using diffusion regeneration for better image quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invisible watermarking is used to trace AI-generated images, but its vulnerability to adaptive removal attacks is not well understood. This work addresses the security gap by proposing an attack that targets the latent representation of images rather than pixel space, exploring a previously overlooked attack surface.

Method: The proposed Latent Frequency Masking attack works by selecting and replacing Fourier coefficients in the latent representation of watermarked images. Two replacement strategies are used: (1) Gaussian noise sampling for computational efficiency, and (2) diffusion regeneration for improved perceptual quality. The authors also derive a theoretical distortion bound linking the reconstructed adversarial image to the latent-frequency perturbation.

Result: LFM successfully removes or substantially weakens watermarks from six different diffusion-based watermarking methods on images from DiffusionDB and MS-COCO prompts, while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared to existing attacks.

Conclusion: Latent-frequency manipulation represents a practical and effective attack surface against image watermarking systems. The authors conclude that robustness evaluations for generative image watermarking should incorporate such latent-frequency attacks to better assess security guarantees.

Abstract: Invisible watermarking has become a central tool for tracing AI-generated images, but its robustness against adaptive removal attacks remains an open security question. We introduce Latent Frequency Masking, an attack that erases watermark evidence by replacing selected Fourier coefficients in the latent representation of a watermarked image. The replacement can be sampled from Gaussian noise for efficiency or derived from diffusion regeneration for improved image preservation. We provide a theoretical distortion bound relating the change between the reconstructed adversarial image and the masked latent-frequency perturbation. We evaluate the proposed attack against six diffusion watermarking methods on images generated from DiffusionDB and MS-COCO prompts. Latent Frequency Masking removes or substantially weakens several watermarks while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared with existing attacks. These results identify latent-frequency manipulation as a practical attack surface and highlight the need to include such attacks in robustness evaluations of generative image watermarking.

</details>


### [8] [Domain generalization and synthetic data in object detection: the enabler, the probe, and the gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00030)
*Elfi I. S. Hofmeijer,Ella P. Fokkinga,Friso G. Heslinga,Klamer Schutte,Jörgen M. Karlholm*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper reviews Domain Generalization (DG) for object detection, examining synthetic data's role from three perspectives: as an enabler through diversification/alignment strategies, as a probe for understanding failure modes, and as a source of synthetic-to-real gap challenges. The authors argue future research needs representation-aware methods addressing both localization and classification under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Object detection models suffer performance degradation under distribution shifts (weather, environment, object appearance changes). While Domain Generalization (DG) aims to develop robust models for unseen domains, DG research specifically for object detection is scarce despite additional challenges in localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data offers a promising solution for large-scale diverse sample generation.

Method: This is a review paper that examines the role of synthetic data in DG for object detection from three complementary perspectives: (1) synthetic data as an enabler via diversification and alignment strategies to improve robustness, (2) synthetic data as a probe for controlled experimentation to identify failure modes, and (3) analysis of the synthetic-to-real gap when deploying synthetic-trained models on real-world data.

Result: The review identifies limitations of current DG approaches for object detection and argues that future research requires representation-aware methods that explicitly address both localization and classification under domain shift.

Conclusion: Future DG research for object detection must develop representation-aware methods that explicitly handle both localization and classification challenges under distribution shifts, rather than treating these as separate problems.

Abstract: Object detection models often experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, caused by for example changes in weather type, operational environment, or object appearance. Domain Generalization (DG) aims to develop models that remain robust under such shifts and generalize well to unseen domains. DG research specifically focused on object detection models is scarce, although these models face additional challenges around localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data is a promising tool to support in DG, by enabling large-scale generation of diverse new samples. In this paper, we present an object detection-centric review of DG and examine the role of synthetic data from three complementary perspectives. First, synthetic data acts as an enabler of DG through diversification and alignment strategies that aim to improve robustness to distribution shifts. Second, it serves as a probe that enables controlled experimentation to identify and understand failure modes. Third, we discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, a particularly challenging form of domain shift that arises when models trained on synthetic imagery are deployed on real-world data. Through reviewing these perspectives, we identify limitations of current DG approaches for object detection and argue that future research requires representation-aware methods that explicitly address both localization and classification under domain shift.

</details>


### [9] [Seeing the City or Recognizing the Place? What Street-View Imagery Adds Beyond Existing Urban Data in VLM Urban Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00031)
*Kaizhen Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether street-view imagery adds predictive value beyond existing urban data sources across seven urban attributes (road damage, curb ramps, house price, population, building type, building function, and low-rise floor count). The study compares image-based predictions using three Vision-Language Models (VLMs) against five public data resources, testing source reliance through image replacements and conflicting records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Street-view imagery is increasingly used to infer urban attributes, but predictive accuracy alone does not reveal how much a photograph contributes beyond data already available for the same place. The authors aim to determine when and where images provide additional information value compared to existing urban data sources.

Method: The study compared image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes from five public resources and three VLMs. The same urban units were evaluated using images, task context, nearby observations, and public records. Image replacements and conflicting records were used to test source reliance. OpenFACADES floor annotations were generated using OpenStreetMap floor values for validation.

Result: Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price. Neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population. Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count. For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labelled building and declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame. Models frequently followed conflicting records. OpenFACADES floor annotations showed the opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only reruns.

Conclusion: Street-view image value depends on visual legibility and local data coverage. Images are more valuable when the attribute is visually observable and existing data is sparse or inaccurate. The study provides a framework for comparing images with existing urban data to guide image collection and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps.

Abstract: Street-view imagery is increasingly used to infer urban attributes, but predictive accuracy alone does not reveal how much a photograph contributes beyond data already available for the same place. We compare image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes from five public resources and three VLMs. The same urban units are evaluated using images, task context, nearby observations, and public records, while image replacements and conflicting records test source reliance. Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price, while neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population. Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count. For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labelled building and declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame. Models frequently followed conflicting records. OpenFACADES floor annotations were generated with OpenStreetMap floor values and showed the opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only reruns. Street-view image value therefore depends on visual legibility and local data coverage. Comparing images with existing urban data can guide image collection and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps.

</details>


### [10] [DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00040)
*Thanh-Khoi Nguyen,Thien-Phuc Tran,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DSSR-3D is an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on 3D Gaussian Splatting fields. It addresses the limitation that existing methods cannot resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. The framework uses two interfaces: pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning, instantiated via a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting-based referring segmentation methods embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. This limits their ability to handle viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding tasks.

Method: DSSR-3D formalizes the problem as two interfaces: (1) pose-invariant semantic localization and (2) pose-conditioned spatial reasoning. Any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation without retraining the underlying semantic field. The two interfaces are instantiated with: (1) a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and (2) a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step. The method also introduces ViewRef-GS benchmark for evaluating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, along with an augmented Ref-LERF.

Result: Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field. The method transfers zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation.

Conclusion: DSSR-3D successfully enables view-dependent referring segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields through a training-free approach. The proposed framework is generalizable to different semantic fields and achieves improved performance on viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding tasks without requiring retraining.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field

</details>


### [11] [Reachability Is Not Generalization: Understanding Verb--Noun Decomposition in Assembly Action Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00064)
*Changyi Li,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper investigates why verb-noun decomposition only partially generalizes to unseen action combinations in assembly recognition tasks. Through systematic analysis across three datasets, the authors find that decomposition gains are limited by training data co-occurrence patterns, vocabulary asymmetry between components, and component entanglement from shared encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Atomic action classifiers fail on unseen component combinations (zero probability by design). While verb-noun decomposition is widely adopted as the solution, it was unclear how well it truly generalizes beyond the training distribution. The authors sought to understand the limits of compositional generalization in this approach.

Method: Systematic analysis across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, IMPACT) with varying characteristics. The authors analyzed: (1) primitive support in training data, (2) vocabulary asymmetry effects, and (3) component entanglement from shared-encoder training. They compared performance on unseen compositions and measured the gap between interpolation and true recombination.

Result: Decomposition escapes the "atomic ceiling" but only partially generalizes. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to training data co-occurrence structure—gains come primarily from interpolation within densely supported regions rather than true recombination. Failures concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component. IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs. Shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, causing reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly, trailing independent recombination by up to 6.0× in harmonic mean.

Conclusion: The three connected sources of error—primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement—explain why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. The authors provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy.

Abstract: Assembly actions are compositional: they combine a manipulation with a part or tool. In deployment, systems routinely encounter novel combinations of familiar components, yet an atomic action classifier assigns every unseen combination exactly zero probability by construction. The prevailing solution is verb--noun decomposition, which predicts components separately and recombines them to reach unseen actions. While widely adopted, how decomposition generalizes under compositional shift remains poorly understood. We present a systematic analysis of verb--noun decomposition across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT). Although decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling, its generalization extends only partially beyond it. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to the co-occurrence structure of the training data, indicating that much of the observed gain arises from interpolation within densely supported regions of the compositional space rather than from unconstrained recombination. Across datasets, failures consistently concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component, and IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs. We further show that shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions and trailing independent recombination by up to $6.0\times$ in harmonic mean. Taken together, these findings explain why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. By identifying primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement as connected sources of error, we provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy. Code: https://github.com/hisalaheiyo/assembly.

</details>


### [12] [Robust Online Aero-Engine Blade Defect Detection via Dual-Alignment Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00067)
*Zhaoyang Wang,Haiyong Chen,Dongying Li,Yining Wang,Huapeng Wu,Xinwei Lv,Atik Shahariar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ABDD is an online adaptive detection framework for aero-engine blade defect inspection that addresses domain shift problems between training and deployment data. It employs a Dual-Alignment Strategy combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment, uses Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering to reduce error accumulation from unreliable pseudo labels, and incorporates a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aero-engine blade manufacturing faces domain shifts due to varying production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. These shifts cause mismatch between training and deployment data, degrading deep defect detector reliability. The challenge is compounded by sparse defects in blade images, making pseudolabel-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions.

Method: The proposed ABDD framework has three key components: (1) Dual-Alignment Strategy that jointly adapts global visual style and local defect morphology through feature-statistics alignment and pseudo-box alignment; (2) Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism that evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy to reduce error accumulation; (3) Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. Evaluation uses TTA strategies under unified RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture.

Result: ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD datasets across multiple domain-shift scenarios. The approach is validated on an industrial inspection platform, demonstrating practical applicability.

Conclusion: The proposed ABDD framework effectively addresses domain shift challenges in aero-engine blade defect detection through its dual-alignment strategy and uncertainty-aware filtering mechanism. The method achieves robust detection performance under various domain shifts while maintaining parameter efficiency, making it suitable for industrial deployment.

Abstract: Reliable visual inspection is essential for quality assurance in aero-engine blade manufacturing, where defect appearance may vary across production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. Such domain shifts cause a mismatch between training and deployment data and degrade the reliability of deep defect detectors in online inspection. This problem is particularly challenging because aero-engine blade images usually contain sparse defects, making pseudolabel-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions. To address this issue, we propose Aero-engine Blade Defect Detector (ABDD), an online adaptive detection framework based on test-time adaptation. ABDD introduces a Dual-Alignment Strategy to jointly adapt global visual style and local defect morphology by combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment. To reduce error accumulation from unreliable pseudo labels, an Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy. In addition, a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module enables parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. ABDD is evaluated on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD under multiple domain-shift scenarios, with TTA strategies compared under a unified RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture. Experiments show that ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts, and its practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.

</details>


### [13] [What Builds the Scene? Luminance Dominates Geometry Formation in 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00749)
*Rezvan Joshaghani,Steven Cutchin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates how luminance and chroma contribute to geometry learning in 3D Gaussian Splatting through controlled ablation experiments with different channel supervision patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 3DGS learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma individually contribute to the learned representation.

Method: Train models under different channel supervision (luminance-only, chroma-only, RGB), freeze non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity), re-estimate appearance with the same solver, and compare held-out reconstruction quality across 11 benchmark scenes with 4 independent runs each.

Result: Geometry learned from luminance alone performs 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry. Higher-order spherical harmonics improve PSNR by 1.44 dB for luminance vs 0.19 dB for chroma. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only. Chroma can be largely recovered after geometry forms, but densification partially explains the gap.

Conclusion: Geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive. Much chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed, but luminance is the primary driver of geometry learning.

Abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma contribute to the learned representation. We study this by training models under different channel supervision, freezing their non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, and opacity), and re-estimating appearance with the same solver before comparing held-out reconstruction. Across eleven benchmark scenes with four independent runs each, geometry learned from luminance alone supports held-out reconstruction 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry on average. If chroma is deleted from a trained model, a sufficiently expressive solver can re-fit it on the frozen geometry to the original quality or slightly better. Higher-order spherical harmonics contribute much more reconstruction quality to luminance than to chroma, improving PSNR by 1.44 dB versus 0.19 dB on average, although on mirror-like surfaces hue does still change with viewpoint. The luminance advantage is even larger when geometry is being formed. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision after the same appearance solve; densification explains part of this gap. Overall, geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive, and much of the chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed.

</details>


### [14] [A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00069)
*Vivek Chavan,Jörg Krüger*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework called Work Environment Model (WEM) that converts continuous workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory. The system uses event segmentation theory to detect boundaries through multiple modalities (visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction) and converts video segments into compact, auditable event cards with rich metadata.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon ego/exo workplace video data is rich in procedural evidence but is redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. There is a need for a compact representation that enables efficient storage, retrieval, and documentation while preserving privacy constraints (on-premise processing).

Method: The framework detects event boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence—rather than fixed time windows or visual novelty alone. Each detected segment is abstracted into an "event card" containing: actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. The system uses frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders for visual features and a local language model for processing, with incremental WEM updates.

Result: The authors instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model. They outline evaluation criteria for: (1) segmentation quality, (2) memory compression, (3) retrieval fidelity, and (4) long-horizon question answering.

Conclusion: The WEM framework provides a compact, auditable, and privacy-preserving approach to summarizing and retrieving procedural information from long-horizon workplace video. It enables efficient on-premise processing while maintaining evidence-linked documentation suitable for downstream QA and retrieval tasks.

Abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

</details>


### [15] [DramaAgent: Agentic Storytelling Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00097)
*Ting Huang,Biao Wu,Ronghao Chen,Zeyu Zhang,Tengfei Cheng,Qizhen Lan,Huacan Wang,Hao Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DramaAgent is a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework that addresses the challenge of generating coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio. It operates as an upper-level control layer over existing video generation backbones, decomposing the task into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided targeted repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent diffusion and autoregressive models have improved text-to-video generation, but producing coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio remains challenging. Existing methods suffer from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences.

Method: DramaAgent introduces a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework with four key components: (1) Story planning - decomposes the generation process; (2) Persistent character conditioning - maintains character consistency; (3) Scene-wise synthesis - generates individual scenes; (4) Reflection-guided targeted repair - diagnoses and fixes failures like identity drift, missing scene semantics, temporal discontinuity, and cross-modal mismatch. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes.

Result: Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines.

Conclusion: Hierarchical agentic control is a practical direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation. The approach does not improve the underlying video backbone itself but rather adds an upper-level control layer for better coherence and consistency.

Abstract: Recent diffusion and autoregressive models have substantially improved text-to-video generation, yet producing coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio remains challenging. Existing methods often suffer from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences. We propose DramaAgent, a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework for long-form text-to-video-and-audio generation. Rather than improving the underlying video backbone itself, DramaAgent introduces an upper-level control layer that decomposes generation into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided targeted repair. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes, diagnoses failures such as identity drift, missing scene semantics, temporal discontinuity, and cross-modal mismatch, and repairs problematic clips in a stage-specific manner. Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines. These results suggest that hierarchical agentic control is a practical direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DramaAgent. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DramaAgent.

</details>


### [16] [LiteReality-Agent: An Agentic System for Interactable 3D Indoor Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01863)
*Zhening Huang,Yueyan Li,Johnathan Chiu,Xiaoyang Lyu,Matt Zhou,Yuxin Yao,Joan Lasenby,Shangzhe Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LiteReality-Agent is an agentic 3D reconstruction system that formulates indoor environment reconstruction as a coding problem, where a coding agent iteratively edits a Python script (Room.py) to produce simulation-ready 3D digital twins from RGB-D scans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creating realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from real indoor environments is challenging. Current frontier models (Astra, Fable) lack sufficient geometric accuracy, visual realism, and simulation compatibility for downstream embodied AI tasks.

Method: The system uses an observe-edit-verify harness where a coding agent gathers evidence using specialized tools and iteratively edits a Python script (Room.py) that can be executed to produce a 3D digital twin. The framework supports evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimization, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout reconstruction.

Result: LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than recent frontier models (Astra and Fable). The system provides specialized tools, structured workflows, and robust verification mechanisms.

Conclusion: LiteReality-Agent serves as a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems. It remains a strong orchestration framework for future agents as capabilities continue to improve, offering a foundation for high-quality 3D scene reconstruction suitable for simulation and embodied AI tasks.

Abstract: We present LiteReality-Agent, an agentic system for reconstructing real indoor environments as realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from RGB-D scans. At its core, LiteReality-Agent formulates 3D reconstruction as a coding problem, in which a coding agent gathers evidence using specialised tools and iteratively edits a Python script, Room.py, which can be executed to produce a 3D digital twin of the room. With this formulation, we develop a robust observe-edit-verify harness that supports evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimisation, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout the reconstruction process. LiteReality-Agent produces high-quality reconstructions suitable for simulation and downstream embodied AI tasks. Furthermore, as agent capabilities continue to improve rapidly, the system introduced by LiteReality-Agent remains a strong orchestration framework for future agents: it equips them with specialised tools, structured workflows, and robust verification mechanisms that substantially improve reconstruction quality and reliability. We demonstrate that LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than those generated by recent frontier models, such as Astra and Fable. We therefore view LiteReality-Agent as a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems. Both the source code and the data-capture application are publicly available. Code:https://github.com/LiteReality/LiteReality-Agent/

</details>


### [17] [A Low Grounding Score Is Not an Ungrounded Judge: Identifying the Perceptibility Confound in Multimodal Oversight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00111)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical flaw in auditing whether multimodal model judges actually use visual evidence. The authors show that the standard counterfactual probe for measuring visual grounding (the Verdict Grounding Score) systematically underestimates grounding, leading to false alarms where auditors incorrectly discard usable judges. They propose a fix using a detection probe on unedited images and validate it across nine judges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model judges increasingly supervise multimodal systems, filtering training data and shaping reasoning models. Before trusting such judges, we need to verify they actually use visual evidence. However, the standard method for checking visual grounding (counterfactual probes) has a fundamental flaw that was previously unrecognized.

Method: The authors formalize the counterfactual probe as the Verdict Grounding Score. They edit images so ground truth flips, hold reasoning traces fixed, and test whether the verdict follows the edit. They prove theoretically that this score is one-sided: it can only make judges appear less grounded, never more. They then show this missing quantity can be identified from three quantities already collected in standard audits. They audited nine judges using this protocol.

Result: The predicted ordering holds strictly across all nine judges. The typical judge acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright—including a judge that detects injected errors essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all.

Conclusion: Image-side counterfactual scores should never be reported alone. A detection probe on the unedited image should be run first to upper-bound the score and certify false alarms. This costs nothing extra since the audit protocol already collects the necessary data. The key insight is that the standard probe creates false alarms (incorrectly flagging grounded judges as ungrounded), which could lead to discarding usable overseers.

Abstract: Model judges now supervise multimodal systems at scale, filtering training data, selecting outputs, and supplying the reward that shapes multimodal reasoning models. Trusting one means first checking that it uses its evidence, and that check is itself worth scrutinizing, so we ask whether a counterfactual probe of visual grounding measures what it claims to. The probe edits the image so the ground truth flips, holds the reasoning trace fixed, and asks whether the verdict follows. We formalize it as the Verdict Grounding Score and show it cannot be read the way such scores are read. A verdict responds only to an edit that reaches the judge's decision-relevant reading, so the score is capped by how perceptible the edit is, and unless editing makes the attribute easier to read, the error is one-sided: the score can only make a judge look less grounded than it is. The practical failure is therefore a false alarm, an auditor discarding a usable overseer. Under assumptions we state, we show this missing quantity is not merely bounded but identified from three quantities the same audit protocol already collects, which makes the false-alarm rate directly measurable rather than merely a concern. Auditing nine judges, we find the predicted ordering holds strictly across our entire primary pool, and the typical judge there acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright, the clearest being a judge that detects the injected error essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all. The rule that follows is that an image-side counterfactual score should never be reported alone: a detection probe on the unedited image upper-bounds it, certifies its false alarms, and costs nothing extra to run.

</details>


### [18] [MosaiChunk: Compositing Spatio-Temporal Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02153)
*Yiwen Zhang,Haocheng Xi,Michael Tian-Yue Liu,Alexei A. Efros,Hadar Averbuch-Elor,Qianqian Wang,Haiwen Feng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MosaiChunk addresses long-horizon video generation by using a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value entries, enabling a frozen video generator to recover fine-grained visual details when objects reappear after falling out of context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by finite context windows. When objects or scenes fall out of context, their fine-grained visual details are lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance. Existing methods like sliding-window inference or whole-chunk retrieval have limitations in retaining and retrieving such visual details efficiently.

Method: MosaiChunk introduces a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value (KV) entries across space and time. The approach keeps the video generator fixed and learns only a lightweight router that determines which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. The method is evaluated on RememBenchmark, a new benchmark with long-horizon revisits for both text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) settings.

Result: MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

Conclusion: The proposed MosaiChunk method effectively addresses the context window limitation in long-horizon video generation by adaptively selecting and composing historical KV entries into a spatio-temporal mosaic, enabling a frozen generator to recover fine-grained visual details without requiring generator retraining.

Abstract: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by a finite context window. When an object or scene falls out of context, its fine-grained visual details may be lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance. To retain access to such visual details, we introduce MosaiChunk, a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value (KV) entries across space and time. Our approach is motivated by the observation that a frozen video generator can directly consume such non-contiguous historical KV and recover the corresponding visual content. We therefore keep the generator fixed and learn only a lightweight router that determines which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. We further introduce RememBench, a benchmark of long-horizon revisits with prompt-driven text-to-video (T2V) and camera-driven image-to-video (I2V) splits. Our experiments show that MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

</details>


### [19] [Evaluating the Robustness of Anti-UAV Detection under Controlled Fog Degradation: Fog-Aware Training and Clear-Sky Tradeoff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00141)
*Gur Levy Birkental,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for vision-based anti-UAV detection, revealing that detection performance degrades sharply and non-linearly with fog severity, with a 96% reduction in mAP from clear to thickest fog. Fog-aware training partially mitigates this but cannot prevent collapse under extreme conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility conditions, yet existing benchmarks use only clear-sky footage. Prior robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition, failing to capture the impact of fog severity on ground-to-air UAV detection.

Method: The authors created a synthetic fog benchmark at ten severity levels applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset. They compared a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline against a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images.

Result: Detection performance drops sharply and non-linearly with fog severity. Degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta ≈ 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, primarily due to lost recall and confidence. On mAP@0.5, this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in prior benchmarks. Fog-aware training improves detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, but cannot prevent collapse under extreme fog.

Conclusion: Reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, meaning simple clear vs adverse weather tests significantly underestimate operational risk. The study highlights the need for severity-controlled benchmarks to properly assess anti-UAV system performance in real-world fog conditions.

Abstract: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility, yet most benchmarks use only clear-sky footage, and previous robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition. As a result, the impact of fog severity on ground-to-air UAV detection remains poorly understood. This work presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for this task: synthetic fog at ten severity levels is applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset, comparing a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline to a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images. Detection performance drops sharply and non-linearly: degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta approximately 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, mainly due to lost recall and confidence. On the comparable metric (mAP@0.5), this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in the closest prior benchmark. Fog-aware training boosts detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, raising the threshold for reliable detection while not preventing collapse under extreme fog. Since reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, simple clear vs adverse tests underestimate operational risk.

</details>


### [20] [GPEC: Efficient Pre-LLM Gaussian Process Embedding Correction for Cardiac Video Caption Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00196)
*Arefeh Rezaei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GPEC is a computationally efficient pre-LLM error-correction method that improves VideoChat2's visual representations for cardiac ultrasound caption generation using sparse variational Gaussian Processes, achieving better caption quality with minimal inference overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show performance decline in specialized medical imaging domains like echocardiography. This limits their utility for cardiac ultrasound caption generation, which requires high accuracy for clinical applications.

Method: The paper introduces Gaussian Process Embedding Correction (GPEC), a modular pre-LLM error-correction method. GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model, learning a residual correction that moves projected visual representations toward annotation-guided targets. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating fixed-format reference captions, and mapping them into the language-model embedding space. The correction uses a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel, while keeping original VideoChat2 components frozen.

Result: Results show improved caption similarity and content alignment after applying GPEC. The method adds less than 0.05 seconds of inference-time overhead per video, demonstrating minimal computational cost.

Conclusion: GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational overhead, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for video understanding and caption generation, but their performance may decline in specialized medical imaging domains such as echocardiography. This work introduces Gaussian Process Embedding Correction (GPEC), a modular and computationally efficient pre-LLM error-correction method that improves the visual representations used by VideoChat2 for cardiac ultrasound caption generation. GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model and learns a residual correction that moves the projected visual representation toward an annotation-guided target. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating a fixed-format reference caption, and mapping it into the language-model embedding space. The correction is modeled using a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel, while the original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.The method is evaluated using representation-level, caption-level, content-oriented, and execution-time metrics by comparing the original VideoChat2 with VideoChat2 + GPEC under identical input and reference conditions. Results show improved caption similarity and content alignment after applying the proposed correction. Furthermore, GPEC adds less than 0.05 s of inference-time overhead per video in the evaluated setting. These findings indicate that GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.

</details>


### [21] [Query Independent Variable Rate Visual Token Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00204)
*Hongbo Zhang,Zihao Yang,Liuyang Song,Daqian Yang,Haoyang Yao,Yan Wen,Zhengtao Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a transform coding approach for visual-token compression in vision-language models. Instead of the conventional selection-based method (deciding which tokens to keep/discard), the authors keep all tokens but allocate varying bit rates to each token based on its distortion-rate curve. This creates a single compressed representation that works for any query, unlike attention-ranked pruning which is question-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current visual-token compression methods treat the problem as token selection, ranking tokens by attention scores from the language model. This creates a question-dependent compressed representation that works well in single-turn benchmarks but fails when one compressed representation must answer multiple different questions (e.g., cached conversations or device-server transmission). The authors recognized this limitation and sought a question-agnostic compression approach.

Method: The proposed method uses classical transform coding: (1) measure each token's distortion-rate curve, (2) distribute a fixed bit budget across all tokens using exact integer rate-distortion optimization, (3) no text/query enters the compression pipeline, creating a single universal compressed representation.

Result: At equal bit budgets on two datasets and two model capacities, the method preserves the model's output distribution and answers better than: uniform-rate coding, closed-form water-fill, and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the specific question it was tuned for, and outperforms it when the compressed image must answer different questions about the same image.

Conclusion: Transform coding with rate-distortion optimization provides a more versatile and effective compression approach for vision-language models. By keeping all tokens but varying their rates, the method achieves question-agnostic compression that maintains accuracy across multiple queries, outperforming conventional selection-based pruning methods especially in multi-query scenarios.

Abstract: Visual-token compression for vision--language models is posed almost entirely as a selection problem: decide which tokens to keep and discard the rest. The criteria that work best rank tokens by the attention the language model pays them, which makes the ranking a function of the question being asked. That is invisible in a single-turn benchmark and decisive whenever a compressed representation is written once and read many times, as when it is cached across the turns of a conversation or transmitted between a device and a server. We take the other half of the classical transform-coding toolkit instead: keep every token and vary its rate. A transform code exposes each token's measured distortion--rate curve, and a fixed bit budget is distributed across tokens by exact integer rate--distortion optimisation on those curves. No text enters the pipeline, so one compressed representation serves any query. At equal bit budgets, on two datasets and two capacities, it preserves the model's output distribution and its answers better than uniform-rate coding, the closed-form water-fill and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the question pruning was tuned for, and overtakes it once the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.

</details>


### [22] [Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion U-Net for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00279)
*Eirini Cholopoulou,Dimitrios E. Diamantis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes MRFFU-Net, a novel deep learning architecture for MRI segmentation that integrates a Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF) module into U-Net-like architectures. The MRFF module, combined with attention mechanisms and skip connections, enables extraction of features at multiple resolutions to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Learning architectures like U-Net struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information in MRI segmentation. This is particularly challenging for MRI data where anatomical structures have irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale.

Method: The proposed MRFF module is integrated at all levels of the encoder-decoder structure, along with attention mechanisms and skip connections. This enables the model to extract features at multiple resolutions, capturing both fine-grained details and global contextual information.

Result: MRFFU-Net was evaluated on two benchmark MRI datasets: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) segmentation in spinal MR scans and left atrium cardiac segmentation from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge. Experimental results show that MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: The MRFFU-Net architecture demonstrates effectiveness in MRI segmentation across different anatomical structures, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models.

Abstract: The segmentation of anatomical structures in medical images and particularly in MRI scans, is essential for clinical diagnosis and monitoring disease progression. While Deep Learning (DL) architectures, such as U-Net and its extensions are very effective in medical image segmentation tasks, they often struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information. This is especially challenging for MRI data segmentation, where anatomical structures are characterized by irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale. To address this challenge, we propose a novel DL architecture for MRI segmentation across different anatomical structures. Specifically, the architecture introduces a module, named Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF), that can be easily integrated into any U-Net-like architecture. The MRFF is integrated in all levels of an encode-decoder structure, along with attention mechanisms and skip connections to extract features at multiple resolutions, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information. We evaluate the MRFFU-Net on two publicly available benchmark MRI datasets of different anatomical targets; one for Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) segmentation in spinal MR scans, and one for left atrium cardiac segmentation, from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge. Experimental results indicate that MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in MRI segmentation.

</details>


### [23] [LENS-GRF: Permutation-Invariant Lesion Evidence Network with Gated Residual Fusion for Acne Severity Grading and Multi-Rater Clinical Oracle Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00294)
*Muhammad Muhtasim Shahriar,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LENS-GRF is an interpretable multi-stage framework for automated four-class acne severity grading that combines global facial context via Vision Transformer with local lesion evidence through a Lesion Set Transformer, using Gated Residual Fusion to adaptively combine both. The method achieves 95.89% accuracy with ground-truth lesion annotations on ACNE04 but only 35% in zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation, revealing significant domain shift challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acne severity grading requires both whole-face context (global appearance) and fine-grained lesion evidence (localized patches). Existing methods lack proper integration of these two complementary information sources, and current datasets suffer from data integrity issues and limited cross-dataset generalization.

Method: The proposed LENS-GRF framework consists of: (1) Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation to isolate facial region; (2) Global Vision Transformer prior for whole-face context; (3) Permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer that encodes localized lesion patches and spatial geometry; (4) Gated Residual Fusion that adaptively controls local residual contribution, reducing to global prediction when gate is zero.

Result: On ACNE04: 80.82% accuracy (fully automated with YOLOv11s), 95.89% ± 0.59% accuracy with ground-truth lesion annotations, QWK = 0.9753. A data integrity audit identified 15 cross-split duplicate image pairs including 5 with conflicting severity labels. On PLSBRACNE01 zero-shot: 35.00% accuracy (vs 42.50% baseline). Best oracle accuracy: 47.97% with ground-truth inputs, QWK = 0.5799. Oracle agreement: 49.32% to 66.22%.

Conclusion: LENS-GRF achieves near-human performance (95.89% accuracy, QWK=0.9753) on ACNE04 with ground-truth lesions, demonstrating the importance of combining global context with local lesion evidence. However, significant domain shift exists between datasets (only 35% accuracy in zero-shot), and annotation variability among dermatologists (oracle agreement 49-66%) highlights the challenge of inconsistent grading criteria. The findings emphasize the need for better detector generalization, standardized annotation protocols, and cross-criterion alignment.

Abstract: Automated acne severity grading requires both whole-face context and fine-grained lesion evidence. We propose LENS-GRF (Lesion Evidence Network with Set-Transformer and Gated Residual Fusion), an interpretable multi-stage framework for four-class acne severity grading. The method combines Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation and a global Vision Transformer prior with a permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer that encodes localized lesion patches and spatial geometry. Gated Residual Fusion adaptively controls the local residual contribution and reduces to the global prediction when the gate is zero. On ACNE04, fully automated LENS-GRF with YOLOv11s achieved 80.82% accuracy; with ground-truth lesion annotations, it achieved 95.89% +/- 0.59% accuracy and a Quadratic Weighted Kappa of 0.9753. A data-integrity audit identified 15 cross-split duplicate image pairs, including five with conflicting severity labels. In locked zero-shot evaluation on the full PLSBRACNE01 cohort (200 subjects, 600 views), automated LENS-GRF achieved 35.00% accuracy versus 42.50% for the global baseline. On the 148-subject common cohort used for three-dermatologist oracle analysis, ground-truth lesion inputs increased the best oracle accuracy to 47.97%, while the highest oracle QWK was 0.5799. Pairwise oracle agreement ranged from 49.32% to 66.22%, highlighting detector domain shift, annotation variability, and cross-criterion mismatch.

</details>


### [24] [Decoding the Disaster: Multi-Task Geospatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models and Crowdsourced Imagery for Disaster Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00302)
*Wenping Yin,Fabian Desuer,Ziqi Liu,Naixia Mou,Weijia Li,Pedram Ghamisi,Xiao Xiang Zhu,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GRDisaster is a multi-task Geospatial Reasoning Disaster mapping framework that uses vision-language models (VLMs) to understand, geolocalize, and reason over crowdsourced disaster imagery. It combines cross-view geolocalization with multi-view fusion to transform unstructured crowdsourced imagery into actionable GeoAI for disaster response.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowdsourced imagery provides timely, fine-grained street-level observations for disaster mapping but is often unstructured, spatially ambiguous, and lacks reliable geographic metadata, making manual geolocalization and interpretation labor-intensive and difficult to scale.
