The inference pipeline consists of three stages: (1) Video Preview provides cheap global coverage using low-resolution frames, (2) Video Evidence Indexing constructs a compact high-resolution Evidence Set, and (3) Answer Generation combines both inputs for final visual question answering. To address missing frame-level supervision, the method adopts privileged self-distillation, where an answer-aware teacher guides the test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. A single policy is trained to support multiple preview resolutions (1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame).

Result: Experiments demonstrate that Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets. Self-distillation further enhances both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization performance.

Conclusion: The VEI approach effectively balances visual token efficiency with question answering accuracy by intelligently selecting relevant moments for high-resolution processing, while self-distillation provides additional performance gains without requiring explicit frame-level annotations.

Abstract: Long-video question answering is limited by the high cost of visual tokens and by the fixed context width of current VLMs. A long-video question may require broad temporal coverage, but the answer is often supported by only a compact set of moments. To locate these moments efficiently, we propose token-budgeted Video Evidence Indexing (VEI): given a dense low-resolution Video Preview, the model constructs a compact high-resolution Evidence Set for final reasoning. We treat VEI as a policy that must jointly solve \textit{evidence localization}, which finds question-relevant moments, and \textit{budget planning}, which decides where to spend the limited high-resolution frame budget. We implement this idea with an inference pipeline: the Video Preview provides cheap global coverage, Video Evidence Indexing constructs the Evidence Set, and Answer Generation combines both inputs for final VQA. To address missing frame-level supervision, we adopt privileged self-distillation, where an answer-aware teacher guides the normal test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. We explore previews at 1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame, training a single policy that supports all four resolutions. Experiments show that Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets, and self-distillation further improves both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization.

</details>


### [47] [VTV-FM: Flow Matching through Variational Terminal-Velocity Closure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00785)
*Haoyang Jiang,Yuheng Li,Di Yang,Yanhai Xiong,Haipeng Chen,Yi He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VTV-FM is a second-order flow matching framework that addresses the limitation of first-order bridges (linear paths) in modeling curved motion. It derives missing terminal velocity information by minimizing acceleration energy, providing a closed-form solution for static datasets. This variational construction simultaneously defines OT pairing costs and acceleration targets for training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current flow matching methods use first-order bridges (straight-line motion with constant velocity) between paired source and target samples. This linear bridge structure limits the model's ability to represent curved motion, acceleration, and changing directions. Additionally, learning second-order phase-space dynamics requires target-side terminal-velocity information that static datasets do not provide.

Method: VTV-FM proposes a variational terminal-velocity approach that derives the missing velocity by minimizing acceleration energy. This yields a closed-form closure for static data. The same minimum-acceleration variational construction serves dual purposes: (1) defining the optimal transport (OT) pairing cost, and (2) providing acceleration targets used for training the model.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that VTV-FM improves transport geometry and generation quality across three domains: low-dimensional datasets, PDE-governed physical fields, and CIFAR-10. The method outperforms both first-order and high-order flow matching baselines.

Conclusion: VTV-FM successfully extends flow matching to second-order dynamics by solving the terminal-velocity problem through variational minimization. This enables modeling of more complex motion patterns while maintaining tractability for static datasets, leading to improved generative quality across various data domains.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) learns generative transport by fitting continuous-time motion from a simple source distribution to the data distribution. Most existing methods use first-order bridges: once a source and a target sample are paired, the path is a straight motion with constant velocity. FM with optimal transport (OT) improves the pairing, but the bridge itself remains linear, limiting its ability to model curved motion, acceleration, and changing directions. A natural remedy is to use second-order phase-space dynamics; however, learning the bridge requires target-side terminal-velocity information that static datasets do not provide. We propose Variational Terminal-Velocity Flow Matching (VTV-FM), a second-order FM framework that derives the missing velocity by minimizing acceleration energy, yielding a closed-form closure for static data. The same minimum-acceleration variational construction also defines the OT pairing cost and the acceleration targets used for training. Experiments on low-dimensional datasets, PDE-governed physical fields, and CIFAR-10 show that VTV-FM improves transport geometry and generation quality over first-order and high-order FM baselines.

</details>


### [48] [Paying for Too Many Tokens? Valid and Cost-Efficient Multimodal LLM Annotation with Simple Heuristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00809)
*Zhixi Zhu,Kristina Gligoric*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates cost-saving heuristics for Vision-Language Model (VLM) video annotation in computational social science tasks, finding that accuracy and validity diverge, text-only can suffice, and single image grids can achieve full-video understanding at ~15% token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLM video annotation costs accumulate rapidly (millions of tokens for 60-second videos), but it remains unclear which cost-saving heuristics preserve downstream conclusions. Researchers use various approaches (frame sampling, image grids, single modality) without understanding their impact on validity.

Method: Systematic evaluation of heuristics on short-form videos for sentiment and topic classification, assessing three dimensions: classification accuracy, validity of downstream inference, and per-video token cost. Tested configurations include different frame sampling rates, image grid compression, and modality combinations (text vs. video).

Result: Three key findings: (1) Accuracy and validity diverge—the highest-accuracy configuration can produce incorrect conclusions; (2) Text alone yields strong performance, meaning adding modalities can add cost without adding signal; (3) A single 2×8 image grid using shot-transition detection achieves full-video understanding (κ within ~0.05) at ~15% of token cost, decoupling cost from video length.

Conclusion: Cost-aware VLM annotation is feasible in CSS. Guidelines derived from this work can enable significant cost reduction while preserving downstream inference validity. The highest-accuracy method is not always the best choice for valid conclusions.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable video annotation at scale, but costs accumulate quickly: processing a typical 60-second short-form video at one frame per second requires millions of tokens. To reduce costs, researchers rely on heuristics such as sampling a subset of frames, compressing videos into image grids, or using only a single modality. However, it remains unclear which heuristics save cost, and whether they preserve the downstream conclusions these annotations enable. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic evaluation of these heuristics using short-form videos, on two computational social science (CSS) tasks: sentiment and topic classification. We evaluate each configuration along three axes the literature typically treats separately: classification accuracy, validity of downstream inference, and per-video token cost. First, we find that accuracy and validity diverge: the highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions. Second, modality value is not guaranteed: text alone can yield strong performance, indicating that adding modalities can add cost without adding signal. Finally, we find that cost can be decoupled from video length when annotating short-form videos: a single $2\times8$ image grid built via simple shot-transition detection approaches full-video understanding ($κ$ within~.05), at $\sim 15\%$ of the token cost. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines that can enable cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS.

</details>


### [49] [Video Generation Models: A Survey of Post-Training and Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00812)
*Chaoyu Li,Xiaoyi Gu,Yogesh Kulkarni,Eun Woo Im,Mohammadmahdi Honarmand,Zeyu Wang,Juntong Song,Fei Du,Xilin Jiang,Kexin Zheng,Tianzhi Li,Fei Tao,Pooyan Fazli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This survey presents the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment strategies for video generation models. It addresses the challenge of adapting pretrained video models to follow human intent, maintain temporal coherence, and satisfy physical/safety constraints without full retraining. The paper proposes a taxonomy of four alignment categories: supervised fine-tuning, self-training/distillation, preference-based, and inference-time methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generation has advanced significantly in resolution and duration, but pretrained models struggle with reliable human intent following, temporal coherence, and constraint satisfaction. Unique challenges include error accumulation, motion-appearance coupling, multi-objective trade-offs, and limited temporal supervision. This motivates systematic post-training strategies that adapt models without full retraining.

Method: The authors frame post-training as a unifying framework, distinguishing between implicit alignment (where alignment signals are indirectly enforced) and explicit alignment (direct enforcement). From this perspective, they organize approaches into four categories: (1) supervised fine-tuning methods, (2) self-training and distillation methods, (3) preference- and reward-based methods, and (4) inference-time methods.

Result: The survey provides a structured taxonomy organizing existing alignment approaches, reviews commonly used datasets and benchmarks, and evaluates current practices. It identifies key open challenges including scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation.

Conclusion: This survey establishes a coherent conceptual foundation and provides practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models. It serves as a foundational reference for researchers working on post-training and alignment in video generation, while highlighting critical open problems for future research.

Abstract: Video generation has rapidly progressed from short, low-quality clips to high-resolution, long-duration sequences with complex spatiotemporal dynamics. Despite strong generative priors learned through large-scale pretraining, pretrained video models often fail to reliably follow human intent, maintain temporal coherence, or satisfy physical and safety constraints. Compared with image and text generation, alignment in video generation presents unique challenges, including error accumulation over time, motion-appearance coupling, multi-objective trade-offs, and limited supervision for temporal properties. These challenges motivate systematic post-training strategies that adapt pretrained models without retraining them from scratch. In this survey, we present the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment in video generation models. We frame post-training as a unifying framework and distinguish between implicit alignment and explicit alignment based on how alignment signals are enforced. From this perspective, we organize existing approaches into four broad categories: supervised fine-tuning methods, self-training and distillation methods, preference- and reward-based methods, and inference-time methods. This taxonomy provides a coherent view of how alignment signals shape model behavior across both training and deployment. Beyond methodological advances, we review commonly used datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation practices, and discuss open challenges such as scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation. This survey aims to provide a structured conceptual foundation and practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models.

</details>


### [50] [Align Then Reason: A Multimodal Lip-Sync Judge for Dubbing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00825)
*Rui Liu,Bhavin Jawade,Haoqi Li,Shivam Mehta,Karan Saxena,Yinghong Lan,Cameron R. Wolfe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ATR (Align Then Reason) is a multilingual lip-sync judge that determines if a candidate text line matches a speaker's visible articulation in content and timing using only silent video and text. It first aligns frame-level lip representations with phonetic units, then uses an LLM to reason over this alignment for final judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dubbing quality control requires reference-free judgment of whether candidate text matches speaker's lip motion in content and timing. Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models are insensitive to temporal errors even when fine-tuned for lip reading.

Method: ATR uses a two-stage approach: (1) establishes monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and phonetic units of candidate text using an alignment scorer, (2) provides the LLM with local evidence for each phonetic unit and calibrated global alignment score to reason jointly about content and timing. The method works with various LLM backbones (Qwen3.5, LLaMA-3.1, Mistral).

Result: On a seven-language benchmark, ATR improves mean AUC by 59.4%, 50.2%, and 50.8% over Qwen3.5 SFT baselines with 2B, 4B, and 9B reasoners. Gains generalize across LLM families (45.9% over LLaMA-3.1-8B, 46.6% over Mistral-7B). Transfers to three unseen MuAViC languages. On downstream tasks: 52.0% improvement on dub-line reranking and 17.7% on script-to-clip assignment over best lip-reading baselines.

Conclusion: ATR significantly outperforms existing lip-reading and visual speech recognition methods for lip-sync quality control by combining alignment scoring with LLM reasoning, enabling effective evaluation of dubbed content across multiple languages and downstream applications.

Abstract: Dubbing quality control requires a reference-free judge that can determine whether a candidate text line matches a speaker's visible articulation in both content and timing, using only silent video and text because dubbed audio may not yet exist. Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models are poorly suited to this setting: even when fine-tuned to recover spoken content from lip motion, they remain largely insensitive to temporal errors. We introduce $\textit{Align Then Reason}$ (ATR), a multilingual lip-sync judge that first establishes a monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and the phonetic units of the candidate line, then reasons over this alignment to make the final judgment. An alignment scorer provides the LLM with both local evidence for each phonetic unit and a calibrated global alignment score, enabling it to reason jointly about content and timing. On a seven-language benchmark, our method improves mean AUC over the corresponding Qwen3.5 SFT baselines by 59.4%, 50.2%, and 50.8% with 2B, 4B, and 9B reasoners, respectively. The gains generalize across LLM families, reaching mean AUC improvements of 45.9% and 46.6% over the best baseline for LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, respectively. They also transfer across datasets to three unseen MuAViC languages. Furthermore, we evaluate on two downstream tasks built from real dubbing lines. On dub-line reranking, ATR-9B outperforms the best lip-reading baseline by 52.0%, while on script-to-clip assignment, ATR-9B improves over the best lip-reading baseline by 17.7%.

</details>


### [51] [Geometric Similarity in VLM Low-Level Vision Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00848)
*Shao-Jun Xia,Huixin Zhang,Zhen Lei,Anlan Sun,Yuner Zhang,Xiaoyang Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes GeoSim, a unified four-level framework to analyze how vision-language models (VLMs) organize representations across 24 low-level image restoration tasks. It compares autoregressive (AR) models and Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) to understand their geometric organization for pixel-level perception, aiming to enable better transferability in unified restoration models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field lacks understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations and whether structurally distinct paradigms (AR vs DiTs) share common geometric organization for pixel-level perception. This understanding is prerequisite for building highly transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters.

Method: The authors propose GeoSim, a unified four-level framework that analyzes task-conditioned representations from: (1) global similarity, (2) local geometry, (3) sparse feature decomposition, and (4) topological verification perspectives. The framework applies to analyzing hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings.

Result: The study reveals the organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing their limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement.

Conclusion: GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability in low-level vision and diagnosing model limitations in task- or model-specific scenarios.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as powerful candidates for universal vision backbones, with representative architectures including autoregressive (AR) models and diffusion transformers (DiTs). Yet, adapting them efficiently for all-in-one low-level image restoration remains a challenge. Crucially, the field lacks an understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations and whether these structurally distinct paradigms share a common geometric organization for pixel-level perception. Such shared organization is a prerequisite for building highly transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters. In this paper, we systematically investigate representational similarity across 24 low-level tasks spanning 5 categories. We propose GeoSim, a unified four-level framework that analyzes task-conditioned representations from global similarity, local geometry, sparse feature decomposition, and topological verification perspectives. Our formulation applies to the analysis of hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings. Our results reveal the organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing their limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement. Ultimately, GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability in low-level vision and diagnosing model limitations in task- or model-specific scenarios.

</details>


### [52] [SmoothOperator: Enhancing Representations for Fine-grained Open-set Recognition via Modulated Label Smoothing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00851)
*Thiru Thillai Nadarasar Bahavan,Yu Xia,Sachith Seneviratne,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses Open Set Recognition (OSR), where models must classify known classes while rejecting unknown classes. The authors identify that label smoothing in spherical representation learning applies uniform smoothing to all samples, and propose SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), which adaptively sets smoothing coefficients based on sample "prominence" - measuring how well a sample's class stands out against competitors. The method integrates into existing spherical representation learning methods with minimal overhead, achieving up to 4.7% improvements in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy on the Semantic Shift Benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge in OSR is that unknown classes cannot be modeled during training since their distribution is unbounded. While spherical representation learning methods have shown success by shaping feature spaces to make known classes compact and well-separated, label smoothing - a key driver of this success - applies the same coefficient to all samples regardless of their embedding quality. This one-size-fits-all approach is suboptimal.

Method: The authors first theoretically analyze spherical representation learning objectives in OSR, discovering they share a single alignment-uniformity structure where labels only affect the alignment term. Label smoothing acts as an alignment dial, but with a fixed coefficient for all samples. They propose SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), a plug-in method that sets the smoothing coefficient per-sample based on "prominence" - an embedding-space signal measuring how distinctly a sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class. High-prominence samples receive strong smoothing to reduce alignment and relax their pull in the feature space.

Result: SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors on the Semantic Shift Benchmark, with gains of up to 4.7% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed SmoothOP provides a principled way to apply adaptive label smoothing in spherical representation learning for OSR. By tailoring the smoothing coefficient to each sample based on its prominence, the method achieves consistent improvements over base objectives without significant computational overhead.

Abstract: Open Set Recognition (OSR) aims to enable models to accurately classify known classes while rejecting samples from unseen classes. A key challenge in OSR lies in the inability to model the unbounded distribution of unknown classes during training, often leading to the misclassification of samples from these classes. Rather than modeling unknowns, recent work shapes the feature space so that known classes are compact and well separated, and spherical representation learning methods have achieved strong results this way. Label smoothing has been identified as one of the key drivers of this success, yet it applies the same coefficient to every training sample, regardless of how well each sample is already embedded. We show that the spherical representation learning objectives used in OSR share a single alignment--uniformity structure in which labels enter only through the alignment term. Label smoothing therefore acts as an alignment dial, and a fixed coefficient sets this dial to the same value for every sample. We propose a plug-in, SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), which sets the smoothing coefficient of each sample from its \textbf{prominence}, an embedding-space signal measuring how clearly the sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class. Our method integrates into four existing spherical representation learning methods at minimal training overhead. SmoothOP assigns strong smoothing to samples with high prominence, which reduces their alignment and relaxes their pull. On the Semantic Shift Benchmark, SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform their base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors, with gains of up to 4.7\% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

</details>


### [53] [Lang3DSeg: Annotation-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation with Point Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00855)
*Cigdem Kokenoz,Amir Salarpour,Alkim Domeke,Christopher Salas,Pedram MohajerAnsari,Long Cheng,Mert D. Pesé,Bing Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Lang3DSeg is an open-vocabulary 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation method using point transformers, trained without manual annotation. It addresses depth ambiguity in 2D-to-3D label projection through class-priority compositing and depth-based instance truncation, achieving state-of-the-art 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI among annotation-free methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised LiDAR segmentation relies on costly manual annotation and closed taxonomies. Existing open-vocabulary methods use voxel-based sparse convolutions, while point transformers have been limited to indoor environments. The authors aim to establish point transformers for outdoor LiDAR segmentation without annotation, requiring novel solutions to noise in 2D-to-3D label projections.

Method: Lang3DSeg uses a point transformer backbone trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. It addresses depth ambiguity in 2D-to-3D projection through two mechanisms: (1) class-priority rule for mask compositing and (2) truncating projected instances at the first gap in depth distribution to correct projection errors.

Result: Lang3DSeg achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods on both benchmarks. Inference runs in real-time without vision-language models on single LiDAR sweeps.

Conclusion: Point transformers can serve as effective backbones for open-vocabulary outdoor 3D LiDAR segmentation. The proposed depth-aware projection correction methods significantly improve label quality from noisy 2D-to-3D projections, enabling annotation-free training that matches or exceeds prior methods.

Abstract: Accurate 3D semantic perception is critical for safe autonomous navigation. However, supervised LiDAR segmentation remains tied to closed taxonomies and to the cost of point-wise manual annotation. Open-vocabulary methods avoid that cost by projecting the output of 2D vision-language models onto LiDAR and distilling it into a 3D network. These methods rely almost exclusively on voxel-based sparse convolutions, and point transformers have so far been limited to indoor environments, where 3D data is dense and bounded. We present Lang3DSeg, which establishes a point transformer as the backbone for annotation-free open-vocabulary segmentation of outdoor 3D LiDAR, and is trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. This training paradigm necessitates addressing the inherent noise in 2D-to-3D label projections; specifically, naive projection often suffers from depth ambiguity, where points behind an object are erroneously assigned its semantic label. We therefore composite masks using an explicit class-priority rule and truncate each projected instance at the first gap in its depth distribution, correcting the projection error directly rather than averaging it over registered sequences. Lang3DSeg achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods on both benchmarks. Every 3D semantic segmentation is on a single LiDAR sweep, and inference operates in real-time without running vision-language models.

</details>


### [54] [CtrlWAM: Controllable World Action Models with Aligned Intent and Foresight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00859)
*Chensheng Peng,Wenhao Ding,Ran Tian,Zewei Zhou,Jef Packer,Maximilian Igl,Peter Karkus,Yan Wang,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone,Yuxiao Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CtrlWAM addresses a training mismatch in world action models (WAMs) where perturbed actions imply counterfactual futures but noisy video remains tied to ground truth. The method executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with noised visual consequences, using warped video-action noise schedules to maintain visual layout responsiveness. It also extends from ego-only to multi-agent control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard WAM training adds noise to both actions and video simultaneously, but this creates a fundamental mismatch: perturbed actions should produce counterfactual visual futures, yet the noised video stays tied to the original recording. In low-noise regimes, scene geometry and dynamic behavior remain visible despite added noise, undermining the model's learning.

Method: CtrlWAM executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. It introduces warped video-action noise schedules to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. The action interface is extended from ego-only control to variable numbers of agent streams for unified multi-agent future prediction.

Result: Driving experiments show more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, and better command following. Robotics experiments demonstrate stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support benefits of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity.

Conclusion: CtrlWAM provides a more controllable world action model through simulated action execution, tailored noise scheduling, and multi-agent support, validated in both driving and robotics domains.

Abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions (intent) and visual future (foresight). Standard training adds noise to recorded actions and video simultaneously, but such training paradigms introduce a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visual, while the noised video remains tied to the GT recording. In low-noise regime, the scene geometry and even the dynamic behavior remain clearly visible from the noisy future frames despite the added noise. We present CtrlWAM, which executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. To accommodate the different denoising requirements of video and actions, we introduce warped video--action noise schedules that aim to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. We further extend the action interface from ego-only control to a variable number of agent streams, allowing a unified model to represent predicted or commanded futures for multiple agents. Driving experiments show more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, and better following of supplied commands; robotics experiments show stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support the benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity. Together, these findings contribute to a more controllable world action model. Project page: https://ctrl-wam.github.io/

</details>


### [55] [Machine Translation for Sign Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00881)
*Ozge Mercanoglu Sincan,Anton Pelykh,Edward Fish,Harry Walsh,JianHe Low,Karahan Sahin,Oline Ranum,Sobhan Asasi,Steven Emery,Richard Bowden*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This is a comprehensive review paper on sign language machine translation, covering the evolution from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end systems, technical challenges, linguistic properties, and ethical considerations. The paper emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary collaboration between computer vision, sign language linguistics, deaf studies, and deaf communities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field of sign language machine translation has progressed substantially over the past decade, but faces unique challenges compared to spoken language translation. The authors seek to provide a balanced review that addresses both technical challenges and stakeholder considerations, particularly ethical issues around data governance and community involvement.

Method: This is a comprehensive review paper that traces the evolution of sign language recognition, translation, and production systems. It examines linguistic properties, technical challenges, and ethical considerations by drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies.

Result: The paper identifies key challenges: limited datasets compared to spoken-language resources, inadequate evaluation metrics for linguistic quality, and the need for models to capture the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. It also addresses ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use.

Conclusion: Continued progress in sign language machine translation requires sustained collaboration across computer vision, sign language linguistics, deaf studies, and most importantly, with deaf communities. The review emphasizes that technical advancement must be coupled with ethical considerations and community involvement.

Abstract: Sign language machine translation has progressed substantially over the past decade, evolving from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end translation systems. Advances in pose estimation, transformer architectures, and large-scale dataset collection have driven progress, yet challenges remain. Datasets are limited compared to spoken-language resources; evaluation metrics inadequately capture the linguistic quality of output; and models must capture the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. This manuscript provides a comprehensive review that seeks to balance technical challenges with stakeholder considerations. We examine the linguistic properties that make sign languages computationally unique, trace the evolution of recognition, translation, and production systems, and analyze ongoing technical challenges. Crucially, we address ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies, our analysis emphasizes that continued progress requires sustained collaboration across these fields and with deaf communities.

</details>


### [56] [EyeTAG: Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00922)
*Jungmin Lee,Niamat Ullah,Yoseob Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EyeTAG is a multi-frame gaze estimation framework that uses an explicit first-order gaze prior by differentiating recent predictions to create a kinematic token representing gaze trajectory. This approach reduces jitter and improves accuracy by modeling motion explicitly rather than learning it implicitly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-frame gaze estimation methods suffer from output jitter due to treating each frame independently. Existing multi-frame methods reduce jitter but learn motion implicitly within appearance features, without making gaze trajectory an explicit variable. This limits their ability to properly model temporal motion dynamics.

Method: EyeTAG uses a causal multi-frame framework with an explicit first-order gaze prior. At each time step, it differentiates its recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. This token is translation-invariant in gaze space, making it subject-invariant rather than capturing personal gaze offsets. The system uses face and eye streams with visual evidence fused via cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder.

Result: EyeTAG reduces mean angular error by approximately 1.0° on Gaze360 dataset and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56° vs. 2.58°). Ablation studies show the differential formulation specifically removes systematic saccade bias that persists even with absolute gaze-history prior, demonstrating that the improvement comes from the motion modeling rather than just temporal context.

Conclusion: The explicit modeling of gaze trajectory through differencing provides significant improvements in gaze estimation accuracy. The differential formulation is key to removing systematic saccade bias, outperforming approaches that only use absolute gaze history. The subject-invariant nature of the kinematic token allows the model to generalize well across different individuals.

Abstract: Gaze estimation under natural head-eye motion underpins applications from driver monitoring to human-computer interaction. Single-frame methods predict each frame independently, so consecutive outputs fluctuate as jitter. Multi-frame methods reduce this, but they learn motion implicitly inside appearance features, so the gaze trajectory is never an explicit variable. We propose EyeTAG (Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation), a causal multi-frame framework built around an explicit first-order gaze prior: at each step it differentiates its own recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. Because differencing is translation-invariant in gaze space, this token carries subject-invariant motion rather than personal gaze offsets. Face and eye streams supply visual evidence, fused by cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder. EyeTAG reduces the mean angular error by about 1.0$^\circ$ on Gaze360 and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56$^\circ$ vs. 2.58$^\circ$). Within-model ablations, which keep the encoder and the rest of the architecture fixed and vary only the gaze history, show that the differential formulation, rather than temporal context alone, removes the systematic saccade bias that persists even with an absolute gaze-history prior. Our code is available at https://github.com/peter8366/EyeTAG.

</details>


### [57] [Joint Branch-Space Transform Coding for Diffusion Activation Quantization with Classifier-Free Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00930)
*Mingrun Jiang,Yuejia Liu,Zishan Shao,Ting Jiang,Qinsi Wang,Hancheng Ye,Yixiao Wang,Rui-Feng Wang,Kangning Cui,Yixuan Chen,Fan Yang,Xiang Cheng,Hai Li,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses post-training quantization (PTQ) for diffusion models by exploiting cross-activation structure between conditional and unconditional branches in Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG). The authors propose branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via a 2x2 orthogonal matrix, and derive the Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform (GCBT) that jointly incorporates CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. The method achieves statistically significant fidelity gains while maintaining the existing quantization pipeline unchanged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion quantization methods treat conditional and unconditional branches independently, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. The authors observe that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated two-dimensional source, and the choice of branch coding basis materially affects quantization fidelity under a fixed bit budget.

Method: The paper introduces branch-space transform coding that rotates matched CFG branches via an offline-derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix, requiring minimal modifications to model parameters or the quantization pipeline. The Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform (GCBT) is derived to jointly incorporate the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. GCBT admits a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search under an equal-rate quantization-noise surrogate.

Result: Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

Conclusion: The proposed GCBT method effectively exploits cross-activation structure in CFG diffusion models, providing consistent fidelity improvements without modifying the existing quantization pipeline. This approach represents a novel direction in diffusion model quantization by considering the correlation between conditional and unconditional branches.

Abstract: Post-training quantization for diffusion models increasingly exploits timestep, feature, and layer structure. While recent work has begun incorporating CFG structure into diffusion quantization, activation quantization still operates independently across conditional and unconditional coordinates, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. We show that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated two-dimensional source and that, under a fixed bit budget, the choice of branch coding basis materially affects quantization fidelity. Motivated by this observation, we introduce branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via an offline derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix, requiring minimal modifications to model parameters or the quantization pipeline. We further derive the Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform (GCBT), which jointly incorporates the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. Under an equal-rate quantization-noise surrogate, GCBT admits a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search. Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

</details>


### [58] [A Matched-Budget Audit Framework for Recaptioned Image-Text Supervision Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00952)
*Giyeong Oh,Junghun Park,Yuhan Bae,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a matched-budget audit framework for evaluating recaptioned image-text corpora used in text-to-image training. The framework assesses five axes at a fixed text budget (B=64): prompt-side coverage, image-conditioned faithfulness, and caption-surface health, using controllable basic units (CBU) as the common metric. Applied to seven paired comparisons across five public corpora, the framework reveals significant improvements (+3.39 to +6.36 CBU per caption) in cross-corpus pairs and exposes a consistent long-vs-dense frontier on CC12M.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for auditing recaptioned supervision distributions have critical limitations: length-correlated proxies fail to capture caption-register artifacts, and downstream T2I benchmarks entangle corpus evaluation with training choices, making it difficult to assess the quality and characteristics of caption distributions at scale.

Method: The authors propose a reusable matched-budget audit framework (D_{π,V_c,C}) that evaluates recaptioned corpora across five axes at a fixed text budget of B=64 tokens. The framework measures: (1) prompt-side coverage, (2) image-conditioned faithfulness, and (3) caption-surface health, using controllable basic units (CBU) as the common claim unit. They instantiate this framework on seven paired comparisons across five public source corpora, using Qwen and Gemma as judges.

Result: Across four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by +3.39 to +6.36 under both Qwen and Gemma judges. On CC12M, the framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier that remains consistent across both judges and four different budgets. The audited multi-source recap corpus (~490M) and audit-artifact bundle are released.

Conclusion: The matched-budget audit framework provides a standardized, reproducible method for evaluating recaptioned image-text corpora. It successfully identifies significant improvements in caption quality across corpora and reveals consistent trade-offs between caption length and density, offering valuable guidance for T2I training data curation.

Abstract: Recaptioned image-text corpora are now standard for text-to-image (T2I) training, with vision--language model (VLM) captioners replacing sparse alt-text by dense descriptions. A recaptioned corpus is a supervision distribution induced by a documented captioning policy ($π$), captioner ($V_c$), and source corpus ($C$). Length-correlated proxies miss caption-register artifacts and downstream T2I benchmarks entangle the corpus with training choices, so this distribution is hard to audit at corpus scale. We introduce a reusable matched-budget audit framework for recaptioned supervision distributions $D_{π,V_c,C}$: at a fixed text budget of $B = 64$ it reports a five-axis profile spanning prompt-side coverage, image-conditioned faithfulness, and caption-surface health, with claimed controllable basic units (CBU) as the common claim unit. We instantiate the framework on seven paired comparisons over five public source corpora. Across the four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by $+3.39$ to $+6.36$ under both Qwen and Gemma Judges, and on CC12M the same framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier that is consistent across both judges and four budgets. We release the audited multi-source recap corpus ($\approx$ 490M) together with the audit-artifact bundle.

</details>


### [59] [Two Clocks in Diffusion MLLMs: When Answers Stabilize Before Rationales Unfold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00953)
*Keuntae Kim,Yong Suk Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates the temporal dynamics of answer stabilization versus rationale generation in masked diffusion Multimodal Language Models (MLLMs). The study reveals that most rationale canvas remains unwritten when answers stabilize, and identifies coverage as the primary driver of prompting-induced accuracy changes across different benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how answer candidates stabilize in masked diffusion MLLMs while rationales are still being generated. The authors aim to distinguish between retrospective stabilization and token commitment, and examine how these timing mechanisms affect model performance across different visual question-answering scenarios.

Method: The study employs three key methodologies: (1) Analyzing temporal dynamics between answer stabilization and rationale generation across three VQA benchmarks; (2) Examining block length effects (128 vs 8) on V*Bench; (3) Testing EOS-enabled prompting strategies on Nemotron, LaViDa, and other models; (4) Conducting matched-canvas image ablations to measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization.

Result: Key findings include: (1) 89.4-98.1% of rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs; (2) Reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%; (3) EOS-enabled prompting improves Nemotron's accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA but reduces LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points; (4) Coverage rather than conditional accuracy accounts for the larger absolute component of each change.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity are distinct temporal phenomena in masked diffusion MLLMs. Coverage emerges as the dominant component explaining prompting-induced performance differences across benchmarks, suggesting that timing mechanisms and generation coverage are critical factors in model performance.

Abstract: An answer candidate in a masked diffusion MLLM can stabilize while its rationale is still unfolding. We distinguish retrospective stabilization of the logged candidate from token commitment, and examine these two clocks relative to rationale generation. Analyzing our results across three visual question-answering benchmarks, we find that 89.4-98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs. On V*Bench, reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, together with answer coverage and the eligible observation window. Under EOS-enabled prompting, direct instructions improve Nemotron's overall accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA, but reduce LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points. A symmetric decomposition associates the larger absolute component of each change with coverage rather than conditional accuracy. Matched-canvas image ablations measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization, separating the two temporal readouts. Together, these measurements distinguish answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity, and identify coverage as the larger component of the prompting differences.

</details>


### [60] [Video-Index: A Curated Meta-Benchmark for Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00960)
*Enxin Song,Yinuo Xu,Shusheng Yang,Wenhao Chai,Jiatao Gu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the "attack pyramid" framework to audit video benchmarks for shortcut vulnerabilities, revealing that many benchmarks can be exploited without seeing actual video frames. The authors release Video-Index, a curated dataset of 840 verified difficult items across 4 capability groups, and show that even the best models (Claude Opus 5) have significant room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video benchmarks often claim to measure video understanding capabilities, but models can exploit shortcuts in answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence rather than truly understanding video content. The authors aim to expose these vulnerabilities and create more reliable evaluation benchmarks.

Method: The authors introduce the "attack pyramid" - five levels of shortcut attacks with increasing access to each item: (1) no frame access, (2) answer options only, (3) question text only, (4) partial visual evidence, and (5) full video. They audit 115 video benchmarks using this framework, screen 505,518 QA pairs from 112 benchmarks, and use a deterministic selector with red-team gate to create reproducible benchmarks.

Result: On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see a frame approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames retain 96% of full-video accuracy. Near-duplicate questions comprise at least half the items in 63 benchmarks. Video-Index contains 210 hardest verified items in each of four capability groups (840 items from 76 sources). Claude Opus 5 outperforms all open-source models by over 37 percentage points, and agent tools add approximately 20 more percentage points, but all systems still have room for improvement in efficiency and accuracy.

Conclusion: Current video benchmarks have significant shortcut vulnerabilities that inflate model performance. The release of Video-Index provides a more rigorous evaluation benchmark, but even state-of-the-art models like Claude Opus 5 show substantial room for improvement on video understanding tasks.

Abstract: A video benchmark should reward the capability it claims to measure, yet models can exploit answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence. We introduce the attack pyramid, five levels of shortcut attacks with increasing access to each item, and audit 115 video benchmarks with it. On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see a frame approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames keep a median 96% of full-video accuracy. Near-duplicate questions make up at least half the items in 63 benchmarks. We screen 505,518 question-answer pairs from 112 of them into an audited pool. Agents turn evaluation requests into specifications, and a deterministic selector with a red-team gate composes reproducible benchmarks. We release Video-Index, the 210 hardest verified items under these attacks in each of four capability groups, 840 items from 76 sources. With the same fixed input, Claude Opus 5 outscores every open-source model by over 37 percentage points, and agent tools add about 20 more, yet all systems leave room to improve efficiency and accuracy. Blog: https://www.enxinsong.com/blog/video-index/ GitHub: https://github.com/Espere-1119-Song/Video-Index Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Video-Index/Video-Index

</details>


### [61] [RelationVGGT: Visual Geometry Transformers for 3D Spatial Relation Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00970)
*Minsu Kim,Jaesung Choe,Jiwoo Lee,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang,Seon Joo Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces RelationVGGT, a feed-forward framework for 3D spatial relation segmentation that segments target objects based on a visually specified subject and a relational text query, without requiring category names, per-scene optimization, or known camera poses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D reconstruction and semantic scene understanding methods remain confined to object-centric perception, neglecting spatial relations between objects. The authors aim to move beyond this limitation by formulating a new task: pose-free, multi-view spatial relation segmentation.

Method: RelationVGGT integrates: (1) semantic features from a visual foundation model, (2) geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model, and (3) a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction. The authors also provide an automated annotation pipeline built on ScanNet++ using VLMs and LLMs for scalable training data generation.

Result: The paper proposes a novel feed-forward framework that can segment targets based on spatial relations to a subject, without requiring per-scene optimization or known camera poses.

Conclusion: This work bridges the gap between object-centric 3D perception and relational understanding by enabling feed-forward inference for spatial relations in multi-view settings, with scalable data generation via automated annotations.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction have progressed from per-scene optimization to feed-forward inference, and semantic scene understanding has followed suit -- yet existing methods remain confined to object-centric perception, neglecting spatial relations between objects. We formulate 3D spatial relation segmentation in a feed-forward, pose-free multi-view setting: given a visually specified subject and a relational text query, the model segments the target across views without receiving its category name. To this end, we propose RelationVGGT, a novel feed-forward framework that integrates semantic features from a visual foundation model with geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model and leverages a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction -- requiring neither per-scene optimization nor known camera poses. We additionally provide a fully automated annotation pipeline built on ScanNet++ with VLMs and LLMs, enabling scalable training data generation for this new task.

</details>


### [62] [Concept Driven Domain Adaptation: Finding an Abstract Needle in a Haystack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00973)
*Haiming Zhao,Tai Wang,Kun Zhang,Xicheng Peng,Zhiyang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses concept-to-example video retrieval, where teachers search for documentary clips illustrating abstract scientific concepts. The authors propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework that adapts vision-language models to bridge the abstraction gap between high-level curriculum concepts and concrete visual evidence in documentaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Science teachers search for video excerpts by querying abstract concepts they intend to teach, but existing language-based video retrieval methods assume queries describe observable events. This creates an abstraction gap: teachers need to find concrete visual phenomena that instantiate underlying scientific principles—a problem the authors term "concept-to-example retrieval" or "abstract-needle-in-a-haystack."

Method: The authors propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework for adapting two-tower vision-language models: (1) Structure the textual embedding space using textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs; (2) Transfer concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder; (3) Jointly adapt both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps.

Result: On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

Conclusion: The staged alignment approach of CDDA successfully bridges the abstraction gap in concept-to-example retrieval, enabling vision-language models to ground compact curriculum concepts in temporally sparse documentary evidence without sacrificing pretrained concrete image description alignment.

Abstract: Science teachers frequently search for documentary excerpts not by describing what appears on screen, but by querying the abstract concepts they intend to teach. This use case exposes a limitation of existing language-based video moment retrieval methods, which typically assume that queries describe observable events, whereas instructional search requires retrieving concrete visual phenomena that instantiate an underlying scientific principle. We study this setting as concept-to-example video retrieval, an abstract-needle-in-a-haystack problem where compact curriculum concepts must be grounded in temporally sparse documentary evidence. To bridge this abstraction gap, we propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework for adapting two-tower vision-language models to concept-level retrieval. CDDA treats concepts as intermediate semantic anchors: it first structures the textual embedding space with textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs, then transfers this concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder, and finally jointly adapts both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps, thereby encouraging concept-level adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's concrete image description alignment. On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

</details>


### [63] [VIEScore2: Unified Image Evaluation with Spatially Grounded Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00994)
*Xianda Du,Max Ku,Weiming Ren,Zhi Rui Tam,Chunlin Ren,Ping Nie,Min-Hung Chen,Wenhu Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VIEScore2 is a unified evaluator for image generation and editing tasks that jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass by representing images as an N x N grid. It combines supervised fine-tuning with GRPO training and achieves SRCC of 0.601, outperforming Gemini-3-Flash (0.491) and specialized spatial evaluators on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic image evaluators only provide scalar quality scores without identifying which image regions support the score, limiting interpretability and actionable feedback.

Method: 1) Represent images as N x N grid for text-native representation
2) Train on 38K examples spanning score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision
3) Apply GRPO with rewards combining cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity
4) Use parameter-free parser to convert structured predictions into readable explanations

Result: 1) Overall-score SRCC of 0.601 vs 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash (strongest zero-shot VLM baseline)
2) Outperforms both general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on 3/6 benchmarks in per-image grid IoU
3) Ranks among top three on 5 benchmarks, including datasets beyond training sources

Conclusion: VIEScore2 successfully provides both quality scores and defect localization in a unified model, demonstrating superior performance over existing evaluators and general-purpose VLMs across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Existing synthetic image evaluators typically provide only a scalar quality score and do not identify the image regions that support it. We introduce VIEScore2, a unified evaluator for image generation and editing tasks with optional conditioning images. VIEScore2 represents an image as an N x N grid and jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass. Its text-native grid representation provides a common interface for heterogeneous spatial supervision and enables directly verifiable post-training objectives. We train on 38K examples spanning score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision across generation and editing tasks. Starting from supervised fine-tuning, we further apply GRPO to improve defect localization using rewards that combine cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity. A parameter-free parser converts the structured predictions into readable explanations. On the primary suite, VIEScore2 achieves an overall-score SRCC of 0.601, compared with 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash, the strongest zero-shot general-purpose VLM baseline under matched inputs. For defect localization, VIEScore2 outperforms both general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on three of six benchmarks in per-image grid IoU and ranks among the top three on five, including datasets beyond its training sources.

</details>


### [64] [VASC: Value-Aware Sparse Attention with Cross-Layer Memory for Efficient 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01013)
*Junyi Wu,Fanqing Kong,Leyang Chen,Shaoqiu Zhang,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VASC is a training-free sparse attention method for feed-forward 3D vision models (VGGT, π³) that combines value-aware block selection with execution-aware cross-layer memory to reduce computational cost while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward 3D vision models like VGGT suffer from quadratic global attention that makes long sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may select redundant value regions despite high query-key relevance.

Method: VASC introduces two mechanisms: (1) Value-aware block selection that integrates pooled query-key relevance with neighboring value contrast to reduce redundancy while preserving distinctive content; (2) Execution-aware cross-layer memory that tracks unserved demand across layers and updates based on actual execution, allowing underserved blocks to compete within fixed computation budget.

Result: Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D demonstrate improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, with up to 2.29× faster inference than dense VGGT.

Conclusion: VASC achieves a favorable trade-off between efficiency and accuracy for long image sequences in 3D vision tasks, providing a training-free sparse attention solution that maintains query-relevant and distinctive content while optimizing computational resource allocation.

Abstract: Feed-forward 3D vision models such as VGGT have achieved remarkable progress, unifying camera estimation and dense scene reconstruction in a single pass. However, their quadratic global attention makes long image sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may favor highly attended yet value-redundant regions. To address these limitations, we introduce VASC, a training-free sparse attention method combining value-aware block selection and execution-aware cross-layer memory. Our value-aware block selection integrates pooled query--key relevance with neighboring value contrast, reducing redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content. Cross-layer memory tracks unserved demand across layers and updates this state according to actual execution, enabling previously underserved blocks to compete under a fixed computation budget. Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D with VGGT and $π^3$ demonstrate improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, together with up to $2.29\times$ faster inference than dense VGGT. Code is available at https://github.com/kosakayamahoo-design/VASC.

</details>


### [65] [FutureWorlds: Learning Robotic World Models from Alternative Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01019)
*Hao Wu,Shengju Qian,Weiyan Wang,Fan Xu,Fan Zhang,Yuanpeng He,Qingsong Wen,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FutureWorlds is a framework for robotic world models that predicts action-conditioned future scenes using diverse beam search and candidate-specific bounded memory. It includes MemSPO, which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages for policy optimization. The method achieves significant improvements in visual quality (LPIPS reduction of 14.78% on RT-1, 20.84% on BridgeV2, and 9.12% on RoboCasa) and more accurate motion prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key challenges in robotic world models are: (1) similar candidate predictions limit informative quality comparisons, (2) diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of individual histories. The paper aims to unify candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality to improve prediction quality and enable continued learning beyond the training horizon.

Method: FutureWorlds uses: (1) a multimodal discrete autoregressive model as the foundation, (2) diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures balancing confidence and diversity, (3) candidate-specific bounded memory to preserve scene states and ensure matching histories between generation and policy scoring, (4) MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization) to convert video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages for optimizing the world model.

Result: FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78% (RT-1), 20.84% (BridgeV2), and 9.12% (RoboCasa) relative to the strongest baseline. With only 200 MemSPO updates under fixed evaluation configurations, both generation quality and prediction capability beyond training horizon improve. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation confirm gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states.

Conclusion: FutureWorlds successfully addresses the challenges of candidate construction and history maintenance in robotic world models. The combination of diverse beam search, bounded memory, and MemSPO enables high-quality future predictions with accurate motion and object consistency. The method demonstrates continued improvement beyond training horizon with minimal updates, showing promise for real-world robotic applications.

Abstract: Robotic world models predict action-conditioned future scenes, providing a foundation for understanding action outcomes. However, turning alternative predictions into useful learning signals remains challenging: similar candidates limit informative quality comparisons, while diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories. We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality. Built on a multimodal discrete autoregressive model, FutureWorlds uses diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity. Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states and ensures that generation and policy scoring use matching histories. We further propose MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model. On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation show that these gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states. Project page and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/FutureWorlds.

</details>


### [66] [Towards Automatic Video Annotation with ASH: Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Tracking and Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01022)
*Arash Rocky,Q. M. Jonathan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces SAM3-ASH, a training-free video instance segmentation pipeline that enables fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video length. It addresses memory limitations and single-prompt constraints of existing memory-attention VIS methods through two contributions: Generalized Presence Token (GPT) for efficient multi-prompt processing and Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) for arbitrary-length sequence handling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-attention-based VIS methods face two critical limitations: (1) substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips, and (2) their single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive. These constraints prevent scalable, training-free automated video annotation.

Method: Two technical contributions: (1) GPT reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1); (2) ASH extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to arbitrary-length sequences through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training.

Result: SAM3-ASH achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB.

Conclusion: The proposed SAM3-ASH establishes a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation, combining zero-shot capability with efficient memory usage and multi-category open-vocabulary tracking.

Abstract: Memory-attention-based Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) methods have demonstrated strong zero-shot tracking capability, yet their substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips and their single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive. This work introduces two contributions toward fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video. The Generalized Presence Token (GPT) reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1) with no modifications to any learned component. The Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to sequences of arbitrary length through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training. Instantiated on SAM3, the resulting pipeline -- SAM3-ASH -- achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB, establishing a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation.

</details>


### [67] [Bootstrapping Video Interaction Generation with Synthetic State Transitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01039)
*Jiho Jang,Jinyoung Kim,Nojun Kwak,Kyungjune Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical limitation in video generative models: their inability to portray plausible physical interactions and resulting state transitions. The authors propose a framework that generates scalable synthetic datasets of controllable interactions using a structured taxonomy and image editing models to create visual anchor points (start/end states), combined with a novel State-Guided Sampling (SGS) technique to generate seamless videos between these anchors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generative models can synthesize high-fidelity videos but struggle with physical interactions and state transitions. This is a critical bottleneck for applications in robotics and VR/AR, where understanding and generating plausible physical interactions is essential.

Method: The framework consists of three main components: (1) A structured taxonomy to organize different types of physical interactions; (2) State-of-the-art image editing models to create explicit 'start' and 'end' state images as visual anchors; (3) State-Guided Sampling (SGS), a novel sampling technique designed to mitigate artifacts common in naive conditional generation. Additionally, a new automated evaluation system was developed that aligns with human judgments.

Result: Fine-tuning a base model on the generated dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible interactions, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework and dataset.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses the challenge of generating plausible physical interactions in videos. By using visual anchors and the SGS technique, the method produces higher quality videos with proper state transitions. The developed evaluation system ensures data quality aligns with human judgments, making this approach valuable for robotics and VR/AR applications.

Abstract: While recent video generative models can synthesize high-fidelity videos, they struggle to portray plausible physical interactions and the resulting state transitions, a critical bottleneck for applications in robotics and VR/AR. To address this, we introduce a framework to generate a scalable synthetic dataset of controllable interactions. Our pipeline leverages a structured taxonomy and state-of-the-art image editing models to create explicit `start' and `end' state images, which serve as visual anchors for the interaction. To generate a seamless video utilizing these anchors, we propose State-Guided Sampling (SGS), a novel sampling technique that mitigates artifacts common in naive conditional generation. Furthermore, we develop and validate a new automated evaluation system that aligns with human judgments to ensure data quality. Experiments show that fine-tuning a base model on our dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible interactions.

</details>


### [68] [Towards Subject Consistency over Dynamic Subject Sets in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01052)
*Tongcheng Zhang,Jun Zhu,Jianfei Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces DynSC-Eval, an evaluation framework for assessing subject consistency in long video generation by dynamically tracking subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measuring continuity/identity preservation using six complementary metrics. The framework is validated through synthetic experiments and applied to improve models via DiffusionNFT post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As video generation extends to longer durations, existing metrics fail to properly evaluate subject consistency over dynamic subject sets (subjects appearing/disappearing throughout the video). There is a need for an evaluation framework that can track subjects dynamically and measure both local continuity and global identity preservation.

Method: 1) DynSC-Eval framework with six complementary object-level metrics tracking eligible subjects throughout their visible lifespans; 2) Synthetic experiments with injected inconsistency events to validate sensitivity; 3) Application of DiffusionNFT post-training using rewards from DynSC-Eval; 4) Curriculum learning for extended generation (10s, 30s).

Result: On 5s generation: 13.82% average reduction in six inconsistency metrics for Wan-2.1-1.3B, 5.66% for SANA-2B, with improvements also on ReSim I2V model. Consistency optimization remains effective for 10s and 30s generation while largely preserving other capabilities.

Conclusion: DynSC-Eval effectively measures subject consistency in long video generation and exposes substantial differences obscured by conventional metrics. The rewards derived from this framework can successfully improve models through post-training, demonstrating its utility for both evaluation and optimization.

Abstract: We argue that as video generation extends to longer durations, subject consistency should be evaluated over \textit{dynamic subject sets}. We therefore introduce \textbf{DynSC-Eval}, an evaluation framework that dynamically tracks eligible subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measures local continuity and global identity preservation using six complementary object-level metrics, with explicit detection of inconsistency events. To validate its effectiveness, we design synthetic experiments that actively inject inconsistency events, demonstrating both the sensitivity of DynSC-Eval and the limitations of existing metrics. Evaluations of diverse models on 5s, 15s, and 60s video generation further reveal substantial subject consistency differences that are obscured by conventional metrics. Beyond evaluation, we construct rewards from DynSC-Eval and apply DiffusionNFT post-training in an autonomous-driving testbed. On 5s generation, our approach reduces the six inconsistency metrics by an average of 13.82\% for Wan-2.1-1.3B and 5.66\% for SANA-2B, with improvements also observed on the I2V model ReSim. Qualitative comparisons further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. We then extend generation to 10s and 30s through curriculum learning and show that consistency optimization remains effective while largely preserving other capabilities.

</details>


### [69] [HierGF: Hierarchical Gaussian Fields via Geometry-perception Message Passing for Sparse-view 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01056)
*Bi'an Du,Zhimin Zhang,Daizong Liu,Baoquan Chen,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses sparse view 3D reconstruction, a challenging scenario where only limited random views are available. Existing methods struggle with insufficient multi-view consistency and under-sampled regions causing missing structure. The proposed Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF) method uses a hierarchical geometry-perception approach, transforming coarse 3D geometry and 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision through a two-stage network, with a learnable confidence network and geometrically consistent densification module.
