<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is important for AR/VR content creation, cultural heritage digitization, and robotic applications. However, sparse views pose two major challenges: (1) too few images for matching, making multi-view consistency difficult to establish; (2) insufficient view coverage leads to missing parts in under-sampled regions. Existing methods rely on limited reprojection errors and regularization terms, prone to overfitting and inconsistent appearances, and often use heuristic density control lacking reliable guidance.

Method: The paper proposes Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF), which revisits sparse-view reconstruction from a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective. Key components include: (1) a two-stage geometry-perception backbone network that transforms coarse 3D geometric information and additional 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision; (2) a learnable confidence network to guide gradients toward cross-view consistent content; (3) a geometrically consistent densification module to improve reconstruction of multi-view alignment and under-sampled regions.

Result: The method enhances multi-view consistency with very few input views by converting limited observations into reliable self-generated supervision beyond fixed priors and heuristic density control.

Conclusion: HierGF successfully addresses sparse view 3D reconstruction challenges by moving beyond fixed priors and heuristic density control, providing reliable guidance for under-sampled regions through hierarchical geometry-perception learning and geometrically consistent densification.

Abstract: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is an important and common scenario in multimedia applications, such as augmented reality/virtual reality (AR/VR) content creation, cultural heritage digitization, and certain robotic applications, where only a limited number of randomly captured views may be available. However, sparse views contain only limited 3D information, posing two major challenges:1) too few images are available for matching, making it difficult to build multi-view consistency; 2) insufficient view coverage leads to a lack of information in under-sampled regions, resulting in missing parts of object structure. Existing methods mostly still rely on limited reprojection errors and regularization terms, which are prone to overfitting to a single view and inconsistent appearances across views. In geometrically under-sampled regions, they often rely on heuristic density control, lacking reliable guidance and often resulting in blurring and structural holes.To address these issues, this paper proposes Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF), which revisits sparse-view reconstruction from a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective and converts limited observations into reliable self-generated supervision beyond fixed priors and heuristic density control. In particular, we transform coarse 3D geometric information and additional 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision through a two-stage geometry-perception backbone network, thereby enhancing multi-view consistency with very few input views. In addition, we introduce a learnable confidence network to guide gradients toward cross-view consistent content, and a geometrically consistent densification module to improve the reconstruction of multi-view alignment and under-sampled regions.

</details>


### [70] [Overcoming Kernel Redundancy for Scaling Logic Gate Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01069)
*Sejin Park,Hongjae Lee,Changwoo Han,Seung-Won Jung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates width scaling in differentiable logic gate networks, addressing the issue of kernel redundancy that limits performance when scaling network width. The authors propose a dynamic logic kernel framework with input-dependent kernel routing to improve kernel utilization and specialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While scaling model capacity is a central principle in deep neural networks that typically improves performance, this practice has not been well-explored in logic gate networks. The authors aim to investigate whether similar scaling benefits can be achieved in logic gate networks and understand why naive width scaling often leads to performance saturation due to kernel redundancy.

Method: The authors propose a dynamic logic kernel framework that reorganizes kernel utilization by promoting specialization across kernel groups. This approach uses input-dependent kernel routing to better utilize increased width, with both routing and computation implemented entirely with gate-level Boolean operations at inference time. They specifically focus on addressing kernel redundancy at the first gate level, where it is most pronounced.

Result: The proposed approach improves kernel utilization and increases kernel diversity, leading to higher accuracy with improved parameter efficiency compared to naive width scaling approaches.

Conclusion: The dynamic logic kernel framework successfully enables logic gate networks to benefit from width scaling by addressing kernel redundancy through input-dependent routing and early-stage adaptation. This work demonstrates that scaling benefits similar to those in deep neural networks can be achieved in logic gate networks when properly designed.

Abstract: Differentiable logic gate networks, which operate using only logic gates, have recently attracted attention as an efficient alternative to conventional neural networks. However, despite their efficiency, the scaling behavior of logic gate networks remains underexplored. By contrast, scaling model capacity is a central design principle in deep neural networks and typically leads to improved performance. This discrepancy raises a key question: Can similar scaling benefits also be achieved in logic gate networks? In this work, we focus on width as a primary scaling axis and conduct a systematic analysis of its behavior in logic gate networks. We observe that naive width scaling often introduces redundancy among logic kernels, limiting the effective use of additional kernels and leading to performance saturation. To address this limitation, we propose a dynamic logic kernel framework that reorganizes kernel utilization by promoting specialization across kernel groups. This enables the network to better utilize increased width via input-dependent kernel routing, while ensuring that both routing and computation are implemented entirely with gate-level Boolean operations at inference time. We further find that kernel redundancy is most pronounced at the first gate level, motivating an early-stage dynamic logic kernel strategy that concentrates adaptation at this level. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves kernel utilization and increases kernel diversity, leading to higher accuracy with improved parameter efficiency.

</details>


### [71] [Ego2Act: Evaluating Goal-Directed Manipulation in Egocentric Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01092)
*Patrick Amadeus Irawan,Iskandar Muda Rizky Parlambang,Rava Maulana,Qinrong Cui,Erland Hilman Fuadi,Zayd M. K. Zuhri,Nanda Ryaas Absar,Ahmed Elshabrawy,Wilfried Ariel Mulyawan,Shoubin Yu,Yue Zhang,Mohit Bansal,Alham Fikri Aji*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Ego2Act is a goal-directed benchmark for evaluating video generation models as world simulators in egocentric planning tasks. It contains 2,640 videos from 110 real-world tasks and includes a reference-free evaluation pipeline (Ego2ActJudge). The benchmark reveals that current models struggle with multi-step task execution and fine-grained physical dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generation models are being explored as world simulators for embodied planning, but existing benchmarks focus on single short actions, leaving multi-step physical reasoning underexplored. There's a need for a benchmark that evaluates whether models can simulate proper execution to accomplish high-level goals through multiple real-world manipulations.

Method: Ego2Act benchmark with 2,640 videos from 110 real-world tasks across day-to-day settings, varying object clutter and multi-step complexity. Given an initial scene image and a high-level goal, the benchmark evaluates whether video generation models can produce realistic egocentric videos of hand manipulating objects. Ego2ActJudge provides reference-free evaluation for task completion and physics plausibility.

Result: Models' generated simulations often skip or partially execute steps, leaving later steps missing dependent states, leading to unfulfilled goals. Models consistently fail at fine-grained physical dynamics, particularly during complex object manipulation and persistent world modeling.

Conclusion: Ego2Act provides a rigorous testbed for advancing video models toward physically plausible, goal-directed simulation. Current models need significant improvement in multi-step planning and physical reasoning.

Abstract: Video generation models are increasingly being explored as world simulators for embodied planning and learning. To do so effectively, these models must not only generate visually appealing frames, but also predict how environments dynamically evolve when executing goal-directed actions. While evaluating these capabilities is crucial, existing benchmarks focus mainly on single short actions or step-by-step instructions. This leaves multi-step physical reasoning underexplored, especially in egocentric video generation that requires planning to simulate proper execution to accomplish high-level goals by carrying out multiple real-world manipulations. We introduce Ego2Act, a goal-directed benchmark featuring 2,640 videos from 110 real-world tasks across day-to-day settings, varying object clutter and multi-step complexity. Given an initial scene image and a high-level goal, Ego2Act evaluates whether video generation models can produce realistic egocentric videos of a hand manipulating objects to carry out the task. To support scalable evaluation, we also introduce Ego2ActJudge, a reference-free evaluation pipeline that achieves better task completion and physics plausibility evaluation alignment with human consensus compared to relevant baselines. Our findings reveal that models' generated simulations often skip or partially execute steps, leaving later steps missing dependent states, which leads to unfulfilled goal. Furthermore, models consistently fail at fine-grained physical dynamics, particularly during complex object manipulation and persistent world modeling. We hope Ego2Act provides a rigorous testbed for advancing video models toward physically plausible, goal-directed simulation.

</details>


### [72] [MVDG: Efficient Multi-view 3D Disambiguation on Unconstrained Real-World Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01098)
*Hanyuan Xiao,Gonglin Chen,Haolin Xiong,Wenbin Teng,Haiwei Chen,Yajie Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MVDG is a multi-view disambiguation framework that addresses the problem of illusory matches between visually similar 3D surfaces (doppelgangers) in large-scale 3D reconstruction and visual localization. It builds on the VGGT 3D foundation model and enables joint reasoning over arbitrary numbers of multiview images, reducing O(n²) complexity of prior pairwise approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Doppelgangers (distinct yet visually similar 3D surfaces) are a fundamental obstacle for large-scale, in-the-wild 3D reconstruction and visual localization. Prior pairwise classifiers are limited in multi-view contextual reasoning and incur O(n²) inference complexity for downstream structure-from-motion (SfM).

Method: 1) Build on VGGT 3D foundation model with 3D-aware multi-view features
2) Joint reasoning over arbitrary number of multiview images in single pass
3) Construct pseudo-pairwise training set from AerialMegaDepth to handle label ambiguity
4) Fine-tune on sampled subsets for stable optimization and generalization
5) Derive predictive relationship between regular SfM metrics and pseudo-pairwise classification accuracy for efficient validation

Result: Achieves comparable pairwise accuracy while improving both SfM accuracy and inference speed over baselines.

Conclusion: MVDG provides a scalable solution for multi-view disambiguation that reduces computational complexity and improves reconstruction quality. The pseudo-pairwise training strategy enables stable fine-tuning under noisy supervision, and the derived validation metric allows efficient evaluation without expensive full SfM pipelines.

Abstract: Illusory matches between distinct yet visually similar 3D surfaces--doppelgangers--remain a fundamental obstacle for large-scale, in-the-wild 3D reconstruction and visual localization. Prior work mitigates this issue with pairwise classifiers, but this design limits multi-view contextual reasoning and incurs O(n^2) inference complexity for downstream structure-from-motion (SfM). We present MVDG, a scalable multi-view disambiguation framework built on the 3D foundation model VGGT, which jointly reasons over an arbitrary number of multiview images. By incorporating 3D-aware multi-view features, our method reduces dependence on pairwise comparisons by encoding and decoding views in a single pass. We further observe that direct multi-view fine-tuning of VGGT can be unstable under noisy supervision; motivated by label ambiguity in Doppelgangers, we construct a pseudo-pairwise training set from AerialMegaDepth and show that fine-tuning on sampled subsets yields stable optimization and strong generalization to held-out scenes. Finally, because full SfM evaluation (even with faster pipelines such as GLOMAP) remains expensive, we process a pseudo-pairwise dataset for efficient validation; we derive a predictive relationship between regular SfM metrics and the classification accuracy on this pseudo-pairwise test. Experiments show that our method achieves comparable pairwise accuracy while improving both SfM accuracy and inference speed over baselines.

</details>


### [73] [Affine-Aligned Atlas for Canonical Gaussian Construction in Video Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01114)
*Masaya Takabe,Hiroshi Watanabe,Sujun Hong,Tomohiro Ikai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation to address the limitation of existing Gaussian-based video methods that struggle with large global motion (camera movement). The key insight is to construct canonical Gaussians in an affine-aligned atlas space where frame-wise affine transforms absorb global motion before canonical Gaussian construction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Gaussian-based video representations decompose videos into canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation. However, when videos contain large global motion (e.g., camera movement), the canonical representation becomes misaligned with individual frames, significantly increasing the burden on the temporal deformation model and degrading reconstruction quality.

Method: The proposed method introduces an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation that constructs canonical Gaussians in a larger affine-aligned atlas space. Frame-wise affine transforms are used to absorb global motion before canonical Gaussian construction, reducing the gap between the canonical representation and target frames. This approach only modifies the canonical construction stage, allowing integration into existing canonical-Gaussian-based methods with negligible additional parameter cost.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that the method improves reconstruction quality especially for sequences with large camera motion. The approach maintains compatibility with existing methods while effectively handling global motion artifacts.

Conclusion: The affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation provides an effective solution for Gaussian-based video representations to handle large camera motions. By absorbing global motion through frame-wise affine transforms in an atlas space, the method reduces the burden on temporal deformation models and improves reconstruction quality. Its modular design allows easy integration into existing canonical-Gaussian-based frameworks with minimal overhead.

Abstract: Gaussian splatting has recently emerged as an efficient representation for images and videos due to its explicit structure and fast rendering capability. Existing Gaussian-based video representations often decompose a video into canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation. However, when a video contains large global motion such as camera movement, the canonical representation may become misaligned with individual frames, increasing the burden on the temporal deformation model. In this paper, we propose an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation, which constructs canonical Gaussians in a larger affine-aligned atlas space. Frame-wise affine transforms absorb global motion before canonical Gaussian construction, reducing the gap between the canonical representation and target frames. Since the proposed method only modifies the canonical construction stage, it can be integrated into existing canonical-Gaussian-based methods with negligible additional parameter cost. Experiments show that our method improves reconstruction quality especially for sequences with large camera motion.

</details>


### [74] [Open Vocabulary Word Recognition From Transcribed Bangla Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01134)
*Faias Satter,Sk. Md. Masudul Ahsan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of recognizing handwritten Bangla words using deep learning-based object detection models. The study implements three models (SSD with MobileNetV2, Faster R-CNN with InceptionResNetV2, and an ensemble) on a custom dataset of 9841 handwritten Bangla word images, achieving an F1-score of 92.61% with the ensemble model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop a reliable OCR system for Bangla handwritten text, which is challenging due to the complexity of Bangla script and the variability in handwriting styles. Word recognition is identified as the critical stage in OCR that directly impacts overall system performance.

Method: The study employs three object detection models: SSD with MobileNetV2, Faster R-CNN with InceptionResNetV2, and an ensemble combining both. A modified Non-Maximum Suppression technique is introduced to improve detection results. A custom dataset of 9841 handwritten Bangla word images with diverse handwriting styles was compiled for training and testing.

Result: The ensemble model achieved the best performance with an F1-score of 92.61%. At the word level, the ensemble model correctly recognized 96.12% of the words to some extent.

Conclusion: The ensemble model demonstrates superior performance in handwritten Bangla word recognition. Future improvements could include adding a post-processing phase to correct errors generated by the system.

Abstract: An optical character recognition (OCR) can scan a paper and extract text using technology, making people's jobs easier. While various OCR systems are available in the software industry, finding a reliable equivalent solution for Bangla takes much work. When it comes to handwritten texts, the situation is much more unusual. Recognizing words from word images is the most critical stage in any OCR process. It is the second stage after segmenting words from text pictures. If this stage fails, the overall performance of the OCR will be poor, regardless of how well the other phases perform. This study aims to recognize words using deep learning in a handwritten Bangla word image. Three object detection models, SSD with MobileNetV2, Faster R-CNN with InceptionResNetV2, and an ensemble model of these two, have been used to train and test handwritten word images. A modified Non-Maximum Suppression has been introduced to enhance the effectiveness of the models' results. A customized dataset of 9841 handwritten Bangla word images has been compiled, featuring diverse handwriting styles from various individuals. All three models' performances have been checked against the test dataset, and the ensemble model has been the most impressive, with an F1-score of 92.61%. Also, at the word level, the ensemble model correctly recognizes 96.12% of the words to some extent. The system can be further improved by introducing a post-processing phase to correct errors generated by the system.

</details>


### [75] [The RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm (RSNA-ICA) Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01135)
*Maria Correia de Verdier,Rachit Saluja,Jason Sho,Maryam Vabarizad,Rennie Yung-Chieh Chen,Uyen N. T. Nguyen,Mona Alrehaili,Layal Aweidah,Deniz Bulja,Wesley C. Chan,Hernan Chaves,Madhavi Duvvuri,Huseyin Ekin Ergin,Undrakh-Erdene Erdenebold,Ekim Gumeler,Mohamed Sobhi Jabal,Chin-Chi Kuo,Fatima Mubarak,Sevde Nur Emir,Scott Riley K. Ong,Johanna Ortiz,Almudena Pérez-Lara,Andreas M. Rauschecker,Shayan Sirat Maheen Anwar,Charit Tippareddy,Tam Tran,Sorawis Visrutaratna,John Mongan,Adam E. Flanders,Robyn Ball,Greg Zaharchuk,Peter D. Chang,Felipe Kitamura,Errol Colak,Luciano Prevedello,Tyler Richards,Data Contributor Group,Dataset Annotator Group,Evan Calabrese,Jeffrey D. Rudie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm (RSNA-ICA) Dataset is a large, publicly available, expert-annotated dataset of 7,202 image series from 4,278 patients across 21 institutions in 12 countries, designed to support AI algorithm development for aneurysm detection on CTA, MRA, and MRI scans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intracranial aneurysm rupture causes significant morbidity and mortality, but detection remains challenging—especially for small lesions on routine non-angiographic imaging. There was a need for a large, diverse, well-annotated dataset to advance AI-based detection algorithms.

Method: Dataset curated by RSNA in collaboration with ASNR, SNIS, and ESNR. Included 2,566 CTA, 2,166 MRA, and 2,470 MRI series from adult patients with and without saccular aneurysms. Expert annotations indicate aneurysm presence, location, and 178 series include 3D segmentations of vascular locations. 5,041 series publicly available via MIRA; remainder used for challenge test sets.

Result: The dataset provides substantial geographic (12 countries, 5 continents) and imaging modality diversity. It was used for the 2025 RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection Challenge, enabling development and evaluation of AI algorithms across both angiographic and routine neuroimaging examinations.

Conclusion: RSNA-ICA is a comprehensive, freely available resource for non-commercial research, poised to significantly advance AI-based aneurysm detection in clinical practice.

Abstract: Intracranial aneurysm rupture is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet aneurysm detection remains challenging, particularly for small lesions and on routine non-angiographic imaging examinations. To support the development and evaluation of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms for intracranial aneurysm detection and localization, the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), in collaboration with the American Society of Neuroradiology (ASNR), the Society of Neurointerventional Surgery (SNIS), and the European Society of Neuroradiology (ESNR), curated the RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm (RSNA-ICA) Dataset. Developed for the 2025 RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection Challenge, RSNA-ICA is a large, publicly available, expert-annotated dataset comprising 7202 CTA, MRA, and MRI series from 4278 adult patients collected across 21 institutions in 12 countries spanning five continents. The dataset includes 2566 CTA, 2166 MRA, and 2470 MRI series from patients with and without intracranial saccular aneurysms, providing substantial geographic and imaging diversity. Expert annotations indicate both aneurysm presence and location, and 178 series additionally include three-dimensional segmentations of challenge-defined vascular locations. RSNA-ICA was used to develop and evaluate algorithms in the 2025 RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection Challenge. Of the 7202 image series, 5041 are publicly available through MIRA (https://mira.rsna.org/dataset/7), while the remainder were used for challenge public and private test sets. The dataset is freely available to the research community for noncommercial use and provides a comprehensive resource for advancing AI-based aneurysm detection across both angiographic and routine neuroimaging examinations.

</details>


### [76] [OptimusMesh: Compact Autoregressive Mesh Generation from Point Clouds via Sparse Latent Pivots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01148)
*Mazhar Iqbal,Naoya Chiba,Xuanmeng Sha,Tomohiro Mashita,Yuki Uranishi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OptimusMesh is a framework for direct compact triangle mesh generation from point clouds using sparse latent pivot conditioning. It compresses 2,048 oriented input points into only 16 sparse latent pivots, reducing the conditioning set by 128×, and uses a two-stage autoregressive framework that generates mesh vertices first, then predicts triangular faces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Point clouds are unordered and sparse while meshes have irregular structure and varying topology. Existing approaches rely on implicit representations followed by surface extraction, which can produce dense or over-smoothed meshes requiring computationally expensive post-processing and simplification.

Method: The method compresses 2,048 oriented input points into 16 sparse latent pivots (128× reduction). These pivots serve as a compact structural representation shared across a two-stage autoregressive framework: first generating mesh vertices, then predicting triangular faces conditioned on the generated vertices and the same pivots. Compared to methods using 257 decoder-conditioning tokens, OptimusMesh uses only 16.

Result: OptimusMesh produces the most compact outputs among compared autoregressive methods, using 25.7%--94.1% fewer faces while maintaining competitive geometric fidelity and distributional quality. The conditioning sequence is 16.1× shorter.

Conclusion: The sparse latent pivot conditioning approach enables direct compact mesh generation from point clouds with significant reduction in output faces while preserving geometric fidelity, avoiding the need for implicit representations and subsequent surface extraction pipelines.

Abstract: Generating compact and geometrically faithful 3D meshes directly from point clouds remains a fundamental challenge. Point clouds are unordered and sparse, whereas meshes exhibit irregular structure and varying topology. As a result, many existing approaches rely on implicit representations followed by surface extraction or reconstruction. Although effective, these pipelines can produce dense or over-smoothed meshes, often requiring computationally expensive post-processing and simplification. We present OptimusMesh, a framework for direct compact triangle mesh generation from point clouds using sparse latent pivot conditioning. Our key idea is to compress $2{,}048$ oriented input points into only $16$ sparse latent pivots, reducing the geometric conditioning set by $128\times$. These pivots provide a compact structural representation shared across a two-stage autoregressive framework that first generates mesh vertices and then predicts triangular faces conditioned on the generated vertices and the same pivots. Compared with the evaluated recent point-cloud-conditioned autoregressive methods, which use $257$ decoder-conditioning tokens, OptimusMesh uses only $16$, yielding a $16.1\times$ shorter conditioning sequence. Experiments show that OptimusMesh produces the most compact outputs among the compared recent autoregressive methods, using $25.7\%$--$94.1\%$ fewer faces while maintaining competitive geometric fidelity and distributional quality.

</details>


### [77] [PhysicsLENS: Diagnosing Physical Property Blindness in Video Generation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01162)
*Isaiah Milkey,Som Sagar,Aditya Taparia,Xinyuan Liu,Jiqing Wen,Ransalu Senanayake*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhysicsLENS is a dataset and benchmark for evaluating physical plausibility in robot video generation. It addresses the problem that current video generation benchmarks evaluate visual fidelity rather than physical accuracy, and that generated videos can complete tasks through physically implausible behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video world models for robots can generate physically implausible videos that violate physical principles, limiting their reliability for robot learning and planning. Existing benchmarks only evaluate visual fidelity, not the underlying accuracy of physics that is hidden by visuals (weight, viscosity, friction, etc.).

Method: PhysicsLENS uses matched scenario pairs with the same conditioning frame and task but varying underlying physics. Scenarios are curated from public robot video sources and annotated across seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. Four video generation models were evaluated, producing over 400 human-annotated labels.

Result: Results show that 34 out of 47 plausible-looking videos actually ignore the stated physical property. Stating the property only slightly and not significantly lowers plausibility.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals a significant gap between visual plausibility and physical accuracy in video generation models, highlighting the need for better evaluation of physical properties in robot video generation.

Abstract: Reliable video world models could provide scalable predictive environments for robot learning, planning, and evaluation. However, generated robot videos can violate physical principles and complete tasks through physically implausible behavior, limiting their reliability for robot learning and planning. Current video-generation benchmarks exclude physics that are inherently hidden by visuals (e.g., weight, viscosity, friction). Due to this, video models are evaluated on the fidelity of physics, not the underlying accuracy of physics. We introduce PhysicsLENS, a dataset and benchmark for evaluating plausibility of physical properties grounded in robotics. PhysicsLENS uses matched scenario pairs that hold the same conditioning frame and task, while varying underlying physics in the scene description. Scenarios are curated from public robot video sources and annotated across seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. We evaluate across four video generation models, producing over 400 human-annotated labels. Results show that plausible-looking videos often ignore the stated property (34 of 47), and that stating the property lowers plausibility only slightly and not significantly.

</details>


### [78] [CineMR: Tool-Integrated Vision-Language Reasoning for Quantitative Cardiac MRI Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01166)
*Kunyang Li,Hai Nguyen,Joshua Lowe,Chenguang Zhao,Peace C. Madueme,Mehdi Hedjazi Moghari,Mubarak Shah,Pegah Khosravi,Yuzhang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CineMR is a tool-augmented vision-language model that integrates cardiac image-analysis tools for quantitative cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment, achieving 35.9% pass@1 on a multi-cohort benchmark, significantly outperforming baseline VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical VLMs cannot reliably derive quantitative measurements from multidimensional cine CMR images without dedicated analysis tools, limiting their utility for clinical cardiac assessment.

Method: CineMR combines a VLM backbone with cardiac image-analysis tools (segmentation, phase selection, volumetry, morphometry, regional wall motion analysis). Training involves supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on tool-interaction traces followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with conditional tool-use rewards. A multi-cohort visual question answering benchmark was constructed covering quantitative metric extraction, multiclass diagnosis, and differential diagnosis.

Result: CineMR achieves 35.9% pass@1 and 58.9% pass@4, compared with 1.5% for Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, 0.0% for LLaVA-Med v1.5, and 7.0% for MedGemma-4B. Correct tool invocation reaches 99.8% after GRPO (up from 78.9% after SFT). Live tool outputs improve ventricular measurement accuracy by 20.4-23.7% over direct predictions. Removing all tools reduces pass@1 from 35.9% to 27.9%.

Conclusion: CineMR demonstrates that reliable tool use is crucial for quantitative cine CMR reasoning. The tool-augmented VLM approach shows promise for assistive cardiac image assessment in clinical practice.

Abstract: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), including cine imaging, is a reference standard for the noninvasive assessment of cardiac morphology and ventricular function. Cine CMR interpretation integrates qualitative visual assessment with quantitative measurements of ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, myocardial mass, wall thickness, and regional wall motion. Current medical vision-language models (VLMs) cannot reliably derive quantitative measurements from multidimensional cine images without analysis tools. We present CineMR, a tool-augmented VLM that invokes cardiac image-analysis tools and integrates their outputs into interleaved reasoning for quantitative CMR assessment. We also construct a multi-cohort visual question answering benchmark covering quantitative metric extraction, multiclass diagnosis, and differential diagnosis, together with tools for segmentation, phase selection, volumetry, morphometry, and regional wall motion analysis. CineMR is trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on tool-interaction traces followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with conditional tool-use rewards. On the multi-cohort cine CMR benchmark, CineMR achieves 35.9% pass@1 and 58.9% pass@4, compared with 1.5% pass@1 for the Qwen3-VL-8B backbone and 0.0% and 7.0% pass@1 for LLaVA-Med v1.5 and MedGemma-4B, respectively. Correct tool invocation reaches 99.8% after GRPO, up from 78.9% after SFT. Live tool outputs improve ventricular measurement accuracy by 20.4--23.7% over direct model predictions, and removing all tools reduces pass@1 from 35.9% to 27.9%. These results highlight the importance of reliable tool use for quantitative cine CMR reasoning and support CineMR as a promising approach for assistive cardiac image assessment. Code, benchmark resources, and model weights are available at https://github.com/AI-MIND-Lab/CineMR.

</details>


### [79] [Skeleton-and-Strategy Prompting: Training-Free Negation Understanding for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01180)
*Yuliang Cai,Mohammad Rostami,Jesse Thomason*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A training-free method called Skeleton-and-Strategy Prompting (SSP) that improves Vision-Language Models' ability to understand negation in VQA tasks by using in-context learning without parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language Models consistently fail to understand negation and produce incorrect answers when questions involve negated clauses, despite strong performance on standard VQA tasks.

Method: SSP works in three steps: (1) abstracts the question structure into a skeleton, (2) retrieves same-skeleton questions from a lightweight pool, (3) prompts the VLM to analyze the shared negation pattern and synthesize an answering strategy. The skeleton and strategy are prepended to guide the test sample.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple negation VQA benchmarks while remaining computationally efficient.

Conclusion: SSP provides an effective training-free solution for improving VLM negation understanding, demonstrating that in-context learning can address specific linguistic limitations without requiring model fine-tuning or parameter updates.

Abstract: Despite the strong performance of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on a wide range of visual question answering (VQA) tasks, these models consistently struggle to understand negation and produce incorrect answers when questions involve negated clauses. To address this limitation, we propose Skeleton-and-Strategy Prompting (\textbf{SSP}), a training-free, in-context learning method that improves VLM negation understanding capabilities without any parameter updates. Given a negation question, our method first abstracts the underlying question structure into a skeleton, retrieves a small set of same-skeleton questions from a lightweight question pool, then prompts the VLM to analyze their shared negation pattern and synthesize a single-sentence answering strategy. The skeleton and strategy are prepended to the test sample to guide the model correctly tackle the negation problems. Experiments on multiple negation VQA benchmarks show that SSP achieves state-of-the-art performance on negation-focused VQA tasks while remaining computationally efficient.

</details>


### [80] [Color Independent Word Segmentation From Transcribed Bangla Passages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01191)
*Faias Satter,Noor Masrur,Sk. Md. Masudul Ahsan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This research focuses on word segmentation for handwritten Bangla text images, addressing the lack of reliable OCR solutions for Bangla script. The proposed system can process smartphone-captured images with varying paper and ink types, including shadow interferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the scarcity of dependable OCR systems for Bangla, particularly for handwritten text. Word segmentation is identified as the critical first step in OCR pipeline - if this stage fails, the entire OCR performance suffers regardless of later stage quality.

Method: The research uses a custom dataset containing 7374 words with 7278 bounding boxes. The system is designed to handle smartphone-captured images with various obstacles including shadow interferences, different paper colors, and ink types. Adaptive thresholding and dilation filters are employed.

Result: The system achieves 90.60% recall, 91.80% precision, and 91.20% F1-score on the dataset.

Conclusion: The word segmentation system shows promising results for Bangla handwritten text. Future improvements can be made by handling bounding boxes containing multiple words through nested operations and fine-tuning adaptive thresholding and dilation filter sizes for better precision.

Abstract: An optical character recognition(OCR) system can scan paper and extract text, making people's jobs easier. While numerous OCR systems are accessible in the software sector, finding a dependable equivalent solution for Bangla is tough. When it comes to handwritten texts, the case is even more rare. The first fundamental step to any OCR is to segment words from text images. If this stage fails, the total OCR's performance will be poor no matter how promising the later stages perform. This research aims to segment words in a handwritten Bangla text image. This research can be implemented on any smartphone-captured image, irrespective of the color and type of paper and ink. Furthermore, as smartphone-captured images can create shadow interferences, the custom dataset built for this research is created in such a way that every possible obstacle that can be faced is included. For 7374 words, a total of 7278 bounding boxes are generated, which have recall of 90.60 %, precision of 91.80 %, and F1-score of 91.20 %. The system can be further improved with nested operations on bounding boxes containing several words or by adjusting the adaptive thresholding and dilation filter sizes to a more precise level.

</details>


### [81] [FlashBack: Knowing When to Remember in Streaming Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01192)
*Yi Chen,MingMing Yu,Rui-Qi Wang,Boran Wang,Xiaohang Cao,Chu Tang,Jingmin Chen,Jie Gu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FlashBack is a training-free framework for selective memory retrieval in streaming vision-language models. It uses a frozen VLM to determine whether a query requires historical evidence, then either stays on a native real-time trajectory or invokes a recall trajectory with a side-KV pathway that preserves temporal continuity without modifying the persistent state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming VLMs face a tension between real-time perception and long-term memory under bounded compute. Historical recall can be counterproductive - unnecessary history introduces irrelevant context and interferes with native perception. The key insight is that memory retrieval should be selective, not automatic.

Method: FlashBack uses the frozen streaming VLM to assess whether a query requires historical evidence before retrieval. This creates two trajectories: (1) Native trajectory for real-time inference, (2) Recall trajectory that combines recent context with retrieved long-term memory via a query-local Side-KV pathway, preserving local temporal continuity without modifying the persistent Native state.

Result: Implemented on StreamingVLM and Mage-VL-4B, evaluated on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench. Results show improvements on long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks while largely preserving real-time perception. Performance is competitive with strong training-based streaming methods despite requiring no additional training.

Conclusion: FlashBack demonstrates that selective, training-free memory retrieval can effectively balance real-time perception with long-term memory in streaming VLMs. The approach achieves competitive results without requiring additional training, making it a practical solution for resource-constrained streaming vision-language applications.

Abstract: Streaming vision-language models must process continuously growing video streams under a bounded compute budget, creating a persistent tension between real-time perception and long-term memory. Retrieving historical information provides a natural remedy, yet historical recall is not uniformly beneficial: unnecessary history may introduce irrelevant context into current reasoning and interfere with native real-time perception. Effective streaming memory should therefore address not only what to remember, but also when and how to access it. To this end, we introduce FlashBack, a training-free framework for selective, multi-level memory in streaming vision-language models. Before retrieving history, FlashBack draws on the semantic understanding of the frozen streaming VLM to infer whether a query calls for historical evidence. This assessment determines whether inference remains on the Native trajectory or invokes an isolated Recall trajectory. The Recall trajectory combines recent context with retrieved long-term memory through a query-local Side-KV pathway, preserving local temporal continuity without modifying the persistent Native state. We instantiate FlashBack on StreamingVLM and Mage-VL-4B and evaluate it on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench. The results show improvements on several long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks while largely preserving real-time perception, with performance competitive with strong training-based streaming methods despite requiring no additional training. Our code will be announced later.

</details>


### [82] [iSEE: Object Permanence Through Self-Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01201)
*Pramish Paudel,Ajad Chhatkuli,Luc Van Gool,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: iSEE is a self-supervised framework that achieves object permanence in videos—tracking object identity and position during occlusion—without any labels. It uses three novel components: object evidence modeling (detecting occlusion via slot attention changes), appearance-position separation (two streams for re-identification vs. position tracking), and permanence from reappearance (training on reappearance cues only).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Object permanence is essential for video understanding tasks like tracking, prediction, and planning. Existing methods either require labeled data (trackers) or lose object slots under occlusion (slot attention). The problem is challenging because it requires detecting occlusion, re-identifying objects upon reappearance, and maintaining continuous hidden position estimates using only reappearance as the learning signal.

Method: iSEE proposes three key components: (i) Object evidence modelling: comparing a slot's current attention with its past to detect when the object is hidden; (ii) Appearance-position separation: using two parallel slot streams—one for appearance (held for re-identification) and one for position (continuously updating); (iii) Permanence from reappearance: a walker that tracks hidden object positions, trained solely on where objects reappear.

Result: On LA-CATER static dataset, iSEE achieves 86% correct re-identification after occlusion (vs. 32% for SlotContrast), and localizes hidden objects within 4.1 mAP of the label-trained state-of-the-art RAM method. The two-stream architecture also enables downstream planning, with the position stream serving as the action for a world model.

Conclusion: iSEE successfully achieves self-supervised object permanence, solving the occlusion problem without any human annotations. It combines detection of occlusion, re-identification, and continuous position tracking in a unified framework. The appearance-position separation is key to enabling both re-identification and downstream planning applications.

Abstract: Object permanence, keeping track of an object's identity and position while it is occluded, is central to video representations that track, predict and plan. Trackers that achieve it learn from boxes, track identities and visibility labels. On the other hand, self-supervised object-centric methods discover objects without labels: through slot attention, it represents a video as slots that bind to objects and follow them across frames. However, these slots are lost under occlusion, making the desired permanence impossible. Reasoning permanence is a hard problem because it requires to detect when an object becomes occluded, re-identify when object reappears, and keep the object's hidden position continuous, using reapperance as the only learning cue. To address this, we propose iSEE, a novel framework that offers all three aforementioned requirements, without any labels whatsoever. We built iSEE using the following three proposed components: (i) Object evidence modelling: a slot's attention, compared with its own past, reveals when its object is hidden. (ii) Appearance-position separation: two slot streams let the appearance be held for re-identification while the position keeps changing. (iii) Permanence from reappearance: a walker follows the hidden object's position, trained only on where the object reappears. On LA-CATER static, iSEE returns a reappearing object to its own slot after 86% of occlusions, against 32% for SlotContrast, and localises it while hidden within 4.1 mAP of the label-trained SoTA RAM. The two streams also allow downstream planning, with the position stream as the action of a world model. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/iSEE/

</details>


### [83] [Semantic RGB--Depth Based Surgical Skill Assessment in Microscopic Stereo Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01205)
*Jecia Z. Y. Mao,Sue M. Cho,Francis X. Creighton,Deepa Galaiya,Russell H. Taylor,Manish Sahu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a semantic RGB-Depth framework for automated microsurgical skill assessment from stereo microscope videos. It combines sparse stereo depth with dense monocular depth estimates, integrated with semantically decomposed instrument and anatomy streams, using a hierarchical attention architecture. The method achieved F1=0.938 for skill-level classification, outperforming semantic RGB (0.696) and matching semantic depth (0.929) approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video-based surgical skill assessment relies on RGB images and misses 3D spatial relationships. While stereo microscopes provide depth information, conventional stereo matching produces sparse/unreliable depth estimates under high-magnification conditions, limiting automated skill assessment.

Method: The framework uses: (1) Regression-based depth fusion combining sparse metric stereo depth with dense monocular depth estimates to create dense geometric representation; (2) Semantic decomposition of RGB streams into individual surgical instruments and surrounding anatomy; (3) Hierarchical attention architecture to jointly encode these streams and capture discriminative patterns of instrument use and instrument-anatomy interaction.

Result: Evaluated on 33 ex vivo transoral microlaryngeal procedures by 6 surgeons using leave-one-surgeon-out cross-validation. Semantic RGB-Depth achieved F1=0.938 vs semantic RGB (0.696) and semantic depth (0.929). The model also provides interpretable attention patterns for spatial, temporal, and semantic analysis.

Conclusion: Geometric (depth) information improves automated surgical skill assessment from microscopic stereo videos. The combination of RGB and depth with semantic understanding provides the best classification performance, demonstrating the value of integrating 3D spatial relationships with instrument-anatomy interaction analysis.

Abstract: Objective assessment of microsurgical technical skill is essential for competency-based training and quality assurance, yet existing video-based approaches predominantly rely on RGB images and therefore overlook the 3D spatial relationships that characterize instrument-anatomy interactions. Although stereo operating microscopes provide complementary depth information, conventional stereo matching algorithms can produce sparse and unreliable depth estimates under high-magnification imaging conditions, limiting their use for automated skill assessment. This work presents a semantic RGB-Depth framework for surgical skill assessment from microscopic stereo videos. A regression-based depth fusion method combines sparse metric stereo depth with dense monocular depth estimates to generate a dense geometric representation of the surgical scene. This representation is integrated with semantically decomposed RGB streams corresponding to individual surgical instruments and surrounding anatomy. A hierarchical attention architecture jointly encodes these streams to capture discriminative patterns of instrument use and instrument-anatomy interaction across surgeons at different training levels. The framework was evaluated on 33 ex vivo transoral microlaryngeal procedures performed by six surgeons, comprising attending surgeons and surgical residents, using leave-one-surgeon-out cross-validation. The proposed semantic RGB-Depth model achieved an F1 score of 0.938 for skill-level classification, compared with 0.696 for semantic RGB and 0.929 for semantic depth. These results suggest that geometric information can improve automated surgical skill assessment from microscopic stereo videos. The learned spatial, temporal, and semantic attention patterns also support qualitative examination of the scene regions, video segments, and semantic streams emphasized by the model.

</details>


### [84] [Resolving Mixed Single-Photon LiDAR Returns for Foreground-View and Hidden Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01206)
*Ziting Wen,Runrong Deng,Zili Zhang,Haitao Zheng,Yuecong Xu,Xiaoqiang Ren,Guodong Shi,Kemi Ding*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing hidden scenes behind partially transmissive occluders using single-photon LiDAR. The authors propose a state-aware framework that identifies echo evidence (no surface, single return, or two returns) to route supervision for a two-head neural field, enabling accurate geometry localization through partially transmissive materials.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional LiDAR systems struggle with partially transmissive occluders because they either discard weak hidden returns (peak-based systems) or fit a single scene representation that fails under occlusion. The core problem is that accurate transient fitting doesn't guarantee correct geometry when both foreground and hidden echoes overlap, forming broad peaks or subtle shoulders that could also be explained by a displaced single surface.

Method: The authors propose a state-aware framework with three key components: (1) Local echo evidence estimation for each ray to identify no reliable surface, single-return, or two-return states; (2) A two-head neural field where all rays constrain waveform reconstruction while reliable anchors provide geometry localization; (3) A real paired single-photon LiDAR occlusion dataset with occluded and clean captures at fixed poses for training and evaluation.

Result: Experiments on the real dataset demonstrate improved hidden scene depth and point-cloud accuracy over baseline methods, showing that single-photon layered reconstruction is a practical approach for 3D perception through partially transmissive occluders.

Conclusion: The state-aware framework successfully enables reconstruction of both foreground and hidden scenes from single-photon LiDAR data with occluders. This approach represents a practical route for 3D perception through partially transmissive materials, with potential applications in robotic inspection, autonomous navigation, and security systems.

Abstract: Partially transmissive screens and protective covers are common in robotic inspection, but they create mixed LiDAR returns from both the foreground material and the scene behind it. Conventional peak-based LiDAR usually discards weak hidden returns, while single-photon LiDAR records time-resolved histograms that preserve attenuated and overlapping echoes. However, existing transient reconstruction methods typically fit a single scene representation to the measured waveform. Under occlusion, weak or nearby foreground--hidden echoes can form a broad peak or subtle shoulder. Because such waveforms can also be explained by a displaced single surface or a thick density distribution, accurate transient fitting does not necessarily imply correct geometry. We propose a state-aware framework for foreground-view and hidden scene reconstruction from occluded single-photon histograms. For each ray, we estimate local echo evidence, identifying no reliable surface evidence, single-return evidence, or two returns. The inferred echo state routes supervision for a two-head neural field: all rays constrain waveform reconstruction, while reliable anchors provide geometry localization. We also introduce a real paired single-photon LiDAR occlusion dataset with occluded and clean captures at fixed poses. Experiments on a real dataset show improved hidden scene depth and point-cloud accuracy over baselines. Our results demonstrate single-photon layered reconstruction as a practical route for 3D perception through partially transmissive occluders.

</details>


### [85] [EgoFound3R: End-to-End Egocentric Hand Reconstruction in World Space with Point-Wise Interaction Attributes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01210)
*Hongming Fu,Jingcheng Shi,Wenjia Wang,Binhua Zuo,Bo Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EgoFound3R is a unified end-to-end model for egocentric video that estimates world-space hand geometry in metric scale and predicts point-wise interaction attributes (visibility, contact, distance) in a single pass, achieving significant MPJPE reductions (43.2%, 22.4%, 11.6%) and 6x higher throughput compared to prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing egocentric video reconstruction pipelines separate hand and scene estimation, use separate models for interaction attributes, and invoke multiple models per video, resulting in no unified model for these attributes and low throughput that constrains large-scale annotation.

Method: EgoFound3R integrates three key designs: (1) structured hand prompts that transfer pretrained geometric priors to world-space hand reconstruction; (2) an explicit hand representation that decodes hand geometry and interaction attributes; (3) a shared-parameter multi-rate design that lowers inference cost.

Result: On OakInk-v2, TACO, and HOI4D datasets, EgoFound3R reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 43.2%, 22.4%, and 11.6% respectively, while predicting point-wise contact and distance alongside geometry in the same pass, and achieving approximately 6x higher throughput.

Conclusion: EgoFound3R successfully provides a unified, efficient solution for world-space hand reconstruction with interaction attribute prediction, significantly outperforming prior methods in accuracy and throughput for embodied AI applications.

Abstract: Egocentric video has become a primary source of supervision for embodied models, and its value rests on recovering hand motion in world coordinates, which camera motion and hand occlusion make difficult. Existing reconstruction pipelines typically separate hand and scene estimation, leave interaction attributes to separate task-specific models, and invoke several models per video, so no prior reconstruction model estimates these attributes and throughput becomes a practical constraint on large-scale annotation. We therefore introduce EgoFound3R, a unified end-to-end model that estimates world-space hand geometry in a metric scale shared with the scene, and predicts point-wise interaction attributes, including visibility, contact, and distance. The model integrates three designs: (i) structured hand prompts that transfer pretrained geometric priors to world-space hand reconstruction; (ii) an explicit hand representation that decodes hand geometry and interaction attributes; and (iii) a shared-parameter multi-rate design that lowers inference cost. Together, these designs predict hand geometry and point-wise attributes in one pass. On OakInk-v2, TACO, and HOI4D, EgoFound3R reduces the mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 43.2%, 22.4%, and 11.6% over previous methods and predicts point-wise contact and distance alongside the geometry in the same pass, while attaining approximately 6x higher throughput.

</details>


### [86] [AutoGUIWorld: Image Generators as Visual World Models for GUI Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01215)
*Cheng Yang,Yifan Wu,Yutao Huang,Zhaohua Zhang,Beiduo Chen,Muxi Chen,Chenchen Zhao,Hexuan Deng,Haolin Yang,Geyuan Zhu,Sa Zhu,Jianhuan Zhuo,Qiuyong Xiao,Jianhao Ruan,Yiran Peng,Jiayi Zhang,Tian Ye,Xinlei Yu,Tianwen Jiang,Jihong Zhang,Yuyu Luo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AutoGUIWorld is a synthetic data generation framework that creates GUI interaction trajectories for training agents without requiring actual software deployment, using image generators combined with planners to synthesize valid action-observation sequences across operating systems and browsers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI agents require diverse interaction trajectories to learn software behavior, but real-world data collection is constrained by the need to deploy and run actual software environments, which imposes significant costs and limitations on diversity.

Method: AutoGUIWorld combines visual priors from image generators with task knowledge from planners: (1) samples initial GUI scenes from structured specifications of OS context, visual appearance, and interface state; (2) generates tasks conditioned on those scenes; (3) uses a planner to specify atomic actions and intended visual consequences; (4) employs an image generator to iteratively edit screenshots to produce subsequent observations; (5) applies action grounding and transition-level quality filtering to ensure validity.

Result: Generated 79,266 spatially annotated step-level training samples across Ubuntu, Windows, macOS, and Chrome. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these trajectories improved mean task score on OSWorld from 33.0% to 40.8% and task success rate on ScienceBoard from 14.0% to 32.2%.

Conclusion: Synthetic trajectories generated by AutoGUIWorld can effectively improve GUI agent performance on real desktop and scientific tasks, demonstrating that image generation combined with planning can replace costly real software deployment for training data synthesis.

Abstract: GUI agents require high-quality interaction trajectories to learn how software environments respond to actions, maintain state, and support multi-step workflows. However, the diversity of available trajectories is constrained by the applications, interface states, and workflows accessible in the underlying environments. Expanding this coverage requires deploying increasingly diverse and complex software, with specialized applications imposing additional installation, configuration, and runtime costs. We introduce AutoGUIWorld, a data generation framework that combines the visual priors of image generators with the task knowledge of a planner to synthesize GUI interaction trajectories without deploying or running the corresponding software environments. AutoGUIWorld samples initial GUI scenes from structured specifications of operating-system context, visual appearance, and interface state, and generates tasks conditioned on those scenes. A planner then specifies atomic actions and their intended visual consequences, while an image generator iteratively edits the current screenshot to produce subsequent observations. Action grounding and transition-level quality filtering yield 79,266 spatially annotated step-level training samples across Ubuntu, Windows, macOS, and Chrome. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on AutoGUIWorld trajectories improves the mean task score on OSWorld from 33.0% to 40.8% and the task success rate on ScienceBoard from 14.0% to 32.2%. These results show that generated trajectories improve GUI-agent performance on real desktop and scientific tasks.

</details>


### [87] [A Compact Explicit 4D Representation for Dynamic Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01229)
*Di Yang,Zhihao Li,Yanhai Xiong,Yufei Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Sparc4D is a feed-forward autoencoder that represents dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video with known cameras. It uses a sparse 4D scene state with static features shared across time and temporal slots for time-varying features. The system produces 2D Gaussian surfels via sparse decoder while preserving fine texture through geometric re-projection of stored source pixels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create a compact dynamic-scene representation that retains both surfaces seen over time and the appearance needed to render them from new viewpoints, enabling efficient novel view synthesis from monocular video.

Method: Feed-forward autoencoder encoding monocular video with known cameras into sparse 4D scene state. Static features are shared across the clip while temporally anchored slots compress time-varying features. A sparse decoder produces 2D Gaussian surfels, with stored source pixels preserving fine texture through geometric re-projection. The state includes one full source frame and dynamic-region pixels sampled every fourth frame, alongside learned features and sparse occupancy.

Result: For 32-frame clips: averages 0.95M 32-bit-equivalent values on random windows and 0.92M on first-32 protocol. Achieves 21.70dB PSNR on first-32, compared with 20.40dB for MoVieS. Comparable PSNR on randomly placed windows. Without stored texture, temporal slots compress time-varying features by 4.0× and reduce mean state from 1.04M to 0.42M values. Transfers to DyCheck and Neu3D datasets with improved LPIPS but slightly reduced PSNR.

Conclusion: Sparc4D achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality (21.70dB PSNR) on MultiCamVideo while maintaining compact representation (~0.92-0.95M values for 32 frames). The temporal slot mechanism provides 4.0× compression of dynamic features with minimal quality loss. The method generalizes to real datasets (DyCheck, Neu3D) without fine-tuning, demonstrating practical applicability.

Abstract: A compact dynamic-scene representation must retain both the surfaces seen over time and the appearance needed to render them from new viewpoints. We present Sparc4D, a feed-forward autoencoder that encodes a monocular video with known cameras into a sparse 4D scene state. Static features are shared across the clip, while spatially anchored temporal slots compress time-varying features. A sparse decoder produces 2D Gaussian surfels, while stored source pixels preserve fine texture through geometric re-projection. The state includes one full source frame and dynamic-region pixels sampled every fourth frame, alongside learned features and sparse occupancy. For a 32-frame MultiCamVideo clip, it averages 0.95M 32-bit-equivalent values on random windows and 0.92M on the first-32 protocol. On first-32, Sparc4D reaches 21.70\,dB, compared with 20.40\,dB for MoVieS. On randomly placed windows, their PSNR scores are comparable. With stored texture disabled, temporal slots compress the time-varying feature state by a median $4.0\times$ and reduce the mean state from 1.04M to 0.42M values, with essentially unchanged target-view reconstruction quality. Without fine-tuning on real data, Sparc4D transfers to DyCheck and Neu3D, where stored texture improves LPIPS while slightly reducing PSNR.

</details>


### [88] [Flow Matching Reinforcement for 3D Mesh Generation via Dynamic Homing Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01233)
*Zhen Zhou,Zhiwei Ning,Puhua Jiang,Sheng Zhang,Yifei Tang,Jie Yang,Xintong Han,Wei Liu,Chunchao Guo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Dynamic Homing Optimization (DHO), a novel RL method for flow matching in 3D generation that reformulates negative-trajectory optimization as positive-sample attraction-guided dynamic homing. The method uses MAM for target assignment and TDC for trajectory correction, leading to the development of Flow3D-Pro, an image-to-3D geometry generation framework that outperforms existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods (DPO, GRPO, NFT) for flow matching in 3D generation are adapted from 2D visual generation without explicitly specifying target velocity fields toward preferred samples. These methods mainly steer predicted velocities away from negative directions but fail to provide constructive guidance. Additionally, constrained by pretrained model capabilities, rollout diversity, and reward-distribution complexity, these methods yield limited gains in geometric quality.

Method: The paper proposes two key innovations: (1) Dynamic Homing Optimization (DHO) - a forward-process RL method that reformulates negative-trajectory optimization as positive-sample attraction-guided dynamic homing, consisting of Minimum-Cost Attractive Matching (MAM) for assigning distinct positive targets to each negative sample, and Time-Aware Dynamic Correction (TDC) for redirecting trajectories using remaining-time-aware corrective velocity; (2) Flow3D-Pro - an image-to-3D geometry generation framework built on asynchronous online DHO.

Result: DHO outperforms representative DPO-, GRPO-, and NFT-style objectives in 3D generation tasks. Flow3D-Pro produces higher-quality 3D geometry than existing mesh generation methods.

Conclusion: The forward-process RL method DHO effectively addresses the limitations of existing RL methods in 3D generation by explicitly guiding negative trajectories toward positive targets. The resulting Flow3D-Pro framework demonstrates superior performance in image-to-3D geometry generation, establishing a new approach for applying reinforcement learning to flow matching in 3D generation tasks.

Abstract: Flow matching is central to 3D generation, yet in practice its reinforcement learning (RL) methods are largely adapted from 2D visual generation. Representative DPO-, GRPO-, and NFT-style objectives, when applied to negative trajectories, mainly steer predicted velocities away from the corresponding directions without explicitly specifying a target velocity field toward preferred samples. In 3D generation, constrained by pretrained model capabilities, rollout diversity, and reward-distribution complexity, directly applying these RL methods yields limited gains in geometric quality. We introduce a forward-process RL method \textbf{Dynamic Homing Optimization (DHO)}, which reformulates negative-trajectory optimization as positive-sample attraction-guided dynamic homing. Specifically, Minimum-Cost Attractive Matching (MAM) assigns each negative sample a distinct positive target, and Time-Aware Dynamic Correction (TDC) then redirects its trajectory toward the target using a remaining-time-aware corrective velocity. Building on asynchronous online DHO, we develop \textbf{Flow3D-Pro}, an image-to-3D geometry generation framework. Experiments show that DHO outperforms representative DPO-, GRPO-, and NFT-style objectives in 3D generation, while Flow3D-Pro produces higher-quality 3D geometry than existing mesh generation methods.

</details>


### [89] [When the Judge Acts: Auditing VLM-Guided Image Selection on Culturally Situated Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01243)
*Huichan Seo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper audits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as judges for selecting the best generated images, revealing significant reliability issues. A 4B-parameter judge barely beats random selection, shows strong position bias (selecting first image 49% of the time vs 28% chance), and changes decisions 60% of the time when candidate order is reordered. An 8B model performs better but filtering mechanisms don't consistently improve outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLM judges are validated by score agreement with human ratings, not by examining the actual images they select. This creates a gap in understanding whether these models reliably pick the best images or are influenced by artifacts like position bias. The motivation is to audit VLM judges as decision-makers using a rigorous methodology that exposes their failure modes.

Method: The researchers conducted an audit on 300 culturally situated prompts. They compared the VLM judge's returned image with human ratings (which the judge never saw) and with random selection. They also repeated every decision with candidates reordered to test for position bias. They evaluated a 4B-parameter judge and an 8B judge, testing whether agreement across reorderings or agreement with a weaker judge could filter good from bad decisions.

Result: The 4B judge barely beats random and falls short of a CLIP similarity baseline. It picks the first image shown in 49% of calls (chance: 28%), and reordering changes its choice on 60% of prompts. Decisions that survive reordering are much better than random for the 4B judge. The 8B judge shows almost no position bias and outperforms CLIP, but filtering by reordering mostly discards good decisions. The 4B judge's slight rise in stereotype ratings is no longer detectable after aggregating across orders or with the larger judge.

Conclusion: VLM judges suffer from significant reliability issues including position bias and order-dependent decision-making. Agreement across reorderings helps only when targeting the specific failure mode - filters must be re-audited whenever the judge changes. The findings suggest that validation metrics should go beyond score agreement to include actual decision quality and position bias testing. Aggregation across multiple orderings can help mitigate some biases, especially for smaller models.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly act as judges that pick the best of several generated images, so their choices decide what users see. Such judges are usually validated by score agreement with human ratings, not by the images they return. We audit VLM judges as decision-makers: on 300 culturally situated prompts, we compare the returned image with human ratings the judge never sees and with random choice from the same candidates, and repeat every decision with the candidates reordered. A 4B-parameter judge barely beats random and falls short of a CLIP similarity baseline. It picks the first image shown in 49% of calls (chance: 28%), and reordering changes its choice on 60% of prompts. For this judge, agreement across orders is informative: decisions that survive reordering are much better than random, whereas agreement with a weaker second judge keeps the wrong ones. An 8B judge shows almost no position bias and outperforms CLIP, yet for it the same filter mostly discards good decisions. Agreement helps only when it targets the judge's failure mode, so filters must be re-audited whenever the judge changes. The 4B judge's slight rise in stereotype ratings is no longer detectable after aggregating across orders or with the larger judge.

</details>


### [90] [PickMoment: Continuous-Time Single-Image-to-Video via Learning Deblurring and Blur-to-Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01279)
*Junseong Shin,Hyeonsu Jo,Daehyun Kim,Tae Hyun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PickMoment introduces a continuous-time approach to motion blur removal that learns to predict sharp images at arbitrary time points within the exposure window, unifying single-image deblurring, blur-to-video generation, and continuous-time recovery in a single model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learning-based methods for motion blur treat it as either a single-image problem (recovering one sharp frame) or a blur-to-video problem (predicting fixed frames), but both approaches ignore the physical model of blur as temporal integration. The authors propose that by understanding blur as the integral of sharp signals over time, a single model can flexibly recover sharp images at any point within the exposure window.

Method: The method uses three complementary losses: (1) empirical reconstruction loss from available subframes, (2) an additivity loss enforcing self-consistency across overlapping sub-intervals (analogy to MeanFlow's average-velocity), and (3) a sharp-frame loss anchored at the zero-interval limit. The model is trained as a deterministic function that directly outputs the interval-mean blur for arbitrary sub-intervals of the exposure.

Result: PickMoment achieves state-of-the-art performance among generative-based deblurring methods on GoPro and HIDE datasets, competitive performance against restoration-based methods on RealBlur, and the highest per-frame fidelity on GoPro-7 blur-to-video benchmark, all in a single forward pass without iterative sampling.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates that a single trained model can unify multiple blur-related tasks (single-image deblurring, blur-to-video, continuous-time recovery) by directly learning the physical blur integral, rather than treating them as separate problems. The approach provides a principled continuous-time formulation that outperforms prior generative methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Motion blur arises from the temporal integration of a continuous sharp signal over a finite exposure window, yet existing learning-based methods sidestep this physical model and predict only the sharp signal itself: most single-image deblurring methods recover a single frame at the exposure center, while blur-to-video methods predict a fixed set of frames. We introduce PickMoment, a continuous-time reformulation that directly learns the interval-mean blur over arbitrary sub-intervals of the exposure with a single deterministic model. Drawing an analogy to MeanFlow's average-velocity formulation, we train the model with three supervisions derived from the blur integral: an empirical reconstruction loss from available subframes, an additivity loss that enforces self-consistency across overlapping sub-intervals, and a sharp-frame loss anchored at the zero-interval limit. A single trained model unifies single-image deblurring, blur-to-video generation, and continuous-time pick-a-moment recovery as different queries to the same network, with no separate training for each task. Our PickMoment achieves state-of-the-art performance among generative-based deblurring methods on GoPro and HIDE while competitive against restoration-based methods on RealBlur, and the highest per-frame fidelity on GoPro-7 blur-to-video, all in a single forward pass without iterative sampling.

</details>


### [91] [ShelfChange3D: Object-Level 3D Change Detection for Retail Shelf Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01283)
*Lingyi Zhou,Yunke Wang,Mengyu Zheng,Wenbo Wang,Zijian Wang,Chang Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper tackles shelf monitoring for retail automation by formulating it as object-level 3D change detection. The authors introduce ShelfChange3D dataset (145K synthetic + 5K real RGB-D pairs) and ChangeBox, an end-to-end framework that predicts 3D change boxes from paired observations. A geometry-based refinement stage improves localization accuracy using depth and gravity prior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing out-of-stock detection methods operate in image space and lack metric 3D localization needed for downstream robotic systems in retail automation.

Method: ChangeBox: end-to-end framework that jointly reasons over paired RGB-D observations to predict object-level 3D change boxes. Includes a geometry-based refinement stage that exploits depth and gravity prior to estimate relative pose and refine predicted boxes.

Result: ChangeBox outperforms existing change detection baselines. The method shows effective transfer from synthetic to real-world observations, with further gains from the refinement stage.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables metric 3D localization for shelf monitoring, supporting downstream robotic manipulation tasks. The combination of synthetic and real data training proves effective for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Reliable shelf monitoring is an important capability for retail automation, yet existing out-of-stock detection methods mainly operate in image space and lack metric 3D localization for downstream robotic systems. We formulate shelf monitoring as object-level 3D change detection: given two RGB-D observations captured at different times, the goal is to identify changed products and localize each change with a 3D bounding box. To support this task, we introduce ShelfChange3D, comprising 145K synthetic and 5K real-world paired RGB-D observations with object-level 3D change annotations. We further propose ChangeBox, an end-to-end framework that jointly reasons over paired observations and predicts object-level 3D change boxes. To improve localization accuracy, we introduce a geometry-based refinement stage that exploits depth and gravity prior to estimate relative pose and refine predicted boxes. Experiments show that ChangeBox outperforms existing change detection baselines, with further gains from refinement and effective transfer from synthetic to real-world observations.

</details>


### [92] [Dyna3: VLM-Guided Training-Free 4D Reconstruction via Depth Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01286)
*Xinhao Xiang,Weiyang Li,Zhijie Zheng,Abhijeet Rastogi,Jiawei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV
