TL;DR: Dyna3 is a training-free framework that extends the depth-only model DA3 for 4D dynamic scene reconstruction without fine-tuning. It leverages motion-discriminative signals from cross-view depth features and uses VLM-generated semantic prompts for SAM 3 segmentation to distinguish static vs dynamic objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing depth foundation models like DA3 assume static 3D scenes, limiting real-world dynamic environment applications. Training-free 4D methods like Easi3R and VGGT4D rely on correspondence-trained backbones, which have cross-frame matching capabilities that depth-only models lack. The authors aimed to extend depth-only models for dynamic scene reconstruction without any fine-tuning.

Method: 1) Exploit DA3's cross-view features combined with best-match feature search to implicitly encode motion-discriminative signals (static surfaces find consistent matches globally, dynamic objects cannot). 2) Use vision-language models (VLM) to automatically generate scene-specific semantic prompts for SAM 3, enabling precise instance-level segmentation. 3) Decouple the scene into a cross-frame aligned static background and per-frame dynamic point clouds for reconstruction.

Result: Dyna3 surpasses correspondence-trained methods with +5.5pp J-Mean over state-of-the-art VGGT4D on dynamic object segmentation, while achieving up to 13x faster pose estimation and 3x faster 4D reconstruction with 4 to 8x lower memory.

Conclusion: Dyna3 enables much denser temporal sampling that prior methods cannot support, demonstrating that depth-only models can be extended for 4D dynamic scene reconstruction without fine-tuning by leveraging implicit motion signals and VLM-guided segmentation.

Abstract: Recent depth foundation models like Depth Anything 3 (DA3) achieve remarkable multi-view depth estimation but assume static 3D scenes, limiting their applicability to real-world dynamic environments. Existing training-free 4D methods like Easi3R and VGGT4D rely on correspondence-trained backbones whose attention encodes cross-frame matching, a property absent in depth-only models like DA3. We present Dyna3, a training-free framework that extends DA3 for 4D dynamic scene reconstruction without any fine-tuning. Our key insight is that DA3's cross-view features, though trained only for depth consistency, implicitly encode motion-discriminative signals when combined with best-match feature search across frames. Its static surfaces find consistent matches globally, while dynamic objects cannot. We further adopt vision-language models (VLM) to automatically generate scene-specific semantic prompts for SAM 3, enabling precise instance-level segmentation that distinguishes which objects move from what objects exist. For reconstruction, we decouple the scene into a cross-frame aligned static background and per-frame dynamic point clouds. Experiments on four datasets demonstrate that Dyna3 surpasses correspondence-trained methods with +5.5pp J-Mean over state-of-the-art VGGT4D on dynamic object segmentation, while achieving up to 13x faster pose estimation and 3x faster 4D reconstruction with 4 to 8x lower memory. Dyna3 could therefore enable much denser temporal sampling that prior methods cannot support.

</details>


### [93] [ODDR: One-Step Deshadow Diffusion via Reward Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01291)
*Junseong Shin,Kijun Kim,Minseong Kim,Dongjin Kim,Tae Hyun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ODDR is a novel framework for efficient single-step shadow removal that uses synthetic data and a self-supervised reward model (ShadowReward) to achieve high-fidelity results without requiring costly real-world paired annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning shadow removal methods rely on real-world paired datasets, which are expensive to collect, limited in scene diversity, and result in poor generalization. This motivates the need for methods that can work without real-world paired supervision.

Method: The method comprises two stages: (1) One-step Deshadow Diffusion (ODD), a baseline model trained on synthetic shadow data for efficient single-step shadow-free image reconstruction; (2) ShadowReward, the first reward model for shadow removal trained without human annotation by ranking synthetically generated images with controlled degradations (texture distortion, boundary artifacts). ODDR is then fine-tuned using this reward-guided approach to close the synthetic-to-real domain gap.

Result: ODD achieves strong performance without real-world paired supervision. ODDR further improves results, narrowing the gap to fully supervised methods trained on real-world paired data while maintaining higher computational efficiency as a single-step model.

Conclusion: The proposed ODDR framework demonstrates that high-fidelity shadow removal can be achieved efficiently without relying on costly real-world paired data, offering a promising direction for domain adaptation in image restoration tasks.

Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning for shadow removal have significantly enhanced image quality and realism. However, most approaches rely on real-world paired datasets, which are costly to collect and often limited in scene diversity, leading to limited generalization. To address these limitations, we propose One-step Deshadow Diffusion via Reward guidance (ODDR), a new framework that achieves efficient and high-fidelity shadow removal without relying on real-world paired supervision. Our method begins with One-step Deshadow Diffusion (ODD), a baseline model trained on synthetic shadow data for efficient one-step shadow-free reconstruction. We further adapt ODD into ODDR using ShadowReward. In contrast to traditional, annotation-heavy approaches, ShadowReward is the first reward model for shadow removal trained entirely without human annotation. It learns to mimic human perceptual judgments by ranking synthetically generated images with controlled degradations, such as texture distortion and boundary artifacts. This reward-guided fine-tuning enables ODDR to close the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Extensive experiments show that ODD achieves strong performance without relying on real-world paired supervision, and ODDR further improves the results, narrowing the gap to fully supervised methods trained on real-world paired data while maintaining higher computational efficiency as a single-step model.

</details>


### [94] [STAGE: Subspace-Targeted Affine Generative Erasure for Text-to-3D Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01302)
*Karol Dziekan,Przemysław Spurek,Dawid Malarz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STAGE is a training-free, closed-form framework for erasing concepts (shape, material, object) in native text-to-3D generation by applying stage-aware editing to either the structural stage, appearance stage, or both, achieving a composite score of 66.7 vs 53.2 for baselines on TRELLIS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing closed-form concept erasure methods were designed for 2D image diffusion and assume a single generative pathway. Native 3D generators synthesize structured 3D representations directly rather than by lifting 2D samples, violating this assumption. Shape and object concepts must be erased in the structural stage while material concepts should be erased in the appearance stage.

Method: STAGE confines each edit to the low-dimensional subspace spanned by differences between erase and anchor embeddings, and relaxes the norm-preserving orthogonal constraint into a least-squares affine correction that maps target activations onto safe anchors subject to a penalty on displacement of retained prompts. The correction applies to structural stage, appearance stage, or both.

Result: On TRELLIS (standard open native 3D generator) across 15 shape, material, and object concepts, STAGE achieves 66.7 on a composite score (balancing forgetting target concept against preserving everything else, aggregating CLIP-based semantic and physical metrics) versus 53.2 for the strongest adapted baseline.

Conclusion: The stage an edit must reach is determined by concept type - shape and object concepts in structural stage, material concepts in appearance stage. STAGE successfully handles concept erasure in native 3D generation by treating it as a stage-aware editing problem.

Abstract: Concept erasure suppresses a target concept while preserving behavior on unrelated inputs. Existing closed-form methods were designed for 2D image diffusion and assume a single generative pathway, so one edit must cover geometry and texture at once. Native 3D generators, which synthesize structured 3D representations directly rather than by lifting 2D samples, violate this assumption. We show that shape and object concepts must be erased in the structural stage of the pipeline and material concepts in the appearance stage. We therefore formulate erasure in native text-to-3D as a stage-aware editing problem and introduce STAGE, a training-free, closed-form framework. STAGE confines each edit to the low-dimensional subspace spanned by the differences between erase and anchor embeddings, and relaxes the norm-preserving (orthogonal) constraint of prior editors into a least-squares affine correction that maps target activations onto safe anchors subject to a penalty on the displacement of retained prompts. The correction applies to the structural stage, the appearance stage, or both. We find that the stage an edit must reach is determined by concept type. On TRELLIS, the standard open native 3D generator, across 15 shape, material, and object concepts, STAGE reaches 66.7 on a composite score that balances forgetting the target concept against preserving everything else, aggregating CLIP-based semantic and physical metrics, versus 53.2 for the strongest adapted baseline.
  Code: https://github.com/gmum/STAGE/
  Project Page https://gmum.github.io/STAGE/

</details>


### [95] [ARROW: Arbitrary Reconstruction and Tracking of 4D Observations in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01314)
*Ilya Fradlin,Christian Schmidt,Jens Piekenbrinck,Karim Knaebel,Gonzalo Martin Garcia,Bastian Leibe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ARROW is a feed-forward model that unifies 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking from arbitrary image sets, using a novel order-invariant querying approach for associating queries with observations across arbitrary inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic scenes captured by moving cameras, multiple video streams, or images at different times reveal complementary aspects of scene geometry and motion. However, combining these observations requires establishing correspondence across viewpoints, capture times, and visibility changes—a challenging problem in computer vision.

Method: The paper introduces ARROW, a feed-forward model with a novel order-invariant querying approach at its core. This technique allows association of queries with observations across arbitrary inputs. The model is trained with a strategy that exposes it to more diverse sets of inputs, leading to improved performance and generalization capability.

Result: ARROW achieves state-of-the-art results in 3D tracking on WorldTrack and TAPVid-3D benchmarks. It outperforms dedicated multi-view trackers on an adapted RGB-only MVTracker benchmark while remaining competitive across 3D reconstruction tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed ARROW model demonstrates that training with diverse input sets improves task performance and enables generalization to a wider range of tasks, including multi-view tracking. The model successfully unifies 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking in a single framework.

Abstract: Dynamic scenes may be captured by a moving camera, multiple video streams, or images taken at different times. These observations reveal complementary aspects of scene geometry and motion, yet bringing them together requires establishing correspondence across viewpoints, capture times, and visibility changes. We introduce ARROW, a feed-forward model that unifies 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking from arbitrary image sets. At its core is a novel order-invariant querying approach, which allows the association of queries with observations across arbitrary inputs. We show that exposing the model to more diverse sets of inputs during training results in improved task performance. Moreover, the resulting model is capable of generalization to a wider range of tasks including multi-view tracking. Trained with this strategy, ARROW establishes a new state of the art in 3D tracking on WorldTrack and TAPVid-3D and outperforms dedicated multi-view trackers on an adapted RGB-only MVTracker benchmark, while remaining competitive across 3D reconstruction tasks. Code and weights are publicly available.

</details>


### [96] [CLASP: Continual Low-rank Adapters for Spatially Placed Concepts from One Hypernetwork](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01331)
*Wojciech Gromski,Patryk Krukowski,Jan Miksa,Maciej Zieba,Przemysław Spurek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A rehearsal-free continual personalization method for text-to-image diffusion models using a fixed-size hypernetwork that dynamically produces concept-specific adaptations without expanding model parameters, while integrating spatial control capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual personalization methods for diffusion models suffer from catastrophic forgetting or require growing parameter storage as new concepts are added, limiting scalability to long concept sequences.

Method: A single fixed-size hypernetwork that produces concept-specific adaptations for a frozen diffusion model, eliminating the need to expand model parameters. The framework integrates spatial control into the personalization process without additional per-concept components.

Result: Strong retention of previously learned concepts and reliable spatial grounding, matching or improving upon existing methods while scaling effectively to long streams of personalization tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed approach enables continual personalization with a parameter footprint that remains independent of the number of learned concepts (aside from compact concept representations), effectively solving the scalability limitation of prior methods.

Abstract: Continual personalization of text-to-image diffusion models requires sequentially acquiring new concepts while retaining previously learned ones. However, existing methods either suffer from catastrophic forgetting or rely on storing additional concept-specific parameters and spatial components, causing their parameter footprint to grow with the concept stream. This limits their ability to scale to long sequences of personalization tasks. We propose a rehearsal-free approach that uses a single fixed-size hypernetwork to continually personalize a frozen diffusion model. Instead of expanding the model as new concepts are acquired, the hypernetwork dynamically produces the concept-specific adaptations required for personalization while preserving previously learned concepts. Our framework further integrates spatial control into the personalization process, allowing users to specify where a personalized concept should appear without introducing additional per-concept components. This formulation enables continual personalization with a parameter footprint that remains independent of the number of learned concepts, aside from compact concept representations. Experiments demonstrate strong retention of previously learned concepts and reliable spatial grounding, matching or improving upon existing methods while scaling effectively to long streams of personalization tasks.

</details>


### [97] [MMVistaReason: Toward Open-Data and Post-Training Recipes for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01352)
*Juekai Lin,Honglin Lin,Yuqian Yuan,Xiaolong Wu,Jie Cao,Liang Liang,Yunqi Cao,Yun Zhu,Wenqiao Zhang,Lijun Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MMVistaReason (MVR) is an open-data post-training recipe for multimodal reasoning models that addresses challenges in data quality, supervision efficiency, difficulty imbalance, and cross-domain interference through three components: broader capability coverage across Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups, efficient SFT/RL data construction (MVR-SFT-528K, MVR-RL-63K), and specialize-then-integrate training via Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open multimodal reasoning models suffer from unreliable post-training due to uneven data quality, inefficient supervision construction, imbalanced difficulty, and cross-domain interference, necessitating a systematic approach to open-data construction and capacity-aware training.

Method: The study proposes three components: (1) broader capability coverage across Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups with structured reasoning vs. visual perception and spatial grounding; (2) efficient SFT and RL data construction via staged cleaning/annotation, difficulty-aware cascaded teacher distillation, answer-likelihood-based trajectory selection for MVR-SFT-528K, and scale-specific frontier filtering for MVR-RL-63K; (3) specialize-then-integrate training with complementary RL experts consolidated through Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD).

Result: MVR-4B achieves 72.8 average across 15 benchmarks, outperforming Qwen3.5-9B and MMFineReason-8B with ~70% fewer samples; MVR-9B achieves 74.4 average, surpassing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. Key findings: smaller models benefit more from selected supervision while larger models are robust to trajectory variation; mixed-domain RL causes negative transfer while MOPD provides consistent capability integration with KL direction varying across model scales.

Conclusion: Systematic open-data construction and capacity-aware post-training provide a practical and scalable path toward reliable multimodal reasoning, with the optimal training strategy depending on model capacity.

Abstract: Open multimodal reasoning models have benefited from large-scale reasoning supervision, yet reliable post-training remains challenging due to uneven data quality, inefficient supervision construction, imbalanced difficulty, and cross-domain interference. We introduce MMVistaReason (MVR), an open-data post-training recipe with three components: (1) broader capability coverage across complementary Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups, emphasizing structured reasoning versus visual perception and spatial grounding; (2) efficient SFT and RL data construction, standardizing heterogeneous open data through staged cleaning and annotation, combining difficulty-aware cascaded teacher distillation with answer-likelihood-based trajectory selection to construct MVR-SFT-528K, and applying scale-specific frontier filtering for MVR-RL-63K; and (3) specialize-then-integrate training, which trains complementary RL experts and consolidates their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Our analyses reveal a capacity-dependent interaction between supervision difficulty, trajectory quality, and model capacity: smaller students benefit more from selected supervision, while larger students are robust to trajectory variation and mixed-domain interference. Mixed-domain RL introduces benchmark-level negative transfer, whereas MOPD provides consistent capability integration, with the preferred KL direction varying across model scales. Across 15 multimodal benchmarks, MVR-4B achieves an average score of 72.8, outperforming Qwen3.5-9B (Instruct) and MMFineReason-8B while using about 70% fewer samples than MMFineReason. Scaling to 9B improves the average to 74.4, surpassing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Instruct). Overall, MMVistaReason demonstrates that systematic open-data construction and capacity-aware post-training provide a practical and scalable path toward reliable multimodal reasoning.

</details>


### [98] [Smoother Flow Matching via Contrastive Trajectory Repulsion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01408)
*Ziqi Jiang,Zhenqi He,Long Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoFlow addresses trajectory crossing issues in Flow Matching by introducing contrastive learning to repel trajectories during training, reducing local Lipschitz constants in the velocity field and improving few-step inference quality on ImageNet 256x256.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trajectory crossing is a critical bottleneck in Flow Matching that causes velocity averaging. Previous works address this indirectly through post-hoc distillation or endpoint coupling without explicitly regulating intermediate trajectories. The authors identify that crossing points induce large local Lipschitz constants in the target velocity field, leading to two problems: (1) neural networks struggle to fit high-frequency signals due to spectral bias, and (2) drastic velocity variations cause severe numerical integration errors in few-step inference.

Method: CoFlow introduces contrastive learning paradigm into Flow Matching. The method is formulated from a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) perspective by injecting a repulsive drift term that actively guides the forward process of positive samples away from negative trajectories, effectively reducing local Lipschitz constants. An equivalent stochastic interpolant formulation is derived to provide a simple design space for controlling negative sample influence.

Result: CoFlow significantly reduces FID compared to standard FM in few-step inference (e.g., 20 steps) on ImageNet 256x256, with no added training overhead.

Conclusion: CoFlow provides a new network learning perspective to address trajectory crossing in Flow Matching. By explicitly repelling trajectories through contrastive learning, the method reduces local Lipschitz constants and improves sample quality in few-step generation, offering a practical solution without additional computational cost.

Abstract: Trajectory crossing remains a critical bottleneck in Flow Matching (FM), and previous works typically view these crossings from a theoretical optimization perspective causing velocity averaging. They attempt to address it indirectly by post-hoc distillation or endpoint coupling, without explicitly regulating the intermediate trajectories. In this paper, we introduce a new network learning perspective: crossing points inherently induce large local Lipschitz constants in the target velocity field, leading to two drawbacks. First, high Lipschitz constants correspond to high-frequency signals in the velocity field that neural networks struggle to fit due to spectral bias. Second, they also imply drastic velocity variations, leading to severe numerical integration errors in few-step inference. To alleviate this, we propose CoFlow, a framework that introduces the contrastive learning paradigm into FM to explicitly repel trajectories during training, thereby lowering the local Lipschitz constants of the velocity field. Specifically, we formulate CoFlow from a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) perspective by injecting a repulsive drift term. This drift actively guides the forward process of positive samples away from negative trajectories, effectively reducing the local Lipschitz constant. Furthermore, we derive an equivalent stochastic interpolant formulation from this SDE, providing a simple and tractable design space to control the influence of negative samples. Extensive experiments on ImageNet 256x256 demonstrate that CoFlow significantly reduces FID compared to standard FM in few-step inference (e.g., 20 steps), with no added training overhead. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/HKUST-LongGroup/CoFlow

</details>


### [99] [Localisation-Aware Uncertainty for Pretrained Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01409)
*Charmaine Barker,Daniel Bethell,Simos Gerasimou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GRACE is a lightweight post-hoc evidential meta-model that estimates uncertainty for object detector predictions without requiring detector retraining or architectural modifications. It uses saliency-guided curriculum learning to train on progressively challenging modifications, combining localisation error, modification level, and prediction instability to guide uncertainty estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying object detectors in real-world scenarios requires reliable uncertainty estimation to handle distribution shift and adversarial attacks. Existing methods impose significant overheads through retraining, architectural changes, or repeated inference, making them impractical for many applications.

Method: GRACE identifies localisation-relevant features automatically and uses saliency-guided modification to construct a curriculum with increasingly challenging inputs. The meta-model is trained on detection-level targets combining localisation error, modification level, and prediction instability. This post-hoc approach keeps the base detector frozen and preserves original localisation outputs.

Result: GRACE achieves up to 22% relative improvement in TP-FP AUROC compared to the strongest comparator under adversarial attacks, while maintaining in-distribution detection performance. The approach requires no detector modifications and adds minimal overhead.

Conclusion: GRACE provides an effective, lightweight solution for uncertainty estimation in object detection that can be applied to existing detectors without retraining. It successfully balances robustness to adversarial attacks with maintaining baseline performance, offering a practical approach for deploying object detectors in safety-critical applications.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying object detectors when distribution/covariate shift and adversarial attacks may occur. Existing approaches often require detector retraining, architectural modification, or repeated inference, which may be infeasible or incur significant overheads. We introduce a lightweight post-hoc evidential meta-model that learns when object localisations should be considered uncertain while keeping the base detector frozen. Our approach automatically identifies localisation-relevant features and uses saliency-guided modification to construct an increasingly challenging curriculum. Detection-level targets combine localisation error, modification level, and prediction instability to guide an evidential meta-model to estimate uncertainty for each predicted bounding box. Our approach requires no changes to the detector and preserves its original localisation outputs. Across adversarial attacks and evaluated strengths, GRACE improves TP-FP AUROC by 22% relative to the strongest comparator in some cases while maintaining in-distribution detection performance.

</details>


### [100] [MWOP: Modality-aware Width-wise Operation Pruning for Efficient MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01434)
*Xudong Wang,Hao Wu,Haozhe Hu,Peiran Yin,Xinghao Chen,Yunpu Ma,Wei Zhang,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MWOP is a method to reduce inference costs in Multimodal Large Language Models by pruning attention paths (V2V, T2V, T2T) and FFN channels separately for visual and textual inputs, using first-order Taylor criterion and LoRA recovery training. Achieves 1.6x prefill speedup with 99.7% performance retention on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, and can be combined with token compression for further speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing operation compression methods treat computation within attention heads and FFN channels as unified units, ignoring finer-grained redundancy. The authors discover that redundancy varies across modality-interaction paths within attention heads and across visual/textual executions of FFN channels, suggesting opportunities for more efficient pruning.

Method: Modality-aware Width-wise Operation Pruning (MWOP) independently prunes: (1) Visual-to-visual (V2V), text-to-visual (T2V), and text-to-text (T2T) attention paths within each layer; (2) FFN channels separately for visual and textual inputs. Uses first-order Taylor criterion to guide pruning, re-evaluates FFN importance after attention pruning, and applies LoRA-based recovery training. Implementation includes path-sparse Triton attention kernels and compact visual-side FFN execution.

Result: On LLaVA-OneVision-7B: 1.6x prefill speedup with 99.7% average performance retention across 12 benchmarks. Combined with token compression methods, increases prefill speedups from 2.0x and 1.9x to 2.9x and 2.7x respectively. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B demonstrate cross-architecture applicability.

Conclusion: MWOP preserves token sequence while reducing attention and FFN computation, making it complementary to token compression methods. It enables simultaneous reduction of sequence length and per-token computation, achieving significant speedups while maintaining high performance across different benchmarks and model architectures.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) incur substantial inference costs when processing long visual-textual sequences. While existing operation compression methods exploit modality-level redundancy, they largely treat computation within attention heads and shared feed-forward network (FFN) channels as unified units, leaving finer-grained redundancy underexplored. We find that redundancy varies both across modality-interaction paths within the same attention head and across visual and textual executions of the same FFN channel. Based on these findings, we propose Modality-aware Width-wise Operation Pruning (MWOP), which independently prunes visual-to-visual (V2V), text-to-visual (T2V), and text-to-text (T2T) attention paths within each layer, and separately selects FFN channels for visual and textual inputs. A first-order Taylor criterion guides the pruning process, with FFN importance re-evaluated after attention pruning and LoRA-based recovery training. To translate the resulting fine-grained sparsity into practical acceleration, we further develop path-sparse Triton attention kernels and compact visual-side FFN execution. MWOP preserves the token sequence while reducing attention and FFN computation, making it complementary to token compression and enabling simultaneous reduction of sequence length and per-token computation. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, MWOP alone achieves a $1.6\times$ prefill speedup with 99.7\% average performance retention across 12 benchmarks. Combined with two representative token compression methods, it further increases their prefill speedups from $2.0\times$ and $1.9\times$ to $2.9\times$ and $2.7\times$, respectively. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B further demonstrate its applicability across architectures. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/MWOP.

</details>


### [101] [The Impact of Processing Parameters on High-Accuracy Measurements in UAV Photogrammetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01438)
*Paweł Ćwiąkała,Edyta Puniach,Elżbieta Pastucha,Wojciech Gruszczyński*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study systematically evaluates 768 processing variants of UAV photogrammetry workflows to determine how Bundle Block Adjustment parameter settings affect 3D accuracy and deformation measurements. Using 10 UAV datasets collected over 1.5 years in a 220 ha study area, the research identifies key parameters influencing accuracy and provides optimization recommendations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While UAV photogrammetry is increasingly used for high-accuracy applications like landslide monitoring and surface change detection, the influence of processing workflow parameters—especially Bundle Block Adjustment settings—remains poorly understood. This gap limits the reliability and repeatability of photogrammetric monitoring.

Method: Full-factorial experimental design evaluating 768 processing variants across 10 UAV datasets collected over 1.5 years in a 220 ha study area. Eight key Bundle Block Adjustment parameters were systematically analyzed, including number of ground control points, camera calibration corrections, and Post-Processing Kinematic GNSS methods.

Result: The study found substantial accuracy variability: RMSE ranged from 16 mm (best) to 303 mm (worst). The three most influential factors were: (1) number of ground control points, (2) additional camera calibration corrections, and (3) use of PPK GNSS method for camera projection center coordinates. Optimized workflow reduced systematic errors by over half in all axes, with vertical median absolute error decreasing from 14 mm to 7 mm, while random displacement errors remained stable at ~6-7 mm RMSE.

Conclusion: This study provides the first large-scale, practice-oriented assessment of processing parameter selection effects on photogrammetric accuracy and deformation indices determination. The results offer actionable guidance for developing robust, repeatable UAV photogrammetry workflows for high-precision monitoring applications.

Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry is increasingly used in applications requiring high accuracy, such as determining ground surface changes caused by landslides, mining, or microrelief transformation. While acquisition strategies have been widely studied, the influence of the processing workflow-particularly Bundle Block Adjustment parameter settings-remains insufficiently explored. This study addresses this gap through a systematic, full-factorial evaluation of 768 processing variants applied to ten UAV datasets collected over 1.5 years in a 220 ha study area. Eight key parameters were analysed. The results show substantial variability in final 3D accuracy: the best performing variant achieved a root mean square error (RMSE) of 16 mm, whereas the weakest reached 303 mm. The most influential factors were the number of ground control points, the application of additional camera calibration corrections, and the use of the Post-Processing Kinematic GNSS method for determining camera projection center coordinates. The study also evaluates how workflow optimization affects the accuracy of displacement, tilt changes, and horizontal strain determination. While random displacement errors remained stable (RMSE of ~6-7 mm), systematic errors were significantly reduced by over half in all axes, with vertical median absolute error decreasing from 14 mm to 7 mm in the optimized configuration compared to the baseline previously used by the authors. This study provides the first large-scale, practice-oriented assessment of how processing parameter selection shapes the accuracy of both photogrammetric products and deformation indices determination. The results offer actionable guidance for developing more robust and repeatable UAV photogrammetry workflows tailored to high-precision monitoring.

</details>


### [102] [Uncertainty-Guided Handshake: Efficient Human-in-the-Loop Refinement for Surgical-Grade Glioma Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01452)
*Samuel Hart,Ahmad Yahya,Ahmed Karam Eldaly*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A Hybrid Structural-Aleatoric Human-in-the-Loop framework for glioma segmentation that achieves sub-2.0 mm HD95 on benchmarks and improves Whole Tumor Dice from 0.891 to 0.914 while requiring only 11.3% interactive workload, addressing catastrophic failures in automated medical image segmentation for safe clinical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art automated models for medical image segmentation suffer from localized, catastrophic failures that preclude safe clinical deployment in neuro-oncology. Existing interactive segmentation frameworks impose prohibitive cognitive and temporal workloads on clinicians.

Method: The method extracts voxel-wise Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) uncertainty and applies hierarchical topological filtering to proactively isolate high-risk structural anomalies. It operates under a simulated Human Oracle to route structural failures.

Result: On an out-of-distribution clinical stress-test cohort (N = 362), the framework improved Whole Tumor Dice from 0.891 to 0.914 and reduced HD95 from 5.82 mm to 4.76 mm. For Tumor Core, mean HD95 was reduced from 17.96 mm to 14.83 mm, improving absolute TC Dice to 0.356. The median interactive workload was 11.3% of the target volume.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates a highly Pareto-efficient pathway for safely deploying clinical AI in neuro-oncology, achieving surgical-grade precision while maintaining feasible human workload requirements.

Abstract: While state-of-the-art automated models for medical image segmentation achieve high mean performance, they frequently suffer from localized, catastrophic failures that preclude safe clinical deployment, particularly in neuro-oncology. Interactive segmentation frameworks mitigate this by incorporating human oversight, but traditionally impose prohibitive cognitive and temporal workloads by requiring clinicians to manually search for errors. In this project, we present an efficient, Hybrid Structural-Aleatoric Human-in-the-Loop framework for glioma segmentation that bridges the gap between automated baseline performance and surgical-grade precision, achieving sub-2.0 mm HD95 on curated benchmarks while providing safety-net routing for structural failures across real-world clinical data. By extracting voxel-wise Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) uncertainty and applying hierarchical topological filtering, our method proactively isolates high-risk structural anomalies. We comprehensively evaluated our approach on a challenging out-of-distribution clinical stress-test cohort (N = 362). Operating under a simulated Human Oracle, the framework improved the Whole Tumor (WT) Dice score from 0.891 to 0.914 and reduced the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) from 5.82 mm to 4.76 mm. Critically for surgical safety, the system rescued severe boundary failures in the Tumor Core, reducing mean HD95 from 17.96 mm to 14.83 mm (improving absolute TC Dice to 0.356). These spatial rescues were achieved while demanding a median interactive workload of just 11.3% of the target volume. Acknowledging this as a simulated upper bound lacking real-world cognitive friction, the framework nevertheless demonstrates a highly Pareto-efficient pathway for safely deploying clinical AI.

</details>


### [103] [FiVOS: A Fish Segmentation Algorithm Based on Interactive Video Object Segmentation and Filter Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01480)
*Yuqing Duan,Song Zhang,Shili Zhao,Daoliang Li,Ran Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes FiVOS, an improved interactive video object segmentation method for fish behavior monitoring in aquaculture. It addresses limitations of existing methods by using a mask block filter with rule-based thresholding and serialized noise filters to correct erroneous propagated masks and eliminate noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The continuous expansion of aquaculture creates need for precise fish behavior monitoring. Existing deep learning-based video segmentation methods overlook dynamic correlations between video frames. IVOS methods are promising but face challenges in aquaculture: data scarcity, error accumulation, and mask loss over long sequence propagation due to high intra-class similarity.

Method: The paper proposes FiVOS with two key components: (1) A mask block filter enabling early detection and correction of erroneous propagated mask blocks, using rule-based thresholding for enhanced filtering accuracy; (2) Serialized noise filters to further eliminate erroneous mask noise, improving model robustness. The method also constructs two fish-specific datasets.

Result: FiVOS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in fish video segmentation tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed FiVOS method provides robust technical support for fish behavior research in aquaculture environments.

Abstract: With the continuous expansion of aquaculture, precise and efficient monitoring of fish behavior has become increasingly critical for improving farming efficiency and reducing economic losses. In particular, with the ongoing enhancement of computational capabilities in deep learning models, vision-based fish segmentation methods are garnering growing attention. By analyzing video segmentation results, fish behavior can be effectively tracked, thereby providing reliable data support for the precise regulation of aquaculture environments. However, existing deep learning-based video segmentation methods for aquaculture scenarios often overlook the dynamic correlations between video frames. In contrast, Interactive Video Object Segmentation (IVOS) employs an interaction-propagation scheme to achieve high-precision segmentation while minimizing user effort, thereby enhancing monitoring efficiency. Yet, IVOS applications in aquaculture remain limited due to data scarcity, and are susceptible to error accumulation and mask loss over long sequence propagation due to high intra-class similarity. In response, this paper proposes an improved interactive video object segmentation method (FiVOS) and constructs two fish-specific datasets. FiVOS utilizes a mask block filter to enable early detection and correction of erroneous propagated mask blocks, enhancing filtering accuracy through a rule-based thresholding approach. Additionally, it serializes noise filters to further eliminate erroneous mask noise, thereby improving model robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that FiVOS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in fish video segmentation tasks, providing robust technical support for fish behavior research.

</details>


### [104] [SALD: Self-Referenced Advantage Learning for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01496)
*Aryan Das,Surjo Dey,Koushik Biswas,Swalpa Kumar Roy,Moloud Abdar,Arnab Bhattacharya,Vinay Kumar Verma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces SALD, a self-referenced training framework for diffusion models that evaluates image-caption pairs at two noise levels to generate training signals without external teachers. The method uses relative error differences between easy (low-noise) and hard (high-noise) paths to adapt the training objective, incorporating three components: AGD (Advantage-Guided Diffusion), TAM (Temporal Advantage Memory), and SAD (Spectral Advantage Decomposition).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from recent work on language-model adaptation showing that models can obtain informative training signals by evaluating their behavior in demonstration or feedback-augmented contexts with teacher networks. The authors aim to enable diffusion models to identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks, applying the "internal-reference principle" to the diffusion model domain.

Method: SALD evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model: (1) Easier lower-noise path evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference; (2) Harder higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Instead of directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hard-path objective. Three components are introduced: (1) Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts relative error into differentiable sample-level weight; (2) Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts future gap between noise levels; (3) Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) compares residual power spectra of two paths and constructs frequency-derived latent-element weight.

Result: Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality. Component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of each proposed component.

Conclusion: The proposed SALD framework achieves improved generation quality in diffusion models through self-referenced training without external teachers. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither external teacher networks nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, with no modification to the inference procedure.

Abstract: Recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that single models can obtain informative training signals by evaluating their behavior in demonstrationor feedback-augmented contexts, with the help of a teacher network, which is driven by the student's learned parameters. Inspired by this internal-reference principle, we investigate how diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks. We introduce SALD, a self-referenced training framework that evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The easier, lower-noise path is evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference, while the harder, higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Rather than directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hardpath objective. The proposed Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts this relative error into a differentiable sample-level weight. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts the future gap between the two noise levels. Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) further compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither an external teacher network nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, and no modification to the inference procedure. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of the proposed components.

</details>


### [105] [VTR-Bench: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Text Rendering in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01499)
*Yu Huang,Jungang Li,Zhiyuan Wang,Yonghua Hei,Song Dai,Jiayu Yang,Deyuan Liu,Xiang Zheng,Xiaoshuang Shi,Hao Cheng,Kaidi Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VTR-Bench is a systematic benchmark for evaluating visual text rendering capabilities in video generation models. It addresses the overlooked dimension of accurate text rendering in generated videos, which can appear visually compelling but still render text incorrectly. The benchmark includes 300 prompts across 5 scenario categories (advertisements, scientific videos, etc.) and an automated evaluation pipeline. A Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework is also introduced to improve text rendering through iterative refinement. Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art models reveal widespread difficulties, with the best model achieving a word error rate (WER) of 0.250.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video generation evaluation benchmarks predominantly assess visual quality, aesthetic appeal, and physical plausibility, while paying limited attention to text rendering accuracy. This is a critical gap because text is an essential medium for conveying information in everyday scenes, and generated videos may appear visually compelling but still render text incorrectly.

Method: 1) VTR-Bench: 300 carefully constructed prompts across 5 scenario categories (advertisements, scientific videos, etc.)
2) Automated evaluation pipeline with human alignments:
   - Text fidelity assessed through carrier-specific transcription
   - Scene and motion requirements assessed through prompt-specific chain of query
3) Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework: A Director agent coordinates image and video generation with visual evaluation, guiding iterative refinement and candidate selection through visual feedback.
4) Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art video generation models

Result: 1) Widespread difficulties in accurately rendering scene text across all 11 models tested
2) Best-performing model recorded an overall word error rate (WER) of 0.250 (25% error rate)
3) Analysis of text rendering failures to characterize challenges faced by current video generation models

Conclusion: Visual text rendering is a key challenge for current video generation models. VTR-Bench provides a practical path toward improvement by establishing a systematic evaluation benchmark and introducing an agentic framework for iterative refinement. The findings highlight the need for significant improvements in text rendering capabilities for video generation models to reach practical application standards.

Abstract: Recent video generation models can produce highly realistic videos from natural language instructions, with visual quality approaching cinematic standards. Existing evaluation benchmarks, however, predominantly assess visual quality, aesthetic appeal and physical plausibility, while paying limited attention to text, an essential medium for conveying information in everyday scenes. A generated video may appear visually compelling and feature lifelike subjects, yet still render the text within the scene incorrectly. To address this overlooked dimension, we introduce \textbf{VTR-Bench}, a systematic benchmark for evaluating the \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}ext \textbf{R}endering capabilities of video generation models. VTR-Bench situates text within concrete application scenarios, such as advertisements and scientific videos, with 300 carefully constructed prompts spanning five scenario categories. We develop an automated evaluation pipeline with human alignments that separately assesses text fidelity through carrier-specific transcription and scene and motion requirements through a prompt-specific chain of query. Beyond evaluation, we introduce a \textbf{Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework} in which a Director agent coordinates image and video generation with visual evaluation, guiding iterative refinement and candidate selection through visual feedback. Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art models reveal widespread difficulties in accurately rendering scene text, with the best-performing model recording an overall word error rate (WER) of 0.250. We further analyze text rendering failures to characterize the challenges faced by current video generation models. These findings highlight visual text rendering as a key challenge for video generation and demonstrate a practical path toward improvement. Code is available at https://github.com/hardenyu21/VTR-Bench.

</details>


### [106] [FedCKA: Representation-Guided Layer Personalization for Federated 3D Perception Across Driving Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01510)
*Jolle Verhoog,Ali Burak Ünal,Holger Caesar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedCKA is a federated learning approach for 3D object detection in autonomous vehicles that uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to dynamically determine which model layers to personalize vs. aggregate globally. It computes layer-wise feature similarities to create client-specific aggregation masks, enabling selective sharing of representation-consistent layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust perception in intelligent vehicles requires 3D object detectors that work under domain shifts (time of day, location, weather). However, annotation costs and rare shifts limit training data in some environments. Traditional federated learning relies on a single global model that struggles with heterogeneous data distributions, and existing personalization approaches use fixed layer partitions or ratios, limiting adaptability to client-specific conditions.

Method: FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training. These similarity scores are converted into client-specific aggregation masks that selectively share representation-consistent layers while personalizing divergent ones. The approach was evaluated on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes.

Result: FedCKA outperforms established federated learning baselines (FedBN, FedRep, FedSelect), improving average NDS (NuScenes Detection Score) by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: FedCKA offers a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across domain shifts in location, weather, and illumination. The method dynamically adapts the personalization-globalization trade-off based on learned feature similarities, reducing rigidity in layer-wise adaptation decisions.

Abstract: Robust perception in intelligent vehicles demands 3D object detectors that remain dependable under domain shifts, such as changes in time of day, location, or weather. However, due to costly annotation and rare shifts, some environments lack sufficient data to train a standalone detector. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving framework for collaborative model training, enabling clients to benefit from shared learning across diverse environments. Yet, this framework traditionally relies on a single global consensus model, which struggles to perform across heterogeneous local data distributions. Local conditions are better captured by adapting a subset of the model, but many personalization approaches rely on predefined layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, thereby limiting adaptation to client-specific divergence. To reduce this rigidity, we propose FedCKA, a Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)-based strategy that dynamically handles the personalization-globalization trade-off. Specifically, FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training. By converting layer-wise similarity scores into client-specific aggregation masks, FedCKA selectively shares representation-consistent layers. Evaluation on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes shows that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The findings offer both a comparative benchmark and a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across shifts in location, weather, and illumination. Code is available at https://github.com/j-verhoog/FedCKA.

</details>


### [107] [VoxelSynth3D: Interpretable Volumetric Image-Domain Metal Artifact Reduction with a Paired Synthetic CLINIC-Metal Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01512)
*Amritesh Banerjee,Abdul Basit,Renil Renji Joseph,Nouhaila Innan,Muhammad Shafique*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VoxelSynth3D is a training-free 3D image-domain framework for reducing metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT scans. It combines support masking, normalized tissue synthesis, deviation gating, and restricted edge refinement to correct metal-induced artifacts while preserving implant voxels. The method was evaluated on a synthetic dataset (Synthetic CLINIC-Metal) and 75 real cases, showing significant RMSE reduction (15.30 HU improvement) compared to baseline and a 3D Gaussian smoother.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT significantly obscure bone-implant and adjacent soft-tissue interfaces, making clinical assessment difficult. Existing metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods either require unavailable raw projections or rely on learned models that may not generalize across different scanners and implants. This necessitates a training-free, robust solution that works directly on reconstructed CT volumes.

Method: VoxelSynth3D is a training-free 3D image-domain framework that operates on reconstructed CT scans. It combines four key components: (1) Support masking to identify implant regions; (2) Normalized tissue synthesis to replace artifacted tissue; (3) Deviation gating to filter out incorrect corrections; and (4) Restricted edge refinement to preserve structural integrity. The method preserves detected implant voxels while targeting metal-induced artifacts in surrounding tissue. Evaluation was conducted using Synthetic CLINIC-Metal (constructed from no-metal CTPelvic1K volumes with clean targets, metal/artifact masks, fixed seeds, and patient-level splits) and 75 unpaired real metal cases.

Result: On 40 held-out test cases, VoxelSynth3D reduced RMSE from 801.48 to 786.18 HU, achieving a paired gain of 15.30 HU (95% CI 11.68-19.23). The method improved every case and exceeded the evaluated 3D Gaussian smoother by 13.58 HU. Clean-edge agreement decreased adjacent to metal but exceeded input beyond 5 mm. Spacing-aware sensitivity analysis confirmed aggregate broad-region improvement and identified near-metal calibration as an area for future improvement.

Conclusion: VoxelSynth3D provides case-consistent within-distribution tissue-error reduction with a localized structural tradeoff. The training-free approach avoids the generalization issues of learned models while maintaining consistent performance across cases. The method demonstrates that image-domain MAR can achieve meaningful artifact reduction without requiring raw projection data or extensive training datasets, though there is a tradeoff near metal interfaces where edge preservation is compromised.

Abstract: Metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT obscure bone-implant and adjacent soft-tissue interfaces. Many metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods require unavailable raw projections or learned models that may shift across scanners and implants. We present VoxelSynth3D, a training-free 3D image-domain framework for reconstructed CT. The framework combines support masking, normalized tissue synthesis, deviation gating, and restricted edge refinement. Detected implant voxels are preserved in the output, while correction targets metal-induced artifacts in the surrounding tissue. We also construct Synthetic CLINIC-Metal, a controlled paired synthetic evaluation resource, from no-metal CTPelvic1K volumes with clean targets, metal/artifact masks, fixed seeds, and patient-level splits; 75 unpaired real metal cases receive qualitative/no-reference evaluation only. The operating point was fixed in a near-flat validation basin. With exact-mask oracle localization, all methods share a metal-excluded tissue ROI. On 40 held-out cases, VoxelSynth3D reduced RMSE from 801.48 to 786.18 HU (paired gain 15.30 HU, 95% CI 11.68-19.23), improving every case and exceeding the evaluated 3D Gaussian smoother by 13.58 HU. Clean-edge agreement decreased next to metal but exceeded input beyond 5 mm. Thus, VoxelSynth3D provides case-consistent within-distribution tissue-error reduction with a localized structural tradeoff. Spacing-aware sensitivity retained aggregate broad-region improvement and identified near-metal calibration as a target.

</details>


### [108] [SuperMotion: Source-Preserving Denoising for Text-Driven Human Motion Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01517)
*Fa-Ting Hong,Peter Wonka*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SuperMotion is a text-driven human motion editing framework that addresses the problem of temporal detail loss in existing diffusion-based editors. It introduces a source-preserving denoising mechanism that explicitly reuses the source motion at each reverse step through a learned preservation gate and clean-space source anchor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion-based human motion editors rely on learned conditioning to preserve unedited content, but their outputs lose temporal detail as denoising proceeds. The authors identify that this smoothing occurs because reconstruction-trained denoisers tend to attenuate high-frequency temporal details.

Method: The method has three key components: (1) Source alignment - aligning source motion to output timeline; (2) Preservation gate - predicting a gate that controls source reuse across frames and feature dimensions; (3) Clean-space source anchor - blending predicted clean motion with aligned source and passing corrected estimate to sampling posterior. Training uses supervised learning against editing target and a temporal high-frequency loss matching second temporal differences. No explicit edit masks are required.

Result: SuperMotion achieves 33.20% full-pool R@1 on MotionFix, improving editing accuracy while reducing temporal-detail attenuation and preserving motion dynamics when realizing requested text-guided changes.

Conclusion: The learned preservation gate is responsible for the performance gain, effectively reusing source to retain unedited content. The clean-space source anchor successfully injects sample-level temporal detail that would otherwise be smoothed away by the denoiser.

Abstract: Text-driven human motion editing aims to realize a requested change while preserving compatible source content. Existing diffusion editors rely largely on learned conditioning for preservation of the unedited part, yet their outputs can lose temporal detail as denoising proceeds. We propose the \textbf{Source-Preserving Denoising framework (SuperMotion)}, which explicitly reuses the source at each reverse step for source preservation. We first align the source motion to the output timeline and predict a preservation gate that controls reuse across frames and feature dimensions. A clean-space source anchor then utilizes the learned preservation gate to blend the predicted clean motion with the aligned source and passes the corrected estimate directly to the sampling posterior. Because the aligned source is a realized motion rather than a regression output, the anchor injects sample-level temporal detail that a reconstruction-trained denoiser tends to smooth away. To learn effective source reuse, we supervise the anchored estimate against the editing target and match its second temporal differences through a temporal high-frequency loss. These objectives require no explicit edit masks. Extensive experiments show that SuperMotion improves editing accuracy, reaching 33.20\% full-pool R@1 on MotionFix, while reducing temporal-detail attenuation and preserving motion dynamics as it realizes the requested changes. Ablations confirm that the learned preservation gate is responsible for the gain and that it reuses the source to retain the unedited content properly.

</details>


### [109] [Synthetic training for long-tail haemorrhagic lesion segmentation in data-scarce settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01542)
*Yuan Cao,Sumeet Dash,Antonia Zachariadis,Stefanie Schreiber,Katja Neumann,Jose Bernal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A synthetic training framework for automated segmentation of cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) that requires no real lesion annotations, using procedural lesion synthesis with clinical priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated segmentation of CMBs and cSS is limited by the scarcity of positive cases and voxel-level annotations, creating a long-tail distribution problem in medical imaging.

Method: The framework starts from anatomical brain parcellations, applies spatial augmentation and voxel resampling, procedurally inserts cSS and CMB labels using clinical priors on lesion location and morphology, and synthesizes images through randomized intensity assignment, blurring, and Rician noise simulation. Models were trained on dynamically generated image-label pairs and evaluated against manual delineations in 10 cSS cases and 13 CMB cases.

Result: For cSS, the hypointensity constrained model achieved higher AUPRC and AUROC than the Frangi filter (AUPRC: 0.284 vs 0.083; AUROC: 0.907 vs 0.731). For CMBs, explicit synthesis of blood vessels as lesion mimics improved performance over the classical baseline (AUPRC: 0.538 vs 0.004; AUROC: 0.999 vs 0.968).

Conclusion: The proposed synthetic training framework is a feasible strategy for data-scarce haemorrhagic lesion segmentation, outperforming classical filter baselines for both cSS and CMB detection.

Abstract: Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) are imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease, but their automated segmentation is limited by the scarcity of positive cases and voxel-level annotations. We propose a synthetic training framework for long-tail haemorrhagic lesion segmentation that requires no real lesion annotations for training and leverages radiological description of the lesions. Starting from anatomical brain parcellations, the framework applies spatial augmentation and voxel resampling, procedurally inserts cSS and CMB labels using clinical priors on lesion location and morphology, and synthesises images through randomised intensity assignment, blurring, and Rician noise simulation. Models were trained on dynamically generated image-label pairs and evaluated against manual delineations in 10 cSS cases and 13 CMB cases. The proposed configurations outperformed classical filter baselines. For cSS, the hypointensity constrained model achieved higher AUPRC and AUROC than the Frangi filter (AUPRC: 0.284 vs 0.083; AUROC: 0.907 vs 0.731). For CMBs, explicit synthesis of blood vessels as lesion mimics improved performance over the classical baseline (AUPRC: 0.538 vs 0.004; AUROC: 0.999 vs 0.968). These results support our proposal as a feasible strategy for data-scarce haemorrhagic lesion segmentation.

</details>


### [110] [Revisiting Cross-Reconstruction for Generalizable Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01544)
*Bingjian Yang,Shilei Zhao,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an artifact-oriented disentanglement framework for robust image forgery detection that preserves artifact diversity instead of enforcing explicit alignment. The method uses semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction with masked frequency-aware reconstruction to learn transferable forensic representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing image forgery detectors suffer from poor generalization to unseen manipulation methods due to limited ability to capture transferable forensic cues. Prior cross-reconstruction methods align heterogeneous artifacts across generators and exclude artifact representations during reconstruction, overlooking the inherent diversity and visual cues of manipulation artifacts.

Method: The framework preserves diverse artifact characteristics through semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction (instead of enforcing explicit artifact alignment). It incorporates artifact representations into the reconstruction process and introduces a masked frequency-aware reconstruction strategy to emphasize manipulation-related residuals while reducing semantic interference.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements under both cross-dataset and cross-generator evaluation settings. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of artifact diversity preservation and artifact-aware cross-reconstruction.

Conclusion: The proposed artifact-oriented disentanglement framework successfully improves generalization of image forgery detection by leveraging artifact diversity as complementary forensic cues rather than undesirable domain variations.

Abstract: Existing image forgery detectors often suffer from generalization to unseen manipulation methods due to the limited ability to capture transferable forensic cues. Recent cross-reconstruction based methods attempt to improve generalization through semantic-artifact disentanglement, but typically align heterogeneous artifacts across generators and exclude artifact representations during reconstruction, which may overlook the inherent diversity and visual cues of manipulation artifacts. In this work, we revisit cross-reconstruction and introduce an artifact-oriented disentanglement framework for robust image forgery detection. We argue that \textbf{artifact diversity}, i.e., the intrinsic variations of manipulation artifacts introduced by different generation processes, contains complementary forensic cues rather than undesirable domain variations. Instead of enforcing explicit artifact alignment, our framework preserves diverse artifact characteristics through semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction. Furthermore, we incorporate artifact representations into the reconstruction process and introduce a masked frequency-aware reconstruction strategy to emphasize manipulation-related residuals while reducing semantic interference. This design enables the model to learn transferable forensic representations from diverse artifacts. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements under both cross-dataset and cross-generator evaluation settings. Further analysis and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of artifact diversity preservation and artifact-aware cross-reconstruction.

</details>
