### [111] [GS-PQM: A Parameter-Domain Quality Metric for Compressed Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00195)
*Pedro Martin,António Rodrigues,João Ascenso,Maria Paula Queluz*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: GS-PQM is a novel full-reference quality metric for Gaussian Splatting compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain, using Support Vector Regression to estimate perceptual quality from parameter-domain distortion errors, outperforming 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable objective quality assessment is essential for comparing GS compression methods and guiding development of more efficient GS codecs. Existing methods rely on rendering-based assessment which depends on selected viewpoints.

Method: GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality from a set of parameter-domain distortion errors using a Support Vector Regression model, operating directly in the GS parameter domain rather than requiring rendering.

Result: GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content.

Conclusion: GS-PQM provides an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment for GS compression.

Abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian Splatting (GS) compression have enabled substantial reductions in GS model size. Reliable objective quality assessment is therefore essential for comparing compression methods and guiding the development of more efficient GS codecs. Existing GS quality assessment typically relies on image and video quality metrics, requiring rendering of predefined viewpoints and making the quality estimate dependent on the selected views. This paper introduces GS-PQM, a novel full-reference quality metric for post-training GS compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain. GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality from a set of parameter-domain distortion errors using a Support Vector Regression model. Experimental results show that GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content, providing an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment.

</details>


### [112] [Diffusion Editing with Soft Mask: Pixel Level Redo of Image and Video with Adjustable Strength](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00359)
*Candi Zheng,Yuan Lan*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: SoftPaint is a zero-shot sampling method that enables fine-grained, pixel-level control in diffusion models using soft masks, allowing continuous spectrum edits from content preservation to complete re-synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion model editing methods are too coarse for pixel-level control. Training fine-grained control requires expensive pixel-wise annotations, and zero-shot methods often produce unsatisfactory results. There is a need for a gradient-free, memory-efficient method that can achieve smooth, pixel-level edits across images and videos.

Method: The method introduces a Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths. It leverages soft masks to enable a continuous spectrum of edits and applies universally to image and video diffusion models.

Result: The method achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones while being gradient-free and memory-efficient.

Conclusion: SoftPaint provides a universal zero-shot solution for fine-grained diffusion model editing, working across both image and video models without requiring additional training or pixel-wise annotations.

Abstract: Diffusion models with prompt and reference image-guided editing have seen rapid progress, yet they remain too coarse for pixel-level control. One promising direction is to incorporate a soft mask that specifies spatially varying edit strengths but training such fine-grained control demands expensive pixel-wise annotations, while existing zero-shot methods often yield unsatisfactory results. We introduce SoftPaint, a new zero-shot sampling method that leverages soft masks to enable a continuous spectrum of edits, from fully preserving the original content to completely re-synthesizing the masked region. Going beyond zero-shot inpainting methods, we design a Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths, which applies universally to image and video diffusion models, enabling tasks such as video editing. The method is gradient-free, memory-efficient, and achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones.

</details>


### [113] [Smooth Curves from Curvature-Driven Subdivision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00020)
*Hassan Ugail*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel interpolatory subdivision scheme where new points are defined using a curvature-profile model instead of traditional affine combinations. The scheme works identically in the plane and on the sphere, reproducing geodesics and circles exactly. The linearization corresponds to the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme, and the refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature (C² in arc length).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be advancing the theory of interpolatory subdivision schemes by using a curvature-profile model rather than traditional affine combinations. The authors aim to establish convergence and geometric regularity, addressing limitations in the straightening condition theory proposed by Ewald, Reif, and Sabin, which fails for this scheme. The authors seek to prove that refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with specific smoothness properties.

Method: The method involves: (1) Estimating curvatures from circumscribed circles on each edge to prescribe a curvature profile; (2) Reconstructing the segment using Frenet integration with geodesic shooting; (3) Placing new points at half arc length. A unique curvature prefilter is used to turn the planar linearization into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The theory is refined by measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion to repair the failing straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin.

Result: The scheme achieves convergence and geometric regularity. The refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, and are twice continuously differentiable in arc length (C²). The scheme reproduces geodesics and circles exactly and works identically in the plane and on the sphere. The regularity is governed solely by the normal companion scheme, as conjectured by Ewald, Reif, and Sabin.

Conclusion: The curvature-profile based subdivision scheme provides a successful alternative to traditional affine-based methods. The key insight is that regularity is governed by the normal companion scheme alone, confirming the conjecture of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin. The scheme achieves the desired smoothness (C² in arc length) while maintaining exact reproduction of geodesics and circles, and works uniformly in both planar and spherical settings.

Abstract: We introduce and analyse an interpolatory subdivision scheme in which each inserted point is defined by a curvature-profile model rather than by an affine combination of its neighbours, and we establish its convergence and geometric regularity. On each edge, curvatures estimated from circumscribed circles prescribe a curvature profile, the segment is reconstructed by Frenet integration with geodesic shooting, and the new point is taken at half arc length. The construction works identically in the plane and on the sphere, reproduces geodesics and circles exactly, and a unique curvature prefilter turns its planar linearisation into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin fails for this scheme. Measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion repairs their theory, and we prove that the refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, twice continuously differentiable in arc length. Regularity is thus governed by the normal companion scheme alone, as these authors conjectured.

</details>


### [114] [Implementation Note 2: Approximating a Smooth Three-Dimensional Function on a Coarse Lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00203)
*Dennis Luxen*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A method for approximating smooth 3D functions using low-resolution 3D lookup tables with tetrahedral interpolation, specifically applied to RGB to CMYK color conversion. The approach uses integer arithmetic only (no floating point or division) and requires only 38 KiB for a 16-cell-per-axis table while achieving 0.08% mean error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable efficient and accurate color conversion for low-power devices and real-time applications where computational resources are limited, while avoiding the need for floating-point arithmetic and large memory storage.

Method: Preprocess by sampling a 3D function on a coarse grid (17^3 nodes for n=16). For each input, locate the enclosing grid cube, select one of 6 tetrahedra, and combine corner values using weighted sum. The 8-bit implementation uses integer arithmetic only - no floating point or division, with all intermediate values fitting in 32 bits.

Result: A table with n=16 cells per axis (17^3 nodes, 16-bit values) requires only 38 KiB. The mean error is 0.08% ink per channel. The integer result differs from exact fractional tetrahedral interpolation by at most 1 unit of 16-bit output, and white/black are reproduced exactly.

Conclusion: This approach is suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications with limited computational resources, providing a good balance between memory efficiency, computational simplicity, and accuracy.

Abstract: A smooth 3D function can be efficiently and accurately approximated by a 3D lookup table of significantly lower resolution combined with tetrahedral interpolation. The function is sampled once on a coarse grid in a preprocessing step. For each input, the enclosing grid cube is located, one of the 6 tetrahedra in this cube is selected, and the values at its 4 corners are combined by a weighted sum.
  For RGB to CMYK color conversion, a particularly frequent application of this, a table with $n = 16$ cells per axis ($17^3$ nodes, 16-bit values) requires 38\,KiB. A full 8-bit table requires 64\,MiB. As shown in an experimental evaluation, the mean error of the $n = 16$ table is 0.08\,\% ink per channel. For 8-bit input, the lookup uses integer arithmetic only (Section~\ref{sec:integer}). It requires no floating point and no division, and all intermediate values fit in 32 bits. Floating point is needed only to build the table, once and offline. The integer result differs from tetrahedral interpolation with exact fractions by at most 1 unit of the 16-bit output, and white and black are reproduced exactly. This makes the approach suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications where computational resources are limited.

</details>


### [115] [Plate-Local River Generation: Deterministic, Terrain-Aware, Downhill-Flowing Rivers for Infinite Procedural Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00301)
*Michael K. Davis*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a deterministic algorithm for generating coherent, downhill-flowing river networks in infinite procedural worlds. The approach uses tectonic plate seeds to define terrain fields and bounded plate domains, traces rivers downhill from highlands to coastlines or minima, and guarantees downhill flow through lazy caching and on-demand height interpolation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing procedural terrain generation methods either produce coherent river networks only on fixed domains or sacrifice network coherence/downhill-flow guarantees when extending to infinite worlds. There was a need for a terrain-aware river generation method that supports efficient on-demand evaluation for interactive procedural worlds.

Method: The method uses tectonic plate seeds to define continuous terrain fields and bounded Voronoi-like plate domains. Within each plate, terrain is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland source nodes to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are monotonically adjusted to ensure every segment descends. Rivers are generated and cached lazily per plate. During full-resolution sampling, distance to the cached river network is computed exactly, and river height is interpolated along nearby segments and blended with local terrain on demand.

Result: The algorithm guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. The bounded warp of plate borders (below river border margin) ensures coherence. The approach supports efficient on-demand evaluation for interactive procedural worlds, as demonstrated by the performance analysis.

Conclusion: The design choices make terrain-aware river generation practical for interactive procedural worlds by supporting efficient on-demand evaluation. The method successfully combines infinite world generation with coherent, downhill-flowing river networks.

Abstract: Existing procedural terrain generation methods produce coherent, downhill-flowing river networks only on fixed domains, whereas approaches that extend to infinite worlds typically sacrifice network coherence or downhill-flow guarantees. This work presents a deterministic, terrain-aware, downhill-flowing river algorithm for infinite procedural worlds. Tectonic plate seeds define both continuous terrain fields and corresponding bounded Voronoi-like plate domains, so localized river preprocessing can operate directly on the geometric domain without sampling terrain fields for the purpose of locating plate boundaries. Within each plate, the terrain field is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland source nodes to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are then monotonically adjusted along each path so that every stored segment descends. The resulting river network is generated and cached lazily per plate, so each plate is processed independently of its neighbors. During full-resolution terrain sampling, the distance to the cached river network is computed exactly, and river height is interpolated along nearby segments and blended with the locally evaluated terrain on demand, without caching the blended result itself. Because the warp of the plate borders is bounded below the river border margin, this guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. Together, these design choices make terrain-aware river generation practical for interactive procedural worlds by supporting efficient on-demand evaluation, as demonstrated by the performance analysis presented in this work.

</details>


### [116] [Dirichlet Splatting: Differentiable Rendering for Wave-Based Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00618)
*Xingyu Chen,Wuqiong Zhao,Xinyu Zhang,Tzu-Mao Li*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: The paper addresses a fundamental mismatch between 3D Gaussian splatting (designed for passive optical rendering) and wave-based coherent imaging (terahertz, synthetic-aperture acoustics, millimeter-wave radar). The authors replace Gaussian primitives with physically exact Dirichlet kernels modulated by surfels, paired with a specialized solver (DSFW) that handles the rugged optimization landscape. Results show 10-50x speedup and 0.018 bin RMSE accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wave-based coherent imaging uses Fourier-processing of finite-length signals with Dirichlet kernel point spread functions, but current 3D Gaussian splatting fails because it discards sidelobe energy (10-20% of total) and phase information critical for coherent interference. This creates a physics mismatch between the rendering primitive and the actual measurement process.

Method: Replace learned Gaussian footprint with Dirichlet kernel (finite-window DFT) modulated by surfels carrying area, normal, and material properties. Use Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW) solver combining: (1) variable projection, (2) residual dual certificates, (3) certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels, and (4) periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction for optimization.

Result: The method achieves 0.018 bin RMSE for reflector center recovery, runs 10-50x faster than waveform-level automatic differentiation, matches FFT ground truth to machine precision, and remains differentiable end-to-end. Gaussian splats fail completely on this task.

Conclusion: The Dirichlet kernel primitive with DSFW solver successfully bridges the physics-to-rendering gap for coherent sensing, providing both computational efficiency and physical accuracy. The O(1) closed-form evaluation enables real-time applications while maintaining exact physics fidelity.

Abstract: Wave-based coherent imaging, including terahertz tomography, synthetic-aperture acoustics, and millimeter-wave radar, forms images by Fourier-processing finite-length signals, with an exact point spread function that is not Gaussian but a Dirichlet kernel: complex-valued, oscillatory, and periodic. However, transplanting 3D Gaussian splatting to coherent sensing fails by construction; Gaussian splats discard the sidelobe energy (10-20% of the total) and the phase that governs coherent interference between reflectors. Our key idea is to replace the learned Gaussian footprint with the physically exact Dirichlet kernel of the finite-window DFT, modulated by a surfel that carries area, normal, and material, so that the rendering primitive matches the measurement physics instead of approximating it. We pair this primitive with a specialized solver, Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW), that combines variable projection, residual dual certificates, and certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels, with periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction, navigating the rugged loss landscape that breaks generic first-order optimizers. The Dirichlet kernel admits an O(1) closed-form evaluation, so the forward model matches FFT ground truth to machine precision while remaining differentiable end-to-end. On dense terahertz reconstruction, our method recovers reflector centers to 0.018 bin RMSE, 10-50x faster than waveform-level automatic differentiation, where Gaussian splats fail.

</details>

### [117] [Supporting Perspective Acquisition and Opinion Formation on Societal Issues Through AI-Generated Japanese Rap Battle Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01179)
*Ryota Mibayashi,Toru Urakawa,Dai Takanashi,Tomoya Morohoshi,Kanata Yamagishi,Ryuho Sekikawa,Yasuhiko Nishimura,Yuta Takeuchi,Hideaki Tamori,Takehiro Yamamoto,Hidenari Kiyomitsu,Hiroaki Ohshima*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This study investigates whether AI-generated rap battle-style debates can support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues. Using GPT-5.4-mini, researchers generated 40 rap battle debates and evaluated them through a user study with 6 participants. Results showed that brief (~1.5 min) AI-generated rap battles nearly doubled participants' identified opinions/discussion points and led to stance reconsideration or change in 52.5% of cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility for learning diverse perspectives. The study explores an engaging alternative format (rap battles) that preserves argumentative structure while being more accessible and concise.

Method: Researchers automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio via a web-based interface. A user study was conducted with 6 participants who viewed 40 debates on societal issues from the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships.

Result: Watching approximately 1.5 minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Furthermore, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases.

Conclusion: Even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues, demonstrating potential as an accessible educational tool for critical thinking development.

Abstract: Acquiring diverse perspectives and forming informed opinions on societal issues are essential for critical thinking and informed decision-making. Although observing debates between opposing viewpoints can promote perspective acquisition, conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility. This study investigates whether brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues. Rap battles are debate-style performances in which opposing viewpoints are expressed through rhymed verses, making them engaging while preserving the structure of argumentative dialogue. To conduct this investigation, we automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio through a web-based viewing interface. We evaluated the educational effectiveness of this approach through a user study involving six participants who viewed 40 debates generated from topics on societal issues used in the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships. The results showed that watching approximately 1.5 minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Furthermore, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases. These findings demonstrate that even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues.

</details>

### [118] [Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00002)
*Jung Min Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "reverse IRT" - a novel methodological framework that adapts Item Response Theory to pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by modeling cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from GDSC2, the method demonstrates superior performance over simple averaging under various missingness regimes, achieves the best Brier score in held-out prediction, and shows methodological robustness in cross-platform validation despite weak rank-order correlation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses a key challenge in pharmacogenomics: how to systematically characterize and compare drug response across diverse cancer types when data is incomplete and fragmented. Traditional approaches like simple averaging fail to handle missing data effectively, and there is no unified framework for estimating both cancer-type-level resistance and drug-level activity on a common scale. The authors aim to provide a principled statistical method that can recover latent rankings even under substantial data missingness.

Method: The authors propose "reverse IRT" - an innovative application of Item Response Theory where cancer types serve as latent "subjects" possessing an underlying resistance ability, while drugs function as "items" with varying evasion difficulty. This framework estimates cancer-type-level in-vitro resistance and drug-level broad activity on a shared latent scale. The model was validated across four missingness regimes (MCAR - Missing Completely At Random, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity) and compared against four other methods using metrics including Delta-rho and Brier score. Bootstrap confidence intervals were used to assess stability of cancer type classifications.

Result: The reverse IRT method demonstrates clear advantages: (1) It recovers the full-data latent ranking better than simple averaging with Delta-rho improvements of +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness across MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity regimes; (2) It achieves the best Brier score among five evaluated methods in held-out prediction; (3) Bootstrap analysis shows 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications; (4) Cross-platform PRISM replication shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25).

Conclusion: The contribution is methodological robustness rather than a universal clinical resistance leaderboard. The weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25) in cross-platform validation indicates that the method provides reliable within-platform inference but cannot serve as a general ranking of clinical resistance across different data sources. The authors appropriately frame this as a methodological contribution that handles fragmented evaluation scenarios, not as a definitive clinical tool.

Abstract: We introduce reverse Item Response Theory (IRT) to pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by treating cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC2) database, the model estimates cancer-type-level in-vitro resistance and drug-level broad activity on a shared latent scale. Validation across four missingness regimes demonstrates that reverse IRT better recovers the full-data latent ranking than simple averaging, with advantages of Delta-rho = +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness under MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity. Held-out prediction confirms IRT achieves the best Brier score among five evaluated methods. Bootstrap confidence intervals show 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications. Cross-platform PRISM replication shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25), indicating the contribution is methodological robustness under fragmented evaluation, not a universal clinical resistance leaderboard.

</details>


### [119] [How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00004)
*Vihaan Paka-Hegde*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the geometric relationship between Adam optimizer and natural gradient descent (NGD), finding that Adam's deviation from NGD varies significantly with conditioning: low in well-conditioned settings but reaching ~10^3 misalignment in neural networks. The study suggests Adam's effectiveness comes from balancing approximation errors with momentum smoothing rather than closely tracking NGD paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the geometric relationship between Adam (the standard deep learning optimizer) and natural gradient descent, which has unresolved questions. The authors aim to quantify how Adam's actual trajectory deviates from the theoretically optimal NGD path across different problem geometries.

Method: The study analyzes Adam's full update rule (including momentum) as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation with three simplifications: diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. They use the scale-invariant γ(Δθ) metric to measure geometric deviation across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network.

Result: Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of ~10^3 in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not prevent reaching low final loss. The improved empirical Fisher (iEF) provides more stable paths than standard empirical Fisher (EF), which often oscillates or diverges.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that Adam's practical optimization power likely stems from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path. This explains why Adam works well despite significant geometric deviation from NGD.

Abstract: Adam is the standard optimizer in deep learning, yet its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) contains unresolved questions. We study Adam's full update rule, including momentum, as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant $γ(Δθ)$ metric, we measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network. Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of $\approx 10^3$ in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not degrade final objective minimization; Adam consistently reaches low loss. Furthermore, the improved empirical Fisher (iEF) tracks more stable paths than the standard empirical Fisher (EF), which frequently oscillates or diverges. Our results suggest Adam's practical optimization power may stem from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path.

</details>


### [120] [FourierQK: Filter Shape, Admissibility and the Leakage-Coverage Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00009)
*Athanasios Zeris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates optimal filter shapes for frequency-collapse attention, which replaces the standard Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. Through controlled ablation on character-level language modeling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT), five hypotheses about filter properties are tested.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to follow up on previous work showing that frequency-collapse attention outperforms standard dot-product attention, and to determine which filter shape works best and why. The key question is understanding the specific filter properties that contribute to performance improvements.

Method: Controlled ablation study on character-level language modeling (TinyShakespeare dataset with 6-layer GPT architecture). Five hypotheses are tested: DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage.

Result: Key findings: (1) DC and Nyquist components are harmful (val ~2.0, equivalent to phase randomization); (2) optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~2 bins centered at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m=2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage—narrowband filters are clean, wideband are leaky; (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context).

Conclusion: FourierQK is effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style like BERT) where full-sequence context is available. Autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK (decoder-style like GPT).

Abstract: Frequency-collapse attention [Zeris, 2026e] achieves large gains over standard dot-product attention by replacing the Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. A natural follow-up question is: which filter shape works best, and why? We test five hypotheses about filter properties -- DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage -- using a controlled ablation on character-level language modelling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT). Our main findings are: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~= 2.0, equivalent to phase randomisation), confirming that oscillatory bandpass structure is essential, not just any low-dimensional spectral summary; (2) the optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~= 2 bins centred at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving a clean gain of Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m = 2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians at the same scale and provide partial protection against bilateral FFT leakage; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage -- narrowband filters (gap > +4) are clean, wideband filters (gap < +2) are leaky; and (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context), motivating word-level experiments in the companion MorletQK paper [Zeris, 2026f]. Together, findings (1)-(5) characterise FourierQK as effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style, e.g. BERT), where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time; autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK [Zeris, 2026f] (decoder-style, e.g. GPT). Code available at: https://github.com/AthanasiosZeris/energy-gated-attention

</details>


### [121] [Integrating Fairness and Explainability in a Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00035)
*Bente Hinkenhuis,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multi-objective framework combining RL-MIL, adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for fair student-at-risk prediction. While the RL-MIL baseline performs well, the hypernetwork extensions fail due to mode collapse, demonstrating that preference conditioning alone cannot guarantee controllable fairness-performance trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting student performance requires models that are both accurate and transparent, while demographic information introduces unfair prediction risks. The authors aim to create a controllable fairness mechanism that allows practitioners to adjust the trade-off between predictive performance and fairness (Equalized Odds).

Method: The study combines: (1) Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) to represent students as bags of weakly labeled interactions; (2) An RL agent to select informative instances for classification; (3) Adversarial debiasing for fairness; (4) Preference-conditioned hypernetworks to control the fairness-performance trade-off via a user-defined preference scalar.

Result: The RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance. However, both hypernetwork variants exhibit mode collapse—changing the preference weight produces little systematic movement along the fairness-performance frontier. The failure is attributed to objective dominance, weak gradient propagation through the conditioning mechanism, and interactions between dynamically generated parameters.

Conclusion: Fairness objectives can be incorporated into interpretable RL-MIL pipelines, but preference conditioning alone does not guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior. Robust fair RL-MIL requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis.

Abstract: Predicting student performance from educational interaction data requires models that are both accurate and sufficiently transparent to support meaningful intervention, while demographic information introduces an additional risk of unfair predictions. This study investigates a multi-objective framework that combines reinforcement learning-based multiple instance learning (RL-MIL), adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for student-at-risk prediction. MIL represents each student as a bag of weakly labeled interactions, while an RL agent selects informative instances for downstream classification. Two hypernetwork variants are evaluated to determine whether a user-defined preference scalar can continuously control the trade-off between predictive performance and Equalized Odds. The underlying RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance, but both hypernetwork extensions exhibit mode collapse: changing the preference weight produces little systematic movement along the intended fairness-performance frontier. The failure is associated with objective dominance, weak gradient propagation through the conditioning mechanism, and interactions between dynamically generated parameters. The results show that fairness objectives can be incorporated into an interpretable RL-MIL pipeline, but preference conditioning alone does not guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior. Robust fair RL-MIL therefore requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis.

</details>


### [122] [Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00049)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates using short polynomial programs (degree-3 or degree-4 in BF16) to accelerate special-function-unit (SFU) operations (sigmoid, tanh, SiLU) in LLMs, achieving 1.19-2.19x speedups in isolated tests and 0.3-8.0% improvements in integrated training tasks, with minimal impact on training loss across four tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU hardware generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, causing kernel bottlenecks to shift. FlashAttention-4 revealed such imbalance in attention mechanisms on NVIDIA Blackwell. The authors investigate whether polynomial approximations can accelerate other SFU operations in LLMs beyond attention.

Method: The authors: (1) Compared native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply-add (FMA) polynomial programs in isolated IEEE FP16 sweeps across L2 and HBM-resident working sets; (2) Replaced native sigmoid, tanh, and SiLU with degree-3 or degree-4 BF16 programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert SwiGLU; (3) Combined analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels; (4) Evaluated model behavior through same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and paired pre-training comparisons.

Result: Isolated path improvements: 1.19-2.19x in L2, 1.00-1.70x in HBM. Integrated task improvements: dense-SiLU improved training-step throughput by 2.7%, tanh-softcapped attention by 2.9%, routed-expert SwiGLU by 8.0%, sigmoid attention improved attention forward by 7.4% and full GPU step by 0.3%. Training loss differences (polynomial minus native) at ~100B tokens ranged from -0.107 to +0.079 across four tasks.

Conclusion: Short polynomial programs can effectively accelerate SFU operations in LLMs with acceptable accuracy trade-offs. The approach provides meaningful speedups across different model components (dense layers, attention, MoE experts) while maintaining training quality, though the actual loss impact varies by operation and task.

Abstract: Graphics processing unit (GPU) generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, so kernel bottlenecks move as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance inside attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. We test whether short polynomial programs can accelerate other special-function-unit (SFU) operations in large language models (LLMs). We first compare native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply--add (FMA) programs in an isolated IEEE binary16 (FP16) sweep spanning L2-resident and high-bandwidth-memory (HBM)-resident working sets. We then replace native sigmoid, tanh, and sigmoid linear unit (SiLU) with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 (BF16) programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU). The programs combine analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels. The isolated paths improve by 1.19--2.19x in L2 and 1.00--1.70x in HBM. The dense-SiLU, tanh-softcapped-attention, and routed-expert substitutions improve complete training-step throughput by 2.7\%, 2.9\%, and 8.0\%, respectively. The sigmoid-attention substitution improves complete-attention forward by 7.4\% and the complete GPU step by 0.3\%. Same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and one paired pre-training comparison per task extend the evaluation to model behavior. At common horizons near 100 billion tokens, the final smoothed training-loss differences (polynomial minus native) range from $-0.107$ to $+0.079$ across the four tasks.

</details>


### [123] [SW-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Stieltjes-Wigert q-Orthogonal Polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00050)
*Amirhosein Azarpour,Seyyed Moein Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SW-KAN introduces Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials on semi-infinite domain (0, ∞) to address domain mismatch in polynomial-based KANs, using exponential-of-tanh mapping and stable three-term recurrence for efficient evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the fundamental challenge of domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and bounded/semi-infinite support of orthogonal polynomial bases in polynomial-based KAN variants, while maintaining parameter efficiency and interpretability.

Method: Employ Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials with semi-infinite domain support; introduce smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping for stable domain bridging; use numerically stable three-term recurrence for O(N) polynomial evaluation without special-function calls; leverage log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter for inductive bias.

Result: SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across image classification and continuous function approximation tasks, outperforming polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks with robust performance under resource-constrained conditions (reduced feature dimensionality, limited training data).

Conclusion: SW-KAN offers a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings, with strong representational capacity for complex multivariate functions using remarkably few parameters.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) represent a paradigmatic shift in deep learning by replacing fixed node activations with learnable univariate functions on edges, offering enhanced interpretability and parameter efficiency. While recent polynomial-based KAN variants have addressed the computational overhead of original B-spline implementations, they introduce a fundamental yet underexplored challenge: the domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and the bounded or semi-infinite support of orthogonal polynomial bases. To address this limitation, we propose the Stieltjes-Wigert Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (SW-KAN), a novel architecture that employs Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on the semi-infinite domain (0, infinity). We introduce a smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping that stably bridges the domain gap while preserving well-conditioned gradients, and leverage a numerically stable three-term recurrence that evaluates polynomial expansions in O(N) operations without special-function calls. Through comprehensive experiments spanning image classification and continuous function approximation, we demonstrate that SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across diverse tasks. The log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter of Stieltjes-Wigert polynomials provide a distinct inductive bias that enables robust performance under resource-constrained conditions, including reduced feature dimensionality and limited training data. The proposed architecture not only outperforms established polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks but also exhibits strong representational capacity for approximating complex multivariate functions with remarkably few parameters, making it a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings.

</details>


### [124] [Uncertainty-Aware RL-Controlled Adaptive 3D Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00188)
*Alpay Ozkan,Tunc Ozan Aydin,Marc Pollefeys,Jelena Trisovic,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive voxel-based 3D reconstruction framework that uses semantic entropy, geometric curvature, and texture richness as cues for principled resolution allocation, controlled by a reinforcement learning agent under a user-specified memory budget. The method outperforms MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines in geometric accuracy, semantic consistency, and memory-accuracy trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-resolution volumetric grids in 3D reconstruction are inefficient—they waste memory in uniform regions and lose detail in complex ones. Existing adaptive methods like MAP-ADAPT rely on heuristics (geometry + semantic class lists) that require expert tuning, lack generalization to unseen objects, and provide no explicit mechanism for memory control.

Method: The paper introduces: (1) A semantic entropy-based refinement criterion that captures label uncertainty, combined with geometric curvature and texture richness as scene complexity cues—this enables principled resolution allocation without semantic taxonomies. (2) A reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter. The result is a multi-resolution TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Function).

Result: The proposed multi-resolution TSDF achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing adaptive voxel methods by using principled complexity cues (semantic entropy, curvature, texture) and an RL-based memory budget controller. It provides explicit, user-controlled accuracy-memory trade-off through a single intuitive parameter, eliminating the need for expert-tuned heuristics.

Abstract: Voxel-based volumetric mapping is fundamental to 3D reconstruction, yet fixed-resolution grids remain inherently inefficient - wasting memory in uniform regions and losing detail in complex ones. Existing adaptive methods, such as MAP-ADAPT, partially address this by varying resolution based on geometry and user-defined semantic class lists, but these heuristics require expert tuning, lack generalization to unseen objects, and provide no explicit mechanism to control memory usage. We propose an adaptive framework that refines voxels based on semantic entropy, which captures label uncertainty, together with geometric curvature and texture richness as scene complexity cues, yielding principled resolution allocation without reliance on semantic taxonomies. To make the accuracy-memory trade-off explicit and user-controlled, we further introduce a reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter. The resulting multi-resolution TSDF achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/UnRL.

</details>


### [125] [Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00053)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents "format-aware fusion" to optimize 4-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Core acceleration by co-designing quantization producers with scale domains and consumer layouts. The approach achieves 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3% MFU) in Llama-3 8B pretraining, with FP4 training loss ending 2.11% above bfloat16, while downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FP4 Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication, but the overhead from scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the performance gains. This overhead is a significant bottleneck that limits the practical benefits of FP4 acceleration.

Method: The authors propose format-aware fusion, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native MXFP, global NVFP, and CTA-local NVFP formats. They evaluate Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy. Key techniques include row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning.

Result: Matched same-accelerator probes show: bfloat16 achieves 18.8K tokens/s/GPU, Transformer Engine NVFP reaches 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, and the fastest custom route reaches 37.9K tokens/s/GPU. MXFP with the proposed techniques achieves 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Notably, downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings.

Conclusion: FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand format, and execution path. The performance and accuracy trade-offs are complex, and downstream task performance (rankings) does not always correlate with training-loss metrics. Format-aware fusion with appropriate techniques can achieve near-bfloat16 performance while significantly improving throughput.

Abstract: Four-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication, but scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the gain. We present \emph{format-aware fusion}, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native \mxfp{}, global \nvfp{}, and cooperative-thread-array-local \nvfp{}. We evaluate Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy. In matched same-accelerator probes, bfloat16 and Transformer Engine \nvfp{} reach 18.8K and 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, while our fastest custom route reaches 37.9K. \mxfp{} with row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3\% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11\% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87\% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, showing that FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path.

</details>


### [126] ["very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00083)
*Jinhao Duan,Zicheng Liu,Zijie Liu,Kaidi Xu,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the gap between human and LLM verbal uncertainty quantification, proposing that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty markers (e.g., "possible," "likely") with numerical levels that differ substantially from human semantics. The authors introduce METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns optimal uncertainty profiles directly from LLM outputs to enable marker-level comparison between human and LLM confidence semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the cognitive perspective that accurate verbal uncertainty reflects metacognitive monitoring (knowing what you don't know). While most LLM uncertainty quantification relies on likelihood- or consistency-based signals, humans naturally express uncertainty through verbal markers. This divergence raises questions about whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty and how LLMs differ from humans in expressing uncertainty verbally.

Method: The authors curate a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature, then benchmark LLMs against this human baseline. They introduce METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs. Instead of estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling, METHODNAME fits a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, discovering how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey.

Result: The key finding is that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. METHODNAME enables direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that there is a significant mismatch between human and LLM semantics for verbal uncertainty markers. METHODNAME provides a way to disentangle this mismatch and reveal systematic disparities, enabling better understanding of LLM confidence expression and potentially improving human-AI communication about uncertainty.

Abstract: Humans express uncertainty verbally via markers (e.g., "possible," "likely"), yet most LLM uncertainty quantification (UQ) relies on costing likelihood- or consistency-based signals. From a cognitive perspective, accurate verbal uncertainty reflects metacognitive monitoring, representing knowledge boundaries ("knowing that you don't know") to support regulation and information seeking. In this paper, we investigate how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification and whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty. We curate a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature and benchmark LLMs against it. We observe that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. We then introduce METHODNAME, a novel optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs. By fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, METHODNAME discovers how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey, rather than estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling. METHODNAME enables a direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, disentangling mismatch and revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

</details>


### [127] [Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00094)
*Pranav Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether belief-based agent memory must calibrate its information sources before improving decisions. The key finding is that learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration (Θ(l^-2) vs Θ(l^-4)), suggesting memory can make reliable decisions without fully recovering source reliability. The work includes empirical validation in MiniGrid environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, but evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. The fundamental question is whether memory must calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions. This addresses a critical gap in understanding the relationship between source reliability estimation and decision-making performance in learning agents.

Method: The paper uses theoretical analysis on a four-model hidden Markov family, separating the problems of learning, calibration, and revision certification. It derives sample complexity bounds for each task and characterizes the sharp identified interval for policy improvement under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel. The robustness extension handles bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying. Empirical validation uses 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes in three MiniGrid memory environments.

Result: Key theoretical results: (1) Learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Θ(l^-2) records, (2) Certifying improvement over an informative incumbent takes O(l^-2) fresh records, (3) Fixed-precision source estimation requires Θ(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. Thus learning/certifying decisions requires quadratically fewer records than source calibration. Empirical results: The new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, versus none for the earlier certificate in MiniGrid.

Conclusion: Memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability in certain settings. This provides a statistical account of when this is possible, though it is not presented as a universally superior memory algorithm. The approach shows that in some cases, one can bypass the traditionally required source calibration step while still achieving reliable decision-making.

Abstract: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, yet its evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. Must a memory calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions? We separate learning, calibration, and revision certification. On one four-model hidden Markov family, learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Theta(l^-2) records and certifying its improvement over an informative incumbent takes O(l^-2) fresh records from the same observation law, while fixed-precision source estimation requires Theta(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. Thus learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A broader model class retains the decision rate and source lower bound. Under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel, we characterize the sharp identified interval for policy improvement and derive a finite-sample certificate using observable witness regions, without pure-class anchors. A robustness extension tolerates bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying; split-trained witnesses apply to arbitrary history spaces with explicit power conditions. We integrate policy-bound receipts with Nous Dimensions and test 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes in three external MiniGrid memory environments with an introduced noisy-report interface. The new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, versus none for the earlier certificate in MiniGrid. Strong established inference baselines remain competitive or better. The result is a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability, not a universally superior memory algorithm.

</details>


### [128] [One Mastery Threshold Does Not Fit All Knowledge Tracing Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00095)
*Xianghui Meng,Yujing Zhang,Jionghao Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study examines how mastery thresholds in tutoring systems interact with different knowledge tracing (KT) models. The authors test 6 KT models across 4 datasets using 12 thresholds (0.50-0.99), finding that the same threshold produces very different outcomes depending on the underlying model. BKT is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become increasingly selective. The same numerical threshold does not represent equivalent mastery across different KT approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tutoring systems use mastery thresholds to decide when students can advance, but the same numerical threshold can lead to very different decisions when the underlying knowledge tracing model changes. This creates a critical gap in how mastery-based decisions are evaluated and implemented.

Method: The authors examined six KT models across four public educational datasets, evaluating 12 thresholds from 0.50 to 0.99 using four metrics: post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. They also identified balanced thresholds across 30 predefined instructional settings.

Result: BKT is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become much more selective as thresholds increase. The best-balanced threshold varied substantially across models and settings. In half the tested settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in selected thresholds. Stricter thresholds did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement—stronger-prior students advanced up to 3.26 times as often as weaker-prior students.

Conclusion: Mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when the KT model or instructional priorities change and evaluated by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and access. The same numerical cutoff does not represent equivalent mastery across different KT models.

Abstract: Tutoring systems use mastery thresholds to decide when students can stop practicing and advance, but the same numerical threshold can lead to very different decisions when the underlying knowledge tracing (KT) model changes. We examine six KT models across four public educational datasets and evaluate 12 thresholds from 0.50 to 0.99 using post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. We also identify thresholds that balance performance, extra practice, and advancement under 30 predefined instructional settings. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become much more selective as thresholds increase. This partly reflects different model outputs: BKT estimates latent mastery probability, whereas neural models estimate the probability of a correct next response, so the same cutoff does not represent the same level of mastery. The best-balanced threshold varied substantially across models and settings. In half of the tested settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in their selected thresholds, although this gap became smaller when greater priority was placed on reducing extra practice and allowing more students to advance. Stricter thresholds also did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement, with stronger-prior students advancing up to 3.26 times as often as weaker-prior students. These results show that mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when the KT model or instructional priorities change and evaluated by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and access.

</details>


### [129] [Uncertainty-Aware Learning from Multi-Expert Interval Targets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00102)
*Samira Alkaee Taleghan,Younghyun Koo,Andrew P. Barrett,Farnoush Banaei-Kashani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of modeling expert labels that contain both within-label imprecision (intervals) and between-expert variation. The proposed method preserves individual expert intervals, separates these two uncertainty sources, and validates predictive uncertainty components against observed expert disagreement. It achieves 31% MAE reduction on sea-ice concentration data compared to hard labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning applications often rely on expert labels, but qualified experts may provide different interpretations of the same observation. Existing methods treat label uncertainty sources separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to consensus, interval-target methods yield single predictions, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate against observed expert disagreement. This creates a gap in handling both within-label imprecision and between-expert variation simultaneously.

Method: The approach has three main components: (1) Harmonize heterogeneous label vocabularies into a common probabilistic label space to separate encoding differences from expert judgment; (2) Retain individual label intervals and model them with a mixture of Beta distributions trained using a proper Cramér-distance objective; (3) Decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, then introduce "decomposition matching" to align predictive components to their intended label-side sources.

Result: On sea-ice concentration tasks, the model reduces MAE by 31% over hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully preserves individual expert intervals, separates within-label imprecision from between-expert variation, and validates corresponding predictive uncertainty components. The decomposition matching technique ensures predictive uncertainty components correspond to their intended label-side sources. This represents a novel approach to handling multi-source label uncertainty in expert-annotated ML applications.

Abstract: Many machine learning (ML) applications rely on expert labels, and qualified experts may provide different but plausible interpretations of the same observation. Such variation across expert labels may reflect genuine disagreement or ambiguity rather than annotation error. When individual experts additionally report intervals rather than exact values, the supervision contains two distinct sources of label uncertainty: within-label imprecision and between-expert variation. Existing methods treat these forms separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to a consensus, interval-target methods often yield a single prediction, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate their uncertainty estimates against observed expert disagreement. To address this problem, we propose an approach that preserves individual expert intervals, separates within-label imprecision from between-expert variation, and validates the corresponding predictive uncertainty components. First, heterogeneous label vocabularies are harmonized into a common probabilistic label space, separating encoding differences from expert judgement. Second, individual label intervals are retained and modeled with a mixture of Beta distributions trained using a proper Cramér-distance objective, preserving distinct expert-reported labels. Third, we decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, and evaluate whether these components correspond to within-label uncertainty, between-label uncertainty, and model error, respectively. Because this correspondence is not guaranteed, we introduce decomposition matching, which aligns the predictive components to their intended label-side sources. On sea-ice concentration the model reduces MAE by 31\% over hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

</details>


### [130] [The Hidden Costs of 99% Accuracy: A Trustworthiness Audit of the Telco Customer Churn Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00118)
*Soumyadeep Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (n=7,043) for trustworthiness failures, identifying four key issues: (1) pre-split SMOTE inflates F1 by 13.1pp via test set leakage, (2) TotalCharges is nearly determined by tenure × MonthlyCharges (R2=0.999) corrupting SHAP interpretations, (3) isotonic regression outperforms temperature scaling for calibration, and (4) cost-optimal thresholds are 5-10× lower than F1-optimal, saving ~$77K per 1,000 customers. A four-component reporting checklist is proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature reports >95% test accuracy on this benchmark, but the authors note that accuracy/F1-centered reporting ignores critical trustworthiness issues. The motivation is to audit the benchmark for common pitfalls that inflate performance metrics and lead to misleading interpretations.

Method: The authors conducted four audits: (1) SMOTE effect measurement across 10 classifiers and 15 seeds, (2) redundancy analysis of TotalCharges using R2 and SHAP attribution, (3) calibration audit using isotonic regression vs temperature scaling across 15 seeds, and (4) cost-sensitive threshold analysis using a $50 retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy. Replication was performed on Iranian Telecom Churn and Bank Customer Churn datasets.

Result: Key findings: (1) ~36% of synthetic SMOTE points are nearest-neighbor interpolations of test instances, inflating F1 by 13.1pp; (2) TotalCharges is determinable from tenure × MonthlyCharges (R2=0.999) but ranks 9th in SHAP attribution; (3) isotonic regression is best for calibration; temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles with bimodal probability distributions; (4) cost-optimal threshold is 5-10× lower than F1-optimal, saving ~$77K per 1,000 customers. F1 generalizes across domains; F2 generalizes only within telecom.

Conclusion: The authors propose a four-component reporting checklist: pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds. They release a reproducible implementation. The benchmark's reported high accuracies are inflated due to data leakage (SMOTE), redundant features, calibration issues, and failure to consider business costs.

Abstract: Customer churn prediction on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (n = 7,043) routinely reports test accuracies above 95%, with the most cited published study reporting 99.01%. We audit this benchmark for four trustworthiness failures invisible to the accuracy- and F1-centred reporting that dominates the literature. First, pre-split SMOTE inflates churn-class F1 by 13.1 percentage points across ten classifiers and fifteen seeds (Wilcoxon p < 10^-4 per classifier); the same leaky pipeline ordering paired with class weighting yields no inflation, isolating the effect to SMOTE's geometric construction. We measure the mechanism directly: approximately 36% of synthetic training points are nearest-neighbour interpolations of test-set instances. Second, the TotalCharges field is approximately determined by tenure multiplied by MonthlyCharges (R2 = 0.999); removing it changes accuracy by less than 0.2 percentage points, yet TreeSHAP ranks it ninth in mean absolute attribution - a pattern that materially corrupts SHAP-based interpretation. We propose an R2 > 0.95 pre-modelling diagnostic. Third, in a 15-seed calibration audit, isotonic regression is the strongest default; temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles whose predicted-probability distribution is bimodal. Fourth, the cost-optimal decision threshold (under a 50 USD retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy) is approximately 5-10 times lower than the F1-optimal threshold, saving approximately 77,000 USD per 1,000 customers. We replicate F1 and F2 on Iranian Telecom Churn (within domain) and Bank Customer Churn (across domain): F1 generalises; F2 generalises only within telecom. We synthesise these findings into a four-component reporting checklist - pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds - and release a reproducible implementation.

</details>


### [131] [Generalized Biomedicine Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00120)
*Luyao Tang,Yingkai Yang,Hanqi Chen,Jiewei Zheng,Chaoqi Chen,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses open-world challenges in medical imaging by introducing Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) and a unified benchmark for long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. The proposed SCAN method follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression to handle subtle medical anomalies by suppressing expected patterns and highlighting unexpected deviations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world medical images face open-world shifts including long-tailed rare diseases, subtle lesions, and hierarchical taxonomies. Existing open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, failing to address these biomedical challenges. The key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty.

Method: SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN) follows a three-stage cognition-inspired perceptual progression: (1) Predictive suppression to filter expected norms, (2) Surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and (3) Complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations.

Result: SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and can be integrated with existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging.

Conclusion: The proposed approach provides a unified framework for biomedical discovery that addresses long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware challenges. SCAN effectively balances known class preservation with novel discovery, offering a practical solution for clinical decision support in open-world medical imaging scenarios.

Abstract: In real-world clinical practice, medical images face open-world shifts: (i) long-tailed rare diseases, (ii) subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (iii) hierarchical taxonomies. Yet most open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, leaving these biomedical demands unresolved. We introduce Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) and a unified benchmark spanning long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. Our key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty. Inspired by expert diagnosis, we propose SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN), which follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression: it applies predictive suppression to filter expected norms, triggers surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and performs complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations. Extensive experiments show that SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and it plugs into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging. Code is available at https://github.com/lytang63/generalized-biomedicine-discovery.

</details>


### [132] [Classification Based on Association Rules Algorithm for Breast Cancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00174)
*Ali Alsalama,Ahmed Kubba,Ghaith Jamjoum,Zaher Al Aghbari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification using a weighted classification approach. The method employs three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction to identify frequent itemsets, create and prune association rules, and classify test data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast cancer is a significant contributor to female mortality worldwide with one of the highest occurrence rates among cancer types. There is a critical need for early breast cancer detection methods, and association rule-based classification offers the benefit of producing results that are readily understandable for medical professionals.

Method: The proposed approach implements three core algorithms: (1) Rule Generation - identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules; (2) Rule Pruning - eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data; (3) Rule Prediction - applies the pruned rules to classify test data.

Result: The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to demonstrate the feasibility and performance of the approach.

Conclusion: The approach proves feasible for breast cancer classification using association rule mining with a weighted classification approach.

Abstract: Breast cancer is a significant contributor to female mortality across the world, displaying one of the highest oc currence rates among the various cancer types. In response to the need for early breast cancer detection, researchers have increasingly turned to association rule-based classification as a favored method. Association Rule mining is a data mining approach which offers the benefit of yielding results that are readily understandable for medical professionals. This paper introduces a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification based on a weighted classification approach. This implementation employs three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction. Rule Generation identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules. Rule Pruning eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data. Rule Prediction applies the pruned rules to classify test data. The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to show the feasibility and performance of the approach.

</details>


### [133] [Four Ways to Grow a Classifier and Why One of Them Cannot Learn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00180)
*Cagri Temel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes four growth decisions in constructive classifiers (tree-structured and constructive models). It identifies that the natural way to deepen soft decision trees (adding gates at leaves) buys nothing because new gate gradients are identically zero. The fix is a small random perturbation. Of the other three decisions: fitting new hidden units to residuals buys smaller networks; splitting leaf with largest expected error buys sparsity; requiring statistical significance before split buys nothing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to understand what each growth decision actually provides in constructive classifiers, as these models add structure during training (levels to trees, units to hidden layers, splits at leaves). There was a need for an exact diagnosis of which growth methods are effective and which are not.

Method: The authors used a fixed protocol across tree-structured and constructive models, conducting three seeds of five-fold cross-validation on Iris, Wine, and Digits datasets. They proved mathematically that the natural way to deepen soft decision trees leaves gradients zero, and tested a fix involving random perturbation of children.

Result: The natural deepening method loses 19.6 accuracy points on Iris, 19.1 on Wine, and 55.6 on Digits.
