Fitting new hidden units to residuals yields smaller networks but not more accuracy (costs accuracy on Digits). Splitting leaf with largest expected error achieves 0.885 accuracy with only 3.7 splits vs 63 for complete depth-six tree, but loses 4.3 points on harder problems. Requiring statistical significance before split makes the tree larger and less accurate. A small random perturbation fix restores learning ability.

Conclusion: Three of four growth decisions buy something: fitting new hidden units to residuals buys smaller networks; splitting leaf with largest expected error buys sparsity; requiring statistical significance buys nothing. The fix for zero gradients is a small random perturbation, with the practical rule being to assert gradient is nonzero after adding parameters.

Abstract: Constructive classifiers add structure while they train: a level to a tree, a unit to a hidden layer, a split at a leaf. This paper asks what each of four such growth decisions actually buys, measured under one fixed protocol in tree-structured and constructive models, and gives an exact diagnosis and a fix for the one that buys nothing.
  The diagnosis concerns the most natural way to deepen a soft decision tree: turn every leaf into a gate whose two children inherit the parent's class distribution, so that the function is unchanged. I prove that this leaves the gradient of every new gate identically zero and, with the gate at 1/2, gives the two children identical gradients, so the added level can never learn. Unlike the symmetry that Net2Net breaks with noise or the saddle point that splitting steepest descent escapes with second-order information, first-order information here is not weak but absent. Over three seeds of five-fold cross-validation the construction loses 19.6 accuracy points on Iris, 19.1 on Wine and 55.6 on Digits against the same depth trained from scratch. The fix is a small random perturbation of the children, whose size barely matters. The practical rule is one line in a test: after adding parameters, assert that their gradient is nonzero.
  The other three decisions each buy one thing. Fitting a new hidden unit to the residual error before installing it buys a smaller network on every dataset, though not a more accurate one, and on Digits it costs accuracy significantly. Splitting the leaf with the largest expected error buys sparsity, reaching 0.885 with 3.7 splits where a complete depth-six tree uses 63, but loses 4.3 points on a harder problem. Requiring statistical significance before a node receives a more expressive split buys nothing: the tree gets larger and less accurate.
  Every number in the paper is inserted from the measurement script.

</details>


### [134] [Energy Time-Series Imputation with Differentially Private Diffusion Models via Clipping-Aware Objective Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00209)
*Huizhen Huang,Yu Li,Tao Huang,Chen Hou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes clipping-aware objective conditioning for privacy-preserving energy time-series imputation using diffusion models trained with DP-SGD. The method addresses gradient clipping issues at late diffusion timesteps (low SNR) by using v-prediction and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In energy time-series systems, missing measurements need reliable recovery while preserving sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with DP-SGD offer privacy-preserving imputation, but late timesteps in cosine diffusion schedules correspond to low SNR conditions where standard ε-prediction induces large pre-clipping gradients that get clipped, reducing optimization signal.

Method: The proposed method includes three key components: (1) v-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, (2) static loss weighting as uniform-scaling control, and (3) diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. The approach formulates the clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD.

Result: Evaluated on five real-world energy time-series datasets across various missingness scenarios (random point, contiguous block, persistent outages) and multiple severities. The method consistently improves imputation utility over ε-prediction baseline under matched DP-SGD settings. Gradient diagnostics show lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps.

Conclusion: Clipping-aware objective conditioning effectively addresses the gradient clipping problem in privacy-preserving energy time-series imputation. The integration of v-prediction with schedule-aware dynamic weighting provides a principled approach to improve utility while maintaining differential privacy guarantees.

Abstract: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems, where fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation. Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard $\varepsilon$-prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal. The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this objective--clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts $v$-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the $\varepsilon$-prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps, supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for energy time-series imputation.

</details>


### [135] [Useful to Whom? Sample Value Is Defined Only Relative to the Learner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00221)
*Yangze Liu,Xiao-Long Yin,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether the optimal coreset selection strategy depends on the target learner model. Through controlled experiments on ImageNet, the authors demonstrate that the crossover boundary between different selection criteria (easy-first vs geometric coverage) changes with the learner's architecture, width, and input processing. They find that a universal scaling law does not exist, and selection strategies must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question driving this research is "what kind of data does a model need in order to learn?" The authors investigate whether the boundary separating different optimal coreset selection criteria (easy-first vs geometric coverage) is fixed by the data or changes with the target learner. This matters because coreset selection aims to keep the most useful samples under a budget constraint, and understanding learner dependence is crucial for practical deployment.

Method: The authors conducted controlled experiments by freezing selected subsets and manipulating only the training learner. They tested on ImageNet-100 (low-resolution) and ImageNet-1k (native-224px), varied ResNet-18 width, compared CNN (ResNet) vs ViT architectures, and manipulated input grids through stride controls and removing last downsampling stride.

Result: Key findings: (1) On ImageNet-100, doubling ResNet-18's width moves the crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class; (2) There is an interaction between input grid and capacity—enlarging the grid shifts the boundary left, and this shift weakens as width increases; (3) Stride controls reproduce and reverse the grid effect without changing the input grid; (4) Under native-224px ImageNet-1k, width effects are smaller and depend on the probe (LFrac remains nearly flat, EL2N shifts modestly right); (5) Swapping CNN for ViT makes coverage win throughout the measured range, even when easy subsets come from the convolutional proxy.

Conclusion: The boundary between optimal coreset selection strategies is learner-dependent, not fixed by the data. Network structure (width, architecture type, input processing) can move this boundary. A universal scaling law does not exist. The practical implication is that a selection strategy's preferred budget regime must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.

Abstract: What kind of data does a model need in order to learn? Coreset selection makes this question concrete: under a budget, keep the samples most useful for training. Easy-first and geometric coverage criteria can win in different budget regimes, separated by a crossover boundary. We ask whether this boundary is fixed by the data or changes with the target learner. Controlled experiments freeze the selected subsets and manipulate only the training learner. On low-resolution ImageNet-100, doubling ResNet-18's width moves the crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class: the learner changes the relative value of the same samples. A wider sweep reveals an interaction between input grid and capacity. Enlarging the grid while retaining the same image information shifts the boundary left, and this shift weakens as width increases. Stride controls reproduce and reverse the grid effect without changing the input grid; removing only the last downsampling stride is sufficient to recover the leftward shift. Under the native-224px ImageNet-1k protocol, width effects are smaller and depend on the probe: LFrac remains nearly flat, while EL2N shifts modestly right. Swapping the convolutional learning system for a ViT makes coverage win throughout the measured range, even when the easy subsets come from the convolutional proxy. These results establish learner dependence through frozen-subset interventions and identify network structure that can move the boundary. They do not yield a universal scaling law. Their practical implication is direct: a selection strategy's preferred budget regime must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.

</details>


### [136] [Constant-Memory Recall: Learned Associations in a Fixed Matrix State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00232)
*Samuel Larson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases for memorizing 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model achieves 99.95% mean accuracy with 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, maintaining near-perfect recall even with extended context up to 1,798 tokens. However, parameter-matched baselines (vector and Transformer) fail to learn this task, preventing a fair memory-efficiency comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study addresses the limitation of fixed-size recurrent memory during inference, examining whether successful recall depends on task complexity and training. The authors aim to understand the memory capacity and recall mechanisms in recurrent models, particularly comparing against Transformer baselines.

Method: A small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases was trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model uses 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state. Experiments tested recall accuracy, the effect of extended pre-query context (filler tokens up to 1,798 tokens), and memory block ablation. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines were also trained for comparison.

Result: The DeltaNet variant achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when choosing among sequence values. Recall remains near perfect with extended context without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block completely removes recall ability. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget. Both vector and Transformer baselines fail to learn the task, remaining near chance even with additional training searches.

Conclusion: The DeltaNet variant demonstrates strong memory recall capabilities for key-value pairings with fixed recurrent state. However, the failure of baseline models (vector and Transformer) to learn the task prevents a meaningful memory-efficiency comparison. The capacity limit remains unresolved, and the first memory block appears critical for recall. Further work is needed to establish fair baselines and understand the underlying mechanisms.

Abstract: Fixed-size recurrent memory limits storage growth during inference, but successful recall depends on the task and training. We study a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases, trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. With 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, it achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when choosing among the sequence's values. Recall remains near perfect when filler extends the pre-query context to 1,798 tokens without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block removes this recall. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget and does not locate a capacity limit. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines remain near chance, including the Transformer after additional training searches. This unresolved baseline failure prevents a memory-efficiency comparison.

</details>


### [137] [Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00890)
*Sushant Mehta,Logan Ritchie,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning on expert-built agentic coding tasks can help coding agents overcome "last mile" failures (missing requirements, inadequate testing, breaking existing behavior, unchecked assumptions). The authors post-train Kimi K2.7 Code (a 1T-parameter MoE model) using GSPO on 1,700 tasks with hidden fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and expert-written verifiers. One epoch of training on a rank-32 LoRA adapter improves pass@1 on all six external benchmarks across three agent harnesses, with statistically significant improvements (p < 0.001) including on benchmarks released after training data collection (p = 0.004).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents often fail in the final stages of tasks: they miss requirements, test only trivial cases, break existing functionality, or validate against incorrect assumptions. This "last mile" gap needs to be addressed to make agents practical for real-world development. The authors ask whether RL on expert-built tasks can close this gap and whether learned behaviors transfer beyond the training distribution.

Method: Post-training Kimi K2.7 Code (1T-parameter, 32B active MoE model) using GSPO (Gradient-Subspace Policy Optimization) with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on 1,700 expert-built coding tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, plus 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. Reward is fraction of target checks passed, dropping to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails.

Result: One epoch of training improved pass@1 on all six external benchmarks: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1→64.8), DeepSWE (31.0→43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4→82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4→12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0→7.6), SWE-Marathon (5.0→25.0). Improvements are significant (p < 0.001 overall, p = 0.004 on post-training benchmarks). Median trajectory lengths reduced by 24-35% on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3. The trained model avoids all four failure modes on newly solved tasks.

Conclusion: RL on expert-built agentic coding tasks effectively closes the "last mile" gap for coding agents, with learned behaviors transferring to held-out benchmarks. The approach demonstrates statistically significant improvements across diverse benchmarks and harnesses, with the model learning to avoid common failure modes. This suggests RL is a viable path for improving agent reliability in real-world software development scenarios.

Abstract: Coding agents often fail in the last mile: they build most of a feature but drop a requirement, test only the cases their implementation already handles, break behavior that was supposed to stay intact, or validate against an unchecked assumption. We ask whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks closes this gap, and whether what the agent learns transfers beyond the training distribution. We post-train Kimi K2.7 Code, a 1T-parameter (32B active) open-weight mixture-of-experts model, with RL alone on 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and by pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The reward is the fraction of target checks passed and drops to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails. One epoch of GSPO on a rank-32 LoRA adapter improves pass@1 on each of the six external benchmarks we evaluated, across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1 to 64.8), DeepSWE (31.0 to 43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4 to 82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4 to 12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0 to 7.6), and SWE-Marathon (5.0 to 25.0). Pooled over the five independent task sets (Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3), the improvement is significant (p < 0.001), and it remains significant on the three sets released after the training data was collected (p = 0.004); the model also improves under both harnesses never used in training. Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 are 24-35% shorter in agent steps. The base model's failed DeepSWE runs are mostly near-misses, and on the tasks the trained model newly solves, paired trajectories show it avoiding each of the four failure modes above.

</details>


### [138] [How Many Categories Are Enough? Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00236)
*Gia Huy Thai,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in few-shot anomaly detection: the practical feasibility of certifying alarm thresholds with controlled false-alarm rates (FAR) for unseen categories. The authors demonstrate that target-only calibration methods are fundamentally limited and fragile, and derive rigorous requirements for how many source categories are needed to provide distribution-free reliability guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot anomaly detectors are typically evaluated by ranking metrics, but real-world deployment requires setting a specific alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). This creates a fundamental challenge: how much normal evidence is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category? The authors identify that this question has been largely overlooked in the literature.

Method: The authors use a frozen DINOv2 PCA residual ranker evaluated on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types. They analyze the limitations of target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration, derive a category-count feasibility calculus for distribution-free 95% upper confidence bounds (UCB), and propose the CRESS protocol that splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles.

Result: Key findings include: (1) LOIO calibration is resolution-limited (rank values cannot fall below 1/(k+1)) and shift-fragile—at α=0.20, empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k=4, which is 1.7 times the nominal level. (2) Even with ideal conditions, distribution-free 95% UCB requires at least 14, 29, and 59 iid category draws at α=0.20, 0.10, and 0.05 respectively. (3) With only 3-4 certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold τ*=0, with the smallest category-level UCB being 0.950. (4) Image-unit analyses select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells, but these bounds only hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw.

Conclusion: The paper provides a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol (CRESS) that specifies when source evidence can and cannot support a transferable reliability claim. The key insight is that achieving distribution-free reliability guarantees for unseen categories requires a substantial number of certification categories, and with realistic numbers of categories, the only reliable threshold is the fail-closed τ*=0. This work establishes fundamental limits on what can be guaranteed in few-shot anomaly detection deployment.

Abstract: Few-shot anomaly detectors are judged by ranking metrics, yet deployment requires an alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). We ask how much normal evidence, in images or category units, is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category. Using a frozen DINOv2 principal component analysis (PCA) residual ranker on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types, we show that target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration is resolution-limited and shift-fragile: rank values cannot fall below $1/(k+1)$, and at the attainable level $α=0.20$, empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at $k=4$, 1.7 times the nominal level. A category-count feasibility calculus is then derived: even with all-zero category losses and no multiplicity charged, any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) requires at least 14, 29, and 59 independent and identically distributed (iid) category draws at $α=0.20$, $0.10$, and $0.05$; these counts are necessary but not sufficient. The Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles. With only three or four certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold $τ^\star=0$, and the smallest category-level UCB is 0.950. Image-unit analyses of the same archive select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells; these bounds hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw. The contribution is a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol specifying when source evidence can, and cannot, support a transferable reliability claim.

</details>


### [139] [Exposing the Cost of Deep Learning Audio Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01619)
*Constance Douwes,Paul Magron,Romain Serizel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the overlooked environmental impact of the development phase in deep learning projects. Using activity logs from the Grid5000 platform, the authors studied audio projects from the Multispeech team and found that development phase energy consumption is 3-256 times greater than training the best-performing model alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing environmental impact studies focus on model training and inference, but ignore the development phase (architecture prototyping and experiments), which is highly energy-demanding. This gap leads to underestimation of deep learning's true carbon footprint.

Method: The authors proposed a methodology to estimate energy costs based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform. They conducted a case study on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team, evaluating four projects and comparing development phase energy to training energy.

Result: The energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone.

Conclusion: The results advocate for systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects, not just training/inference phases.

Abstract: The environmental impact of deep learning has attracted increasing attention over the past decade. Existing studies mainly focus on the energy and carbon emissions of model training and inference, while the whole development phase is often overlooked. Yet, architecture prototyping and intensive experiments are conducted during this stage, which is highly energy-demanding. In this article, we propose a methodology to estimate these costs, based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform used by the LORIA laboratory. As a case-study, we focus on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team. We evaluate the overall energy cost of four projects, and we compare them to those of training the reported models. Our results show that the energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone. These results advocate for a more systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects.

</details>


### [140] [Contingent Exposure Routing for Financial AI: Outage Risk and the Cost of Indivisible Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00239)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a stress testing framework for model failover routing in financial institutions, analyzing how endpoint failures impact decision errors and risk distribution across institutional networks. The study combines mathematical analysis with empirical evaluation across synthetic and real-world data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses a critical infrastructure vulnerability: when primary model endpoints fail and trigger failover to backup systems, this changes which financial institutions share decision errors, potentially creating correlated failures across the network. The goal is to understand and mitigate this systemic risk.

Method: The methodology employs: (1) Mathematical formulation using a local market-impact response matrix to model outage-contingent routing; (2) Analysis of expected squared price displacement; (3) Derivation of exact second moment for independent randomized routing; (4) Conditional-expectation rounding for finite-agent bounds; (5) Swap procedures preserving endpoint counts; (6) Empirical validation across 60 synthetic portfolio networks (11,340 scenarios) and 1,024 recorded API responses.

Result: Key findings: (1) Shared backup systems can create order-one concentration floor as primary endpoints grow; (2) Balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with surviving endpoint count; (3) Risk reduction of 6.57% and 10.53% for single/double endpoint removals in synthetic evaluation; (4) 3.30% held-out reduction in real API replay (CI: 2.07-4.57%); (5) Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification benefits.

Conclusion: The contribution is an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis framework, explicitly disclaiming any real-market crash probability estimation. The paper provides practical tools for assessing failover routing risk while acknowledging limitations from error alignment, endpoint quality variations, and indivisible decision constraints.

Abstract: Model failover restores availability, but changes which financial institutions share decision errors. We formulate outage-contingent routing through a local market-impact response matrix and study expected squared price displacement. A symmetric construction shows that a shared backup can leave an order-one concentration floor as the number of primary endpoints grows, while balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with the surviving endpoint count. For indivisible decisions, we derive the exact second moment of independent randomized routing and an effective-exposure granularity that determines its gap from fractional allocation. Conditional-expectation rounding gives a finite-agent bound without coupled quotas; a separate swap procedure preserves endpoint counts and is assessed against dual lower bounds. Across 60 synthetic portfolio networks and 11,340 scenario evaluations, the latter reduces risk by 6.57% and 10.53% for single and double endpoint removals at the central feedback setting with independent errors. A replay of 1,024 recorded API responses on constructed rebalancing tasks gives a smaller held-out reduction of 3.30% (paired bootstrap interval 2.07--4.57%). Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification. The contribution is an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis, not an estimate of real-market crash probabilities.

</details>


### [141] [The Null Is the Hard Part: Exact Tests for Memorization in Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00251)
*Sushovan Majhi,Pramita Bagchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses fundamental statistical flaws in current memorization audits of generative models. The authors demonstrate that existing benchmarks lack proper null distributions, leading to false conclusions about memorization. They propose two null hypotheses: for whole models (permutation test with exchangeable training/held-out images) and for single images (calibrated against matched controls). Using these methods, they show that most detected memorization disappears under proper statistical calibration, and recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile as a robust statistic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memorization audits read similarity scores against arbitrary thresholds without null distributions, leading to potentially incorrect conclusions about whether generative models memorize training data. The field needs rigorous statistical methods to properly detect and quantify memorization.

Method: The authors proposed two null hypotheses: (1) For whole-model evaluation, a permutation test where training and held-out images are exchangeable given samples; (2) For single-image evaluation, calibration against matched controls with false-discovery rate control. They tested various perturbations (random prompt perturbations, attention rescaling, embedding optimization) and compared results against proper null distributions.

Result: Under proper false-discovery control: two-thirds of certified images are no longer detected under random prompt perturbations, five-sixths under attention rescaling, and all under embedding optimization. The standard data-copying test incorrectly flags 10 of 24 generators. With the new null, nearest-neighbor preference fires on 7/24 generators, but count restricted to near-duplicate scale fires on none (McNemar p=0.016). Calibrated audit certifies 36 of 61 MemBench images at 5% FDR, while the calibrated maximum certifies 46.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that proper null distributions are essential for memorization audits. They recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile (IECP) as it counts distinct images copied and can test whether two models copy the same images. Without calibration, most apparent memorization detections may be false positives.

Abstract: Memorization audits of generative models read similarity scores against thresholds, with no null distribution, and the conclusions they support can be wrong. By MemBench's rule, the benchmark's mitigations roughly halve Stable Diffusion's memorization; audited with false-discovery control, two thirds of the certified images are no longer detected under random prompt perturbations, five sixths under attention rescaling, and all of them under embedding optimization. The field's data-copying test, read against its own null, flags ten of twenty-four generators that reproduce nothing. We argue that for memorization the null is the hard part, and supply two. For a whole model, training and held-out images are exchangeable given its samples, and relabelling them is a permutation test, exact for any statistic when the held-out images are a random split; under it, a nearest-neighbour preference still fires on seven of those twenty-four, and a count restricted to the near-duplicate scale on none (McNemar p=0.016). For single images, the natural nulls fail twice, measurably: ranking an image among random images yields 596 false discoveries among 2,365 controls, and resampling independent generations makes the null three times too narrow. Calibrated against matched controls, the audit certifies 36 of 61 MemBench images at 5% false-discovery rate, held-out controls are certified in 0.01% of calibration splits, and on this benchmark two generations per image recover that count. A calibrated maximum, which reads occasional rather than typical copying, certifies 46. As the scale-restricted statistic we recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile, which also counts distinct images copied and tests whether two models copy the same ones.

</details>


### [142] [Sharp Oracle-Regret Tradeoffs for Projection-Free Online Convex Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00254)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper characterizes the minimax regret in online convex optimization when the learner can only access the feasible set through an exact linear optimization oracle, with a dimension-free bound of Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^(1/4)}) for convex G-Lipschitz losses, diameter D, Q total oracle calls, and B calls per round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding the fundamental limits of online convex optimization when oracle access is constrained is important for practical scenarios where evaluating the feasible set is expensive. The problem captures settings where computing with exact linear optimization oracles is costly, which is common in many real-world optimization problems.

Method: The lower bound uses a universal feasibility construction that forces each action into the hull of the supplied ball and preceding oracle replies, combined with a fixed-body construction coupling fresh phase directions to a shared simplex. The upper bound is achieved through a counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks.

Result: The dimension-free minimax expected regret is Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^(1/4)}). Special cases include: T^(3/4) rate with one call per round, and quadratic total budget needed for √T regret. For prescribed smoothness β, a curvature-dependent lower bound identifies the threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp.

Conclusion: The characterization provides a complete understanding of the tradeoff between oracle call budget, per-round constraints, and achievable regret. The results show that even with severe oracle limitations, sub-linear regret is achievable, and the T^(3/4) rate emerges naturally when only one call per round is allowed.

Abstract: We characterize the regret attainable in online convex optimization when access to the feasible set is limited to an exact linear optimization oracle. The learner is given an inscribed ball and a diameter bound and must remain feasible on every consistent instance. For convex $G$-Lipschitz losses, diameter at most $D$, a total allowance of $Q$ oracle calls, and a strict limit of $B$ calls per round, the dimension-free minimax expected regret is $Θ(GD\max\{\sqrt T,T/(1+\min\{Q,BT\})^{1/4}\})$. The lower bound applies to arbitrary randomized learners. Universal feasibility first forces each action into the hull of the supplied ball and the preceding oracle replies. A fixed-body construction then couples fresh phase directions to a shared simplex, making useful replies costly repeatedly even though all losses have a common minimizer. A counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks attains the matching rate. Total-budget and strict per-round guarantees follow as special cases, including the $T^{3/4}$ rate with one call per round and the quadratic total budget needed for $\sqrt T$ regret. For prescribed smoothness $β$, an analytic construction yields a curvature-dependent lower bound and identifies the threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp.

</details>


### [143] [Verification Pulses and the Cost of Escaping Wrong Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00256)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how limited verification resources can recover populations from wrong consensus in asynchronous binary registers. The authors derive asymptotic budget thresholds and demonstrate substantial differences between mean-field and exact models (9 vs 23 checks needed in their example). Empirical validation with 13,392 language model responses supports risk-calibrated reset scheduling, while revealing how mean prediction errors can underestimate consensus failure risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a critical problem in multi-agent systems: how external verification can correct individual outputs but may fail to correct a self-reinforcing wrong consensus at the population level. The authors seek to understand how to allocate limited verification resources to recover from wrong consensus in asynchronous binary register systems.

Method: The study employs three approaches: (1) Analytical derivation of minimum fuel required to cross basin boundaries under peak verification constraints for general nonlinear response; (2) Exact birth-death calculation for finite populations to compute probability of subsequent wrong consensus after a verification pulse; (3) Empirical validation using 13,392 language model responses including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Critical budget window identified with leading term Nlog(x_0/b) and √N correction; (2) Substantial distinction between models—with 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks cross mean-field threshold but 23 required for 95% eventual recovery in exact model; (3) Empirical results show calibration produces different fitted response regimes but all four adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero; (4) Distributional audit reveals modest mean-prediction error can conceal large underestimate of terminal consensus occupancy.

Conclusion: The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under specified update contracts while distinguishing it from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast. The gap between mean-field predictions and exact calculations highlights the importance of finite-population effects in verification strategy design.

Abstract: External verification can correct individual outputs while leaving a self-reinforcing population in the basin of a wrong consensus. We study how the timing and addressing of a fixed verification budget affect recovery in an asynchronous binary register. For a general nonlinear response, we derive the minimum fuel required to cross a basin boundary under a peak verification constraint. For a finite population, an exact birth--death calculation gives the probability of subsequent wrong consensus after a pulse. Our main asymptotic result identifies the critical budget window: a leading term $N\log(x_0/b)$ and a correction of order $\sqrt N$, with separate variance contributions from repeated verification targets and autonomous amplification after verification stops. The distinction is substantial: with 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks cross the mean-field budget threshold, whereas 23 are required for 95% eventual recovery in the exact model. A prospectively specified experiment records 13,392 language-model responses, including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories. Calibration produces different fitted response regimes, but all four adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero. A distributional audit also finds that modest mean-prediction error can conceal a large underestimate of terminal consensus occupancy. The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under a specified update contract, while explicitly separating it from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast.

</details>


### [144] [Attention Manifolds: Steering or Blocking Language Models by Editing Learned B-Spline Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00257)
*Naveen Mysore*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "attention manifolds," a modification to transformer attention where 2D B-spline surfaces modulate value vectors based on query-key interactions, rather than the standard approach where source tokens send identical values to all receivers. The method preserves pretrained behavior by initializing surfaces to zero.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard transformer attention, the query determines how much to attend but not what to extract - all receivers get the same value vector. This work aims to make attention more selective by allowing query-key interactions to modulate what information is extracted from each value dimension.

Method: The method introduces learned tensor-product cubic B-spline surfaces S_d(q_d, k_d) that modulate each value dimension based on query-key interaction. Each surface is initialized to zero (preserving pretrained behavior) and adds only 0.3% parameter overhead.

Result: Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct, attention manifolds reduce WikiText-2 validation perplexity by 2-2.5 points. Across 112 diverse prompts, surfaces change greedy-decoded output for 69% (1B) to 83% (3B) of cases, with strongest effects on ambiguous/polysemous inputs (94-100% change rate). The method corrects factual errors, increases precision, and adds specificity. The surfaces are mechanically editable - inverting coefficients changes output for 9/10 prompts, and setting coefficients to -1 creates "attention walls" that can block value flow.

Conclusion: Attention manifolds provide a geometric mechanism for model steering that improves both perplexity and output quality. The learned surfaces are interpretable and editable, enabling targeted model behavior modification. A preliminary experiment shows potential for safety applications by redirecting problematic prompts through layer-wide "attention walls."

Abstract: In standard transformer attention, a source token sends the same value vector to every receiver. The query determines \emph{how much} to attend but not \emph{what} to extract. This work introduces \textbf{attention manifolds}: learned 2D B-spline surfaces $S_d(q_d, k_d)$ that modulate each value dimension based on the query-key interaction. Each surface is a tensor-product cubic B-spline initialized to zero, preserving pretrained behavior. Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct, attention manifolds reduce WikiText-2 validation perplexity by 2--2.5 points with 0.3\% parameter overhead. Across 112 diverse prompts, surfaces change greedy-decoded output for 69\% (1B) to 83\% (3B) of cases, with the strongest effects on ambiguous and polysemous inputs (94--100\% change rate). The surfaces improve output quality: correcting factual errors (\emph{``the CAP theorem has three main components''} $\to$ \emph{``it is impossible to guarantee all three''}), increasing precision (\emph{``impossible to know certain properties''} $\to$ \emph{``impossible to know both position and momentum''}), and adding specificity (a generic quote $\to$ an attributed Saint Augustine citation, consistently at both scales). The learned surfaces are also mechanically editable: inverting a layer's coefficients changes greedy output for 9/10 prompts (KL~0.010), providing a geometric mechanism for model steering. Setting surface coefficients to $-1$ creates ``attention walls'' that block value flow through specific dimensions. In a preliminary experiment, a layer-wide wall redirects an explosive-device prompt from specific instructions to general educational content, suggesting a path toward safety-oriented manifold shaping.

</details>


### [145] [FastCI: Efficient GPU-Intensive CI for LLM Training Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01967)
*Tianshuo Qiao,Naiqian Zheng,Xiaopeng Liu,Shuguang Wang,Diandian Gu,Xuanzhe Liu,Xin Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FastCI is a framework that improves CI efficiency for LLM training frameworks by using runtime evidence to select affected tests, prune equivalent tests, prioritize high-risk tests, and optimize test workloads. It reduces CI latency by 77.5% and GPU usage by 63.9% while improving coverage retention by 3.2%, deployed at ByteDance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM training frameworks are growing in size and complexity, requiring GPU-intensive tests for CI. Traditional CI becomes a bottleneck because it relies on complete model training or evaluation, slowing down fast-paced development cycles.

Method: FastCI uses four key strategies: 1) Runtime evidence-based test selection to identify affected tests, 2) Test pruning to eliminate tests executing changed code in equivalent contexts, 3) High-risk test prioritization to expose failures earlier, 4) Test workload optimization along dimensions outside the intended validation scope.

Result: Evaluated on ByteDance's LLM training framework CI workload: 77.5% CI latency reduction, 63.9% GPU resource usage reduction, and 3.2% improvement in modified code coverage retention compared to existing CI pipelines.

Conclusion: FastCI successfully addresses the CI bottleneck in LLM training frameworks through intelligent test selection and optimization. It is now integrated into ByteDance's production CI pipelines, demonstrating practical applicability and significant efficiency gains.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) keep growing in size and complexity, their training frameworks evolve at a rapid pace as well. Therefore, continuous integration (CI) is critical for maintaining the quality and stability of these frameworks. However, unlike traditional software, CI for LLM training frameworks relies on GPU-intensive tests, which usually involve complete model training or evaluation. This leads CI itself to become a new bottleneck for fast-paced development. In this paper, we introduce FastCI, a framework that improves the efficiency of CI for LLM training frameworks. FastCI leverages runtime evidence to select affected tests and prune tests that execute changed code in equivalent contexts. Then FastCI prioritizes high-risk tests to expose potential failures earlier, and optimizes test workloads along dimensions outside the intended validation scope of each test. Evaluated on the CI workload of our LLM training framework, FastCI reduces the CI latency by 77.5% and the GPU resource usage by 63.9%, while improving the modified code coverage retention by 3.2%, compared with the currently deployed CI pipelines. FastCI has now been integrated into the CI pipelines of our LLM training framework at ByteDance.

</details>


### [146] [Large Language Bayes Is Not Reparameterisation-Invariant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00265)
*Jian Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large Language Bayes (LLB) uses language models to sample probabilistic programs, runs approximate inference on each, and averages them with weights proportional to an exponentiated evidence bound. This paper shows that LLB's weighting depends on how a model is written (parameterization), with weights differing by up to 31.9x across parameterizations of the same underlying model, affecting Bayes factors and posterior inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether LLB's weighting scheme produces consistent results regardless of how a probabilistic program is written, since the log marginal likelihood is mathematically invariant to reparameterization but the evidence bound used by LLB is not.

Method: The authors compare centered vs non-centered parameterizations of the same model (eight schools problem), test across likelihood families, dimensions, and funnel severities, examine 360 programs from six language models, and derive a Hilbert-distance bound relating parameterization-induced errors to the spread of bound shortfalls.

Result: The centered and non-centered parameterizations represent the same measure to 5.7×10^-14, yet their weights differ by 6.1×; importance weighting reduces this to 2.2×, and full-covariance Gaussian matching still leaves 1.9× on eight schools and 8.9× in 64 dimensions. The discrepancy reaches 31.9× and reverses sign, meaning no single writing is uniformly preferable. It inverts Bayes factors against eight competitors. Across 360 programs from six language models, parameterization ranges from 0% to 100% centered and is stable within each model.

Conclusion: LLB's weighting is sensitive to parameterization choice, which can significantly affect downstream inferences including Bayes factors. The induced error is controlled by the spread Δ of bound shortfalls through a sharp Hilbert-distance bound. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge different models; verifying reparameterizations generated internally can address this issue.

Abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) answers an informal modelling question by sampling candidate probabilistic programs from a language model, running approximate inference on each, and averaging them with weights proportional to an exponentiated evidence bound. We show that this weighting depends on how a model is written. The log marginal likelihood is invariant to reparameterisation; the evidence bound is not. On eight schools the centered and non-centered programs are the same measure to $5.7\times10^{-14}$, yet their weights differ by $6.1\times$; importance weighting reduces this only to $2.2\times$, and reproducing the inference LLB actually runs, a full-covariance Gaussian matched to the posterior moments, still leaves $1.9\times$ on eight schools and $8.9\times$ in $64$ dimensions. Across likelihood families, dimensions and funnel severities the discrepancy reaches $31.9\times$ and reverses sign, so no single writing is uniformly preferable. It inverts Bayes factors against eight natural competitors, and the induced error in the model posterior, and in any downstream target, is controlled by the spread $Δ$ of the bound shortfalls through a known sharp Hilbert-distance bound. Across $360$ programs from six language models the parameterisation written ranges from $0\%$ to $100\%$ centered and is stable within a model. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge genuinely different models at practical sample budgets; verifying reparameterisations we generate ourselves cannot, and closes the window.

</details>


### [147] [MOVE: Multimodal Open-world Verification and Expansion for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00268)
*Zekai Chen,Jiayang Xing,Xun Wu,Miao Zhang,Xunkai Li,Kairui Yang,Zhengyu Wu,Xu Wang,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOVE addresses the challenge of emerging new classes in multimodal graph learning by proposing a framework that identifies unknown nodes using multimodal information, generates candidate classes via multimodal LLM, and selectively expands the class space only when there is consistent multimodal evidence, avoiding redundant categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal graph learning models are trained with a fixed label space but new classes may emerge after deployment. Existing approaches detect unknown nodes and use LLMs to generate candidate class descriptions, but they fail to determine whether existing classes are insufficient or whether generated classes are reliable enough to expand the class space. Three key challenges were identified: (1) multimodal information beyond individual modalities is required for unknown-node identification, (2) LLM-generated class descriptions may not fully capture multimodal class characteristics, and (3) directly adding candidate classes can introduce redundant categories.

Method: MOVE consists of three main components: (1) Unknown Node Identification - identifies nodes that cannot be assigned to existing classes by jointly considering visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context; (2) Candidate Class Generation - leverages a multimodal LLM to generate candidate classes; (3) Selective Class Expansion - expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories.

Result: MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed MOVE framework effectively addresses the open-world class expansion problem in multimodal graph learning by jointly leveraging multimodal information for unknown node identification, using multimodal LLM for candidate class generation, and implementing selective expansion to avoid redundant categories. This work provides a practical solution for real-world multimodal graph learning systems that need to adapt to emerging new classes.

Abstract: Multimodal graph learning faces a fundamental challenge: new classes may emerge after deployment, while models are trained with a fixed label space. Existing approaches typically detect unknown nodes and use LLMs to generate candidate class descriptions, but they do not determine whether existing classes are insufficient to cover these nodes or whether a generated class is reliable enough to expand the class space. Our empirical study reveals three challenges: multimodal information beyond individual modalities is required for unknown-node identification, LLM-generated class descriptions may not fully capture multimodal class characteristics, and directly adding candidate classes can introduce redundant categories. Based on these observations, we propose MOVE, a multimodal open-world class verification and expansion framework. MOVE identifies nodes that cannot be assigned to existing classes by jointly considering visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context, leverages a multimodal LLM to generate candidate classes, and selectively expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories. Experiments demonstrate that MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87\% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

</details>


### [148] [Coupling Perception and Reasoning in Federated Multimodal Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00277)
*Zekai Chen,Xun Wu,Hailin Zhang,Xunkai Li,Yu Liu,Kairui Yang,Muyan Huang,Xuaner Chen,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses federated adaptation of multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs). Existing methods only update the GNN while freezing the multimodal Encoder, limiting adaptation to information propagation while fixing information extraction. The authors discover that Encoder and GNN adaptations are interdependent. They propose FedCORE, which uses a shared low-dimensional latent state ("core") to jointly represent both Encoder and GNN updates, enabling federated evolution in a shared state space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated GFM adaptation methods only update graph-side modules (GNN) while keeping the multimodal Encoder frozen. This limits adaptation to "how information is propagated" while fixing "what information is extracted." Additionally, empirical studies reveal that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent—they are affected by graph relations, and cross-client module swapping shows substantial pairing sensitivity between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates.

Method: The authors propose FedCORE, a federated adaptation framework that represents Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state. This "core" is jointly optimized from multimodal and structural signals, and federated evolution is performed directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception (Encoder) and reasoning (GNN) adaptations.

Result: FedCORE reduces the Encoder-GNN pairing gap from 30.6 to 5.9, corresponding to an 80.7% reduction over independent joint adaptation.

Conclusion: The proposed FedCORE framework effectively addresses the compatibility issue between Encoder and GNN adaptations in federated settings by using a shared latent state space, achieving significant improvements in pairing performance.

Abstract: Federated multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to adapt pretrained multimodal models to decentralized graph data, where each client owns a private multimodal graph and cannot share raw information. These models typically combine a multimodal Encoder that extracts semantic evidence from heterogeneous modalities and a graph neural network (GNN) that performs relational reasoning over graph structures. However, existing federated GFM adaptation methods mainly update graph-side modules while keeping the multimodal Encoder frozen, limiting adaptation to \emph{how information is propagated} while fixing \emph{what information is extracted}. Through empirical studies, we reveal that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent: Encoder adaptation is affected by graph relations, while cross-client module swapping reveals substantial pairing sensitivity between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{FedCORE}, a federated adaptation framework that represents Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state. FedCORE jointly optimizes this core from multimodal and structural signals and performs federated evolution directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception and reasoning adaptations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCORE reduces the Encoder--GNN pairing gap from $30.6$ to $5.9$, corresponding to an $80.7\%$ reduction over independent joint adaptation.

</details>


### [149] [Stable and Counterfactually Robust Physical World Models from Imposed Structure and Learned Physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00280)
*Yufeng Wang,Parivesh Priye,Lu Wei,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses fundamental limitations of world models in physical systems—they may create energy, drift, or violate physical laws. The authors propose embedding general physical structure (gradient-based dynamics from learned energy, reversible operators, one-way energy dissipation) while learning system-specific physics from data. The model recovers constitutive functions, separates conserving from dissipating systems by 4 orders of magnitude, and predicts interventions 2-17x better than linear models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models that forecast physical system evolution often violate fundamental physical laws—they may create energy, drift, or diverge over long rollouts, and fail to correctly respond to interventions on physical parameters. The authors seek to determine how much general physical structure must be hard-coded versus learned from data to ensure second-law compatible dissipation, correct intervention responses, stability, and robustness.

Method: The proposed framework imposes general physical structure: dynamics generated from the gradient of a learned energy through a fixed reversible operator; energy restricted to a confining class; a one-way port that removes energy but never injects; known drive channel; and intervened parameters enter through separable maps. The model learns the energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings from data. Tested on electromagnetic cavity, particle-in-cell grid, and shallow-water fluid simulations with ~9,000 parameters.

Result: Models with ~9,000 parameters successfully recover constitutive functions with unit slope, separate conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using a single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values. A nonlinear constitutive law is recovered with its curvature preserved and predicts held-out interventions 2-17× better than converged linear models. Baseline models without the same structure perform at chance or worse.

Conclusion: Embedding general physical structure (Hamiltonian-like dynamics, energy confinement, one-way dissipation) enables world models to learn system-specific physics from data while respecting fundamental laws. This approach achieves stability 100× beyond training horizon, correct intervention responses, and superior generalization compared to models without embedded structure. The work demonstrates that hard-coding general physical principles while learning system-specific details is essential for reliable physical world modeling.

Abstract: A world model learns to forecast how a physical system evolves from recorded trajectories, yet the systems it imitates obey physical laws that are neither fully supplied nor reliably respected. The model may create energy, drift or diverge over long rollouts, and answer a changed law query using the law observed during training. We ask how much general physical structure must be hard coded into a world model, and how much system-specific physics can then be learned from data, for four properties to hold simultaneously: second law compatible dissipation, correct responses to interventions on physical parameters, stability out to one hundred times the training horizon, and robustness to disturbances. The imposed structure is general: dynamics are generated from the gradient of a learned energy through a fixed reversible operator, the energy is restricted to a confining class, a one way port can remove energy but never inject it, the drive channel is known, and the intervened parameter enters through a separable map. The model learns the energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings. Across an electromagnetic cavity, a particle in cell grid, and a shallow-water fluid, models with roughly nine thousand parameters recover constitutive functions with unit slope, separate conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using a single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values, where equal-capacity models without the same structure perform at chance or worse. A nonlinear constitutive law is recovered with its curvature preserved and predicts a held-out intervention $2$-$17\times$ better than a converged linear model.

</details>


### [150] [Partial AUC Maximization from Positive-unlabeled Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00284)
*Atsutoshi Kumagai,Tomoharu Iwata,Taishi Nishiyama,Hiroshi Takahashi,Kazuki Adachi,Yasuhiro Fujiwara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of maximizing partial AUC (pAUC) for binary classification when only positive and unlabeled (PU) data are available, without requiring negative data samples. The method derives an empirical estimator from PU data within an empirical risk minimization framework and trains a classifier by maximizing this smoothed estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many real-world applications (cybersecurity, medical care, advertising), high pAUC is desired but labeled negative data are difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or annotation expertise requirements. Existing pAUC maximization methods require both labeled positive and negative data, which is often impractical.

Method: The paper proposes a method within an empirical risk minimization framework that represents the pAUC (including FPR-dependent thresholds) using only positive and marginal densities, then derives an empirical estimator from PU data. A classifier is trained by maximizing the derived smoothed empirical pAUC estimator.

Result: The effectiveness of the proposed method was experimentally demonstrated using ten real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully maximizes pAUC from PU data without requiring negative data, providing a practical solution for scenarios where negative labeled data is unavailable due to privacy or expertise constraints.

Abstract: The partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUC) is an important performance metric for binary classification that summarizes true positive rates within a specific range of false positive rates (FPRs). Classifiers that achieve high pAUC need to be obtained in many real-world applications such as cybersecurity, medical care, and advertising. Although many methods for maximizing the pAUC have been proposed, they typically require both labeled positive and negative data for training. However, in practice, labeled negative data are often difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or the need for high expertise to annotate them. In this paper, we propose a method for maximizing the pAUC from positive and unlabeled (PU) data without negative data. Within an empirical risk minimization framework, we show that the pAUC, including its FPR-dependent thresholds, can be represented using only the positive and marginal densities, and derive an empirical estimator from PU data. A classifier is then trained by maximizing the derived smoothed empirical pAUC estimator. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with ten real-world datasets.

</details>


### [151] [Bellman-Certified Rounding for Sparse Policy Deployment in MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00325)
*Zhaojun Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of rounding continuous policy optimization to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. The authors develop theoretical bounds and practical methods to quantify how much discounted return is retained after rounding, with empirical improvements in certification coverage and bound-to-loss ratios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous policy optimization produces policies with continuous action probabilities, but real-world deployment often requires sparse binary policies with only a few state-level changes. The challenge is to understand and bound the loss in discounted return when converting continuous "row mixtures" to discrete policies, particularly when policy-dependent visitation couples the updates and long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative.

Method: The authors derive reusable envelopes from 2d+2 Bellman solves to support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. They use a rank-two rational representation for each exchange to enable weighted curvature integration along realized trajectories. The approach provides candidate-specific bounds that raise pre-rounding certification coverage.

Result: Theoretical results show that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is computationally hard. Empirical results demonstrate: (1) candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from 48.2% to 74.1% on the structured suite; (2) at γ=0.95, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from 402.3 to 2.08 on coupled instances.

Conclusion: The paper provides a principled approach to policy rounding with theoretical guarantees and practical improvements. The key insight is that candidate-specific bounds with local curvature integration can significantly improve certification coverage and reduce bound-to-loss ratios, though linear dimension dependence is unavoidable and exact global curvature thresholding is hard.

Abstract: Continuous policy optimization may spread an update across many states, even when deployment permits only a few complete state-level changes. We study how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. Policy-dependent visitation couples the row edits, while long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative. From $2d+2$ Bellman solves, we derive reusable envelopes that support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. A rank-two rational representation of each exchange further permits weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. We prove that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from $48.2\%$ to $74.1\%$ on the structured suite. At $γ=0.95$, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from $402.3$ to $2.08$ on coupled instances.

</details>


### [152] [Beyond Diagonal State Space Models: Exact Non-Abelian Group Tracking, Solvability Barriers, and Geometric Physical Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00329)
*Zeyu Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM) that lift state transitions from diagonal matrices to compact Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)) to overcome limitations of existing SSMs bounded by transition matrix commutativity and solvable affine transformation groups. The method uses Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms to achieve norm-preserving isometry, with specialized readouts and quaternion parallel prefix scans. Experiments show significant improvements: 100% tracking on non-solvable groups (A_5, S_3, D_4, Q_8) vs 6.60% baseline, 50.92% on S_5 vs 5.25% baseline, and excellent manifold preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing selective state space models (Mamba, S4D, LRU) are constrained by transition matrix commutativity and solvable affine transformation groups (Aff_D of derived length ≤ 2). Stacked multi-layer diagonal networks suffer severe optimization degradation on non-solvable simple groups like A_5 because they require exponential circuit emulation depth to simulate non-abelian commutators. This limits their ability to model complex algebraic structures and achieve long-range associative memory.

Method: The paper proposes three novel architectures: (1) NC-SSM lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)); (2) SO(3)-SSM using real-orthogonal transformations; (3) Cayley-SSM for arbitrary dimensions. Key technical contributions include: closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms for exact norm-preserving isometry (||U_t|| = 1); pure Hopf-fibration Bloch projective readouts (S^3/{±1} ≅ S^2 ≅ SO(3)) to eliminate sign ambiguity; true quaternion parallel prefix scans achieving 9.06x speedup at T=2048; and Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate sparse syntax phase drift.

Result: Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes demonstrate: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking accuracy on S_3, D_4, Q_8 and simple group A_5, while 3-layer deep diagonal baseline collapses to 6.60% (p = 8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on symmetric group S_5 (50.92% vs diagonal 5.25%, p = 0.0015), delivering 7.8x variance reduction over SO(3); (3) SO(3)-SSM preserves Riemannian manifolds across 300 steps (< 3.12e-6 drift, > 580,000x advantage), achieving 0.04° dead-reckoning error with active tangent denoising; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p = 0.0081); (5) Ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

Conclusion: Lifting state transitions to non-commutative Lie groups is mathematically necessary and practically effective for modeling non-abelian algebraic structures. The proposed NC-SSM, SO(3)-SSM, and Cayley-SSM architectures achieve state-of-the-art results on group tracking, language modeling (Dyck-2, AST), and manifold preservation tasks, with strict isometry being essential for lossless long-range associative memory. This work opens new directions for state space models that can naturally handle non-commutative symmetries.

Abstract: Selective state space models (SSMs), such as Mamba, S4D, and LRU, are bounded by transition matrix commutativity (A_t A_t' = A_t' A_t) and solvable affine transformation groups (Aff_D of derived length <= 2). Consequently, stacked multi-layer diagonal networks face severe optimization degradation on non-solvable simple groups such as A_5 due to the exponential circuit emulation depth required to simulate non-abelian commutators. We propose Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM), their real-orthogonal counterpart SO(3)-SSM, and arbitrary-dimension Cayley-SSM, lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups SU(2), SO(3), and SO(N). Via closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms, NC-SSM achieves exact norm-preserving isometry (||U_t|| = 1). We introduce pure Hopf-fibration Bloch projective readouts (S^3/{+-1} =~ S^2 =~ SO(3)) to eliminate sign ambiguity, true quaternion parallel prefix scans (9.06x speedup at T=2048), and Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate sparse syntax phase drift. Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes show: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking on S_3, D_4, Q_8 and simple group A_5, where a 3-layer deep diagonal baseline collapses to 6.60% (p = 8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on symmetric group S_5 (50.92% vs diagonal 5.25%, p = 0.0015, delivering 7.8x variance reduction over SO(3)); (3) SO(3)-SSM preserves Riemannian manifolds across 300 steps (< 3.12e-6 drift, > 580,000x advantage), achieving 0.04 deg dead-reckoning error and active tangent denoising; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p = 0.0081); and (5) ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

</details>


### [153] [The Weakest Link: Distilling LLM Reasoning with Worst-Case Constrained Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00332)
*Matthieu Zimmer,Xiaotong Ji,Tu Nguyen,Haitham Bou-Ammar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses reasoning distillation from large LLMs to smaller students by formulating it as a constrained RL problem that maximizes task reward while enforcing worst-case teacher log-likelihood constraints on every trajectory prefix. This avoids the averaging problem in prior methods where a chain-of-thought's validity is undermined by a single weak link.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current distillation methods face a fundamental tension: pure RL (GRPO) leads to reward hacking where students produce correct answers through flawed reasoning, while KL-based regularization dilutes task performance and allows compensation between steps. The key insight is that reasoning validity is determined by the weakest step, not an average.

Method: The authors formulate reasoning distillation as constrained RL with worst-case constraints on teacher log-likelihood along every trajectory prefix. They derive an unaugmented constrained MDP that preserves hard-constraint semantics, admits low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms, and provably satisfies constraints in the penalty limit.

Result: The method significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. It matches the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL while drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, achieving the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed constrained RL formulation successfully addresses the fundamental tension in reasoning distillation by enforcing worst-case constraints rather than averages. This yields students that maintain high task performance while producing reasoning that better aligns with the teacher, setting a new state-of-the-art for rigorous reasoning success.

Abstract: Distilling the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) into smaller students is a central challenge for efficient deployment. Current approaches face a fundamental tension: optimizing purely for verifiable task rewards (e.g., via GRPO) leads to reward hacking, where students arrive at correct final answers through flawed intermediate logic, while regularizing with soft divergence penalties against a teacher (e.g., KL-based distillation) dilutes task performance and, critically, allows the student to compensate for severe logical violations at one step with high teacher agreement at others. We argue that this averaging is fundamentally misaligned with the nature of reasoning: a chain-of-thought is only as valid as its weakest link. Motivated by this observation, we formulate reasoning distillation as a constrained reinforcement learning problem in which the task reward is maximized subject to a worst-case constraint on the teacher log-likelihood along every prefix of the trajectory. To avoid the prohibitive cost of dual Lagrangian solvers and the test-time teacher dependence of state-augmented methods such as Saute, we derive an unaugmented constrained MDP whose reward transformation preserves the hard-constraint semantics, admits a low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms, and provably satisfies the worst-case constraint almost surely in the penalty limit. Through extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, we demonstrate that our method significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. By matching the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL and drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, we ultimately achieve the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across all evaluated settings.

</details>


### [154] [Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00346)
*Amir Rafe,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares three classes of AI models for automated decision-making: typed decision models (System One), supervised classifiers, and generative language models. Under various conditions, decision models generally outperform zero-shot classifiers, with small trained classifiers performing best on intent tasks when labeled data is available. The study provides condition-dependent design rules for implementing automated decision gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to establish design guidelines for when to use different types of AI models (decision models, classifiers, generative models) for automated branching decisions in software systems. The authors aim to identify which model class performs best under different conditions.

Method: The researchers used a controlled harness comparing 8 decision-model checkpoints from 6 families (including hosted model "Jev") against two generative comparators. They evaluated supervised and zero-shot classifiers on the same workflow, intent, and social-science items.
