They tested various conditions including: with/without labels, different temperature settings, threshold tuning, and a two-stage escalation approach.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Small trained classifiers are most accurate on intents with own labels; (2) Decision models exceed zero-shot classifiers on workflows/intents without labels; (3) Larger generative models match Jev on workflows/intents; (4) Fine-tuned decision checkpoints improve over backbones; (5) Temperature fitting on few options raises calibration error with many options; (6) Jev accepts 0.310 of out-of-scope requests at 5% risk threshold; (7) Swapping yes/no flips 50.5 answers/100 for Jev; (8) Two-stage approach achieves 43% of Jev's cost with equal accuracy.

Conclusion: The results yield condition-dependent design rules for automated decision gates. The optimal model choice depends on: availability of labeled data, task type (intent vs workflow), computational cost constraints, and required accuracy/cost tradeoffs. Decision models are preferred without labels; classifiers with labels; and two-stage approaches can reduce costs significantly.

Abstract: Software that hands branching decisions to a model needs a declared option and a probability it can threshold. Typed decision models, also called System One models, return such probabilities without generating text, while supervised classifiers and generative language models are the established alternatives. Under matched conditions, one harness sends eight decision-model checkpoints from six families, including the hosted model Jev, and two generative comparators the same semantic requests, and scores supervised and zero-shot classifiers on the same workflow, intent and social-science items. The ranking of the model classes depends on the conditions. With the task's own labels, small trained classifiers are the most accurate on intents and not significantly different from the best decision models on workflows. Without labels, every decision model except the encoder-based checkpoints exceeds a zero-shot entailment classifier on workflows and intents. Read through option-key likelihoods, a larger generative model is level with Jev on workflows and intents and accepts more workflow decisions at five percent risk, and fine-tuned decision checkpoints gain intent accuracy over their untuned backbones. Stored temperatures fitted on few options raise calibration error with many options, and a held-out threshold for five percent in-scope risk still lets Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests. Swapping yes and no flips 50.5 answers per hundred for Jev, while fine-tuned checkpoints cut their backbones' social-science flips. An intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matches its accuracy at 0.43 of its cost at full graphics-processor utilization. The results yield condition-dependent design rules for automated decision gates.

</details>


### [155] [Deep Learning for Anomaly Detection in Railway Systems: A Structured Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00363)
*Ammar Bouketta,Smail Niar,Hamza Ouarnoughi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey of deep learning-based anomaly detection methods for railway systems, organized by anomaly location, data representation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics, with practical deployment guidelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for safe and reliable railway operations drives the adoption of data-driven monitoring and intelligent fault detection, enabled by growing heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure.

Method: Systematic literature review organizing deep learning approaches into a unified taxonomy: classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid paradigms, covering CNNs, RNNs, attention, autoencoders, GANs, and transformers.

Result: Survey identifies four learning paradigms, examines data-centric challenges, evaluation metrics, and deployment aspects including edge-cloud architectures and computational constraints.

Conclusion: Provides a decision-oriented framework linking anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms, serving as a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions while highlighting open challenges for reliable intelligent monitoring.

Abstract: Ensuring safe and reliable operation of modern railway systems increasingly relies on data-driven monitoring and intelligent fault detection. Deep learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for railway anomaly detection, driven by the growing availability of heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure. This paper presents a structured survey of deep learning-based anomaly detection approaches for railway systems. The surveyed methods are organized using a unified taxonomy covering anomaly location, data representation and manifestation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. Existing approaches, including convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures, autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and transformers, are structured into classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning paradigms. The survey also examines data-centric challenges, evaluation practices, performance metrics, and practical deployment aspects, including edge-cloud architectures, computational constraints, and hardware-aware optimization. Finally, a decision-oriented framework links anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms and deployment configurations. This work provides a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions for railway anomaly detection and highlights open challenges toward reliable and scalable intelligent monitoring systems.

</details>


### [156] [Manifold-Constrained Initial Noise Optimization for Efficient Generative Model Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00365)
*Jinho Chang,Jong Chul Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeNOVA is a stable and efficient initial noise alignment method that operates in a gradient-free manner for black-box reward scenarios in generative models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios.

Method: ZeNOVA addresses black-box scenarios through three key techniques: annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping.

Result: ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing the initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior.

Conclusion: The method demonstrates practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment tasks, as validated by extensive experiments on image and video generative models.

Abstract: Recent advances in distillation and flow-map models have enabled deterministic one- or few-step generation for high-quality data, facilitating a new branch of reward alignment approaches that directly optimize the initial noise from a Gaussian distribution. However, most existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios. Here, we introduce ZeNOVA, a stable and efficient initial noise alignment method in a gradient-free manner. Specifically, we address existing algorithms' major challenge in black-box scenarios through annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping. Extensive experiments on image and video generative models show that ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing the initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior, demonstrating its practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment.

</details>


### [157] [MoRA: MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00367)
*Yushuai Sun,Zikun Zhou,Lin Gao,Jun Yu,Wenjie Pei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoRA is a structured MoE expert pruning framework that introduces learnable router biases optimized with language-modeling loss and a routing-diversity regularizer, combined with an expert approximation mechanism for post-pruning enhancement. It outperforms SOTA pruning algorithms on three models (Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Moonlight-16B-A3B) across nine zero-shot benchmarks when pruning 25% and 50% of experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models enable parameter scaling with limited computation but require loading all experts into memory. Existing pruning methods either use poorly-aligned ranking criteria or are computationally expensive, and they overlook routing-behavior redundancy among retained experts.

Method: 1) Learnable router bias for each expert, optimized by minimizing language-modeling loss + routing-diversity regularizer to sharpen routing probabilities and identify critical experts while encouraging diverse routing preferences. 2) Expert approximation mechanism using affine transformation to approximate outputs of pruned experts from remaining experts.

Result: MoRA outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms on nine zero-shot benchmarks when removing 25% and 50% of routed experts in each MoE layer across three models.

Conclusion: MoRA provides an effective framework for structured MoE expert pruning that addresses routing-behavior redundancy through router bias learning and improves pruned model performance via expert approximation.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable parameter scaling with limited per-token computation by activating only a small subset of experts for each token, but deploying them still requires loading the complete expert pool into memory. Structured expert pruning can effectively reduce the memory usage by removing experts. However, existing pruning methods either use expert ranking criteria that are not well aligned with model performance or rely on effective expert subset searching that is computationally expensive. Moreover, these methods typically overlook the routing-behavior redundancy among the retained experts. In this paper, we propose MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation (MoRA), a framework for structured MoE expert pruning. We introduce a learnable router bias for each expert and optimize these biases by minimizing the language-modeling loss and a routing-diversity regularizer. The learned router biases sharpen the routing probability distributions to identify experts critical to model performance while encouraging the selection of experts with diverse routing preferences. In addition, we introduce an expert approximation mechanism as a post-pruning enhancement. It leverages the remaining experts to approximate the outputs of pruned experts by affine transformation, further improving the performance of the pruned model. We evaluate MoRA on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and Moonlight-16B-A3B, removing 25\% and 50\% of the routed experts in each MoE layer. Extensive experiments on nine zero-shot benchmarks show that MoRA outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms. Our code will be released.

</details>


### [158] [M$^2$Weather: A Benchmark for Joint Multi-Station and Multi-Variable Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00370)
*Rongwen Li,Xiao Wang,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M²Weather is a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting, addressing the gap of separately modeling spatial dependencies and physical coupling among weather variables. It includes 2,809 stations with 5 variables across three spatial scales (France, Europe, Global) with unified evaluation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing weather forecasting studies consider spatial dependencies across stations and physical coupling among weather variables separately, using different datasets and experimental settings. This hinders systematic assessment of their individual and joint contributions to forecasting accuracy.

Method: The paper introduces a benchmark with: (1) multi-criteria quality control and station stratification to collect 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled weather variables across three spatial scales; (2) unified training and evaluation protocols for fair comparison; (3) a lightweight plug-and-play adapter to introduce missing station-variable relationships without retraining. Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models was conducted.

Result: Jointly modeling station and variable relationships provides benefits. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets. The multi-scale design confirms conclusions persist from national to global station networks.

Conclusion: Complementary information across stations and variables represents an important resource for improving station weather forecasting. The adapter enables fair and efficient investigation of station-variable relationships without requiring full model retraining.

Abstract: Station weather forecasting is fundamentally shaped by both complex spatial dependencies across stations and strong physical coupling among weather variables. However, existing studies often consider these relationships separately and use different datasets and experimental settings, hindering systematic assessment of their individual and joint contributions. In this paper, we introduce $M^2$Weather, a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting. Through multi-criteria quality control and station stratification, we collect 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled weather variables across three spatial scales: France, Europe, and Global. This multi-scale design lets us examine whether conclusions persist from national to global station networks. We also introduce unified training and evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison of different station-variable modeling paradigms. To further examine the benefits of modeling station-variable relationships, we design a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter. With a trained weather forecasting model, this adapter can introduce missing station or variable relationships without retraining the model. This enables fair and efficient investigation of station-variable relationships. Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models shows the benefits of jointly modeling station and variable relationships. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets. Together, these results identify the complementary information across stations and variables as an important resource for improving station weather forecasting. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/M2-Weather.

</details>


### [159] [When Do Attention-Head Ablations Support Causal Claims? Projection-Level Confounds, Floor Effects, and Matched Controls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00373)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that attention-head ablation as an interpretability method is fragile and requires careful validation. The authors show that post-projection ablation is nearly uncorrelated with corrected pre-projection ablation (r=0.057), and that metric choice (binary accuracy vs log-probability) significantly affects results. Using proper controls and held-out splits, they find stable ranking of important heads (rho=0.974) but limited task specificity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Attention-head ablation is commonly used to infer causal responsibility of specific components in language models for behaviors. However, the authors identify that this inference can be fragile due to unclear intervention semantics, inadequate evaluation metrics, and lack of proper controls.

Method: The authors compared post-projection vs pre-projection ablation implementations, binary accuracy vs gold-token log-probability metrics, and used discovery/held-out splits with 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws. Experiments were conducted on GPT-2 small and replicated on DistilGPT2.

Result: Post-projection ablation is nearly uncorrelated with corrected pre-projection ablation (Pearson r = 0.057) and selects a completely disjoint top-5 set of important heads. Binary accuracy hides effects at behavioral floors and ceilings, while log-probability remains graded. The corrected per-head effect ranking is highly stable across splits (Spearman rho = 0.974), with top-5 heads significantly exceeding control distributions (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). However, evidence for task specificity is not robust on GPT-2, though findings replicate on DistilGPT2.

Conclusion: Single-head ablation does not by itself justify a causal claim. Defensible interpretation requires: (1) correct intervention placement (pre-projection), (2) non-saturated continuous metrics (log-probability), and (3) matched held-out controls. The method can work with proper validation but is fragile without these safeguards.

Abstract: Attention-head ablation, zeroing a head and measuring the resulting change in task performance, is a common method for inferring which components of a language model are causally responsible for a behavior. We show using GPT-2 small that this inference can be fragile unless the intervention semantics, evaluation metric, and controls are carefully validated. A natural post-projection implementation of "zeroing a head" is nearly uncorrelated with a corrected pre-projection ablation (Pearson r = 0.057) and selects a completely disjoint top-5 set of important heads. We also show that binary accuracy can hide effects at behavioral floors and near ceilings, whereas gold-token log-probability remains graded. Using a discovery/held-out split and 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws, the corrected per-head effect ranking is highly stable across splits (Spearman rho = 0.974), and the top-5 selected heads significantly exceed both control distributions (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). However, evidence for task specificity is not robust on GPT-2. Replication on DistilGPT2 preserves the intervention-semantic and matched-control findings. These results show that single-head ablation does not by itself justify a causal claim; defensible interpretation requires correct intervention placement, a non-saturated continuous metric, and matched held-out controls.

</details>


### [160] [A First Glance at Jev for Network Traffic Classification: Accuracy, Processing Time, and Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00376)
*Shenghe Xu,Lifan Mei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates Jev, a general-purpose decision model, for application classification of network flows using only the first 10 packets' metadata. The study compares Jev against tree ensembles (Random Forest, Extra Trees) and GPT-5.6 Sol on the CESNET-QUICEXT-25 dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: This is the first empirical study of general-purpose decision models for application classification of network flows. The researchers aim to evaluate whether Jev can compete with traditional machine learning approaches and large language models in network traffic classification.

Method: Classification using only first 10 packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. Tested Jev with 40 and 150 labeled examples, compared against Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records, and GPT-5.6 Sol via Azure.

Result: Jev's accuracy improved from 9.80% to 28.42% with 40 examples, and 34.50% with 150 examples. Random Forest achieved 69.95% and Extra Trees 66.80%, both outperforming Jev. In a 100-record subset, Jev achieved 29% accuracy at 0.750s vs GPT's 37% at 6.036s, with lower API costs.

Conclusion: Labeled examples substantially improve Jev's performance, but Jev remains less accurate than trained tree ensembles. The comparison with GPT-5.6 Sol is inconclusive due to unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations. The accuracy gap between Jev and tree ensembles cannot be attributed to a single cause.

Abstract: We evaluate Jev on ten dataset-defined application labels in CESNET-QUICEXT-25 using only the first ten packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first empirical study of general-purpose decision models, represented here by Jev, for application classification of network flows. Across 52,000 records from 26 collection weeks following the training period, 40 fixed labeled examples raise Jev's accuracy from 9.80% to 28.42%. Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records achieve 69.95% and 66.80% and outperform Jev in every week. Increasing Jev's context to 150 examples yields 34.50% on the first test week. On a paired 100-record subset, Jev with 40 examples achieves 29% accuracy at a median request time of 0.750 s, versus 37% and 6.036 s for the generative language model OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort through Azure; Jev also incurs lower API charges. The paired subset does not establish an accuracy advantage for either service, and the timing reflects different service configurations. Thus, labeled examples substantially improve Jev, but the tested Jev configurations remain less accurate than trained tree ensembles; unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations prevent attributing the gap to a single cause.

</details>


### [161] [STCFormer: Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Modeling with Dynamic Cluster Transformer for Station-based Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00377)
*Rongwen Li,Haixin Xie,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Kun Fang,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STCFormer is an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer for station-based weather forecasting that dynamically groups stations within each temporal patch. It combines local attention within clusters and global attention over regional summaries, with theoretical guarantees via Lipschitz bound analysis. Achieves state-of-the-art results on 8 weather forecasting tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current clustering-based weather forecasting methods have two key limitations: (1) fixed grouping across observation windows obscures local changes in station relationships, and (2) intra-cluster interactions alone miss important global context. Additionally, the theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity were not well understood.

Method: STCFormer uses dynamic station grouping based on local evolution within each temporal patch. The Cluster-Guided Attention Block combines: (1) fine-grained local attention within clusters, and (2) global attention over regional state summaries, allowing cross-cluster information access. Theoretically, a Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention is derived, showing it is no larger than fully connected attention, explaining robustness benefits.

Result: STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks. It ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons. Ablations and case studies confirm the benefits of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions.

Conclusion: STCFormer successfully addresses the limitations of previous clustering-based methods through dynamic grouping and dual local-global attention. The theoretical Lipschitz bound analysis provides justification for the robustness of selective interactions, and the design of InfoLoss is motivated by this analysis. The method demonstrates consistent superior performance across diverse weather datasets and forecasting tasks.

Abstract: Station-based weather forecasting supports daily life and economic activity, yet accurate forecasts require modeling complex spatial dependencies among stations. Recent clustering-based selective modeling offers a promising alternative to dense inter-station interactions. However, a grouping shared across an observation window may obscure local changes in station relationships, while intra-cluster interactions alone may miss important global context. The theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity also remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose STCFormer, an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer that dynamically groups stations according to their local evolution within each temporal patch. Its Cluster-Guided Attention Block combines fine-grained local attention within clusters and global attention over regional state summaries, allowing each station to access information beyond its own cluster. We further show that a derived Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention is no larger than its fully connected counterpart, explaining a potential robustness benefit and motivating the design of InfoLoss. Experiments on three real-world weather datasets spanning eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks show that STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight tasks and ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons. Ablations and case studies further confirm the benefits of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/STCFormer.

</details>


### [162] [Fusion techniques of time frequency-based images to predict the outcome of rTMS depression therapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00380)
*Wael Korani,Md Fahimul Kabir Chowdhury,Mohammed Aledhari,Reza Rostami,Reza Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images with fusion techniques (montage and blending) and a lightweight CNN to predict rTMS treatment response for depression. The study reveals a critical finding: when using proper subject-disjoint cross-validation (no data leakage), prediction performance drops significantly, with most models performing near random chance (AUC 0.31-0.54), suggesting the high accuracy reported in segment-level CV was due to overfitting rather than true generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting rTMS treatment outcome for depression is clinically challenging due to high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain EEG analysis. The authors aim to develop a more robust prediction method using fused TF representations from EEG data.

Method: The authors introduced two fusion techniques (montage and blending) to extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency images. They trained a lightweight custom CNN on these fused TF representations. Experiments were conducted on two datasets (15 and 46 patients) using two validation approaches: segment-level 10-fold CV (allowing data leakage) and strict subject-disjoint CV (preventing data leakage).

Result: With segment-level CV, Montage CWT_ST fusion achieved 99.90% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90% on the secondary. However, with strict subject-disjoint CV, performance collapsed: most configurations had AUC 0.31-0.54 with 95% CIs containing 0.5. The best subject-level result was Montage CWT_ST on the primary cohort (AUC 0.874 ± 0.183, 82.7% accuracy), but a permutation test returned p=0.703, indicating this result was not statistically significant.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that high accuracy in segment-level CV is misleading due to data leakage (same patient's segments in both training and testing). With proper subject-disjoint validation, predicting rTMS response from EEG remains extremely challenging, with performance near random chance. The authors emphasize the importance of strict subject-level cross-validation in medical ML applications to avoid overoptimistic results.

Abstract: Depression is a mental condition that can lead to suicide and self-harm. Predicting the outcome of depression treatment is one of the most difficult tasks for clinicians. Among various treatment options, repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a widely used non-invasive method. Predicting rTMS response using Electroencephalogram (EEG) data is difficult because of high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain analysis. We introduce two fusion techniques, montage and blending, to overcome these limitations and extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images. We then propose a lightweight custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on fused TF representations. \textcolor{black}{We use a primary dataset of 15 patients and a secondary dataset of 46 patients. We run two sets of experiments. The first set uses segment-level 10-fold cross-validation. In this setup segments from the same patient can appear in both training and testing. The Montage CWT\_ST fusion reaches 99.90\% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90\% on the secondary dataset. The second set uses strict subject-disjoint cross-validation. All segments of a patient stay in one fold and no patient appears in both training and testing. Performance collapses. We test four time-frequency methods, six fusion mechanisms, and fourteen model architectures. With one exception, every configuration on both cohorts falls between AUC 0.31 and 0.54 and every 95\% confidence interval contains 0.5. A patient-level permutation test on the best standalone method returns $p = 0.703$. The best subject-level result is Montage CWT\_ST on the primary cohort, which reaches AUC $0.874 \pm 0.183$ and 82.7\% accuracy.

</details>


### [163] [OmniMed-Jev: Calibrating LVLM Confidence for Trustworthy Medical Multimodal Decisions via System One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00381)
*Luyao Tang,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces OmniMed-Jev, a decision-native interface for medical AI that represents decisions as explicit probability distributions over candidate sets (Choices, Nouls, or Scores) rather than generated text. This approach significantly improves confidence calibration compared to generative baselines while maintaining comparable point-prediction accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical models are judged on whether reported confidence matches actual accuracy. Current generalist multimodal medical models express decisions (diagnoses, findings, cell counts) as generated text, where the reported probability reflects next-token probability rather than the decision itself. This creates a fundamental mismatch between reported confidence and actual decision accuracy.

Method: OmniMed-Jev represents each medical decision as a Choice (mutually exclusive classes), Noul (binary presence of a finding), or Score (bounded ordered value) over a runtime-supplied candidate set. The model returns a full distribution over that set. The design is "omni" in three respects: (1) accepts diverse imaging modalities, (2) covers different prediction tasks, and (3) expresses them through one candidate-conditioned probability model, making heterogeneous outputs comparable probabilities.

Result: In interface-controlled comparison against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data, and schedule, OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness far more closely. It reduces calibration error by up to an order of magnitude (10x) and reliability error by up to two (2x), while point-prediction performance remains comparable. The exception is counting tasks, where the generative baseline maintains better performance.

Conclusion: Making the decision distribution the model's output transforms reported numbers into probabilities that accurately reflect confidence. The results support explicit decision modeling as a way to make reported confidence meaningful. However, the comparison cannot separate the interface from associated training differences, and the results do not evidence clinical readiness. Code is available at github.com/lytang63/OmniMed-Jev.

Abstract: Medical models are judged not only on correctness, but on whether reported confidence matches actual accuracy. Generalist multimodal medical models have expanded what a single model can perceive, yet they still express bounded decisions such as diagnoses, findings or cell counts as generated text, so the reported probability reflects the next token rather than the decision itself. Motivated by decision-native interfaces such as Jev, we introduce OmniMed-Jev, which represents each medical decision as a Choice, Noul or Score decision over a runtime-supplied candidate set and returns a full distribution over that set: mutually exclusive classes, binary presence of a finding, or a bounded ordered value. The design is omni in three respects: it accepts diverse imaging modalities, covers different prediction tasks, and expresses them through one candidate-conditioned probability model, so heterogeneous outputs become comparable probabilities rather than task-specific strings. In an interface-controlled comparison against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data and schedule, OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness far more closely, reducing calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two, while point-prediction performance remains comparable; counting is the one family where the generative baseline stays ahead. Making the decision distribution the model's output is not a format change but what turns reported numbers into probabilities that mean what they say. These results support explicit decision modeling as a way to make reported confidence meaningful within the evaluated tasks, and they are not evidence of clinical readiness: the comparison cannot separate the interface from associated training differences, which we state alongside the results. Code is available at github.com/lytang63/OmniMed-Jev.

</details>


### [164] [EvoGen-Harness: Learning Where and How to Evolve Image-Generation Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00383)
*Jiabin Luo,Yinan Liu,Chunlei Meng,Yufei Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoGen-Harness is a generator-agnostic framework that enables multi-responsibility evolution for text-to-image systems without modifying the frozen generator. It uses Trace (Trajectory-Relative Attribution and Coordinated Evolution) to aggregate evidence across stochastic executions, attribute failures to specific responsibilities, and coordinate evolution across multiple dimensions while preventing harmful updates via No-Patch validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2I adaptation approaches only optimize single predefined dimensions (prompts, routing, or workflows), limiting the space for correcting generation failures. While allowing multiple responsibilities to evolve provides broader adaptation space, it introduces a new challenge: visual feedback reveals failures but not where evolution should occur or how to explore this space efficiently.

Method: The proposed Trace method aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities, and employs No-Patch and held-out validation to prevent unnecessary or harmful updates.

Result: EvoGen-Harness improves over strongest baselines by +0.2633 on GenEval2, +0.0720 on T2I-CompBench++, and +0.0752 on WISE. It achieves 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation, demonstrating that coordinating evolution across multiple responsibilities with proper failure attribution and validation is effective for improving text-to-image generation.

Abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems can be improved without modifying generator parameters by adapting the external system around frozen generators. However, existing approaches typically optimize a predefined dimension, such as prompts, routing, or workflows, restricting the space in which generation failures can be corrected. Allowing multiple generator-external responsibilities to evolve provides a broader adaptation space, but introduces a new challenge: visual feedback reveals what failed, but not where persistent evolution should occur or how this space should be explored efficiently. We introduce EvoGen-Harness, a generator-agnostic framework for multi-responsibility image-generation harness evolution, together with Trace (Trajectory-Relative Attribution and Coordinated Evolution). Trace aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, and progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities, while No-Patch and held-out validation prevent unnecessary or harmful updates. Across GenEval2, T2I-CompBench++, and WISE, EvoGen-Harness improves over the strongest evaluated baselines by +0.2633, +0.0720, and +0.0752, respectively, while achieving 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression. These results demonstrate that attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation.

</details>


### [165] [FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00385)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Tianshu Fu,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FAER is an auditable full-trajectory replay framework that addresses the gap between replay selection metrics (format feedback, confidence, freshness) and downstream learner utility. It introduces training-free fixed selectors and learner-aware selectors (FAER-UTILITY) fitted on calibration blocks. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, FAER-UTILITY achieves 0.6624 quality vs 0.5482 for uniform selection, demonstrating that learner-aware selection significantly outperforms format-feedback approaches despite format-feedback selecting records with higher correctness (0.6953 vs 0.3594).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Replay selectors typically rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, but cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. This selection-to-learning gap leads to suboptimal training performance.

Method: FAER framework with: (1) Training-free fixed selector as protocol baseline; (2) FAER-UTILITY as learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks; (3) Normalized gradient alignment as baseline; (4) Disposable optimizer-aware virtual update for magnitude-aware utility surface; (5) Audit contract that freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined.

Result: On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: Fixed selector achieves 0.6329 quality vs 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches 0.6476 ± 0.0139 (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval [+0.079,+0.122]) at 63,276 target-run tokens. FAER-UTILITY achieves 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953 vs 0.3594 for fixed selector, revealing the selection-to-learning gap.

Conclusion: Learner-aware selection (FAER-UTILITY) significantly outperforms format-feedback and uniform selection approaches. The key insight is that metrics correlated with cache-level correctness (like format-feedback) do not necessarily translate to better downstream learning performance, highlighting the importance of directly optimizing for learner utility in replay selection.

Abstract: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, although cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. We formalize this selection-to-learning gap and introduce FAER as an auditable full-trajectory replay framework. Its training-free fixed selector is a protocol baseline; FAER-UTILITY is the learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks. The normalized gradient alignment is reported as a baseline, while a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update supplies a magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the matched learner study reports quality 0.6329 for the fixed selector, compared with 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches $0.6476\!\pm\!0.0139$ over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval $[+0.079,+0.122]$) at 63,276 target-run tokens; its recorded full cost is 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. The completed FAER-UTILITY row reaches 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens and 4.26 GPU-hours. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953, compared with 0.3594 for the fixed selector, despite the different downstream ranking. The completed comparison surfaces report the learner-aware ablation, same-seed gap, policy-optimization rows, and strict zero-shot transfer.

</details>


### [166] [T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388)
*Bo-Wen Zhang,Junwei He,Maoqi Liu,Feiran Li,Song-Lin Lv,Wentao Ma,Rongyi Lin,Shuhan Zhong,Lan-Zhe Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: T2SPO uses past successful trajectories to provide step-level feedback for training LLM agents in multi-step interactive tasks, employing a TabPFN regressor to estimate remaining distance to success at each state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many interactive tasks, rewards reflect only final outcomes, providing limited guidance on intermediate decisions. This sparse supervision makes it difficult for reinforcement learning agents to learn which intermediate steps advance toward task completion.

Method: T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with state representations. A pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates remaining distance at each state of new rollouts. Changes in distance estimates across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. Newly completed trajectories refresh the estimator's context without updating its parameters.

Result: Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO.

Conclusion: T2SPO effectively addresses the sparse reward problem in multi-step LLM agent training by providing step-level feedback through trajectory-based remaining distance estimation, leading to consistent performance improvements over baseline methods.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to learn multi-step behaviors through interaction with their environments. However, rewards in many interactive tasks reflect only the final outcome, providing limited guidance on which intermediate decisions advance the task. Successful training trajectories contain intermediate states that can provide supervision for subsequent interactions. We introduce Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization (T2SPO), a method that uses past interaction trajectories to provide step-level feedback for policy learning. T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with representations of the states visited along the way. Conditioned on these examples, a pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates the remaining distance to success at each state of a new rollout. Changes in this distance estimate across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. As training proceeds, newly completed trajectories refresh the estimator's context, incorporating new experience without updating its parameters. Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO.

</details>


### [167] [MatrixReward: Reward from Rubric Matrix for Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00389)
*Zihan Shen,Qi Liu,Zixuan Yang,Yiqun Chen,Chenglong Zhao,Xiaozhao Wang,Lei He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MatrixReward addresses the challenge of reward design for open-ended query generation by constructing rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix. It uses column spread to measure rubric distinguishability and column correlations to detect rubric repetition, combining these with prior weights to compute relative-closeness quality rewards based on distances to ideal profiles. The method achieves 63.02 average score on Qwen3-8B, outperforming baselines by ~2.0%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-ended query generation lacks standard answers, making reward design challenging. Existing pointwise scoring rubrics provide limited information about relative quality between sample answers under the same prompt, and merging multiple rubric judgments into a single score can mask important differences between answers.

Method: MatrixReward constructs a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix by comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. It uses column spread to capture how strongly each rubric distinguishes current rollouts, and correlations between columns to reveal rubric repetition. These statistics yield data-dependent rubric weights, which are combined with prior weights. After column normalization and weighting, per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles. Each rollout's distances to these ideals determine its relative-closeness quality reward.

Result: Evaluated using Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, MatrixReward achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by approximately 2.0%.

Conclusion: Matrices derived from relative comparisons can be used to construct rewards more reasonably for open-ended generative reinforcement learning.

Abstract: Open-ended query generation lacks standard answers, thus necessitating an effective reward mechanism. Pointwise scoring rubrics provide limited information about the relative quality of sample answers under the same prompt; merging multiple rubric judgments into a single score may also mask the differences between these answers. We propose MatrixReward, which constructs rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix obtained by comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. The spread of each matrix column captures how strongly that rubric distinguishes the current rollouts, while correlations between columns reveal rubric repetition; together, these statistics yield data-dependent rubric weights. We combine these weights with the prior weights of rubrics. After column normalization and weighting, the observed per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles. Each rollout's distances to these two ideals determine its relative-closeness quality reward. Evaluated using Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, MatrixReward achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by approximately 2.0%. These results support the idea that matrices derived from relative comparisons can be used to construct rewards more reasonably for open-ended generative reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [168] [Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00391)
*Michael Vasilakakis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel framework using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) for generating synthetic medical tabular data. The approach uses linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets to represent clinical features and encodes inter-feature dependencies as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated through FCM propagation followed by defuzzification. The method handles mixed data types and domain constraints, running exclusively on CPU while achieving competitive performance against deep generative models like TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing probabilistic and deep generative models for synthetic medical data lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications in computer-based medical systems (CBMSs). Real clinical data is often restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations.

Method: The proposed method uses Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) where: (1) Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets; (2) Inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections; (3) Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types and domain constraints common in health records.

Result: Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets using Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol shows: Accuracy up to 0.81 and AUROC up to 0.90 on Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines. Fidelity metrics: KS Complement up to 0.91, Correlation Similarity up to 0.95. Privacy (DCR Baseline Protection) scores consistently exceed those of TVAE. The method runs exclusively on CPU.

Conclusion: Causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling using FCMs offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs, with strong privacy guarantees and competitive accuracy.

Abstract: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.

</details>


### [169] [Forking: Sudden Overfitting Under Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00394)
*Shanbin Yu,Shaoyang Guo,Haoran Zhao,Danni Yu,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies and studies "forking," a generalization failure in neural language models where training and validation loss sharply diverge at epoch boundaries under data replay conditions, particularly in models with over-encoding n-gram memory branches. The phenomenon is reproduced in both vanilla NanoGPT and DeepSeek-style models, and is linked to repeated updates that sharpen observed continuations while suppressing unseen ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch, to understand its mechanism and implications. This study is motivated by the need to document and understand unexpected phenomena from autoregressive agent-proposed techniques, similar to grokking and double descent.

Method: The researchers reproduce forking in controlled settings using vanilla NanoGPT and a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. They analyze the mechanistic underpinnings by examining how repeated updates affect continuation probabilities, study the role of n-gram modules in creating context-specific subspaces, and investigate factors that suppress or amplify the effect (training budget, table crowding, context frequency).

Result: Forking manifests as a sharp separation of training and validation loss at epoch boundaries under data replay. The phenomenon is driven by repeated updates that sharpen observed continuations while suppressing unseen ones, with loss growing on unseen continuations. Low-frequency contexts contribute most to the gap. Larger training budgets and crowded tables suppress forking. The phenomenon also appears in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes.

Conclusion: Forking represents a previously undocumented generalization phenomenon in deep learning, joining grokking and double descent. The authors caution that while autoresearch agents produce many seemingly useful results, unexpected and unpleasant by-products like forking can emerge, warranting careful evaluation of such proposed techniques.

Abstract: This paper studies forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch. Under data replay, models with an over-encoding n-gram memory branch show a sharp separation of training and validation loss at epoch boundaries, resembling the shape of forks. We study this phenomenon in a controlled vanilla NanoGPT setting and reproduce it in a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. Mechanistically, repeated updates sharpen the continuations observed in training while suppressing the probability of unseen continuations, whose loss grows with each pass. The n-gram module creates weakly interacting context-specific subspaces, amplifying this effect. Low-frequency contexts contribute most of the gap, whereas larger training budgets and heavily crowded tables suppress it. We also observe forking in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes. The contributions of this paper are twofold: (1) Forking reveals yet another curious phenomenon in deep learning, in addition to grokking and double descent. (2) Forking is an unexpected and unpleasant by-product of tricks proposed by autoresearch agents. While these agents produce an enormous number of results that seem useful, we should always be careful with their results.

</details>


### [170] [Specificity-Aware Diffusion Steering via Variance-Reduced Sequential Monte Carlo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00395)
*Luran Wang,Linrui Ma,Hannes Stärk,Regina Barzilay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a specificity-aware steering method for diffusion models that selectively suppresses undesired reference distributions while preserving the desired distribution in overlap regions. It formulates this as a target-design problem, derives an overlap-based objective, and uses a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with variance-minimized proposals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key problem is that existing inference-time steering methods (like negative guidance) cannot effectively distinguish between positive and negative reference distributions when they overlap. Repelling negative samples also erodes positive samples in overlap regions, causing undesired distortion of the target distribution.

Method: The method has three main components: (1) A target-design formulation deriving a time-dependent target distribution from an overlap-based objective that retains the desired distribution only where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired one; (2) A Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler with variance-minimized local proposals for sampling from the target path; (3) A practical fixed-noise optimization procedure using Jacobian-vector products with desired and undesired score fields.

Result: Experiments across four domains—synthetic tasks, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image synthesis, and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder prediction—demonstrate that the method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing SMC weight collapse compared to negative-guidance baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed specificity-aware steering framework successfully addresses the overlap problem in diffusion model steering by explicitly modeling the preference between distributions. The likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity provides a principled way to handle distribution overlap, and the SMC sampler with variance-minimized proposals enables stable sampling from the derived target.

Abstract: Inference-time steering enables pretrained diffusion models to satisfy new constraints without full retraining. However, specificity-aware generation is difficult: repelling samples from a negative reference distribution can also erode the positive distribution where the two overlap. The key challenge is to suppress negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution. We address this problem by formulating specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem and deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective. The resulting target keeps the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired reference distribution, giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity. To sample from the corresponding time-dependent target path, we develop a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal. We further introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure with the Jacobian--vector products with the desired and undesired score fields. Experiments on synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image tasks and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder show that the proposed method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing the SMC weight collapse compared with negative-guidance baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/WangLuran/Specificity-Aware-Diffusion-Steering

</details>


### [171] [NEUROTOKEN: Joint Source and Directional AAD with Envelope Decoding via Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00397)
*Ali Alavi,Donald S. Williamson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces NEUROTOKEN, a neural network for auditory attention decoding (AAD) that uses conditional flow-matching (ATTUNEFLOW) to estimate the conditional likelihood of attended speech envelope given EEG signals. The method addresses limitations in existing AAD approaches by providing a likelihood-based framework rather than single statistics. Two inference-time ensembles (QUADTRACK and ENV-FLOW) are proposed to handle per-statistic failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The cocktail-party problem - identifying which speaker a listener attends to in noisy environments - is crucial for next-generation hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces. Current AAD methods have significant limitations: directional-AAD cannot map side to stream, regression-based methods use noisy Pearson correlations at real-world time windows (1-5s), and envelope reconstruction lacks a native AAD rule. The authors argue that the conditional likelihood (not any single statistic) is the right objective.

Method: NEUROTOKEN uses a single network with three heads sharing one EEG front-end. The key innovation is ATTUNEFLOW, a conditional flow-matching head that scores candidate streams by an integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio. Two inference-time ensembles are proposed: QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalized QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) to absorb per-statistic failure modes.

Result: At 5-second windows on KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU datasets: ATTUNEFLOW improves per-segment source-AAD by 9-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline; across-subject variance is reduced by ~3x; trial-level fusion exceeds 93% accuracy on two of three datasets. Additionally, canonical 95-97% direction-AAD numbers collapse by 17-45% under strict trial-disjoint protocol, revealing true performance ceilings.

Conclusion: The likelihood-based formulation (conditional flow-matching) provides superior AAD performance compared to traditional statistics. The findings clarify the true ceiling of direction-AAD under strict protocols and demonstrate the importance of likelihood-based approaches for practical AAD systems operating at real-world time windows.

Abstract: Identifying which speaker a listener is attending to in a noisy room -- the cocktail-party problem -- is the missing ingredient for next-generation hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces: it tells the device whose voice to amplify. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) reads this answer from EEG, but the literature splits into disconnected pieces: directional-AAD classifies side but does not map side to stream; regression-based source-AAD ranks candidate streams by a single Pearson correlation that is intrinsically noisy at the 1-5 s windows real devices need; and envelope reconstruction has no native AAD rule. We argue the right object is not any single statistic but the conditional likelihood of the attended envelope given EEG, and we make this practical with NEUROTOKEN: a single network whose three heads share one EEG front-end, with a conditional flow-matching head (ATTUNEFLOW) that scores candidates by an integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio. Two inference-time ensembles -- QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalised QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) -- absorb per-statistic failure modes for free. On KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU at 5 s, ATTUNEFLOW lifts per-segment source-AAD by 9%-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline and shrinks across-subject variance by ~3x; trial-level fusion exceeds 93% on two of three datasets. In parallel reproductions we show that canonical 95-97% direction-AAD numbers collapse by 17%-45% under a strict trial-disjoint protocol, clarifying both the true ceiling and why a likelihood-based formulation is needed.

</details>


### [172] [WIPSNet: Deep Learning for Paediatric Wheeze Detection from Overnight Impedance Pneumography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00398)
*Felix Oury,Harley Day,Karina Mayoral,Ville-Pekka Seppä,Sejal Saglani,Reiko J. Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes WIPSNet, a 3D ResNet-based deep learning model that uses continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight impedance pneumography (IP) signals to classify nocturnal wheeze in paediatric patients. It significantly outperforms the traditional EVI metric and other deep learning approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The current clinical standard (EVI) compresses entire overnight IP recordings into a single scalar, yielding poor classification performance (AUC = 0.633). This motivated the exploration of more sophisticated time-frequency representations and deep learning architectures to capture richer temporal dynamics in paediatric respiratory monitoring.

Method: WIPSNet uses 3D ResNet architecture operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform (CWT) scalograms of overnight IP signals. The model was evaluated on 15 patients (60 nights, 281 hours of data) and compared against EVI, a state-space model (Mamba), and two sleep-staging architectures.

Result: WIPSNet achieved an AUC of 0.783 ± 0.026, substantially outperforming EVI (0.633), Mamba, and the other architectures. The optimal performance required 32 minutes of temporal context (volumetric depth), indicating that multi-scale temporal aggregation is important for modelling nocturnal respiratory dynamics.

Conclusion: Structured time-frequency representations (CWT scalograms) combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series. This approach captures multi-scale temporal patterns that are lost in traditional scalar-based metrics like EVI.

Abstract: Overnight impedance pneumography (IP) is used to monitor paediatric respiratory health. Its current clinical readout, the Expiratory Variability Index (EVI), compresses each IP recording into a single scalar and achieves an AUC of 0.633 for night-level wheeze classification. We introduce Wheeze Impedance Pneumography Scalogram Network (WIPSNet), a 3D ResNet operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight IP signals. On a 15-patient cohort (60 nights, 281 hours), WIPSNet achieves an AUC of $0.783 \pm 0.026$, outperforming EVI, a state-space model (Mamba), and two modern sleep-staging architectures. Performance peaks at a volumetric depth corresponding to 32 minutes of temporal context, suggesting that multi-scale temporal aggregation is important for modelling nocturnal respiratory dynamics. Overall, these results indicate that structured time-frequency representations combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series.

</details>


### [173] [Metacognitive Reasoning in Energy Based Models using Instance Based Learning Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00399)
*Tailia Malloy,Prateek Kumar Rajput,Serge Lionel Nikiema,Cleotilde Gonzalez,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces MERITED, a framework combining Energy-Based Models (EBMs) with Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) to enable metacognitive reasoning in AI systems. The framework allows dynamic allocation of computational resources based on uncertainty estimation, addressing limitations of current LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs cannot estimate uncertainty without first responding, nor can they dynamically allocate computational resources during reasoning. This limits their ability to implement metacognitive processes similar to human decision-making about cognitive effort allocation.

Method: The authors propose combining EBMs (for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic compute allocation) with Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) to model human-like metacognitive decisions. The framework controls computational effort in the EBM based on uncertainty estimates.

Result: The paper reports two main contributions: (1) a trained 191M parameter reasoning EBM with open weights, and (2) an implementation of the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model.

Conclusion: This work enables metacognitive control over reasoning effort in AI systems, allowing them to dynamically allocate computational resources based on uncertainty while remaining computationally efficient, drawing on human cognitive models.

Abstract: Metacognition involves reasoning about cognitive processes themselves. An example is in resource allocation where we choose how much time and effort to put into a reasoning task before we begin based on our confidence. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot estimate their uncertainty about an output without first responding, and cannot dynamically allocate resources to producing an output, making this type of metacognitive process difficult. A recently proposed alternative to classic transformer architectures that addresses these two concerns is the Energy Based Model (EBM) which allows for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic allocation of compute resources. While EBMs can allow for control of these two processes, the actual metacognitive task of determining compute allocation based on uncertainty is not directly addressed. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides an approach to modeling human-like decisions from experience that has previously been applied to predicting human metacognitive reasoning. In this paper we introduce a framework for MEtacognitive Reasoning with Instance-based Learning Theory and Energy Dynamics (MERITED). Grounded in IBLT, this framework allows for control of the computational effort allocated in an EBM to allow for metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty while remaining computationally efficient. This work has two main contributions, the training and open weight sharing of a 191M parameter reasoning EBM, and an implementation of the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model.

</details>


### [174] [Representation Transitions Reveal Emerging Safety Risks in Multi-Turn LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00400)
*Haoyu Wang,Wei Zhao,Yedi Zhang,Christopher M. Poskitt,Jun Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents DART, a runtime defense framework that detects multi-turn attacks on agentic systems by monitoring accumulated representation transitions in the model's internal states, using a denoising technique to filter out benign representation drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn attacks compose individually harmless actions into harmful outcomes, evading defenses that assess actions in isolation. Existing defenses struggle to detect these attacks because they lack a mechanism to identify the accumulated harm signature across context updates.

Method: The authors propose DART, which detects harmful representation transitions by: (1) identifying triggering contexts from representation shifts, (2) denoising the safety direction by anchoring benign traffic at zero and removing leading variation directions, and (3) intervening with targeted reminders at runtime. No auxiliary model is required.

Result: On MT-AgentRisk: attack success reduced from 84% to 25%, with 12% false-alarm rate. On ASEval: reduced from 97% to 52%, with 0% benign non-refusal. DART outperforms ToolShield (55% vs 25% on MT-AgentRisk). Denoising is critical—undenoised monitor catches only 7-40% vs 60-85% for denoised. Covers single-turn indirect injection without modification, adding only 0.14-0.56s overhead per step.

Conclusion: DART provides an effective, lightweight runtime defense against multi-turn attacks by leveraging internal representation dynamics with denoising. The approach successfully reduces attack success rates significantly while maintaining low false-alarm rates and minimal overhead, offering a practical complement to computation-heavy speculative defenses.

Abstract: Multi-turn attacks on agentic systems can compose individually permissible actions into harmful outcomes, challenging defenses that assess actions or states in isolation. We show that such attacks leave a detectable signature in the agent's internal representations: harmful behavior emerges as an accumulated representation transition across context updates, whose triggering context can be identified from the same signal. We further find that naive aggregation is confounded by benign representation drift, as a contrastive safety direction need not assign zero to benign transitions. We address this by denoising the direction, anchoring benign traffic at zero and removing its leading variation directions, with no runtime cost.
  These findings motivate DART, a runtime framework that detects and attributes representation shifts and intervenes with targeted reminders. Across six models and two multi-turn benchmarks, DART reduces attack success from 84% to 25% on MT-AgentRisk, catching every attack at a mean false-alarm rate of 12%, and from 97% to 52% on ASEval, at costs in benign non-refusal of 8% and 0%, respectively. On MT-AgentRisk, it outperforms ToolShield, the state-of-the-art multi-turn defense, on all six models: under the same protocol, ToolShield reaches only 55%. Denoising is critical: on ASEval, the undenoised monitor catches only 7%-40% of attacks, while the denoised monitor catches 60%-85%. The same monitor covers single-turn indirect injection without modification and adds only 0.14-0.56 s overhead per monitored step without requiring an auxiliary model, making it a lightweight complement to computation-heavy speculative defenses.

</details>


### [175] [The Conflict Between Logic and Memory: Learning Higher-Order Interactions in Shallow MLPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00403)
*Gongyue Zhang,Honghai Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural networks can learn to fit training data without capturing the true underlying rule. This paper studies single-hidden-layer MLPs on synthetic tasks, examining how optimization methods (SGD, Adam, Muon) and nuisance inputs affect the learning of higher-order rules (parity functions).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand why neural networks sometimes achieve high training accuracy but fail to generalize to the true rule that generated labels. The separation between "fitting examples" and "recovering the rule" is a fundamental issue in deep learning.

Method: Synthetic tasks controlling interaction order and nuisance inputs; experiments with different optimizers (SGD, Adam, Muon); interventions including freezing first-layer weights and removing nuisance inputs at test time; analysis of Bayes posterior and ReLU network representations.

Result: SGD, Adam, and Muon achieve different performance on higher-order parity tasks: at order 2, all reach 100%; at order 3, they achieve 96.25%, 50.87%, and 76.82% respectively; Muon reaches 99.21% at order 4. Freezing nuisance-connected weights improves AdamW accuracy from 44.73% to 95.07%. Nuisance-weight learning affects training outcomes beyond prediction. Both SGD and Muon learn orders 5-8 in compact regime, with higher SGD accuracy at orders 9-11.

Conclusion: Optimization dynamics and nuisance learning significantly constrain the higher-order rules that shallow networks can realize. Different optimizers show distinct capabilities for learning interaction order, and the presence of nuisance inputs fundamentally changes training outcomes through their effect on weight learning, not just predictions.

Abstract: A network can fit its training examples while failing to recover the rule that generated their labels. We examine this separation in single-hidden-layer multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), using synthetic tasks that control interaction order and the presence of nuisance inputs. We establish elementary benchmark properties: pure parity contains no predictive lower-order marginals, admits an exact Bayes posterior, and can be represented on clean latent inputs by a width-$k$ ReLU network. Experiments then identify distinct optimization outcomes. In a matched order-2--4 sweep, SGD, Adam, and Muon all reach 100\% peak test accuracy at order two; at order three they reach 96.25\%, 50.87\%, and 76.82\%, respectively, while Muon reaches 99.21\% at order four. In a separate mixed-order task, freezing only the first-layer weights connected to independent nuisance inputs raises AdamW's epoch-10 accuracy from 44.73\% to 95.07\%. Removing the same inputs only at test time raises it to 48.38\%. Thus, nuisance-weight learning changes the training outcome beyond its immediate effect on prediction. Bias interventions expose a connection between target symmetry and shallow ReLU representations. In a compact signal-only regime, both SGD and Muon learn orders five through eight, with higher SGD peak accuracy at orders nine through eleven. Together, the results show how optimization and nuisance learning constrain the higher-order rules realized by a shallow network.

</details>


### [176] [RACE: Residual-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Neighbor-Rich Time-Series Foundation Model Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00405)
*Hao-Nan Shi,Tong Wu,Chen-Cong Sun,Yuan Jiang,Han-Jia Ye,De-Chuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RACE is a two-stage framework that improves time-series foundation model (TSFM) forecasting by leveraging neighbor series evidence without modifying the backbone model. It retrieves compatible neighbors, aligns residuals, and uses a lightweight Gate to determine when corrections are beneficial, showing improvements across multiple TSFMs and domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series foundation models perform well in forecasting but struggle with neighbor-rich settings where related but non-identical historical series are available. Existing methods either fine-tune for each target (costly, limited transferability) or append retrieved series without verification. The key challenges are conflicting residual evidence from neighbors and varying residual patterns across different TSFMs and tasks.

Method: RACE uses a two-stage approach: (1) RACE-TF (training-free): retrieves query-compatible neighbors, aligns their residuals to query scale, and aggregates coherent evidence; (2) Full RACE: adds a lightweight domain-specific Gate that learns when applying the correction is beneficial. The training workflow is reusable across TSFM backbones.

Result: Across four TSFMs, RACE improves all three domain-aggregate metrics on both primary domains (CGM and Web/cloud workloads), with largest gains on high-error queries. The Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to other backbones without adaptation, improving all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons over matched frozen targets.

Conclusion: Test-time neighborhood scaling (using same-domain neighbor evidence without modifying the backbone) is an effective approach for improving TSFMs in neighbor-rich forecasting scenarios. RACE achieves significant improvements with zero backbone modifications and excellent cross-backbone transferability, making it a practical solution for deploying TSFMs in real-world forecasting applications.

Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) perform strongly across forecasting tasks, but their per-series inference is ill-suited to neighbor-rich forecasting, where each query has access to related but nonidentical historical series. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and Web/cloud workloads exemplify this setting: CGM trajectories share physiological patterns but vary across individuals, devices, and conditions, while Web/cloud workloads combine common operating regimes with non-stationarity, heavy tails, and bursts.
