DARA computes its weights from each rollout batch, adapting to changes in reward activity throughout training without modifying the underlying policy optimization objective. Experiments on tool calling and mathematical reasoning show that DARA learns the targeted behaviors faster than GDPO, reaching high format compliance in up to 26% fewer training steps on tool calling and near-saturated length compliance in up to 65% fewer steps on mathematical reasoning, while remaining competitive in final performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhaihaotian/DARA.

</details>


### [200] [From Task Mixtures to Specialized Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00580)
*Hojat Allah Salehi,Mehrdad Mahdavi,Andrew Arash Mahyari,M. Hadi Amini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses compound heterogeneity in federated learning, where data distributions vary both across and within clients. When tasks share the same feature geometry, the optimal model for a client's task mixture under squared loss is a convex combination of optimal models for underlying tasks. This motivates routing inputs to specialized experts. With small task-labeled public samples, a convex program recovers task experts. The proposed FedSEE method avoids negative transfer and improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional federated learning addresses heterogeneity across clients but fails to handle latent task mixtures within each client. This compound heterogeneity (heterogeneous data both across and within clients) is common in practice but underexplored.

Method: The study analyzes adaptation over a common frozen representation. When tasks share the same feature geometry, the optimal model for a client's task mixture under squared loss is a convex combination of optimal models for underlying tasks. With access to a small set of task-labeled public samples, a convex program is derived to recover task experts and match them to corresponding tasks. Task-aligned routing is proposed, and FedSEE is developed based on this analysis.

Result: When task optima form a simplex, task-aligned routing achieves lower risk than any single adapted model for genuinely mixed clients. FedSEE avoids negative transfer observed in evaluated baselines and improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile.

Conclusion: Effective specialization requires input-dependent expert selection aligned with each client's task mixture. FedSEE effectively addresses compound heterogeneity in federated learning by leveraging task-specific routing and expert recovery.

Abstract: In collaborative foundation model fine-tuning, client data is rarely homogeneous. Instead, clients typically possess unknown mixtures of distinct data distributions, or tasks. Conventional federated learning primarily addresses heterogeneity across clients without explicitly resolving latent task mixtures within each client. We study this setting as compound heterogeneity, where data is heterogeneous both across and within clients. We study adaptation over a common frozen representation and show that, when tasks share the same feature geometry, the optimal model for a client's task mixture under squared loss is a convex combination of the optimal models for its underlying tasks. Thus, a single locally trained model represents the client's overall task mixture, while individual inputs may be drawn from different underlying task distributions. This motivates routing inputs to specialized experts, and we show that, when the task optima form a simplex, task-aligned routing achieves lower risk than any single adapted model for genuinely mixed clients. With access to a small set of task-labeled public samples, we derive a convex program to recover task experts and match them to their corresponding tasks. Our routing analysis shows that effective specialization requires input-dependent expert selection aligned with each client's task mixture. Motivated by this analysis, we propose FedSEE. Across our experiments, FedSEE avoids the negative transfer observed in the evaluated baselines and improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile.

</details>


### [201] [Right In-Place (RiP) Convolution: A Simple, General, and Near-Optimal Strategy for Memory-Efficient CNN Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00586)
*Opegbemi Matthias Busoye,Tolulope Matthew Busoye,Eghonghon-aye Eigbe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses memory optimization for CNN inference on microcontrollers by correcting bugs in prior in-place convolution work and proposing Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, achieving 12.5-33.5% memory reduction while maintaining bit-identical outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation memory (not compute) limits CNN inference on constrained hardware like microcontrollers. Existing in-place convolution solutions have bugs and limitations (valid padding, unit stride/dilation, odd square kernels only), and the non-sequential traversal incurs 2× inference time overhead.

Method: The authors identified two regimes where prior work fails: (1) under-allocation of (k-1)C_in mod (C_out-C_in) scalars causing silent input corruption; (2) unbounded overestimate up to 2432× when the critical leg leaves the output grid. They corrected both issues and generalized to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. They proposed RiP convolution where each layer reads input right-aligned in shared workspace and writes output left-aligned from index zero, using piecewise affine debt evaluation in O(1) time.

Result: Across 10,000 random layers, RiP produced no corruption. Across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures, it matched herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81 layers, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Deployed to Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it reduced peak activation memory across 11 MCUNet models by 12.5-33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising models fitting Pico 1's 256KB SRAM from 6 to 9.

Conclusion: Right In-Place (RiP) convolution is a practical, memory-efficient solution for CNN inference on microcontrollers that generalizes prior work while eliminating bugs. It achieves significant memory savings (12.5-33.3%) without performance degradation, enabling more deep learning models to run on memory-constrained devices.

Abstract: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Direct in-place convolution removes the dual-buffer cost, but the memory-optimal formulation of Gural and Murmann assumes valid padding, unit stride, unit dilation, and odd square kernels, and needs a non-sequential traversal costing $2\times$ inference time in transposes. We identify two regimes in which their published closed form does not hold: (1) an under-allocation of exactly $(k-1)C_{in} \bmod (C_{out}-C_{in})$ scalars, active on every convolutional layer of their own deployed network and manifesting as a silent corruption of still-live input; (2) an unbounded overestimate, up to $2{,}432\times$, once the critical leg leaves the output grid. We correct both and generalize to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. We then propose Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a bit-identical operation in which every layer reads its input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes its output left-aligned from index zero. The debt is piecewise affine in the output pixel index, so evaluating its breakpoints in $O(1)$ yields the minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid, with row-major access preserved. Across $10{,}000$ random layers RiP produced no corruption, and across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures it matches the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Written into TinyEngine's kernels and deployed to a Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it cuts peak activation memory across eleven MCUNet models by 12.5 to 33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising the number of models that fit the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.

</details>


### [202] [ALER: Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00592)
*Oleg Shchendrigin,Egor Cherepanov,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces ALER (Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting), an RL agent that addresses three memory requirements in partially observable environments: retention, rewriting (updating decision-relevant content), and experience fusion (transforming old content based on later observations). The authors also propose Rune-Mazes, a suite of three environments testing these capabilities. ALER combines an LSTM with a slot memory using Gumbel-Softmax writes and learned gates, achieving state-of-the-art results across 16 Endless T-Maze configurations (≥0.82 success rate), 5 Rune T-Maze compositions (≥0.99), and outperforming baselines on Rune Multi-Corridor and pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory architectures and benchmarks for partially observable RL primarily test retention (keeping information unchanged). However, real-world scenarios require updating stored information based on new observations and transforming old content through learned rules. This work addresses the gap by formalizing two additional memory requirements—rewriting and experience fusion—and creating benchmarks that specifically test these capabilities.

Method: The authors formalize three memory requirements: retention (keeping information unchanged), rewriting (setting decision-relevant content to a value independent of the old one), and experience fusion (transforming old content via rules specified by later observations). They introduce ALER, which pairs an LSTM with a slot memory using: (1) an independently addressed Gumbel-Softmax write mechanism that concentrates weight on one slot for overwriting, and (2) a learned gate that fuses retrieved content with the recurrent state before policy and value heads. They also create Rune-Mazes environments where rune observations invert, cancel, reset, or repeat updates to a hidden cue.

Result: ALER achieves at least 0.82 success rate on all 16 Endless T-Maze configurations and at least 0.99 on all five Rune T-Maze compositions. It has the highest mean success rate on four-branch Rune Multi-Corridor with an Invert rune. On pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory, ALER outperforms PPO-LSTM in 8 of 10 configurations. The study also finds that several baselines reach their lowest success rates on compositions requiring more memory states.

Conclusion: The three requirements (retention, rewriting, experience fusion) provide a useful framework for evaluating memory in partially observable RL. ALER's architecture with slot-based memory and Gumbel-Softmax writes effectively addresses these requirements, demonstrating superior performance across diverse benchmark configurations. The Rune-Mazes suite offers valuable testbeds for evaluating memory mechanisms beyond simple retention.

Abstract: In partially observable reinforcement learning (RL), a later observation can make stored information obsolete or change what it implies for the next decision. Memory architectures and benchmarks for RL mostly test retention, the ability to keep information unchanged until it is needed. We formalize two further requirements. Rewriting sets the decision-relevant content to a value independent of the old one, and experience fusion transforms the old content by a rule that a later observation specifies. For tasks built from such updates, we count the memory states that a solution needs, and several baselines reach their lowest success rates on compositions that need more states. We introduce ALER (Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting), an agent that pairs an LSTM with a slot memory. An independently addressed Gumbel-Softmax write that concentrates its weight on one slot overwrites that slot, and a learned gate fuses the retrieved content with the recurrent state before the policy and value heads. We also introduce Rune-Mazes, three environments in which rune observations invert, cancel, reset, or repeat updates of a hidden cue under vector and pixel observations. Against seven baselines, ALER reaches a success rate of at least $0.82$ in all sixteen Endless T-Maze configurations and at least $0.99$ on all five Rune T-Maze compositions, and it has the highest mean success rate on four-branch Rune Multi-Corridor with an Invert rune. On pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory, it has a higher mean success rate than PPO-LSTM in eight of ten configurations. Project page: https://quartz-admirer.github.io/ALER-Adaptive-Learnable-Experience-Rewriting/.

</details>


### [203] [MIKASA-Robo-VLA: Benchmarking Memory in VLA Models for Long-Horizon Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00604)
*Egor Cherepanov,Nikita Kachaev,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MIKASA-Robo-VLA is a benchmark of 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks designed to evaluate how vision-language-action policies handle information that disappears during task execution. Most tasks (80) hide the cue an action depends on, while 10 are reactive controls. The benchmark includes 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types, with a reference baseline achieving 21.1% mean task success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language-action policies typically see only one or a few recent frames, making it difficult to evaluate how they utilize information that disappears during a task. Existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of memory-dependent policies.

Method: The benchmark constructs 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks where memory-dependent tasks hide task-relevant cues during specified time intervals. An information gap measures when cues are provably absent. A reference π₀.₅ baseline using only current images and proprioception (no observation history or explicit memory) was fine-tuned on 14 tasks.

Result: The baseline achieves 0.211 ± 0.044 mean task success. For 70 tasks, environment phase timings specify an information gap, and for 28 of them the gap exceeds the 16-frame window of the widest fixed-context VLA surveyed. The baseline shows lower success on Long-split tasks, confounded by open-loop chunking and memory types.

Conclusion: MIKASA-Robo-VLA provides a systematic benchmark for evaluating memory-dependent vision-language-action policies. The low baseline success (21.1%) indicates significant challenges in handling temporal information gaps, particularly for long-horizon tasks. The benchmark releases 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types to facilitate research in this direction.

Abstract: Vision-language-action policies often see only one or a few recent frames, which makes it difficult to evaluate how they use information that disappears during a task. We introduce MIKASA-Robo-VLA, a benchmark of 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks. All but 10 hide the cue an action depends on. Those 10 are reactive controls. MIKASA-Robo, the suite it rebuilds, has 32 tasks and uses language only in a representative VLA subset. Here every task provides an instruction, while memory-dependent tasks hide a task-relevant cue and reactive controls keep it available. For 70 tasks, environment phase timings specify an information gap, and for 28 of them the gap exceeds the 16-frame window of the widest fixed-context VLA we survey. The gap counts only the interval the cue is provably absent, not the full duration a policy must retain it, so every memory-dependent task still requires memory by construction, including the ones whose measured gap is short. We release 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3. A reference $π_{0.5}$ baseline with current images and proprioception, but no observation history or explicit memory module, is fine-tuned on 14 tasks and achieves 0.211 $\pm$ 0.044 mean task success. Its lower success on the evaluated Long-split tasks is confounded by open-loop chunking and the memory types represented in that subset. Project page: https://mikasarobo.github.io/

</details>


### [204] [Learning the identity: a case study of how SGD selects among functional decompositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00615)
*Andy Arditi,Weian Xie,David Bau,Liu Ziyin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates why stochastic gradient descent (SGD) prefers certain solutions over others when training deep linear residual networks to learn the identity function. The key insight is that while there exists a manifold of population-loss minimizers (all achieving zero loss), SGD consistently favors specific decompositions of the identity across network layers. The authors explain this through "entropic loss" - which includes a term for expected squared norm of minibatch gradients - and show that this framework predicts the structure of solutions favored by SGD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors were motivated by the observation that learning the identity function with deep linear residual networks, which should be trivial (weights can simply collapse to zero), actually exhibits complex behavior. SGD reproducibly favors particular solutions on the manifold of population-loss minimizers, even without explicit regularization like weight decay. This challenges the conventional understanding of neural network training dynamics.

Method: The authors use analytical methods to characterize the entropic loss and its minimizers on the identity manifold. They also conduct experiments with different parameterizations (factoring weight matrices into products) and varying label noise conditions to validate their theoretical predictions.

Result: The key findings are: (1) There exists a manifold of population-loss minimizers for identity learning, not just the zero-weight solution; (2) SGD favors particular decompositions of the identity across layers, even with weight decay; (3) Changing parameterization while keeping realizable functions unchanged causes weights to collapse to zero; (4) The entropic loss framework accurately predicts the structure of solutions favored by SGD; (5) Networks trained with SGD closely match theoretical predictions.

Conclusion: The identity learning task serves as a clean case study demonstrating that entropic loss provides a useful lens for understanding SGD's implicit bias. This framework explains why SGD favors certain decompositions of the same input-output function over others, even when the population loss is identical across all solutions.

Abstract: One might think that learning the identity function with a deep linear residual network is trivial - the path along residual connections already implements the identity, and so the network need only drive its weights to zero. However, this zero-weight solution is just one point on an entire manifold of population-loss minimizers, each corresponding to a different decomposition of the identity across the network's layers. Although the population loss does not distinguish among these solutions, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) reproducibly favors particular ones. For instance, under anisotropic label noise, the learned layers exhibit a noise-dependent spectrum; even with weight decay, SGD does not generally recover the zero-weight solution. Changing only the parametrization, while leaving the set of realizable functions unchanged, yields different behavior: factoring each weight matrix as a product of two matrices causes the weights to collapse to zero, even without explicit weight decay.
  While perhaps mysterious and unintuitive at first, these phenomena can be understood through the lens of entropic loss, which augments the population loss with a term proportional to the expected squared norm of the minibatch gradient (Ziyin et al., 2025). On the identity manifold, the population loss is constant, while the entropic term distinguishes among these decompositions. We characterize its minimizers analytically and use them to derive predictions for the structure of solutions favored by SGD. Networks trained with SGD closely match these predictions.
  Overall, the identity learning task studied here serves as a clean and simple case study of how the lens of entropic loss can clarify why SGD favors particular decompositions of the same input-output function.

</details>


### [205] [Misalignment of Low-Loss Regions Causes Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00620)
*Yongding Tian,Zaid Al-Ars,Maksim Kitsak,Peter Hofstee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Grokking refers to the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. Although first observed in small algorithmic tasks trained with transformers, its underlying mechanism remains unsettled. In this work, we develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. The framework predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking: under a symmetry-preserving train/validation split, we observe a stable anti-grokking case in which validation performance does not recover. This counterexample challenges several existing correlational explanations of grokking. More broadly, our analysis framework and results further suggest that grokking arises when the low-loss regions induced by the training and validation partitions are misaligned. Once these regions become well aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking and the observed dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior.

</details>


### [206] [Learning Linear Systems under Heavy-Tailed Noise: A Non-Asymptotic Analysis from A Single Trajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00637)
*Xiaomian Yang,Sungho Shin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Establishes non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for least-squares estimation of vector autoregressive models with heavy-tailed noise, achieving error rate of Õ(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p}) under p-th moment boundedness (p > 2).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analysis of autoregressive models typically assumes light-tailed noise (sub-Gaussian), while real-world systems often exhibit heavy-tailed noise characteristics. This work addresses the gap by providing finite-sample guarantees for exponentially stable systems with heavy-tailed noise.

Method: Least-squares estimation on a single observed trajectory under assumptions of i.i.d. noise, bounded noise covariance, and persistent excitation. Uses a unifying approach applicable to broad noise distributions including sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian cases.

Result: Error bound: Õ(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p}) where T is samples, r is noise dimension, and p > 2. The bound also applies to ARX models with dimension factor independent of model order.

Conclusion: The derived bounds provide finite-sample guarantees for VAR estimation under heavy-tailed noise, with the approach being generalizable to various noise distributions. The dimension factor independence from model order in ARX models is a notable finding.

Abstract: We establish non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for the least-squares estimation of vector autoregressive models for exponentially stable systems with heavy-tailed noise based on a single observed trajectory. By assuming i.i.d. noise, bounded noise covariance, and persistent excitation, we show that the estimation error is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p})$ under bounded $p$th moment for $p > 2$, where $T$ is the number of samples, $r$ is the noise dimension, and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic terms. We also introduce a unifying approach to sample complexity analysis applicable to broad classes of noise distributions and showcase this by deriving error bounds for sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian noise distributions. Finally, we specialize our analysis to autoregressive models with exogenous inputs and show that the dimension factor of the error bound is independent of the model order.

</details>


### [207] [Group-Invariant Statistics Determine Embedding Geometry: Harmonic Analysis of Representations from Bach to the Night Sky](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00647)
*Liam Storan,Andreas Tolias,Nina Miolane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper generalizes the explanation for geometric structures (circles, Pringle manifolds) observed in language model embeddings. The key insight is that when word co-occurrence statistics are invariant under a group G, the learned embeddings consist of irreducible representation (irrep) matrix elements of G. This theory is verified across three settings: cyclic group Z_12 for months, dihedral group for musical chords/circle of fifths, and spherical harmonics for celestial objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work only explained circles and Pringle manifolds through translation symmetry on abelian lattices. The authors seek to generalize this to arbitrary symmetry groups, providing a unified theoretical framework that explains various geometric structures observed in learned word embeddings.

Method: Theoretical analysis using group theory and representation theory. The authors prove that group-invariant co-occurrence statistics lead to embeddings that are matrix elements of irreducible representations (irreps) of the symmetry group. Three experimental settings are used for verification: (i) Z_12 cyclic group for months, (ii) dihedral group for musical triads, (iii) spherical harmonics for celestial objects.

Result: The theory successfully explains: (1) circular geometry of months via Z_12 irreps, (2) circle of fifths emergence in chord embeddings via dihedral group symmetry (T/I group), (3) spherical representations of celestial objects as spherical-harmonic embeddings. All three cases demonstrate that geometric structure in embeddings derives from statistical symmetry of underlying data.

Conclusion: The geometry of learned representations in language models is often a direct consequence of the statistical symmetry present in the underlying data. This provides a unifying theoretical framework that connects group theory, representation theory, and emergent geometric structures in neural language models.

Abstract: The representations that language models learn for concepts such as months, weekdays, and places display consistent geometric structure: circles and saddle-shaped "Pringle" manifolds. Recent work traced these structures to $\textit{translation symmetry}$ in word co-occurrence statistics, deriving the observed Fourier geometry when co-occurrence depends only on distance on an abelian lattice of concepts. We demonstrate that more general notions of symmetry lead to equally structured predictions. Considering symmetries defined by arbitrary finite groups, compact groups, and homogeneous spaces, we prove that whenever the co-occurrence statistics of a word family are invariant under a group $G$, the learned word embeddings consist of matrix elements of the irreducible representations (irreps) of $G$. Circles and Pringles arise when $G$ is cyclic, in which case the irreps are Fourier modes. We verify the irrep structure in three experimental settings. (i) The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$: for the months of the year we recover the known circular geometry. (ii) A dihedral group acting on the major and minor triads: we unify two classical observations -- that transposition and chord inversion form a group ($T/I$) acting on chords (music theory), which $\textit{implies}$ that the well-known "circle of fifths" emerges in learned chord embeddings (machine learning). (iii) We explain and reproduce a recently discovered spherical representation of celestial objects in large language models (LLMs) as a spherical-harmonic embedding derived from our theory. Our results demonstrate that the geometry of learned representations is often a consequence of the statistical symmetry of underlying data.

</details>


### [208] [Exploring More, Reasoning Better: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive GRPO for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00661)
*Yue YU,Bowen Zuo,David Crandall,Yinglun Zhu,Dongruo Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StepRS-GRPO introduces a risk coefficient that varies across denoising states in diffusion LLM training, improving mathematical reasoning performance and answer diversity compared to centered GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs generate text by denoising sequences in parallel, but RLVR reuses terminal feedback across decisions even as conditioning context changes. The authors identify this mismatch and propose stepwise risk-sensitive optimization to address it.

Method: StepRS-GRPO varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, this transformation is a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection.

Result: Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. Mass-matched controls support contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and gains persist after matching RMS of advantages. Reasoning-trace diagnostics show diversity gains extend beyond final-answer strings.

Conclusion: StepRS-GRPO effectively addresses the temporal inconsistency in RLVR for diffusion LLMs by adapting risk sensitivity across denoising states, achieving superior accuracy and coverage while maintaining diverse reasoning traces.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by denoising a sequence or successive blocks, allowing several tokens to be revealed in parallel. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions, even as their conditioning context changes. We propose stepwise risk-sensitive GRPO (StepRS-GRPO), which varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, we show that this transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection. Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. In our ablation studies, mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and the gains persist after matching the root mean square (RMS) of the advantages to that of centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics further show that the diversity gains from StepRS-GRPO extend beyond final-answer strings.

</details>


### [209] [Analysis of Quantized and Efficiently Adapted Protein Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00665)
*Ilan Yaniv Zeisler,Sebastian Clancy,Pouriya Bayat,Saaim Raad,Ivan Kraskov,Matthew Xie,Vivian White,Spencer Perkins,Serena Singh,Sepehr Bayat,Keith Pardee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 4-bit quantization and QLoRA (quantized low-rank adapter fine-tuning) across multiple protein language models (PLMs) for both prediction tasks and unconditional generation. The study benchmarks 7 models (ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, Profluent-E1) and 5 generative models, finding that quantization can retain >90% of full fine-tuning performance while achieving up to 90% GPU memory savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protein language models are powerful but computationally expensive. This study addresses the gap in understanding how quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (QLoRA) affect PLM performance, representations, and generation capabilities.

Method: Evaluated 4-bit quantization and QLoRA across 7 PLMs (ESM-2, ESM-C, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, Profluent-E1) for protein prediction tasks, and 5 generative models (ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM, ESM3) for unconditional generation. Assessed performance, GPU memory usage, representations, training speed, and power effects.

Result: For prediction tasks: many model-task pairs retained >90% of full fine-tuning performance; peak GPU memory savings reached ~90% for largest models; QLoRA preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle/late layers. For generation: 4-bit quantization largely preserved structural/sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions.

Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization effectively reduce PLM computational requirements (especially GPU memory). QLoRA is recommended as first-pass strategy for memory-limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures, or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis to detect quantization-induced shifts.

Abstract: Background: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used for sequence generation and property prediction, but their size makes fine-tuning and deployment expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations and generation remain insufficiently characterized. Results: We evaluated 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) across ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3 and Profluent-E1. Across protein prediction tasks, many model-task pairs retained more than 90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings approached 90% for the largest models, although performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers, resembling full fine-tuning with smaller representational changes. Training speed and power effects were more varied. For unconditional generation with ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM and ESM3, 4-bit quantization largely preserved predicted structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions. Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization reduce PLM computational requirements, particularly GPU memory usage. Our results support QLoRA as a first-pass strategy for memory limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts. These approaches can broaden access to large-scale protein modelling while requiring model- and task-specific validation.

</details>


### [210] [ORBIT-FMIB: Tracking Order-Resolved Epistatic Information Through ESM-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00672)
*Maryam Rahimimovassagh,Ivan Garibay,Niloofar Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation, to test whether ESM-2 protein foundation models retain higher-order epistatic information as strongly as lower-order information. Initial results suggested higher-order information loss, but independent replication showed the effect was not robust, leaving the directional question open.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but it is unclear what forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. The study specifically asks whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy.

Method: The study developed ORBIT-FMIB, combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method was validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before application to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations. An initial production run was followed by an independent replication under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, with multiple evaluation-pairing choices applied to trained critics.

Result: Initial production run showed ESM-2 retained higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information (Δ_HO-LO = -0.107). However, independent replication substantially reduced this contrast (Δ_HO-LO = -0.017), and the sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices (-0.011 to +0.015).

Conclusion: There is currently no robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The study demonstrates why probing interaction structure in protein foundation models requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before outputs are treated as biological findings. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for future studies.

Abstract: Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance alone does not reveal which forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. We ask whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy, introducing ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method is validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before being applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations.
  An initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.107$). An independent replication of the complete measurement grid, under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, substantially reduced this contrast ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.017$), and its sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics ($-0.011$ to $+0.015$). We therefore do not currently have robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its documented removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and is unaffected by this finding. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models; this study's own replication result illustrates why such probing requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before its output is treated as a biological finding.

</details>


### [211] [LabBook: Harnessing Experimental History for Efficient LLM-Driven Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00675)
*Bo Yuan,Wenqian Ye,Zelin Zhao,Lama Moukheiber,Henry Kautz,Aidong Zhang,Yongxin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LabBook introduces a single-agent discovery harness with an agent-maintained memory that separates complete history retention from selective context construction in LLM-driven discovery, improving quality-cost trade-off over evolutionary baselines without requiring explicit population or branching search structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery either generate programs from a small set of selected ancestors (omitting useful evidence from other experiments) or include the full experimental history (producing long, redundant contexts).

Method: A simple, single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook - an agent-maintained memory serving two complementary roles: guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log and informing generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence to jointly produce the next program and an updated LabBook.

Result: On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks.

Conclusion: LabBook effectively separates complete history retention from selective context construction without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure, demonstrating superior quality-cost trade-off across diverse tasks.

Abstract: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery often generate new programs from a small set of selected ancestors. This keeps contexts manageable but can omit useful evidence from other experiments, whereas including the full experimental history produces long, redundant contexts. We introduce a simple, single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook, an agent-maintained memory that serves two complementary roles: guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log and informing the generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence and jointly produces the next program and an updated LabBook. This separates complete history retention from selective context construction, without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure. On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over the evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/LabBook.

</details>


### [212] [Learning Transferable Skills using Goal-Conditioned Bisimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00676)
*Mohammad Amin Abbasfar,Farbod Azimmohseni,Mohammad Hossein Rohban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses generalization in unsupervised skill discovery for reinforcement learning. It proposes learning action-aware temporal representations with functional equivariance, combined with bisimulation-based skill discovery that focuses on state features affecting skill execution. This enables skills to transfer across different environment layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unsupervised skill discovery methods either require expert data or exhibit limited generalization - they fail to transfer to previously unseen layouts. The key challenge is learning representations that capture temporal structure while remaining robust to variations across layouts.

Method: 1) Learn action-aware temporal representations satisfying functional equivariance while preserving local temporal structure. 2) Use bisimulation-based unsupervised skill discovery that conditions skill behavior exclusively on state features directly affecting skill execution. This enforces invariant behavior across different layouts.

Result: Skills learned in a given environment can be effectively applied to solve downstream tasks in various environment layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables transferable skills that generalize across different environment configurations, solving the generalization limitation of prior unsupervised skill discovery methods.

Abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery has emerged as a promising approach for leveraging reward-free datasets to pretrain general-purpose policies. However, current skill discovery methods either require access to expert data or exhibit limited generalization, failing to transfer effectively to previously unseen layouts. A key challenge is to learn representations that capture the temporal structure of the environment while remaining robust to variations across layouts. To address this issue, we present an objective for learning action-aware temporal representations that satisfy the functional equivariance property while preserving the local temporal structure of the environment. Building upon this embedding, we further propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation, which learns transferable skills by conditioning the behavior of skills exclusively on the subset of state features that directly affect their execution. This enforces invariant behavior across different layouts, enabling skills to transfer effectively to other configurations. Finally, through comprehensive empirical evaluations, we show that skills learned in a given environment can be effectively applied to solve downstream tasks in various environment layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization.

</details>


### [213] [Curvature Under Attack in hZACH-ViT: Gauge Symmetry, Boundary Saturation, and Adversarial Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00680)
*Athanasios Angelakis,Marta Gomez-Barrero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the interaction between curvature, coordinate scale, logit temperature, and numerical safeguards in Vision Transformers by comparing Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical prototype heads on MedMNIST datasets. It finds that Poincare models show lowest adversarial attack success at c=1 but also lowest clean accuracy, and that curvature changes have implementation-dependent effects that do not establish intrinsic hyperbolic robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the interaction between curvature (treated as intrinsic property of representations) and empirical factors including coordinate scale, learned logit temperature, and numerical safeguards, which jointly affect recognition and adversarial robustness.

Method: Comparing hZACH-ViT (compact Vision Transformer) with Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical prototype heads, matched across backbone architecture, seed-specific initialization, 50-per-class training subset, and optimization protocol across three MedMNIST datasets and five seeds. PGD and CE+DLR multi-restart attacks were used for evaluation.

Result: At fixed curvature c=1, Poincare has lowest PGD attack-success in all 12 dataset-budget cells but also lowest clean MacroF1. Reducing Poincare curvature to c=0.1 improves clean MacroF1 in all 15 paired comparisons but increases strong attack success on OrganAMNIST from 89.7% to 99.3% (paired difference +9.57 points). 40-47% of clean Poincare features are hard-clipped at c=1, with nearly zero radial Jacobian and inefficient attack trajectories.

Conclusion: Results do not establish intrinsic hyperbolic robustness. Instead, they identify an implementation-sensitive regime where curvature, scale, and proximity to the Poincare boundary jointly organize clean recognition and adversarial representation motion. The spherical head serves as a control showing that its curvature change is an exact scale gauge.

Abstract: Curvature is often treated as an intrinsic property of a representation, although its empirical effect also depends on coordinate scale, learned logit temperature, and numerical safeguards. We study this interaction in hZACH-ViT, a compact Vision Transformer with Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical prototype heads. The backbone architecture, seed-specific initialization, 50-per-class training subset, and optimization protocol are matched across three MedMNIST datasets and five seeds. At the fixed comparison curvature $c=1$, Poincare has the lowest class-macro PGD attack-success rate in all 12 dataset-budget cells and under a stronger CE+DLR multi-restart attack on all three datasets, but it also has the lowest clean MacroF1. An end-to-end curvature intervention changes the interpretation. Reducing Poincare curvature to $c=0.1$ improves clean MacroF1 in every one of the 15 paired seed-dataset comparisons and removes hard boundary clipping, yet on OrganAMNIST it increases strong attack success from $89.7\%$ to $99.3\%$ (paired difference $+9.57$ points; 95\% hierarchical bootstrap CI $[+5.52,+14.03]$). At $c=1$, $40$-$47\%$ of clean Poincare features are hard-clipped, the radial Jacobian of the inherited map is nearly zero, and dimensionless attack trajectories are unusually long and inefficient. The spherical head provides a control: its curvature change is an exact scale gauge to floating-point precision and produces much smaller attack differences. These results do not establish intrinsic hyperbolic robustness. They identify an implementation-sensitive regime in which curvature, scale, and proximity to the Poincare boundary jointly organize clean recognition and adversarial representation motion.

</details>


### [214] [Grand Canonical Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00683)
*Andreas Burger,Malte Franke,Luka Mucko,Kjell Jorner,Alan Aspuru-Guzik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grand Canonical Generators (GCG) extend Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble, enabling joint sampling of particle number and configuration conditioned on chemical potential, with applications to Lennard-Jones fluids and methane adsorption in zeolites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Boltzmann generators are limited to the canonical ensemble (fixed particle number), but many physical systems require the grand canonical ensemble where particle number fluctuates at fixed chemical potential. This work aims to bridge this gap.

Method: Two designs: (1) Variable-size generative model conditioned on chemical potential for joint sampling; (2) Factorization into particle-number distribution and canonical Boltzmann density, enabling use of existing Boltzmann generators and supporting self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS).

Result: GCG accurately reproduces grand canonical observables on Lennard-Jones fluid and methane adsorption in zeolite, demonstrating generalization across chemical potentials and correction via SNIS and grand canonical Monte Carlo.

Conclusion: GCG successfully extends Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble, providing a tractable likelihood framework with broad applicability to variable-particle-number systems in statistical mechanics.

Abstract: We introduce Grand Canonical Generators (GCG), a generative framework that extends Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble. We present two designs. The first conditions a variable-size generative model on the chemical potential, sampling particle number and configuration jointly. The second factorizes the grand canonical distribution into a particle-number distribution and the corresponding canonical Boltzmann density. This factorized formulation can use any existing Boltzmann generator for the canonical component, encodes the known linear chemical-potential dependence analytically, and yields a tractable likelihood that supports self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). Empirically, GCG accurately reproduces grand canonical observables on a Lennard--Jones fluid and methane adsorption in a zeolite, demonstrating generalization across chemical potentials and correction via SNIS and grand canonical Monte Carlo.

</details>


### [215] [SkillSpec: Consensus-Gated Agent Skill Evolution via Representation Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00704)
*Huancheng Chen,Xiaodi Sun,Zhaoqiong Huang,Shenyang Huang Shreya Singhal,Jingwen Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SkillSpec is a two-phase framework for optimizing natural-language skills (procedural memories) in LLM agents. It addresses the limitation of treating skills as monolithic documents by separating what knowledge to retain from how to organize it. The framework uses consensus-gated evolution for validation and representation specialization for structuring knowledge into flat, graph, or hybrid formats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat skills as static or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores, but this restricts optimization to textual content only. The key insight is that retaining knowledge (what) and organizing it (how) are distinct objectives - textual updates should be validated through execution evidence first, then structured according to procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements.

Method: SkillSpec has two phases: (1) Consensus-gated evolution - complementary editing intents generate candidate skills; updates are committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus (sufficient overall improvement + non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation). (2) Representation specialization - signals of process and redundancy sensitivity from the full optimization trajectory (including accepted and rejected candidates) guide selection of flat, graph, or hybrid representation.

Result: SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across three target language models and six benchmarks.

Conclusion: Reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference. This two-phase approach effectively separates the validation of textual knowledge from the structuring of that knowledge for optimal retrieval and execution.

Abstract: Natural-language skills are textual procedural memories through which large language model (LLM) agents retain reusable task knowledge without updating model weights. Existing methods typically treat skills as either static artifacts or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores as feedback. However, representing a skill as a monolithic document restricts optimization to its textual content, without explicitly modeling the structure through which procedural knowledge is retrieved and executed. We identify a key distinction between learning what knowledge to retain and determining how to organize it: textual updates should first be validated through execution evidence, after which the retained knowledge should be structured according to its procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements. To this end, we introduce SkillSpec, a two-phase framework comprising consensus-gated evolution and representation specialization. In the consensus-gated phase, complementary editing intents generate complete candidate skills. An update is committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus, requiring sufficient overall improvement and non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation. In the specialization phase, signals of process and redundancy sensitivity derived from the full optimization trajectory, including accepted and rejected candidates, guide the selection of a flat, graph, or hybrid representation.Across six benchmarks and three target language models, SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across the three models. These results demonstrate that reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference.

</details>


### [216] [Initialization Improves LLM-Driven Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00707)
*Mansi Sakarvadia,Marco Ciccone,Colin Raffel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how to improve LLM-based discovery systems by analyzing the relationship between population dynamics and discovery success. The authors develop 12 different "harnesses" (optimization frameworks) and discover that success is highly sensitive to harness design, with "mode collapse" (loss of diversity) being a common failure. They propose using initial parallel exploration to improve subsequent iterative optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Language Models have shown promise for novel discovery across domains (algorithms, theorems, drugs), but the factors determining discovery success are not well understood. The authors aim to generalize past work on harness design and understand why discovery success is often brittle.

Method: The authors developed a suite of 12 harnesses called "Modular" and characterized their performance across 5 diverse discovery tasks. They studied the relationship between population diversity and discovery success, tested existing diversity interventions, and proposed a new intervention involving initial parallel exploration.

Result: Discovery success was found to be brittle and sensitive to harness design. Mode collapse (dramatic drop in diversity of iterates) was identified as a common failure mode. Popular state-of-the-art harnesses and diversity interventions yielded inconsistent gains. However, early discovery performance was found to be predictive of eventual success.

Conclusion: The authors propose a universally applicable intervention that performs an initial stage of parallel exploration to initialize subsequent iterative optimization. This method provides consistent gains across many harnesses and target applications, confirming the importance of initialization in LLM-driven discovery.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been used for novel discovery of algorithms, theorems, drugs, and other tasks through the use of harnesses that prompt an LLM to iteratively optimize an objective. In this work, we study the relationship between the population of previous iterates and eventual discovery success. We generalize past work on harness design to develop a suite of 12 harnesses called 'Modular' and characterize their performance across 5 diverse discovery tasks, finding that discovery success is brittle and sensitive to harness design. We uncover mode collapse, characterized by a dramatic drop in the diversity of iterates, as a common failure mode. We find that popular state-of-the-art harnesses and diversity-inducing harness interventions, which aim to prolong this collapse, yield inconsistent gains. Our results instead uncover that the performance of early discoveries is predictive of eventual success. We therefore propose a universally applicable intervention that performs an initial stage of parallel exploration in order to initialize subsequent iterative optimization. Our method provides consistent gains across many harnesses and target applications, confirming the importance of initialization in LLM-driven discovery.

</details>


### [217] [Beyond Unimodal Bases: Pullback Geometry for Multimodal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00708)
*Honglei Brinkmann,Lucas Ng,Georgios Batzolis,Mark Girolami,Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb,Willem Diepeveen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a pullback geometry for data supported on mixtures of manifolds, using a latent Gaussian mixture distribution instead of the traditional unimodal Gaussian. The method defines a Riemannian metric as the matrix square of responsibility-weighted expected component precision, and is instantiated in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning. Experiments on synthetic, multi-view image, and MNIST data demonstrate reduced transport distortion and improved interpolation realism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scalable pullback geometry methods typically use a unimodal Gaussian latent distribution, assuming data resides close to a single manifold. For multimodal data, mapping separated modes into one Gaussian region requires substantial transport deformation and compromises the resulting geometry.

Method: The proposed method defines a Riemannian metric as the matrix square of the responsibility-weighted expected component precision. This metric is smooth and positive definite and recovers the existing Gaussian construction in the single-component limit. For structured overlapping mixtures, conditions are established under which the log-density is concave along geodesics. The geometry is instantiated in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, allowing the number of active components to emerge from data.

Result: Experiments on synthetic geometric data, controlled multi-view image setting with known reference trajectory, and MNIST show: (1) reduced transport distortion, (2) competitive path support, (3) close reference-trajectory recovery, and (4) improved interpolation realism.

Conclusion: This work extends scalable pullback geometry beyond datasets that reside close to a single manifold while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure. The method successfully handles multimodal data by leveraging Gaussian mixture latent distributions and adaptive mixture learning.

Abstract: Data-driven Riemannian geometry provides nonlinear interpolation and geometric representations of high-dimensional data. For these operations to be statistically meaningful, paths between observations should preferentially traverse high-likelihood regions. Existing scalable pullback constructions typically use a unimodal Gaussian latent distribution, assuming that the data reside close to a single manifold. For multimodal data, mapping separated modes or local structures into one Gaussian region can require substantial transport deformation and compromise the resulting geometry.
  We introduce a pullback geometry for data supported on mixtures of manifolds. Using a latent Gaussian mixture, we define its Riemannian metric as the matrix square of the responsibility-weighted expected component precision. The metric is smooth and positive definite and recovers the existing Gaussian construction in the single-component limit. For structured overlapping mixtures, we establish conditions under which the log-density is concave along geodesics, providing a formal connection between the proposed geometry and paths through high-likelihood regions, and derive the corresponding local curvature relations.
  We instantiate this geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, allowing the number of active components to emerge from the data and supporting component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation. Experiments on synthetic geometric data, a controlled multi-view image setting with a known reference trajectory, and MNIST show reduced transport distortion, competitive path support, close reference-trajectory recovery, and improved interpolation realism. These results extend scalable pullback geometry beyond datasets that reside close to a single manifold while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure.

</details>


### [218] [WOMBAT: Whitebox Oracle for Molecular Benchmarking and Attribution Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00713)
*Dominik Matuszek,Bartosz Zieliński,Tomasz Danel,Dawid Rymarczyk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WOMBAT is a benchmark of 14 whitebox GNNs with known decision rules designed to detect specific SMARTS motifs, enabling systematic evaluation of GNN explainers by providing attribution ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When GNN explainers produce unexpected attributions, it is unclear whether the explainer failed or the model learned a shortcut. There is a need for ground truth to evaluate explainer correctness.

Method: The authors constructed 14 whitebox GNNs with hand-crafted message-passing weights to detect specific SMARTS motifs. Each model's decision rule is known by construction. They validated models on millions of PubChem molecules and evaluated post-hoc explainers (GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, Integrated Gradients).

Result: The benchmark enables identification and study of explainer errors. The authors demonstrated that Integrated Gradients can spread attribution across the graph even when the model reliably detects the intended motif.

Conclusion: WOMBAT provides a valuable benchmark for developing and evaluating XAI tools for GNNs by providing known ground truth attribution. The dataset, models, and evaluation code are released to support research.

Abstract: When a graph neural network (GNN) explainer produces an unexpected attribution on a molecule, the attribution alone cannot reveal whether the explainer has failed or the model has learned a shortcut. We introduce WOMBAT, a benchmark of 14 whitebox GNNs, each with message-passing weights set by hand to detect a specific SMARTS motif. Each model's decision rule is known by construction, providing attribution ground truth against which explainer errors can be identified and studied. We validate the models on millions of PubChem molecules and evaluate post-hoc explainers including GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, and Integrated Gradients. Guided by our qualitative analysis, we construct a model that causes Integrated Gradients to spread attribution across the graph, even though the model reliably detects the intended motif. We release the dataset, models, and evaluation code to help researchers in the development of newer XAI tools for GNNs.

</details>


### [219] [JEPA-TTT: Persistent Test-Time Training of Latent World Models for Planning under Dynamics Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00722)
*Zheyuan Zhang,Suyu Ye,Nakul Agarwal,Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub,Ehsan Moradi Pari,Daniel Khashabi,Tianmin Shu,Vaishnav Tadiparthi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JEPA-TTT is a method that adapts a pretrained Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture world model during test time to handle dynamics shifts. It updates only the latent dynamics predictor using self-supervised learning with dense replay, without requiring goal images or online rewards for planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models enable agents to plan by predicting future environment states, but their predictions become unreliable when test-time dynamics differ from training dynamics. This domain shift problem requires methods that can adapt the model without extensive environment interactions or task-specific rewards.

Method: JEPA-TTT adapts the latent dynamics predictor of a pretrained action-conditioned JEPA world model during test time through self-supervised updates. The visual encoder and reward head remain fixed to preserve pretrained representations and task objectives. The method uses dense replay, creating prediction windows at every temporal offset, retaining them in a growing buffer, and sampling minibatches for predictor updates. Planning requires neither goal images nor online environment rewards.

Result: Across eight dynamics shifts in four continuous-control environments, JEPA-TTT improves planning on every shift. After 500 test-time episodes, it reduces autoregressive latent prediction error by 83% on average and improves planning performance by 153% over the frozen JEPA world model.

Conclusion: Persistent self-supervised test-time training can effectively adapt a pretrained latent world model under changed dynamics, demonstrating that continuous adaptation during deployment enables reliable planning even when environment dynamics shift significantly from training.

Abstract: World models enable agents to plan by predicting future states of the environment, but their predictions can become unreliable when test-time dynamics differ from those seen during training. We present JEPA-TTT, which adapts the latent dynamics predictor of a pretrained action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture world model throughout test time. Self-supervised updates accumulate across episodes, while the visual encoder and reward head remain fixed, preserving the pretrained representation and task objective. Planning requires neither a goal image nor online environment reward. JEPA-TTT uses dense replay, which forms prediction windows at every temporal offset, retains them in a growing buffer, and samples minibatches from that buffer for predictor updates. Across eight dynamics shifts in four continuous-control environments, JEPA-TTT improves planning on every shift. After 500 test-time episodes, it reduces autoregressive latent prediction error by 83% on average and improves planning performance by 153% over the frozen JEPA world model. These results show that persistent self-supervised test-time training can adapt a pretrained latent world model under changed dynamics.

</details>


### [220] [Benchmarking Generative Models for Weather Data Assimilation on Real Station Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00728)
*Ruizhe Huang,Qidong Yang,Jonathan Giezendanner,Sherrie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first controlled benchmark evaluating generative deep learning models for weather data assimilation on real NOAA weather station observations. It compares design choices (diffusion vs flow matching, pixel vs latent space, conditioning strategies) against classical 3D-Var, finding that learned generative priors outperform Gaussian priors (35.7% vs 33.3% RMSE reduction), full-gradient guidance is most effective, while other choices show minimal difference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weather reanalysis relies on computationally intensive numerical weather predictions and data assimilation. While deep generative models offer cheaper alternatives, existing approaches have only been evaluated on synthetic data or under inconsistent evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world performance.

Method: Controlled benchmark using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous US with four weather variables. Methods were evaluated while holding dataset, observation operator, and deep learning architecture fixed. Compared: diffusion vs flow matching, pixel vs latent-space formulations, multiple inference-time conditioning strategies, against classical 3D-Var baseline. Evaluated both dense and sparse station settings.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Learned generative priors outperform 3D-Var's Gaussian prior (35.7% vs 33.3% RMSE reduction over ERA5) without using ERA5 background field at inference; (2) Full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization; (3) Diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically, and latent-space variable mixing provides no measurable benefit. Advantages are more pronounced under sparse station settings.

Conclusion: This work identifies which components of generative weather data assimilation actually improve performance on real station observations: learned generative priors and full-gradient guidance. It establishes a standardized benchmark for future work in this domain.

Abstract: Weather reanalysis products rely on computationally intensive numerical weather predictions followed by data assimilation that corrects the forecast toward observations. Deep generative models offer a cheaper alternative that shifts much of this cost from inference to offline training. However, existing generative approaches have been evaluated on synthetic observations or under different datasets and evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world data assimilation. We present the first controlled benchmark of generative weather data assimilation on real weather station observations. Using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous United States and four weather variables, we evaluate methods while holding the dataset, observation operator, and deep learning architecture fixed. The benchmark compares the major design choices, including diffusion versus flow matching, pixel versus latent-space formulations, and multiple inference-time conditioning strategies, against a classical 3D-Var baseline. The benchmark reveals three clear conclusions. First, learned generative priors outperform the Gaussian prior of 3D-Var (35.7% vs. 33.3% RMSE reduction over ERA5) despite using no ERA5 background field at inference. Second, full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization. Third, other choices provide little measurable benefit: diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically under matched conditions, and latent-space variable mixing does not help. We further evaluate both dense and sparse station settings and find advantages from generative AI and full-gradient guidance more pronounced under sparsity. Together, these results identify which components of generative weather data assimilation improve performance on real station observations and establish a standardized benchmark for future work.

</details>


### [221] [Reward as Observation: Learning Reward-Based Policies for Rapid Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00729)
*Morgan Byrd,Maks Sorokin,Robert Wright,Sehoon Ha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reward-based policy conditioned only on rewards and actions (not observations) to achieve zero-shot transfer between environments with completely different observation spaces. The method enables adaptation to new environments without any fine-tuning or samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities to new environments, but deep neural network policies typically struggle to adapt to new environments and require substantial training samples for successful transfer. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a policy that can transfer zero-shot to environments with completely different observation spaces.

Method: The authors propose a novel reward-based policy that is only conditioned on rewards and actions, rather than observations. They discuss the challenges and feasibility of such an approach and develop a practical algorithm for training the reward-based policy. The key innovation is conditioning the policy on scalar reward signals rather than high-dimensional observations.

Result: The reward-based policy was trained in three environments (Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing) and successfully transferred in zero-shot manner to target environments with completely different observations, including different color palettes, 3D rendering, and Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim. Additionally, the reward-based policy was shown to guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

Conclusion: The reward-based policy approach enables effective zero-shot adaptation to new environments with different observation spaces. This method provides a promising direction for transfer learning in reinforcement learning, where the policy can generalize across vastly different observation representations. Furthermore, the reward policy can serve as a guide for training observation-based policies in target environments.

Abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

</details>


### [222] [Reformulation-Contrastive Learning for Mixed Integer Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00730)
*Ousema Bouaneni,Mathis Le Bail,Clément Elliker,Maël Jenny,Sonia Vanier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces ReMILP, a self-supervised learning framework that leverages MILP reformulations (integrality-preserving variable changes and redundant constraints) to learn general-purpose representations of MILP variables and constraints. It uses graph neural networks and hypernetworks to predict how embeddings transform under changes of variables, achieving invariance and equivariance without solver-derived labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MILPs model many real-world decision problems, but solving them is computationally expensive. The authors aim to exploit recurring structure in MILP formulations through machine learning. The key insight is that MILPs have many equivalent formulations (reformulations), which can serve as a source of self-supervision for learning representations without requiring expensive solver-derived labels.

Method: The method involves: 1) Characterizing affine reformulations valid for every input instance, distinguishing re-descriptions (leaving variables unchanged) from substitutions (predictable transformations); 2) Building on equivariant self-supervised learning, jointly training a graph neural network (GNN) and a hypernetwork; 3) The GNN learns representations while the hypernetwork predicts how variable embeddings transform under changes of variables.

Result: ReMILP learns representations that exhibit the intended invariance and equivariance on unseen problem classes without any solver-derived labels. Across three tasks (binary solution prediction, constraint activity prediction, and integrality gap prediction), these representations carry task-relevant information when frozen and provide useful initialization for fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that reformulations can serve as effective self-supervision for learning MILP representations. The learned representations generalize to unseen problem classes and are useful for various downstream tasks, suggesting the potential for learning general-purpose MILP representations that can accelerate solving across different problem types.

Abstract: Mixed-integer linear programs (MILP) model many real-world decision problems, motivating machine-learning methods that exploit recurring structure to accelerate MILP solving. MILPs can admit many equivalent formulations: integrality-preserving changes of variables and the addition of redundant constraints can alter their formulations while preserving the optimization problem. We leverage these reformulations as a source of self-supervision for learning general-purpose representations of MILP variables and constraints. We characterize the affine reformulations that are valid for every input instance, and distinguish re-descriptions, which leave variables unchanged, from substitutions, which transform them predictably.
