Building on equivariant self-supervised learning, we introduce ReMILP (reformulation-contrastive MILP representation learning), which jointly trains a graph neural network and a hypernetwork to predict how variable embeddings transform under changes of variables. Without solver-derived labels, ReMILP learns representations that exhibit the intended invariance and equivariance on unseen problem classes. Across binary solution, constraint activity and integrality gap prediction, these representations carry task-relevant information when frozen and provide a useful initialization for fine-tuning.

</details>


### [223] [Signal-Noise Factorization Isolates Nuisance Variation into Removable Subspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00751)
*Sakin Kirti,Joel Zylberberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates representation geometry properties in deep neural networks—specifically signal-noise factorization (SNF) and signal-signal factorization (SSF)—and implements regularizers to reinforce these properties during training. SNF regularization improved performance on CIFAR-100 and BloodMNIST with corruptions, while SSF regularization showed no benefit. The key mechanism is that SNF-regularized models represent noise in distinct subspaces separate from class-relevant signal, allowing projection of corruption-induced directions for improved accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent theoretical work identified fundamental properties of representation geometry that shape inference ability in deep neural networks. The researchers wanted to understand how these properties (SNF and SSF) can be reinforced during training to improve model performance, particularly on computer vision tasks with out-of-distribution image distortions.

Method: Built regularizers that reinforce SNF and SSF properties during training. Compared networks trained with these regularizers to L2-regularized baselines on CIFAR-100 classification. Also tested on BloodMNIST dataset with MedMNIST-C corruptions at five severity levels. Analyzed nuisance subspaces across regularization regimes and estimated dominant corruption-induced directions on held-out data to project out of representations.

Result: Enhancing SNF via regularization improved model performance on CIFAR-100, but enhancing SSF did not. On BloodMNIST with MedMNIST-C corruptions, SNF regularizer showed even larger performance gains. SNF-regularized models represent noise in distinct subspaces separate from class-relevant signal. Projecting out corruption-induced directions led to substantial accuracy gains.

Conclusion: Regularizers enforcing signal-noise factorization can produce substantial improvements on computer vision tasks with out-of-distribution image distortions at inference time. Isolating nuisance variables from categorical ones is more important than maintaining factorized representations of categorical variables. The explicit geometry allows estimation and projection of corruption-induced directions.

Abstract: Recent theoretical work identified fundamental properties of representation geometry that shape inference ability of deep neural networks. These include signal-noise factorization (SNF), the ability to segregate signal from noise, and signal-signal factorization (SSF), the ability to segregate task-specific and task-irrelevant signals. Here, we built regularizers that reinforce these two properties during training. We compared networks trained with these regularizers to $L_2$-regularized baseline networks on the CIFAR-100 classification task to understand how our regularizers shape representation geometry and impact performance on a well-known computer vision baseline. Enhancing SNF via regularization improved model performance but enhancing SSF did not. Motivated by biomedical applications, we investigated how our regularizers affected performance on the BloodMNIST dataset treated with MedMNIST-C corruptions at five severity levels, and found even larger performance gains using the SNF regularizer. To understand the mechanism by which SNF-regularization produces improved performance, we analyzed the nuisance subspaces across regularization regimes, finding that the SNF-regularized models represent noise in distinct subspaces, separate from class-relevant signal. Because this geometry is explicit, the dominant corruption-induced directions can be estimated on held-out data and projected out of the representations. This manipulation led to a substantial gain in accuracy. These results show that regularizers that enforce signal-noise factorization can produce substantial improvements on computer vision tasks that contain out-of-distribution image distortions at inference time. They also highlight how shaping representations affects model performance: isolating nuisance variables from categorical ones is more important than maintaining factorized representations of categorical variables.

</details>


### [224] [Increasing Width Allows Greedy Layer-wise Training to Rival End-to-End Backpropagation in Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00753)
*Syon Mansur,Joel Zylberberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how network width and depth affect the performance of greedy layer-wise training versus end-to-end backpropagation in self-supervised learning. The key finding is that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment, with very wide and shallow networks achieving better performance with greedy layer-wise training, and exhibiting more favorable representational geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior studies explored alternative training mechanisms to backpropagation but it remained unclear under what architectural conditions locally optimized networks can learn representations comparable to end-to-end training. This is particularly important for self-supervised learning, a key framework for large-scale pretraining.

Method: The authors compared greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks, systematically varying network width and depth to analyze their effects on performance and representational geometry.

Result: In wider networks, the performance gap between end-to-end backpropagation and greedy layer-wise training shrinks. In relatively shallow and very wide networks, greedy layer-wise training even outperforms end-to-end training. Analysis shows that wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than end-to-end trained networks.

Conclusion: Width can compensate for restricted credit assignment in greedy layer-wise training. Differences in representational geometry represent a potential mechanism explaining the improved performance of wide greedy-trained networks. This provides architectural guidance for training deep networks without end-to-end backpropagation.

Abstract: End-to-end backpropagation has been the dominant mode of training in deep learning, allowing for the coordination of parameter updates across layers of a neural network. Prior studies have explored alternative -- and, in some cases, simpler -- training mechanisms, showing that they can sometimes achieve performance similar to backpropagation. However, the architectural conditions under which locally optimized networks, which avoid end-to-end backpropagation of error, can learn representations comparable to those learned through end-to-end training remain unclear. We aim to answer this question in the context of self-supervised learning, an important framework for large-scale pretraining in artificial intelligence. Here, we investigate how network width and depth affect the efficacy of greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks. We find that in wider networks, the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrink: in relatively shallow and very wide networks, we even observed higher performance in models trained with greedy layer-wise training. Subsequent analysis of the representations formed by these networks shows that very wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than do networks trained end-to-end with backpropagation. This work shows that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment and identifies differences in representational geometry as a potential mechanism for their improved performance.

</details>


### [225] [Scalable Multi-Task Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00758)
*Allen Tran,Jia Wan,Nathan Kallus,Aurélien Bibaut*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-task inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) method that uses low-rank assumption to pool data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment, enabling transfer to new environments with limited coverage requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation addresses a fundamental limitation in IRL: strict coverage requirements for transferring learned rewards to new environments. When agents operate in different environments, their state occupancy varies, making it difficult to evaluate agents in target environments. The authors aim to alleviate these coverage constraints so that each task doesn't need to visit every state, as long as other tasks provide coverage.

Method: The proposed method employs a low-rank assumption when pooling data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment. This approach enables scalable evaluation of multiple tasks under new environments, where computational complexity scales with rank rather than the number of tasks.

Result: The method demonstrates: (1) robustness to limited coverage scenarios, (2) successful reward recovery both on and off each task's support, (3) lower regret transfer to target environments compared to baselines, and (4) computational advantages that widen as the number of tasks grows.

Conclusion: The multi-task IRL method with low-rank assumption successfully addresses coverage limitations in reward transfer, provides theoretical guarantees for reward recovery and policy learning in new environments, and offers significant computational scalability over per-task methods when dealing with multiple tasks.

Abstract: By learning transferable rewards, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) enables counterfactual evaluation of agents under modified environments. Such transfer places strict requirements on coverage since target environments affect agents' state occupancy. We propose a multi-task IRL method that pools data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment under a low-rank assumption. In addition to alleviating coverage requirements, so each task need not visit every state as long as others do, the method offers scalable evaluation of multiple tasks under new environments as computationally intensive planning scales with rank rather than the number of tasks. We provide finite sample guarantees on reward recovery and on policy learning in new environments. Experiments show our method is robust to limited coverage, recovers rewards on and off of each task's support, transfers to target environments at lower regret than baselines, with its computational advantage over per-task methods widening as tasks grow.

</details>


### [226] [Pre-training interventions, ex post facto: Grafting model beliefs across checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00767)
*Peter Nutter,Dani Roytburg,Clément Dumas,Jinghua Ou,Shi Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "grafting," a method to apply synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) interventions at the pre-training stage while reusing existing post-trained models. The approach trains an SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then adds the learned weights to the post-trained model, avoiding the need for costly full post-training runs and reducing artifacts like "reality drift" (where fabricated entities are treated as real).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-training interventions are crucial for alignment research, but applying SDF to already post-trained models causes artifacts and capability degradation. The standard approach of applying SDF post-training creates "reality drift" - treating fabricated entities as real. Additionally, iterating on pre-training interventions requires expensive full post-training runs, making research slow.

Method: The proposed "grafting" method works in two stages: (1) train the SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint to learn weight updates, then (2) add these learned weight updates to the post-trained model. This approximates the faithful approach of mixing synthetic documents during pre-/mid-training while reusing existing post-training. The method was tested across model families up to 284B parameters through experiments including: installing false facts, training misaligned model organisms, and applying a constitutional mid-training intervention.

Result: Grafting installs target beliefs as strongly as SDF on post-trained models while reducing both reality drift and loss of preference coherence by more than half on average. It also stays closer to a faithful mid-training run. The method enables rapid iteration on pre-training interventions at the cost of a single fine-tuning run, since the same adapter can be applied to any later checkpoint.

Conclusion: Grafting provides an efficient way to apply pre-training interventions without requiring full post-training runs. It successfully reduces reality drift and capability degradation compared to standard SDF applied post-training, while maintaining the target belief modification effectiveness. This enables researchers to iterate quickly on alignment interventions at pre-training scale.

Abstract: Pre-training interventions are critical to alignment research, since beliefs formed during pre-training shape how a model generalizes from later training. One recently popular technique for such interventions is synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF), which aims to alter what the model believes. Ideally, synthetic documents would be mixed into pre- or mid-training, but every change to a pre-training corpus must be followed by a full post-training run before its effect can be measured, making iteration slow and expensive. Common practice instead applies SDF to an already post-trained model. This is known to leave artifacts and degrade capabilities, and, as we show, it makes the model treat fabricated entities unrelated to the documents as real, a failure we call reality drift. We propose grafting: train the SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then add the learned weight update to the post-trained model, which approximates the faithful approach while reusing the existing post-training. We demonstrate this by installing false facts, training misaligned model organisms and applying a constitutional mid-training intervention, across model families up to 284B parameters. Grafting installs the target belief as strongly as SDF on the post-trained model while reducing both reality drift and the loss of preference coherence by more than half on average, and it stays closer to a faithful mid-training run. Because grafting requires no post-training, the same adapter can be applied to any later checkpoint, enabling researchers to iterate quickly on pre-training interventions at the cost of a single fine-tuning run.

</details>


<div id='cs.SD'></div>

# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [227] [High-Value Synthetic Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of a Compact Japanese Speech Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00026)
*Sidi Chang,Peiying Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a parameter-efficient approach for adapting a 1.47B audio model to transform Japanese care handoff speech into structured notes, using synthetic data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of collecting private domain speech data and the need for task-specific supervision in compact models. The study aims to develop an auditable synthetic pipeline for Japanese care handoffs.

Method: Used 182 synthetic training and development clips to adapt a 1.47B audio model via two approaches: full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA. Evaluated on a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test set.

Result: Full fine-tuning achieved 0.8664 factuality-recall, LoRA achieved 0.8461 (97.7% of full-tuning), compared to 0.0500 for unadapted model. LoRA used 12.4M trainable parameters (0.85% of backbone).

Conclusion: A compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred synthetic examples. However, this does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to cloud systems. No latency/memory/energy measurements were taken.

Abstract: Private domain speech is difficult to collect and redistribute, while compact models need task-specific supervision. We study an auditable synthetic pipeline that maps Japanese care handoffs directly to six-field structured notes. Using 182 synthetic training and development clips, we adapt a 1.47B audio model by full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA. On a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test, an unadapted model obtains a model-judged factuality-recall score of 0.0500, full tuning 0.8664, and LoRA 0.8461. LoRA reaches 97.7% of the full-tuning aggregate as a descriptive ratio while project telemetry reports 12.4M trainable parameters, about 0.85% of the backbone. Both adaptations show large paired gains over the same base; the full-versus-LoRA interval crosses zero, and differing optimization settings preclude an equivalence claim. This is a parameter-efficient capability-acquisition result, not a device-performance result: latency, memory, energy, and real-time factor were not measured. All evaluation speech and targets are synthetic, references are model-proposed, and the judge is uncalibrated. The evidence shows that a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred provenance-linked synthetic examples; it does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to a clean cloud system.

</details>


### [228] [PLACE: Positional Latent Adaptation via Conditioned Embeddings for Binaural Audio Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00630)
*Tiernon Riesenmy,You Zhang,Gautam Bhattacharya,Andrea Fanelli*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: PLACE is a method that extends pretrained any-to-audio model AudioX for binaural generation from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency in audio generation from diverse input modalities (text, video, audio).

Method: PLACE augments video conditioning with Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text and video representations to derive spatial cues, and applies a conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to the generated latent. The adapter is supervised via decoded-audio interaural level and time difference objectives, trained on MRSAudio dataset.

Result: PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves an improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on the BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation.

Conclusion: PLACE demonstrates flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency for binaural audio generation from diverse input combinations.

Abstract: We present PLACE, a method that extends the pretrained any-to-audio model AudioX for binaural generation from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts. PLACE augments video conditioning with Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text and video representations to derive spatial cues, and applies a conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to the generated latent. The adapter is supervised via decoded-audio interaural level and time difference objectives. Trained on MRSAudio, PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves an improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on the BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation, demonstrating flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency.

</details>


### [229] [How Robust Are Neural Audio Codecs for African Speech? A Multi-Task Benchmark and the Limits of Perceptual Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00154)
*Chibuzor Okocha,Christan Earl Grant*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks seven open-source neural audio codecs on three African speech datasets, evaluating signal-level quality metrics and downstream ASR/ASR tasks. The study reveals that reference-based metrics track downstream performance better than neural MOS predictors, and that degradation is domain-dependent but partly recoverable through efficient codec adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used for speech compression and tokenization, but their robustness on accented and multilingual speech—particularly African languages—remains under-evaluated. This gap limits inclusive deployment of speech technologies.

Method: Benchmarked seven neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets (afrinames, afrispeech dialog, afrispeech multilingual). Evaluated using signal-level quality metrics (NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) and downstream tasks (ASR and ASV). Also tested parameter-efficient codec adaptation using LoRA (~1-3% of parameters) on ~35 hours of African speech.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Reference-based metrics (ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) track ASR/ASV degradation more reliably than neural MOS predictors (NISQA, UTMOS); (2) Intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge across architectures, with rankings depending on ASV backend; (3) Degradation is largest for conversational dialog; (4) Codec adaptation recovers recognition toward uncompressed baseline.

Conclusion: Task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs is essential for inclusive deployment, especially for underrepresented languages and accents.

Abstract: Neural audio codecs enable low-bitrate speech compression and tokenization, yet their robustness on accented and multilingual speech remains under-evaluated. We benchmark seven open-source neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets afrinames, afrispeech dialog, afrispeech multilingual, reporting signal-level quality (NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) alongside two downstream tasks: automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification (ASV). Our analysis yields four findings. First, signal metrics differ sharply in downstream validity: reference-based structural/intelligibility measures (ViSQOL, STOI) and prosodic error (F0-RMSE) track ASR and ASV degradation far more reliably than neural mean-opinion-score predictors (NISQA, UTMOS). Second, intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge sharply across architectures, and the apparent identity ranking itself depends on the ASV backend. Third, degradation is strongly domain-dependent and largest for conversational dialog. Fourth, the resulting degradation is partly recoverable: parameter-efficient \emph{codec} adaptation (LoRA, $\sim$1--3\% of parameters) on roughly 35 hours of African speech reduces the compression-induced word-error-rate gap, recovering recognition toward the uncompressed baseline (developed in companion work). These results motivate task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs as a prerequisite for inclusive deployment.

</details>


### [230] [ProxyMOS: Label-Free Speech Quality Assessment by Multi-Teacher Distillation with Adaptive Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00419)
*Maxim Trokunov,Kirill Borodin,Nikita Vasiliev,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: ProxyMOS combines multiple public MOS (Mean Opinion Score) predictors into a stronger model without requiring new human labels. It benchmarks 8 predictors, selects the 5 most informative, and uses various routing strategies to create an ensemble. This ensemble labels 807k unlabeled utterances to train a wav2vec 2.0 student model, achieving Spearman ρ=0.802 on URGENT and ρ=0.636 on a new Russian TTS benchmark (mos260), outperforming the best individual teacher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human MOS collection is costly, and non-intrusive MOS predictors perform poorly outside their training domain. There is a need for a method to improve MOS prediction without acquiring more human labels.

Method: 1) Benchmark 8 public MOS predictors against human ratings; 2) Select 5 most informative predictors; 3) Test 5 routing strategies (uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimized, adaptive per-utterance); 4) Use best 4-model ensemble to label 807k unlabeled utterances; 5) Train wav2vec 2.0 student on these labels.

Result: On URGENT: student achieves ρ=0.802 vs 0.773 for best teacher. On mos260 (Russian TTS benchmark): student achieves ρ=0.636 vs 0.613 per utterance and 0.95 per condition. Adaptive routing is the only strategy that doesn't degrade when weak predictors are added.

Conclusion: ProxyMOS successfully creates a stronger MOS predictor by ensembling multiple public predictors without new human labels. The wav2vec 2.0 student outperforms the best teacher model. Adaptive routing proves most robust. The model, ONNX exports, and mos260 benchmark are released.

Abstract: Human mean opinion scores (MOS) are costly to collect, and non-intrusive MOS predictors degrade sharply outside their training domain. ProxyMOS turns a pool of public MOS predictors into a single stronger model without new human labels. Eight predictors are benchmarked against human ratings; the five most informative enter a subset search under uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimised and adaptive per-utterance routing; and the best routed four-model ensemble labels 807k unlabeled utterances that train a wav2vec 2.0 student. On URGENT the student reaches Spearman $ρ=0.802$ against $0.773$ for the best teacher. On mos260, a new Russian TTS benchmark of 4,600 utterances from 38 synthesis conditions, it reaches $ρ=0.636$ against $0.613$ per utterance and $0.95$ per condition, matching its own routed ensemble in one forward pass. Adaptive routing is the only rule that does not degrade when weak predictors are added. Model, ONNX exports and mos260 are released. It's about 950 characters; arXiv's limit is 1,920. I kept $ρ$ because arXiv renders it on the abstract page. If you'd rather avoid math, replace $ρ=0.802$ with rho = 0.802 and do the same for the other $...$ values.

</details>


### [231] [Collapse, Not Invariance: Diagnosing Auxiliary Objectives in Speech Anti-Spoofing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00539)
*Ksenia Lysikova,Kirill Borodin,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether auxiliary objectives (AO) can improve speech anti-spoofing systems' generalization across different generators, codecs, and channels. Through 113 experiments on five corpora, the authors find that no auxiliary objective consistently outperforms standard cross-entropy training, despite appearing effective under standard evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when encountering new generators, codecs, or channels. Researchers commonly use auxiliary objectives to shape the embedding space for better generalization. However, EER (Equal Error Rate) only measures ranking performance and cannot reveal whether the embedding space actually becomes more stable or transferable across conditions.

Method: The authors compared seven auxiliary objectives with cross-entropy baseline across 113 runs on five corpora, using AASIST3 (three seeds) plus four pre-trained detectors. They directly measured the embedding space of 24 AASIST3 runs, analyzing factors like cosine consistency, space spread, and decision axis structure.

Result: Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency appear effective, but this is actually due to a smaller embedding space, not improved stability. When normalized by spread, no configuration consistently outperforms cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by a single decision axis (as expected for two-class problems), and training-set structure fails to transfer. Four runs collapsed to near-constant output, which displacement rewards but EER correctly identifies as poor accuracy.

Conclusion: No auxiliary objective maintains an advantage over cross-entropy across different architectures, corpora, and seeds. The apparent effectiveness of auxiliary objectives under standard metrics is an artifact that disappears under proper normalization. The findings suggest that simpler cross-entropy training remains the most robust approach for speech anti-spoofing.

Abstract: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when the generator, codec or channel changes, and a common remedy is an auxiliary objective that shapes the embedding space; whether it does is invisible to EER, a pure ranking metric. We compare seven such objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora, AASIST3 at three seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and measure the embedding space of the 24 AASIST3 runs directly. Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency look effective, but the gain is a smaller space, not a more stable one: normalised by the spread, no configuration consistently improves on cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by the single decision axis expected for two classes, whose training-set structure does not transfer, and four runs collapse to a near-constant output that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective keeps an advantage over cross-entropy across architectures, corpora and seeds.

</details>


### [232] [On Evaluating Quantum Kernel Robustness for Low-Resource Cross-Corpus Audio Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00649)
*Lisan Al Amin,Lei Zhang,Vandana P. Janeja*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study compares quantum kernel methods (QSVM) with classical SVM and MLP for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under limited training data (200 samples). Using 4D PCA-reduced wav2vec 2.0 embeddings, experiments across ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, ADD 2023, and In-the-Wild datasets show QSVM maintains better performance under severe domain shift (AUC 76.0%, EER 27.0%) compared to MLP (AUC ~50%, EER 50.0%), though this advantage is inconsistent across all transfer directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic speech detection faces performance degradation when labeled data are scarce and evaluation conditions differ from training (cross-corpus scenario). This study investigates whether quantum kernel methods can provide advantages over classical approaches under such challenging conditions, particularly with limited training data and severe domain shift.

Method: The study compares QSVM, classical SVM, and MLP, all trained on frozen wav2vec 2.0 embeddings with a strict budget of 200 training samples. Embeddings are reduced to 4 dimensions using PCA to match near-term quantum hardware qubit constraints. Experiments are conducted across four datasets: ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, ADD 2023 Challenge, and In-the-Wild, evaluating cross-corpus transfer performance.

Result: Under severe domain shift (ASVspoof 2019 → ADD 2023), MLP degrades to near-random performance (AUC ~50%, EER 50.0%), while QSVM maintains meaningful discrimination (AUC 76.0%, EER 27.0%). However, this advantage is not consistent—when trained on ADD 2023, QSVM falls below chance on two of three transfers, while MLP performs better. The classical SVM is not explicitly discussed in the results summary.

Conclusion: Quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts and strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide consistent advantage across all transfer directions. The findings represent an empirical characterization of quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift, rather than evidence of quantum advantage, since the 4-qubit kernel can be exactly simulated classically.

Abstract: Synthetic speech detection is critical for audio security, but performance can degrade when labeled data are scarce and evaluation conditions differ from training. This study examines quantum kernel methods and lightweight neural models for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under limited training data. We compare a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), a classical support vector machine (SVM), and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), all trained on frozen wav2vec 2.0 embeddings using a strict budget of 200 training samples. To match the qubit budget of near-term quantum hardware, embeddings are reduced to four dimensions using principal component analysis, and all models use the same reduced features. Experiments on ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, the ADD 2023 Challenge, and the In-the-Wild dataset show that under severe domain shift from ASVspoof 2019 to ADD 2023, the MLP degrades to near-random performance, with an area under the curve of approximately 50% and an equal error rate of 50.0%. In contrast, the QSVM maintains meaningful discrimination, achieving an area under the curve of 76.0% and an equal error rate of 27.0%. This advantage is not consistent across transfer directions. When trained on ADD 2023, the QSVM falls below chance on two of three transfers, while the MLP performs better. These results suggest that quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts and strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide a consistent advantage under near-domain transfer. We interpret these findings as an empirical characterization of quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift, rather than evidence of quantum advantage, since the four-qubit kernel can be simulated exactly on classical hardware.

</details>


### [233] [Balalaika-Longform: A Russian Speech Corpus for Continuous Long-Form Text-to-Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00658)
*Nikita Vasiliev,Kirill Borodin,Vasilii Kudryavtsev,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces Balalaika-Longform, a Russian long-form text-to-speech corpus, and uses it to evaluate how training sequence length affects TTS model performance on continuous synthesis across different text lengths (75, 300, 1,200 words).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form TTS must retain requested words over extended generations, but sentence-level training/evaluation can hide omissions and early stops. The authors aim to isolate the effect of training sequence length under a fixed continuous-generation protocol.

Method: The authors created Balalaika-Longform, an open Russian corpus of 189 hours with continuous units (30 seconds to 15 minutes). They fine-tuned four TTS models (CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, F5-TTS) on either short windows or long targets, then tested continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with unseen voices at three text lengths.

Result: At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER dropped from 99.9% (short-window fine-tuning) to 47.3% (long targets) to 16.6% (punctuated, format-matched transcripts). Long targets favored Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, and marginally F5-TTS (whose WER stayed above 90%).

Conclusion: Training sequence length significantly impacts long-form TTS performance. Long-target fine-tuning substantially reduces word omissions, especially for models like CosyVoice3. Punctuation and format matching provide additional gains. The corpus enables controlled comparisons between short and long training regimes.

Abstract: Long-form text-to-speech must retain requested words over extended generations, yet sentence-level training and evaluation can hide omissions and early stops. We introduce Balalaika-Longform, an open Russian corpus of 189 hours in continuous units of 30 seconds to 15 minutes. Long units and matched short windows support fine-tuning comparisons on the same source recordings, and the accompanying evaluation retains every synthesis attempt. We fine-tune CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2 and F5-TTS on either view and test continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with voices unseen in fine-tuning, at about 75, 300 and 1,200 words. At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER falls from 99.9% after short-window fine-tuning to 47.3% with long targets, and to 16.6% with punctuated, format-matched transcripts; paired intervals favor long targets for Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, and by a small margin for F5-TTS, whose absolute WER stays above 90%. The results isolate the effect of training sequence length under a fixed continuous-generation protocol.

</details>


### [234] [AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00706)
*Pooneh Mousavi,Amir Ivry,Mirco Ravanelli,Cem Subakan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AnchorPrompt is an efficient adaptation method for large audio-language models that learns prompt vectors to improve robustness against various input perturbations (noise, corruption, adversarial injections) while keeping the model frozen. It uses self-distillation training and achieves improved answer consistency across multiple benchmarks and model architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are sensitive to input perturbations such as noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections, which limits their robustness in real-world applications.

Method: AnchorPrompt is proposed - an efficient adaptation method that keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input between audio and question embeddings. Training is performed through self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations. The method uses the model's prediction on clean recordings as targets for answerable inputs and assigns a refusal target when audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. It is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior detection of perturbations.

Result: AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most tested conditions. Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on the remainder of 1.2% at most. It reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations such as choice permutations and reverberation.

Conclusion: AnchorPrompt successfully enhances LALM robustness by reducing hallucinations under severe audio corruption without significantly impacting clean audio performance. The method enables zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions and is perturbation-agnostic at inference, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are sensitive to input perturbations, such as noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections. We propose AnchorPrompt, an efficient adaptation method that keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input, between the audio and question embeddings. We train these vectors through self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations. To improve answer consistency and mitigate hallucination, we use the model's prediction on the clean recording as the target for answerable inputs, and assign a refusal target when the audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. Furthermore, AnchorPrompt is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior detection of perturbations and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions. We evaluate three LALMs across three benchmarks and show that AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most tested conditions. Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on the remainder of 1.2% at most. Crucially, AnchorPrompt reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Finally, these consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations, such as choice permutations and reverberation.

</details>


### [235] [Where the Body Keeps the Beat: Structured Motion Conditioning and Music Dynamics Supervision for Dance-to-Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00726)
*Changchang Sun,Lu Cheng,Yan Yan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Dyna2Music is a latent flow-matching framework for dance-to-music (D2M) generation that synthesizes musically plausible soundtracks aligned with dance performances. It addresses limitations in existing methods by explicitly modeling motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, and introducing a latent dynamics consistency (LDC) objective to supervise local music-latent dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing D2M methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, and standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. The paper aims to improve rhythmic alignment and audio quality by addressing these gaps.

Method: The method decomposes joint velocities into slow and fast components and hierarchically fuses part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features for music generation conditioning. It also introduces latent dynamics consistency (LDC), an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between single-step clean-latent estimates and paired references, without adding trainable parameters or inference computation.

Result: Experiments on AIST++ and TikTok datasets demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines. Empirical analysis quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density.

Conclusion: Dyna2Music effectively combines structured motion conditioning with explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics through LDC, achieving superior performance in dance-to-music generation with variable-length support.

Abstract: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to synthesize musically plausible soundtracks whose temporal structure aligns with a given dance performance. Representative D2M methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, while standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. To address these issues, we propose Dyna2Music, a latent flow-matching framework that combines structured motion conditioning with explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics. An empirical analysis on AIST++ quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density, informing the conditioning design. Accordingly, Dyna2Music decomposes joint velocities into slow and fast components and hierarchically fuses the resulting part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features to condition music generation. To complement this representation, we introduce latent dynamics consistency (LDC), an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between a single-step clean-latent estimate and the paired reference. LDC makes local music-latent variation an explicit training target without adding trainable parameters or inference computation. Dyna2Music supports variable-length music generation, and experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines.

</details>


### [236] [RMS-AQA: A Two-Stage Spatial Audio Question Answering Benchmark for Real-World Domestic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00935)
*Peihao Chen,Qing Wang,Lichun Fan,Yufeng Hao,Zhifeng Kong,Mengyao Zhu,Hengyi Hong,Hang Chen,Hang Su,Yujie Jian,Chao-Han Huck Yang,Shichao Hu,Jun Du,Jian Luan,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: RMS-AQA is a spatial audio question answering benchmark for domestic robots, featuring a two-stage QA format to assess audio-language models' ability to ground sound events and perform spatio-temporal reasoning, using both real Ambisonics recordings and synthetic RIR-based data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied assistants in domestic environments need to infer what happened, where, when it occurred, and how to respond - requiring comprehensive spatial audio understanding.

Method: The benchmark combines authentic first-order Ambisonics recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). A lightweight spatial plug-in injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones.

Result: Primary challenges stem from concurrent sources, far distance, and sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

Conclusion: The benchmark successfully provides a comprehensive testbed for evaluating audio-language models on spatial reasoning in domestic settings, though significant challenges remain in handling complex acoustic scenarios.

Abstract: Embodied assistants in domestic environments must infer what happened, where and when it occurred, and how to respond. To address this, we introduce RMS-AQA, a spatial audio question answering (SAQA) benchmark for real-world domestic environments. The benchmark features a two-stage question-answering (QA) format to comprehensively assess the ability of audio-language models (ALMs) to first ground audible sound events and subsequently perform complex spatio-temporal reasoning based on that grounding. To maximize acoustic realism, our dataset combines authentic real-world first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). Furthermore, we provide a lightweight spatial plug-in that injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones. Experimental results reveal that the primary challenges stem from concurrent sources, far distance, and sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

</details>


### [237] [Toward Elastic Speech Inference: Training-Free Wake-Word Detection from Pretrained ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01182)
*Hwayeon Kim,Youngwon Choi,Hyeonyu Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper explores using pretrained ASR models for wake-up word (WuW) detection without gradient-based fine-tuning, applying SliceGPT's PCA-based structured pruning to extract compact encoders. Experiments show stable WuW detection performance with 50% encoder channel dimension reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the need for generalization across diverse domains and acoustic conditions in ASR systems, while avoiding the computational cost and complexity of additional training or task-specific modules for downstream tasks like wake-up word detection.

Method: Apply SliceGPT's PCA-based structured pruning approach to extract compact encoders from pretrained ASR models (Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base) without gradient-based fine-tuning, then evaluate WuW detection performance.

Result: WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%, demonstrating that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models.

Conclusion: Task-relevant compact encoders can be successfully extracted from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning, offering a promising approach for efficient domain adaptation in ASR systems.

Abstract: Recent ASR development has placed growing emphasis on generalization across diverse domains and acoustic conditions. Existing approaches typically adapt pretrained ASR models to front-end functions such as wake-up word (WuW) detection through additional training or task-specific modules. In this work, we explore the use of a shared pretrained ASR backbone for WuW detection without gradient-based fine-tuning and examine whether a compact encoder can be extracted using the PCA-based structured pruning approach of SliceGPT. Experiments with Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base show that WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%. These results suggest that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [238] [AudioJev: Direct Audio Decisions with Order-Calibrated Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293)
*Sihan Lv,Zhen Li,Zhiqi Cao,Jinshan Zhang,Ying Li,Meng Xi,Jianwei Yin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AudioJev is a model that maps waveform, question, and answer alternatives directly to candidate distributions through a shared full-parameter model, with order calibration to preserve answer probability under meaning-preserving option permutations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio decisions depend on evidence not preserved in transcripts, and probability estimates can depend on how answer options are ordered. Existing approaches may not adequately handle these issues.

Method: AudioJev uses random-derangement SKL training: pairs each question with a reordered view where every alternative changes position, supervises both answers, aligns distributions, and applies a symmetric KL penalty. Inference uses a single forward pass without calibration head or order ensemble.

Result: 68.88%/55.33% mean accuracy on complete MMAU/MMAR benchmarks; reduces random-order SKL by 43.8%/60.5% relative to single-view removal ablation. The model handles intent, environmental sound, note properties, speech activity, and conversational transitions.

Conclusion: AudioJev establishes a direct audio interface with calibration objective acting on candidate meaning rather than presentation position, achieving strong accuracy while maintaining probability stability across different option orderings.

Abstract: Audio decisions often depend on evidence that a transcript does not preserve, while their probability estimates can depend on how answer options are ordered. AudioJev maps a waveform, question and supplied alternatives directly to a candidate distribution through one shared full-parameter model. We define order calibration as preserving an answer's probability under meaning-preserving option permutations. Random-derangement SKL training pairs each question with a reordered view in which every alternative changes position, supervises both answers, and aligns the two distributions before applying a symmetric KL penalty. Inference retains a single candidate-scoring forward, with no calibration head or order ensemble. Across three training seeds, AudioJev reaches 68.88%/55.33% mean accuracy on complete MMAU/MMAR and reduces random-order SKL by 43.8%/60.5% relative to the single-view removal ablation. The same model handles intent, environmental sound, note properties, speech activity and conversational transitions. Paired removal ablations and multi-order evaluation measure predictive accuracy and probability stability together, establishing a direct audio interface whose calibration objective acts on candidate meaning rather than presentation position. Inference code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SihanLv/AudioJev-Inference and https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev.

</details>


### [239] [Multi-Party Backchannel Prediction: a Diagnosis, a Benchmark, and a Ceiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01488)
*Mohammed Hafsati,Ahmed Loughzali*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Multi-party benchmark for backchannel prediction using AMI corpus (682 listener views, 18,697 events). State-of-the-art dyadic models fail zero-shot (AUROC 0.499), but retraining achieves 0.751. Backchannel prediction is listener-specific and fails to transfer to unseen listeners, unlike turn-onset prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backchannel prediction has been studied only in dyadic conversations. This work introduces a multi-party benchmark to investigate whether findings generalize to meeting settings.

Method: Built benchmark from AMI corpus with person-disjoint split. Tested zero-shot transfer of dyadic model, linear probe on frozen features, full retraining, and various techniques (adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, lexical conditioning). Compared backchannel vs turn-onset prediction.

Result: Dyadic model zero-shot performs at chance (0.499 AUROC). Linear probe achieves 0.704, retraining reaches 0.751. Listener conditioning helps seen but not unseen listeners; gap persists under capacity reduction, adversarial training, and adaptation. Adversarial training only partially removes speaker identity info; stronger removal hurts prediction. Turn-onset prediction transfers to unseen listeners; backchannel does not. Backchannel rates vary 2x more across individuals than turn-onset.

Conclusion: Backchannel prediction is inherently listener-specific and cannot transfer to unseen listeners. Speaker identity is entangled with useful backchanneling cues, making it difficult to remove without sacrificing prediction accuracy. The benchmark and evaluation tools are released.

Abstract: Backchannel prediction has been studied almost entirely in dyadic conversation. We introduce a multi-party benchmark based on the AMI corpus, comprising 682 masked-listener views from 171 meetings, 190 speakers, and 18,697 backchannel events, with a person-disjoint held-out split. A state-of-the-art dyadic model applied zero-shot to meeting audio performs at chance (AUROC 0.499); nevertheless, its frozen acoustic features remain informative: a linear probe reaches 0.704, and retraining the predictor raises performance to 0.751. Retraining reveals a second limitation. Listener conditioning improves prediction for listeners seen during training but not for unseen listeners, and the gap remains under capacity reduction, listener-adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, and oracle lexical conditioning. Adversarial training removes only part of the speaker-identity information, while stronger removal hurts prediction, suggesting that identity is entangled with cues that are useful for backchanneling. A within-model control helps explain this pattern: with the same features and data splits, turn-onset prediction transfers to unseen listeners, while backchannel prediction does not. Backchannel rates also vary about twice as much across individuals as turn-onset rates. Since backchannels occupy only about 1% of frames, frame-level F1 is strongly affected by the base rate. We therefore report AUROC alongside event-F1 on listener-active regions. We release the benchmark and evaluation tools at https://github.com/HafsatiMohammed/bc_multiparty_release.

</details>


### [240] [Q-SPT: Learnable Query-Based Compression for Low-Frame-Rate Speech Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01492)
*Jeeyoung Yun,Seohwan Yun,Sungwoong Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Q-SPT is a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer that uses separate learnable query-based compressors for semantic and acoustic representations, with autoregressive text loss supervision, achieving superior reconstruction and downstream performance for speech language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lowering frame rate in neural speech codecs reduces computational and memory costs for SLMs, but existing rule-based compression methods (average pooling or similarity-based merging) struggle to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail simultaneously.

Method: Proposed Q-SPT with: (1) Dual-stream architecture with separate semantic and acoustic representations; (2) Fixed-rate queries that independently attend to each stream as separate key-value sources; (3) Two separately learned, context-aware compressors enabling stream-specific aggregation; (4) Autoregressive text loss explicitly supervising the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information.

Result: Q-SPT achieves: (1) Best reconstruction quality among evaluated codecs at the same frame rate; (2) Best speech recognition accuracy in downstream SLMs; (3) Best text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

Conclusion: The query-based dual-stream approach with separate learnable compressors and explicit linguistic supervision successfully balances preserving linguistic information and acoustic detail at low frame rates, making it a promising tokenizer for speech language models.

Abstract: Neural speech codecs increasingly serve as tokenizers for speech language models (SLMs). Lowering the frame rate reduces the computational and memory costs of SLMs, but makes it difficult to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail. Existing approaches rely on rule-based compression: average pooling can discard linguistic information, whereas similarity-based merging uses a fixed threshold on adjacent-frame similarity and applies the resulting boundaries to the acoustic stream. We propose Q-SPT, a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer with separate, context-aware, learnable query-based compressors specialized for semantic and acoustic representations. In particular, queries at a fixed rate independently attend to the semantic and acoustic streams as separate key-value sources, enabling stream-specific, context-aware aggregation through two separately learned compressors. In addition, an autoregressive text loss explicitly supervises the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information. Experimental results show that Q-SPT achieves the best reconstruction among the evaluated codecs at the same frame rate. In downstream SLMs, it yields the best speech recognition accuracy and text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

</details>


### [241] [Beyond Decodability: Do Acoustic Factors Drive Predictions in Speech-Based Alzheimer's Assessment?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01846)
*Serli Kopar,Alkis Koudounas,Roshan P. Rane,Sam Gijsen,Paula A. Perez-Toro,Kerstin Ritter*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study investigates whether acoustic factors (noise, reverberation) in speech recordings systematically affect Alzheimer's disease (AD) predictions from self-supervised learning (SSL) models. Using controlled interventions on ADReSSo dataset with three SSL backbones, researchers found that acoustic interventions alter AD predictions, with noise showing the strongest effects despite no significant diagnostic-group difference in original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech-based AD assessments increasingly use pretrained SSL models that learn from raw audio, potentially exposing models to recording artifacts. The researchers questioned whether acoustic factors are merely encoded in representations or can systematically alter AD predictions, which is critical for clinical trustworthiness.

Method: The study applied controlled noise and reverberation interventions to participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio from the ADReSSo dataset. They combined layer-wise linear decoding, input- and representation-space interventions, and geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from influence on AD prediction.

Result: Controlled acoustic interventions altered AD predictions across all three SSL backbones. Noise produced the strongest intervention effects despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in original data. These effects were systematically structured relative to the classifier's decision direction, replicated on held-out test sets, and reversed when representation-space intervention direction was reversed.

Conclusion: High predictive performance and absence of significant diagnostic-group difference in measured acoustic factors are insufficient for robustness. Intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

Abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessments increasingly rely on pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) models that learn acoustic representations directly from raw audio, exposing the model to recording factors. We ask whether such factors are merely encoded in SSL representations or can systematically alter predictions. Using ADReSSo and three large SSL backbones, we apply controlled noise and reverberation interventions to participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio. We combine layer-wise linear decoding, input- and representation-space interventions, and geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from influence on AD prediction. Our results show that controlled acoustic interventions alter AD predictions across all three SSL backbones. Noise, despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in the original data, produces the strongest intervention effects. Importantly, these effects are systematically structured relative to the classifier's decision direction, replicate on the held-out test set and reverse when the representation-space intervention direction is reversed. Together, these findings show that high predictive performance and the absence of a significant diagnostic-group difference in a measured acoustic factor are not sufficient for robustness. We argue that intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

</details>


### [242] [From Isolated Feature to Orbits: Discovering Music Concepts via Multi-SAE Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01864)
*Liwei Lin,Gus Xia*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper introduces a structure-based interpretability framework for music foundation models, using pitch transposition as an inductive bias with multi-view SAE alignment to discover organized structures (orbits) of pitch-related features like chords, keys, and melodic patterns, requiring only minimal grounding to interpret entire concept families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current interpretability approaches (probing, SAEs) focus on isolated features, but many music concepts (chords, keys) are better understood as structured relations. The authors argue that learned representations should emerge as organized structures over features, not just individual features.

Method: The framework uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to induce ordered orbits via multi-view SAE alignment. They generate pitch-shifted input pairs and align their SAE representations to discover structured groups of pitch-related features.

Result: Experimental results show the approach recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models, requiring only minimal grounding (e.g., a few anchor examples) to interpret entire concept families.

Conclusion: Structure-based analysis is effective for interpreting music foundation models, revealing how tonal structures (organized in pitch and time space) emerge as organized structures in internal representations.

Abstract: How can we understand what a music foundation model has learned \textit{internally}? Most interpretability approaches, such as probing and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), focus on identifying individual features with minimal structural assumptions. We argue that many concepts are better understood as \textit{structured relations} rather than isolated features. This is especially prominent in music, where tonal structures are organized in the space of pitch and time. For example, concepts such as chords or keys are naturally expressed as structured sets (e.g., the 12 transpositions of a chord or the diatonic system within a key), rather than isolated features. In this study, \textbf{we shift from feature identification to structure-based analysis}, asking whether the learned inner representations of music foundation model emerge as organized structures over features. To this end, we introduce a framework that uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to induce ordered orbits via multi-view SAE alignment. Concretely, we generate pitch-shifted input pairs and align their SAE representations to discover structured groups of pitch-related features. Experimental results show that this approach recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models, while requiring only minimal grounding (e.g., a few anchor examples) to interpret entire concept families.

</details>


### [243] [LAST: Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01926)
*Haider Al-Tahan,Sean O'Brien,Anastasia Razdaibiedina,N. Apurva Ratan Murty*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: LAST (Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer) reuses transformer blocks to refine class tokens over fixed audio features, achieving better performance than deeper sequential transformers with fewer parameters and computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increasing transformer depth improves accuracy but requires more parameters, making it computationally inefficient. The authors explore whether additional processing can focus on integrating already-computed features rather than adding new layers.

Method: LAST first processes all tokens once, then reuses the same transformer blocks to iteratively refine only the class token over fixed audio features, making later passes computationally inexpensive.

Result: On AudioSet, ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mAP, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer MACs, and 9.8% higher throughput. Increasing passes from two to ten improves accuracy with only 1.2% computation increase. Shows improved robustness to temporal masking and auditory augmentations, with better generalization on music, environmental, and event sound classification.

Conclusion: Looped architecture with class token refinement provides a more parameter-efficient and computationally cheaper alternative to deeper transformers, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining robustness to various audio augmentations.

Abstract: Increasing depth of transformer models improves recognition, but it comes at a substantial cost. Each additional layer requires more parameters, which makes the process computationally inefficient. We ask whether additional processing can focus on integrating features already computed. Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer (LAST) first processes all tokens, then reuses the same blocks to refine only the class token over fixed audio features, thereby making later passes inexpensive. On AudioSet, ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mean average precision, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer multiply-accumulate operations, and 9.8% higher measured throughput. Across separately trained models, increasing the pass count from two to ten improves accuracy while adding only 1.2% computation. Further evaluations show improved robustness to temporal masking and various other auditory augmentations, with better generalization on classification tasks with music, environmental, and event sounds.

</details>
