# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [244] [Software Project Management with LLM-Based Automation: Coordination, Validation, and Governance in Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00027)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Italo Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands when LLM-based automation is integrated into software development. Through an exploratory case study in a large multi-project organization, the research finds that LLMs influence planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities without introducing new formal management practices. Key effects include LLMs becoming embedded in everyday work, uneven productivity impacts, increased review/validation needs, and reduced visibility into task execution, leading to greater reliance on managerial judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a gap in software engineering literature, which has predominantly focused on task-level and developer-centered uses of LLMs, while overlooking managerial perspectives on automation. The study aims to understand how LLM-based automation affects software project management work in practice.

Method: An exploratory case study approach was adopted, capturing the experiences of software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization. This methodology allows for in-depth, contextual understanding of managerial perspectives on automation in real-world practice.

Result: The analysis reveals that LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities rather than introducing new formal management practices. LLMs are becoming embedded in everyday project work, producing uneven effects on productivity, increasing the need for review and validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. These effects contribute to greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination.

Conclusion: The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted in contexts where LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice. Learning demands were perceived as experiential and incremental, centered on understanding LLM capabilities and limitations, critically assessing generated artifacts, and guiding responsible use within teams.

Abstract: As software engineering has evolved, development environments have increasingly integrated automated support for tasks such as testing, analysis, and code generation, requiring project management to coordinate both human work and automated workflows. In this paper, we investigate how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands associated with LLM-based automation. Motivated by a gap in software engineering research, which has largely focused on task-level and developer-centered uses of LLMs, we adopted an exploratory case study approach to capture managerial perspectives on automation in practice. Based on the experience of software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization, our analysis indicates that LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities rather than introducing new formal management practices. Participants described LLMs as becoming embedded in everyday project work, producing uneven effects on productivity, increasing the need for review and validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. These effects contribute to greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination. Learning demands were perceived as experiential and incremental, centered on understanding LLM capabilities and limitations, critically assessing generated artifacts, and guiding responsible use within teams. The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted in contexts where LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice.

</details>


### [245] [Localizing Post-Wire Semantic Changes in MCP Agent Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00182)
*Aditi Patodiya*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a differential testing method to verify whether agent frameworks preserve Model Context Protocol (MCP) message distinctions needed by downstream consumers. Testing 18 fixtures across four Python integrations, the method identifies 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfies all primary contracts, while others show interface-specific changes or failures. The study concludes that post-wire regression tests must specify both required information and how consumers read it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that valid MCP messages do not guarantee that an agent framework preserves the distinctions downstream software needs. This creates interoperability issues between MCP providers and consumer applications.

Method: Differential testing method that traces a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. Applied to 18 designed fixtures in four pinned Python integrations (including Google ADK and OpenAI integrations).

Result: 13 unique fixture-task divergences identified involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfies every primary contract; other integrations show interface-specific changes or execution failures. Most OpenAI failures explained by treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null. Exploratory replay shows JSON text parsing recovers more structured values but also returns incorrect values and values for fields absent at source.

Conclusion: Post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases, not production failure rates or model-behavior measurements.

Abstract: Valid Model Context Protocol (MCP) messages do not guarantee that an agent framework preserves the distinctions downstream software needs. We present a differential testing method that follows a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. Applied to 18 designed fixtures in four pinned Python integrations, the method identifies 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfies every primary contract in its observed path; the other integrations show interface-specific changes or an execution failure. Whether a change matters depends on the consumer: treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null explains most of OpenAI's strict rich-content failures. In an exploratory replay, parsing JSON text recovers more structured values but also returns incorrect values and values for fields absent at the source. Documented settings help in conflicting-output stress cases without restoring a separate structured slot. Fault challenges expose an oracle weakness and test its repair on fresh cases. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases, not production failure rates or model-behavior measurements. Its practical implication is that post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it.

</details>


### [246] [Testing and Verification of Quantum Compilers through Assurance Contracts and Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00255)
*Furqan Nasir,Muhammad Arif Shah,Iftikhar Alam*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This survey compares methods for ensuring quantum compiler correctness, including verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential/metamorphic testing, and property-based testing. It provides a source catalogue, extraction matrix, failure case analysis, and a worked example demonstrating why circuit validation under reconstructed interpretation may leave the delivered interface unchecked.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum compiler assurance requires a semantic relation matching intended use with observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. Existing methods lack comprehensive comparison, and there's a need to distinguish formal guarantees from empirical findings to guide method selection.

Method: Integrative survey comparing verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, and property-based testing. Uses source catalogue and focused extraction matrix to distinguish formal guarantees, empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practices. Includes four documented failure cases and a worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits.

Result: Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. The worked example demonstrates why validating a circuit under reconstructed interpretation can leave delivered interface unchecked. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims but don't establish common effectiveness ranking.

Conclusion: Proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as complete system; practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events. Guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes for different quantum compiler assurance methods.

Abstract: Quantum compiler assurance requires a semantic relation that matches the intended use and observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. This critical integrative survey compares verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, property-based testing, and evidence for assurance across revisions. A source catalogue and focused extraction matrix distinguish formal guarantees, reported empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practice. A recorded coverage update and source-level selection decisions make the review auditable within its declared scope. Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. A worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits demonstrates why validating a circuit under a reconstructed interpretation can leave the delivered interface unchecked. An illustrative revision scenario then separates fault detection from change attribution. The resulting guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims and do not establish a common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as a complete system; its practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events.

</details>


### [247] [Code That Works, Environments That Don't: Measuring Environment Reproducibility in AI-Generated Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00425)
*Bhanu Prakash Vangala,Tanu Malik*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in code generation evaluation: environment specification (accurately identifying dependencies needed to execute generated code). The authors develop a three-layer framework (declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies) and evaluate three coding agents across four languages and fifty tasks. Results reveal systematic failures with dependency agreement as low as 7%, indicating this dimension of quality is not captured by current benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While coding agents excel at functional correctness, they frequently misspecify software environment dependencies—the precise packages and libraries needed to execute the code. This gap leads to code that passes functional tests but fails in practice due to missing or incorrect dependencies. The authors argue this is a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that existing benchmarks overlook.

Method: The authors (1) developed an agent protocol for environment specification, (2) introduced a three-layer framework categorizing dependencies: declared (explicitly listed), runtime-installed (automatically installed during execution), and necessary-and-sufficient (complete and minimal set), (3) evaluated three coding agents across four programming languages and fifty tasks, measuring inconsistency, redundancy, and incompleteness in dependency specifications.

Result: Coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures in environment specification: (1) Dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks across agents, (2) Newer agents show no meaningful improvement over earlier ones, (3) Largest divergence occurs between declared and runtime dependency layers, (4) The failure stems from environment priors learned from training distributions rather than task-specific factors.

Conclusion: Environment specification is a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks do not capture. The authors motivate the need for training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability. The failure is not resolved by scale or model recency, suggesting fundamental changes to training are needed.

Abstract: Code generation has emerged as a central capability of large language models, with coding agents now able to produce functionally correct software projects from natural language prompts. However, functional correctness alone does not capture a critical dimension of generation quality: environment specification, defined as the accurate identification of the dependencies required to execute generated code, is equally critical. We develop an agent protocol for environment specification and introduce a three-layer framework comprising declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies to systematically assess coding agents for environment specification. Using this protocol, we evaluate the extent to which coding agents systematically misspecify software environment dependencies and how this misspecification varies across three agents, four languages, and fifty programming tasks. Our results show that current coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures along this dimension, producing dependency specifications that are inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete in ways that functional tests do not detect. Across agents, dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks, and newer agents show no meaningful improvement, suggesting the failure is not resolved by scale or recency. The largest divergence occurs between the declared and runtime dependency layers, implicating environment priors learned from the models' training distributions as the primary driver. Our findings establish environment specification as a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks do not capture, and motivate training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability.

</details>


### [248] [Extending LLM-based support for software engineers with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00555)
*Aarsh Shah,Ronnie de Souza Santos,Italo Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Kiev Gama*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Tether 2.0 is an LLM-based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD by providing structured workflow-oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review phases, with activity-aware context and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering workflows are not designed for developers with ADHD, who face challenges with task initiation, sustained attention, and task completion. Existing LLM-integrated programming tools do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks.

Method: The approach combines structured interaction modes, activity-aware context, and persistent memory. The system was evaluated through expert feedback and hands-on use with a software engineer with ADHD.

Result: Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion, while enabling users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions.

Conclusion: LLM-based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context-aware interaction, specifically for neurodiverse users.

Abstract: Software engineering workflows are often not designed to accommodate the needs of developers with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), despite known challenges related to task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into programming tools, but existing systems do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks. In this work, we present Tether 2.0, an LLM based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD through workflow oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review. The tool was named Tether 2.0 because it builds upon the open source code and foundations of the original Tether system. Our approach combines structured interaction modes, activity aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity. We evaluate the system through expert feedback and hands on use with a software engineer with ADHD. Our results indicate that Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion, while enabling users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions. These findings suggest that LLM based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context aware interaction.

</details>


### [249] [Understanding and Mitigating Library-Related Issues in LLM-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00622)
*Yacine Majdoub,Rinad Hamid,Eya Ben Charrada,Ahmad Abdellatif,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses library-related errors in LLM-generated code by proposing an agentic approach that integrates task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation. The study analyzes 100 LLM-generated files and evaluates the approach on 300 tasks across 5 LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software practitioners increasingly rely on LLMs to generate code that integrates external libraries, but LLMs often produce incorrect library usage (invalid imports, outdated API calls, hallucinated dependencies), leading to compilation or runtime failures that reduce the reliability of AI-assisted software development.

Method: 1) Conducted an exploratory study analyzing 100 LLM-generated code files to characterize library-related issues; 2) Designed an agentic approach integrating task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation; 3) Evaluated on 300 code generation tasks from real-world Python frameworks (LangChain, AutoGen) across five LLMs (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, Llama 3).

Result: 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error, with recurring patterns including incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated library usage, and unused imports. The proposed approach reduces library-related errors by 38.1% - 54.6% and increases code correctness by up to 16% across all evaluated models.

Conclusion: The agentic approach consistently improves code generation quality across all evaluated models, effectively reducing library-related errors and improving code correctness in LLM-generated code.

Abstract: Software practitioners increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate code that integrates external libraries. However, LLMs often produce incorrect library usage, such as invalid imports, outdated API calls, and hallucinated dependencies, leading to compilation or runtime failures that reduce the reliability of AI-assisted software development. In this paper, we propose an agentic approach to mitigate libraryrelated errors in LLM-generated code. More specifically, we first conduct an exploratory study to characterize the library-related issues produced by LLMs. Our analysis of 100 LLM-generated code files reveals that 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error, with recurring patterns including incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated library usage, and unused imports. Based on these findings, we design an agentic approach that integrates task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation to improve library usage during code synthesis. We evaluate our approach on 300 code generation tasks derived from realworld implementations of rapidly evolving Python frameworks, including LangChain and AutoGen, across five LLMs: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, and Llama 3. The results show that our approach consistently improves code generation quality across all evaluated models, reducing library-related errors by 38.1% - 54.6% and increasing code correctness by up to 16%.

</details>


### [250] [ASAD: Adaptive Software Agents for Debugging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00629)
*Yacine Majdoub,Eya Ben Charrada,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ASAD is an adaptive multi-agent debugging system that dynamically configures team size, agent roles, and collaboration strategies based on bug complexity. It uses a central coordinator to orchestrate iterative planning, reflection, and execution—applying minimal coordination for simple bugs and assembling purpose-built teams for complex failures. Evaluated on Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws with multiple LLMs, it improves bug-fix rates by 12-20% over CoT and 4-9% over static multi-agent systems while reducing agent usage by 32%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent debugging systems use rigid, predefined architectures with fixed agent counts, roles, and interaction patterns. This one-size-fits-all approach mismatches the heterogeneous nature of software defects—simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex bugs suffer from insufficient or misaligned expertise.

Method: ASAD analyzes faulty code to dynamically determine: (1) number of agents to deploy, (2) specialized roles they should have, and (3) collaboration strategy to follow. A central coordinator orchestrates the process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution—applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams for complex failures.

Result: ASAD consistently improves bug-fix rates by 12-20% over chain-of-thought prompting and consistently outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4-9% in fix precision while reducing average agent usage by 32%. The system dynamically adjusts agent count and roles based on bug complexity.

Conclusion: Adaptive agent configuration significantly improves debugging efficiency and effectiveness. By matching agent resources to bug complexity, ASAD achieves superior fix rates while minimizing resource waste—resolving simple bugs with minimal coordination and scaling involvement only for complex cases.

Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-agent systems has shown great potential for automated debugging. Yet nearly all current frameworks rely on rigid, predefined architectures: the number of agents, their roles, and their interaction patterns are fixed before any analysis of the bug occurs. This one-size-fits-all approach is fundamentally mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects. Simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex ones suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise. This paper introduces ASAD, an adaptive agentic system for debugging that configures its team according to the nature and complexity of each bug. ASAD initiates the debugging process by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determines the number of agents to deploy, the specialized roles they should have, and the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates this process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution; applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams to tackle more complex failures. We evaluate ASAD on three established benchmarks: Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws, using multiple LLMs, such as DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3 and GPT-5. ASAD consistently improves bug-fix rates by 12--20% over chain-of-thought(CoT) prompting and consistently outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4--9% in fix precision while reducing average agent usage by 32%. Crucially, our system dynamically adjusts the number and roles of agents: it resolves simple bugs with minimal coordination and scales agent involvement only for more complex cases.

</details>


### [251] [FORALL-LEAN-AGENT for Auditable Reasoning in Formal Mathematics and Software Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00885)
*Naing Oo Lwin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FORALL-LEAN-AGENT is a framework for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification that addresses the problem that successful Lean proof compilation doesn't guarantee the proof establishes the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking with traceable verification evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents increasingly automate Lean proof development, but successful compilation alone does not establish that a candidate proves the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. There is a need for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification.

Method: The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. Verification evidence and reviewer decisions are bound to the same candidate artifact, making acceptance traceable.

Result: On the 100-task VeriSoftBench subset, integration with FORALL-LEAN-AGENT raises benchmark-rule success from 93 to 100 for GPT-5.6 Sol at low effort while reducing cost from $69 to $62. The PutnamBench evaluation accepts all 672 problems at an average of $4.72 each.

Conclusion: Agent harness design can improve correctness and efficiency while providing evidence beyond aggregate solve counts. The framework demonstrates that frontend-agnostic approaches can enhance formal verification workflows.

Abstract: Coding agents increasingly automate Lean proof development, but successful compilation alone does not establish that a candidate proves the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. We present FORALL-LEAN-AGENT, a frontend-agnostic framework for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification. The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. Verification evidence and reviewer decisions are bound to the same candidate artifact, making acceptance traceable. We evaluate the framework on VeriSoftBench, PutnamBench, and both problems in the Lean Eval softwareverification track. On the 100-task VeriSoftBench subset, integration with FORALLLEAN-AGENT raises benchmark-rule success from 93 to 100 for GPT-5.6 Sol at low effort while reducing cost from $69 to $62. The PutnamBench evaluation accepts all 672 problems at an average of $4.72 each. These results show that agent harness design can improve correctness and efficiency while providing evidence beyond aggregate solve counts.

</details>


### [252] [Understanding Issues, Causes and Solutions in Open-Source LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00905)
*Asad Ur Rehman,Syed Mohammad Kashif,Ruiyin Li,Peng Liang,Zengyang Li,Arif Ali Khan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper conducts an empirical study on 944 issues collected from 21 open-source LLM-based multi-agent systems to understand the challenges, causes, and solutions encountered by practitioners. The study finds that Orchestration & Execution Issues are most common, with Workflow Problems, Tool Integration Problems, and Memory Problems being the primary causes, and Optimize Workflow being the predominant solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the growing adoption of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) in open-source projects, there is limited understanding of the practical challenges faced by developers, their root causes, and potential solutions. This gap motivates an empirical investigation into real-world issues from open-source LLM-based MAS projects.

Method: The authors collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based MAS projects and applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to identify 944 issues directly related to LLM-based MAS. These issues were then analyzed to identify frequent problems, their underlying causes, and potential solutions.

Result: The study reveals three key findings: (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners; (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are the most frequent causes of issues; (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution approach.

Conclusion: The study provides empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers to improve orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS. The findings highlight the need for better workflow design, enhanced tool integration frameworks, and improved memory management in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: With the advancement of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), an increasing number of opensource projects are adopting multi-agent architectures as the foundation of their core functionality. Although research and practice on MAS have attracted considerable attention, limited studies have explored the challenges faced by practitioners of open-source LLM-based MAS, the causes of these challenges, and potential solutions. To address this gap,we conducted an empirical study to understand the issues that practitioners encounter when developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS, the possible causes of these issues, and potential solutions. We collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-basedMASand applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to reduce the dataset to 944 issues related to LLM-based MAS.We then analyzed these issues to understand the frequent issues encountered by practitioners, their underlying causes, and potential solutions. Our study results show that (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, and (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution to the issues. Based on the study results, we derive empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers aimed at improving orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS.

</details>


### [253] [Groundability, Not Scale Alone: When Weak Reviewers Can Audit Strong Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01023)
*Junyu Guo,Shangding Gu,Ming Jin,Javad Lavaei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates when a weaker reviewer can reliably determine whether an AI-generated code patch actually solves its intended issue. The authors studied 411 execution-labeled traces from three coding agents and 101 controlled cases, finding that structured but unchecked evidence improves defect detection but also increases over-rejection. They evaluated a frozen cascade system using static errors and generated tests, achieving 0.89 coverage and 0.76 catch rate on GPT-5.4 traces, with the main bottleneck being producing reliable checks without official tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can generate plausible patches that omit required behavior, but these failures are difficult to review because long execution traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. The research aims to determine when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue.

Method: The authors studied 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents (GPT-5.4, Gemini, and one unnamed) and 101 controlled cases. They provided official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic, then evaluated a frozen cascade combining patch-caused static errors and generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository. Five of six reviewers tested different formats, with two achieving perfect classification on 122 held-out traces.

Result: On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raised both defect catch and over-rejection. After format selection, five of six reviewers improved both rates on 122 held-out traces; two classified every trace correctly. Reviewer size was not a consistent quality predictor. The frozen cascade achieved: coverage 0.89 (GPT-5.4) and 0.86 (Gemini), risk 0.33 and 0.26, catch 0.76 and 0.80, and over-rejection 0.66 and 0.67. Most false rejections occurred when unresolved cases reached the reviewer.

Conclusion: Official execution evidence demonstrates the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. However, producing equally reliable checks without official tests remains the main bottleneck for practical deployment.

Abstract: Coding agents can return plausible patches that omit required behavior. These failures are hard to review because long traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. We ask when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue. We study 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases. On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raises both defect catch and over-rejection. We then provide official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic. After choosing and freezing one of two formats per reviewer, five of six reviewers improve both rates on 122 held-out traces; two classify every trace correctly. Reviewer size is not a consistent predictor of quality. Because official tests are unavailable in deployment, we also evaluate a frozen cascade with patch-caused static errors and generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository. On 121 scored held-out GPT-5.4 traces and 59 Gemini traces, its coverage is 0.89 and 0.86, risk is 0.33 and 0.26, catch is 0.76 and 0.80, and over-rejection is 0.66 and 0.67. Most false rejections occur when unresolved cases reach the reviewer. Official execution evidence shows the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. Producing equally reliable checks without official tests remains the main bottleneck.

</details>


### [254] [Safety Must Survive Self-Improvement: Why Failures Persist and How Agents Recover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01073)
*Yunbei Zhang,Janet Wang,Saiyue Lyu,Yingqiang Ge,Kaiqu Liang,Zijian Jin,Chandan K Reddy,Jihun Hamm*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies safety challenges in recursive self-improvement (RSI) agents through a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks. The research examines how unsafe programs can persist across generations and explores interventions to maintain safety, including validation, rollback, and strategic editing choices. Key findings show that 22/48 framework histories retain unsafe programs despite correct alternatives existing, and that editing the initial implementation rather than the failed one improves recovery. Full validation achieves fully correct programs with 43% deployment savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address critical safety challenges in recursive self-improvement agents: (1) preventing unsafe behavior from persisting across generations, and (2) enabling recovery when failures occur. The study uses a controlled testbed to systematically examine these issues because RSI allows agents to carry useful changes across generations, which could amplify both beneficial improvements and safety failures.

Method: The researchers used a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks with fixed LLM editors optimizing executable agent components. Independent traces recorded the effects of changes. They employed paired interventions to separate: (1) which revisions pass validation, (2) which program continues running, and (3) which program the editor revises next. They tested interventions including score refreshing, full validation, and validated rollback.

Result: Key findings include: (1) After a new authorization dependency invalidated previously tested optimizations, 22 out of 48 framework histories preserved unsafe programs despite a correct alternative in every affected archive; (2) Refreshing scores restored correctness on the original suite but residual failures remained on independently composed tests; (3) Failures persist under unchanged contracts when all proposals are rejected and the failed incumbent remains active; (4) Editing the initial implementation instead of the failed one improves recovery, though the advantage varies across editors; (5) Full validation and validated rollback achieve fully correct programs in core trajectories while retaining over 43% deployment savings.

Conclusion: Preserving agent safety in RSI systems requires two key practices: (1) checking what will run under current conditions (validation), and (2) choosing which implementation to edit next strategically (editing the initial implementation vs. the failed one). The study demonstrates that safety can be maintained through proper validation and rollback mechanisms while achieving significant deployment efficiency savings.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) allows agents to carry useful changes across generations. Maintaining safety across these generations involves both preventing unsafe behavior from persisting and enabling recovery when failures occur. We study these challenges through a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks, where fixed LLM editors optimize executable agent components and independent traces record their effects. Paired interventions separate which revisions pass validation, which program continues running, and which program the editor revises next. After a new authorization dependency invalidates previously tested optimizations, historical scores preserve the same unsafe programs in 22 of 48 framework histories despite a correct alternative in every affected archive. Refreshing scores restores correctness on the original suite, with residual failures on independently composed tests. Failures also persist under an unchanged contract when all proposals are rejected and the failed incumbent remains active. Starting from shared failures, editing the initial implementation instead of the failed one improves recovery, although the advantage varies across editors. Full validation and validated rollback end with fully correct programs in the core trajectory study while retaining over 43% deployment savings. Preserving agent safety requires checking what will run under current conditions and choosing which implementation to edit next.

</details>


### [255] [CompProv Produces Machine Readable Graphs Encoding Microscopic Algebraic Provenance for Reproducible Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01203)
*Minas Abramyan,Mohammed Alaa Ala'anzy,Nasir Saeed*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CompProv is a Java-based provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by using high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) for auditability without exposing proprietary business logic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing provenance systems operate at coarse granularity (files, datasets, pipeline stages), leaving the internal sequence of algebraic transformations unrecorded. Rounding errors, undocumented substitutions, or missing intermediate values can propagate to final results with no recoverable trace, undermining reliability in scientific research and financial modeling.

Method: CompProv encapsulates numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, capturing operation-level lineage. It produces a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact rather than a discarded byproduct. Evaluated through three case studies: (1) decentralized-finance NAV calculation, (2) interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology, and (3) hydrological model performance evaluation.

Result: Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment. CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing underlying source code. The framework enables numerical integrity auditing without disclosing proprietary business logic, provided the CompProv runtime and wrapper classes are available in the replay environment.

Conclusion: CompProv establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems. Its self-contained structure supports temporal auditability once execution environments become deprecated. Future work should address scaling to high-throughput computing.

Abstract: The reliability of computational results in scientific research and financial modeling increasingly depends on verifiable traceability, not merely on trust in a reported output. Existing provenance systems operate at the granularity of files, datasets, or pipeline stages, leaving the internal sequence of algebraic transformations connecting an algorithm's inputs to its outputs unrecorded; a rounding error, an undocumented substitution, or a missing intermediate value can propagate to a final result with no recoverable trace. This work presents CompProv, a Java-based, audit-oriented provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by encapsulating numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact rather than a discarded byproduct. The framework is evaluated through three heterogeneous case studies: a decentralized-finance NAV calculation, a reconstruction of an interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology under explicitly documented input assumptions, and a hydrological model performance evaluation. Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment, and CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing the underlying source code. These results indicate that, provided the CompProv runtime and wrapper classes are available in the replay environment, a CPG allows numerical integrity to be audited without disclosing proprietary business logic, and that its self-contained structure supports temporal auditability once an execution environment has become deprecated. This framework establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems, with scaling to high-throughput computing identified as a direction for future work.

</details>


### [256] [A Design Theory for AI-Assisted Software Development Derived from Christopher Alexander's Theory of Form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01372)
*Chien-Tsun Chen,Yu Chin Cheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Misfit-Governed Development (MGD), a methodology for ensuring LLM-generated code meets specified requirements by using Alexander's theory of form. The approach models LLMs as non-native vernacular builders and uses a dual-loop process with autonomous LLM iteration against gates and human judgment for specifications. Evidence is provided from building a Scrum system with 64 problem-frame specifications, 1,300 tests, and 28 blocking gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated code cannot be assumed to meet requirements; traditional verification methods (reviews, testing, static analysis) are needed, but it's unclear what harness is sufficient. The paper addresses Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge regarding the generativity dimension of software development.

Method: The methodology engineers four components: (1) explicit representations of problems using Jackson's problem frames and of tradition using a four-form pattern language; (2) deterministic misfit detectors; (3) a fix loop; and (4) a human-gated legislative circuit. The dual-loop process separates an autonomous inner loop (LLM iterates against gates) from a human outer loop (specifications judged against the world). This forms the S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world).

Result: Evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system with four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by about 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, including one applying 188 rules.

Conclusion: The approach addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's challenge. The moral dimension (whether specifications fit the world) requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop. The theory treats LLMs as non-native vernacular builders whose output drifts toward mainstream conventions rather than local tradition.

Abstract: Code generated by large language models (LLMs) cannot be assumed to meet specified requirements. Reviews, testing, and static analysis still apply, but which of them a sufficient harness needs, and in what role, is open. We propose a design theory derived from Christopher Alexander's theory of form, and a methodology for applying it. In Alexander's account, fit between a form and its context can be perceived only negatively, through the absence of identified misfits. We make the organization's tradition explicit and derive the misfits from it and from the problem's classification. The theory models the LLM as a non-native vernacular builder, trained on many codebases but native to none, whose output tends to drift toward mainstream conventions rather than the local tradition. We engineer four pieces of machinery: explicit representations of the problem (Jackson's problem frames) and of the tradition (a four-form pattern language); deterministic misfit detectors; a fix loop; and a human-gated legislative circuit governing the representations and detectors. We call the resulting methodology, a practice of harness engineering, Misfit-Governed Development (MGD). Its dual-loop process separates an autonomous inner loop, where the LLM iterates against the gates, from a human outer loop, where specifications are judged against the world. Together they form the S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world), whose equals signs name relations, not identity. We report evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system of four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by about 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, one applying 188 rules. This addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge. The moral dimension, whether the specification still fits the world, requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop.

</details>


### [257] [Refactoring React Component Hierarchies to Eliminate Prop Drilling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01376)
*Vangelis Gkinis,Vassilis E. Zafeiris*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents ReactRefactor, a Node.js tool that uses static analysis to identify Prop Drilling instances in React codebases and automatically refactors them using Context API or Component Composition strategies. Evaluation on open-source projects shows 76.3% of prop drillings can be automatically eliminated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite React documentation discouraging Prop Drilling and research labeling it as a code smell, there is limited knowledge about its prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring in real-world React applications.

Method: The researchers proposed a static analysis method for identifying Prop Drilling instances and implemented it as a Node.js command line tool called ReactRefactor. They empirically evaluated this tool on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications.

Result: Key findings: (a) Prop drilling occurs frequently across benchmark projects regardless of project size; (b) generally low to moderate complexity in data propagation depth, but more prevalent complexity arises from simultaneous forwarding of multiple properties along the same path; (c) 76.3% of prop drillings can be automatically eliminated, primarily through refactoring to the Context API.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that Prop Drilling is a widespread issue in React projects, and most instances (76.3%) can be successfully automated for refactoring, with Context API being the preferred transformation strategy.

Abstract: In React front-end development, Prop Drilling is the practice of propagating data through component properties across multiple levels of the component hierarchy. Despite being discouraged by React documentation and characterized as a code smell by recent research, little is known about its prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring. In this work, we propose a static analysis method for identifying Prop Drilling instances in a React codebase and eliminating them using two automated refactoring strategies based on Context API and Component Composition. The proposed method is implemented as a Node.js command line tool, ReactRefactor, and empirically evaluated on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications. The main findings of the empirical evaluation indicate (a) the frequent occurrence of prop drillings across benchmark projects, irrespective of project size; (b) their generally low to moderate complexity in terms of data propagation depth, contrasted with the more prevalent complexity arising from the simultaneous forwarding of multiple properties along the same path; and, (c) the potential for automated elimination of a substantial share (76.3%) of prop drillings, primarily through refactoring to the Context API.

</details>


### [258] [Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01611)
*Noman Ahmad,Ruoyu Su,Matteo Esposito,Andrea Janes,Valentina Lenarduzzi,Davide Taibi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a Multivocal Literature Review consolidating research on architectural degradation, examining measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies across 284 studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality, but existing research is fragmented across various approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies. This fragmentation limits understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle.

Method: Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies, using an LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication for screening, data extraction, and classification.

Result: Identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. Remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions with less consolidation.

Conclusion: The field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. The diagnosis-remediation gap is identified as a key direction for future research.

Abstract: Context. Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality. However, existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting our understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle. Aim. We consolidate the state of the art on architectural degradation by examining how researchers measure it, which metrics and tools support its assessment, and how existing approaches address remediation. Method. We conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies. We supported screening, data extraction, and classification with a locally executed LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication. We then analyzed the resulting taxonomies and their cross-dimensional relationships. Results and Conclusions. We identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. In contrast, remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions and shows substantially less consolidation. Overall, the field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. Our results provide a structured view of the available techniques and identify the diagnosis-remediation gap as a key direction for future research.

</details>


### [259] [Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01664)
*Alberick Euraste Djire*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM judges can outperform dedicated code provenance detectors, but reliability varies by model, generator, and prompting strategy. Accuracy alone can mask severe prediction bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code detectors validated on one generation of LLMs may not transfer to the next (detector half-life problem). This study investigates whether general-purpose LLM judges can serve as training-free alternatives to dedicated detectors.

Method: Evaluated 8 general-purpose LLM judges and 3 dedicated detectors on human-written code and code from 7 generators across C++, Java, and Python. Assessed performance across generators and prompting strategies.

Result: Dedicated detectors (DetectCodeGPT, GPT-Sniffer) achieved 0.50 accuracy but 0.00 F1 due to classifying almost all samples as AI-generated, revealing accuracy can mask severe prediction bias. General-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores, outperforming dedicated detectors. However, performance varied considerably across generators and prompting strategies.

Conclusion: General-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance, but reliability depends on judge model, code generator, and prompting strategy. Recommendation: evaluate LLM judges across multiple generators and report macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

Abstract: Code detectors can become obsolete as code-generating models evolve: a detector validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next. We call this limited useful life a detector half-life. We evaluate eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. Our results reveal two problems. First, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting that some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance. Second, accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias. DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved an accuracy of 0.50 but an F1 score of 0.00 across all generators because they classified almost every sample as AI-generated. However, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores. Our results show that general-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. We therefore recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

</details>


### [260] [CONTRA: Discovering and Qualifying Behavior-Changing Questions for Selective Clarification in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01769)
*Zheng Fang,Yongmin Li,Yichang Zhang,Dongming Jin,Haoyu Wang,Shuai Wang,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CONTRA is a training-free method that helps coding agents ask the right clarification questions when requirements are underspecified. It generates candidate questions, filters irrelevant ones, tests for behavioral differences between different plausible answers, and uses interaction history to select questions. It outperforms baselines on ClarifyCodeBench by 13.88 percentage points in F1 and is implemented as a Claude Code plugin.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements behavior the user never intended due to underspecified requirements. When agents silently resolve these underspecified requirements through their own assumptions, subsequent development builds on these assumptions, making corrections increasingly costly. While early clarification can help prevent such mismatches, unnecessary questions can interrupt developers and slow down development. Existing methods struggle to identify key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones.

Method: CONTRA is a training-free method that combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. It works in three stages: (1) Generate candidate questions and filter out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by the requirement; (2) For each remaining question, generate programs conditioned on two plausible answers and check for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs; (3) Use the interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking.

Result: CONTRA achieves the highest F1 on ClarifyCodeBench with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than the coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands.

Conclusion: CONTRA effectively identifies key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones, preventing costly behavior mismatches in coding agent development. The method is practical and has been implemented as a Claude Code plugin for everyday development integration.

Abstract: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements behavior the user never intended. This mismatch can arise when an agent silently resolves underspecified requirements through its own assumptions. As subsequent development builds on these assumptions, correcting the resulting behavior can become increasingly costly. Early clarification can help prevent such mismatches, but unnecessary questions can interrupt developers and slow down development. Existing methods struggle to identify key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones. Therefore, we propose CONTRA, a training-free method that combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. CONTRA first generates candidate questions and filters out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by the requirement. For each remaining question, it generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. It then uses the interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking. Experiments on ClarifyCodeBench show that CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than the coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands. To support practical use, we also implement CONTRA as a Claude Code plugin that integrates selective clarification into everyday development.

</details>


### [261] [Detecting Inconsistencies in Model Specifications with LLM-as-Verifier Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01847)
*Zichen Xie,Mrigank Pawagi,Lize Shao,Yang Hu,Wenxi Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriSpec is the first approach to directly detect inconsistencies in LLM model specifications by auditing specification text itself, using an LLM as a verifier while preserving natural language format.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model specifications may contain defects where two individually reasonable principles prescribe incompatible behavior, but detecting such inconsistencies is challenging because formalizing natural-language specifications risks losing subtle distinctions, while behavior-based testing cannot distinguish specification defects from model behavior differences.

Method: VeriSpec extracts structured, context-aware rules from specifications, constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, and applies LLM-as-verifier reasoning to detect inconsistencies.

Result: Applied to OpenAI Model Spec: extracted 405 rules, manually validated 5 inconsistencies (all reported to developers, who responded positively). Compared with five baselines, VeriSpec achieves highest precision (38.5%) and lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12).

Conclusion: Direct specification auditing is a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching defects at the source before they shape any model.

Abstract: Model specifications define how large language models (LLMs) should behave, guiding alignment training, inference-time behavior, and evaluation. Yet these specifications may themselves contain defects: two individually reasonable principles may prescribe incompatible behavior when applied to the same situation, leaving no response that satisfies both. Detecting such inconsistencies is challenging. Formalizing natural-language specifications risks losing subtle distinctions, while behavior-based testing cannot reliably distinguish specification defects from differences in model behavior. We introduce VeriSpec, the first approach to directly detect inconsistencies in model specifications by auditing the specification text itself. Our key insight is to preserve the specification in natural language while using an LLM as a verifier. VeriSpec extracts structured, context-aware rules, constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, and applies LLM-as-verifier reasoning to detect inconsistencies. Applying VeriSpec to the OpenAI Model Spec, we extract 405 rules and manually validate five inconsistencies, all reported to its developers, who responded positively and have initiated internal discussions. Compared with five baselines, VeriSpec identifies the most validated inconsistencies, achieves the highest precision (38.5%), and incurs the lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12). These results establish direct specification auditing as a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching defects at the source before they shape any model. The code is available at https://github.com/HIPREL-Group/VeriSpec.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

### [262] [Frozen Scenes, Shifting Winners: Configuration Fragility in Text-to-3D Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00447)
*Anson Y. Lam,Shuqing Li,Michael R. Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits whether text-to-3D generation leaderboards remain stable when evaluation protocols (camera settings, caption wording, render factors) are varied. Using 300 frozen scenes from six generators tested across 19 alignment evaluators, the study finds that configuration variance often exceeds generator variance, with 17/19 evaluators showing more variance from protocol changes than from actual generator differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether text-to-3D leaderboard rankings are stable across different evaluation protocols, recognizing that rendered-image evaluation involves camera settings and caption wording that become part of the measurement protocol itself. This is important because leaderboards are used to compare generators, but if their rankings depend heavily on arbitrary protocol choices, comparisons may be misleading.

Method: The study uses 300 frozen scenes from six generators, varying eight render and caption factors across 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control. They test four targeted scene degradations and analyze score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity. Methods include: varying render settings and caption wording, computing variance decomposition (protocol vs. generator), testing pairwise protocol margin envelopes, and evaluating directional discrimination on layout scrambling.

Result: Key findings: (1) Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 17/19 alignment evaluators; (2) Prompt-bootstrap lower bounds exceed 1 for 11/19 evaluators; (3) Rankings are more stable than scores, but 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration; (4) No reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search; (5) No evaluator exceeds 67% tie-adjusted directional discrimination on layout scrambling.

Conclusion: The observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. The audit separates score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity. Recommendations include reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty. The findings suggest that text-to-3D evaluation protocols need standardization and uncertainty quantification to make meaningful generator comparisons.

Abstract: Can a text-to-3D leaderboard change when every generated scene stays fixed? We audit this question for rendered-image evaluation, where camera settings and caption wording become part of the measurement protocol. Across 300 frozen scenes from six generators, we vary eight render and caption factors for 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control, then test four targeted scene degradations. Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 17/19 alignment evaluators, with prompt-bootstrap lower bounds above 1 for 11/19. Rankings are more stable than scores, yet 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. Pairwise protocol margin envelopes show which comparisons keep their direction across the tested settings. Selected pairs have opposite pointwise intervals, but no reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search. Thus the observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. Sensitivity remains separate: no evaluator, even the prompt-free control, exceeds 67% tie-adjusted directional discrimination on layout scrambling, which is diagnostic rather than human-validated ground truth. The audit separates score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity, and recommends reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty.

</details>


### [263] [Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00010)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the evaluation of memory systems in long-horizon language agents, identifying that current benchmarks miss the "shape of memory use" - how memory concentrates on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. The authors propose Core-Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget using exponent τ while retaining a summarized tail. The method achieves 5.9% token reduction on Synthetic Graph World, consistent savings on ALFWorld, and 24.48% reduction on LongMemEval while maintaining accuracy parity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory systems for long-horizon language agents are evaluated only by task success or token cost, ignoring the "shape of memory use" - how memory concentrates under finite context and repeated retrieval. The authors argue this is critical because agent memory can concentrate on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. This observation motivates the need to understand and control the core-tail structure of memory traces.

Method: The authors conduct a "conservative tail audit" to study memory concentration effects, comparing random-walk agents (log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts) with semantic LLM policies (truncated-power-law-compatible core-tail traces). Based on this audit, they propose Core-Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent τ while retaining a summarized tail. Experiments are conducted on Synthetic Graph World, ALFWorld, and LongMemEval benchmarks.

Result: On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to a graph-memory baseline. On ALFWorld, consistent token savings are observed. On LongMemEval, a 24.48% token reduction is achieved with aggregate accuracy parity. Random-walk agents produce log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts, while semantic LLM policies yield the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible core-tail traces.

Conclusion: Heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models. The Core-Tail World Model (CTWM) provides an effective way to manage memory allocation, achieving significant token savings while maintaining accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Long-horizon language agents increasingly rely on external memory as a frozen world model, yet current memory systems are usually judged only by task success or token cost. We argue that the missing object is the shape of memory use: under finite context and repeated retrieval, agent memory can concentrate on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. We study this effect through a conservative tail audit and find that concentration is reproducible but policy-dependent. Random-walk agents produce log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts, whereas semantic LLM policies yield the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible core--tail traces. Motivated by this audit, we propose Core--Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent $τ$ while retaining a summarized tail. On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to a graph-memory baseline. The same paired comparison gives consistent token savings on ALFWorld and a 24.48% token reduction on LongMemEval with aggregate accuracy parity. These results suggest that heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval, but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models.

</details>


### [264] [When Do Causal World Models Help Modular LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00012)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in LLM agent planning: standard world models fit observational traces but fail to capture causal relationships needed for intervention-time planning. The authors propose FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents, and demonstrate that causal structure helps only when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable and presented in a usable form at action time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that observational traces show correlation (e.g., payment precedes shipment) but not causation (payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates, or hidden trigger explains both). Standard world models cannot distinguish between these causal structures, leading to poor intervention-time planning in modular LLM agent systems where actions in one module affect valid transitions in another.

Method: The authors develop FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework where local actions provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. They theoretically prove that: (1) observational world models incur irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, (2) interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and (3) oracle causal composition beats non-causal lower bounds when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled. They validate these predictions through diagnostic agent experiments in structured tool environments versus dialogue/narrative environments.

Result: Theoretical results show causal world models outperform observational models under specific conditions. Empirical testing reveals: causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. In contrast, dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes causal information decision-relevant.

Conclusion: Causal world models in LLM agents help when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable (through intervention-response evidence) and presented in a form the agent can use at action time. This identifies a concrete condition for when causal structure provides practical value: the intersection of causal identifiability and decision-relevant presentation.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act through modular systems, such as order, payment, inventory, and shipment services, where actions in one module change which transitions are valid in another. Standard world models usually fit observational traces, but this is not the quantity needed for intervention-time planning: a trace may show that payment precedes shipment without identifying whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both. We study this gap through FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents in which local actions provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. We first show that observational world models incur an irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, that interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and that an oracle causal composition can beat the non-causal lower bound when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled. We then test the resulting prediction in diagnostic agent settings. Causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments, where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. In contrast, dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes the causal information decision-relevant. These results identify a concrete condition for causal world models in LLM agents: causal structure helps when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable and presented in a form the agent can use at action time.

</details>


### [265] [From Proposal to Verified Effect: Praxa, an Evidence-Bound Harness for Governed AI Agent Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00015)
*Stefan G. Creadore*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Praxa is an agent harness that makes authority-to-effect transitions in LLM agents explicit and testable through deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. Four evidence lanes are reported: unit test passing rates, a Terminal-Bench pilot showing no superiority for reliability layer, a development comparison showing token/cost reductions but no quality improvement, and deployed evidence showing bounded reflection but no production outcome lift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-language-model agents can propose and execute actions, but different claims (proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, and promotion) are conflated. The authors present Praxa to make these states explicit and testable.

Method: Praxa implements five mechanisms: deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. Four evidence lanes are evaluated: (1) author-run repository-local audit with unit tests and coverage, (2) Terminal-Bench Core 0.1.1 pilot with 12 curated tasks comparing baseline and reliability layer, (3) post-debug development comparison with 180 trials, and (4) deployed source/configuration evidence analysis.

Result: Lane 1: 1,027/1,027 unit tests and 89/89 Workerd tests passed, 363 source files instrumented, coverage floors met. Lane 2: Both baseline and reliability layer passed 17/36 trials; reliability layer used 37.49% more input and 50.73% more output tokens—no superiority. Lane 3: Both completed 180/180 trials with equal accuracy; candidate used 37.11% fewer tokens, 33.84% lower cost, 11.63% fewer steps—but no quality/latency improvement established. Lane 4: Bounded reflection, recall accounting, memory compilation, and tool-health paths demonstrated, but no production outcome lift.

Conclusion: Praxa's contribution is an evidence-bound architecture that makes authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable. However, current evidence does NOT establish adversarial security, production safety, general specialist superiority, autonomous recursive optimization, or user benefit. The paper emphasizes evidence-bound claims and transparency about limitations.

Abstract: Large-language-model agents can propose and execute actions, but proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, and serving promotion are different claims. We present Praxa, an agent harness that represents these states explicitly through deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. We report four evidence lanes.
