First, an author-run repository-local audit at a pinned revision passed 1,027/1,027 unit tests and 89/89 Workerd tests, instrumented all 363 expected source files, and met four coverage floors; raw per-test transcripts and independent reproduction are unavailable. Second, in a provider-backed Terminal-Bench Core 0.1.1 pilot across 12 curated tasks, baseline and reliability-layer arms each passed 17/36 strict trials. The reliability layer used 37.49% more input and 50.73% more output tokens, so the pilot does not support superiority. Third, in a post-debug, two-order coordination-proxy development comparison, baseline and a source-authored candidate each completed 180/180 trials with equal measured accuracy, full hermetic crash recovery, and zero protected violations. The candidate used 37.11% fewer tokens, 33.84% lower estimated endpoint cost, and 11.63% fewer steps; this does not establish improved quality, latency, or production behavior. Fourth, deployed source/configuration evidence shows bounded reflection, recall accounting, memory compilation, and tool-health paths, but no production outcome lift. Praxa's supported contribution is an evidence-bound architecture that makes authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable. Current evidence does not establish adversarial security, production safety, general specialist superiority, autonomous recursive optimization, or user benefit.

</details>


### [266] [What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00018)
*Jiameng Zhang,Hongqiu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates what value the rationale (explanation) actually provides when passed from a reasoner to a verifier in QA pipelines. Using a "message-intervention diagnostic" that varies only the rationale while fixing evidence and answers, the authors find that faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy improvement over no rationale, but corrupted rationales significantly impact support judgments (10-55% shift depending on prompt). Only a small fraction of support changes co-occur with answer changes, and humans can detect most corrupted rationales that models accept.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand what the rationale message actually accomplishes in reasoner-verifier QA pipelines - whether it improves answers, support assessment, or introduces new failure modes. The key insight is that rationale sharing is typically evaluated only for answer accuracy, not as a verification mechanism.

Method: The authors introduce a "message-intervention diagnostic" that fixes evidence and candidate answers while varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. They test on 400 examples from MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA using DeepSeek as both generator and verifier. They compare faithful rationales, corrupted rationales, and harmless paraphrases under different verifier prompts (blind vs. explicit rationale-checking).

Result: Key findings: (1) Faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale; (2) Corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments (10-22% shift with blind verifier, 34-55% with explicit rationale-checking); (3) Final answers move less (2-30%), and only 2.9-35.3% of corrupted support flips co-occur with answer changes; (4) Human audits show 16/42 valid corruptions are "corruption-overtrust" cases; (5) Blind humans reject or mark unclear 9/10 audited corrupted rationales that the model accepts.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism, not merely as a route to higher answer accuracy. The rationale channel can be active, amplified, inert, or folded into the task label depending on model and task. The key risk is "corruption-overtrust" - models accept invalid rationales that humans would reject.

Abstract: Role-specialized QA pipelines increasingly pass rationales from a reasoner to a verifier, but it is unclear what this message actually buys: better answers, stronger support assessment, or a new failure surface. We introduce a message-intervention diagnostic that fixes the evidence and candidate answer while varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. On 400 MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA examples with DeepSeek as generator and verifier, faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale, while corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments. Under a blind verifier prompt, harmless paraphrases shift support by only 0--2.5%, whereas corrupted rationales shift support by 10--22%; an explicit rationale-checking prompt amplifies the same pattern to 34--55%. Final answers move less (2--30%), and only 2.9--35.3% of corrupted support flips co-occur with answer changes. Human audits show why this matters: 16/42 valid corruptions are corruption-overtrust cases, and blind humans reject or mark unclear 9/10 audited corrupted rationales that the model accepts. Cross-model and task-boundary checks show when the channel is active, amplified, inert, or folded into the task label. Rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism, not merely as a route to higher answer accuracy.

</details>


### [267] [Measuring the Microtask Eligibility Gap: When Is an Off-the-Shelf SLM Enough for an Agent Harness?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00025)
*Jundong Hu,Shekar Ramachandran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether small language models (SLMs) can handle microtasks around an LLM planner (auto-approving shell commands, writing memory, selecting tools, ranking past turns). Testing Qwen3 models (0.6-8B) and Llama-3.x against practitioner-defined thresholds, they find 0/16 configurations pass eligibility. Quantization does not help. The practical recommendation is to use SLMs only where a baseline fails to meet the CI-backed threshold.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether off-the-shelf SLMs can handle microtasks around a frontier LLM planner. They want to determine if SLMs meet practitioner-defined thresholds, understand why they fail, and whether quantization improves performance.

Method: Built a benchmark of 4 microtasks with fixed prompts and automatic metrics. Each task has a pre-specified threshold τ anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline with CI-aware eligibility rule. Tested Qwen3 models (0.6/1.7/4/8B) at FP16, greedy, one frozen prompt, no tuning. Tested 4-bit quantization (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ). Replicated on Llama-3.x. Tested robustness to anchor choice (τ-sweep) and prompt wording (3 neutral paraphrases per cell).

Result: 0 of 16 configurations pass eligibility (4 tasks × 4 models). A logprob decision-threshold diagnostic separates failures into capability deficits and decoding threshold issues. Quantization damages performance depending on model size and moves no configuration into eligibility. The gap tracks model size more than precision. Replicates on Llama-3.x (12/12 ineligible). Robust to anchor choice and prompt wording (0/112 eligible).

Conclusion: Place SLMs behind a baseline that meets the CI-backed threshold, and use SLM only where the baseline fails. Example: 4B re-ranker over BM25 shortlist beats BM25 (+0.047 [0.020, 0.073]), without itself certifying eligibility.

Abstract: Agent harnesses increasingly want to run small language models (SLMs) on the microtasks around a frontier large language model (LLM) planner: auto-approving shell commands, writing memory, selecting tools, ranking past turns. We ask whether off-the-shelf SLMs meet practitioner-defined thresholds and, when they fail, why, and whether quantization changes the answer. We build a benchmark of 4 such microtasks with fixed prompts and automatic metrics, each with a pre-specified threshold $τ$ anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline and a CI-aware eligibility rule (a configuration passes only if its confidence bound clears $τ$). Sweeping Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B at their best (FP16, greedy, one frozen prompt, no tuning), we find an eligibility gap: 0 of 16 (4 tasks $\times$ 4 models) configurations pass (verified by checking the raw outputs and parser behavior). A logprob decision-threshold diagnostic (T1/T3/T4; T2 via a context-length/cascade probe) separates the failures into capability deficits and failures that can be addressed by changing the decoding threshold (4 regimes). Quantization to 4-bit (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ) does damage that depends on model size and moves no configuration into eligibility (certified on the reconstructable hard-label tasks T1/T3, diagnostic/windowed robustness on T2/T4), so the gap tracks model size more than precision; it replicates on Llama-3.x (12/12 ineligible) and is robust to the anchor choice (a $τ$-sweep) and to prompt wording (0/112 eligible across the original plus 3 neutral paraphrases per cell). The practical implication: place SLMs behind a baseline that meets the CI-backed threshold, and use the SLM only where the baseline fails to meet the threshold; e.g. a 4B re-ranker over a BM25 shortlist beats BM25 ($+0.047$ [0.020, 0.073], without itself certifying eligibility).

</details>


### [268] [Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00047)
*Khawaja Murad ul Hassan,Mehran Ebrahimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), a technique where high-scoring chain-of-thought prefixes are extracted and grafted into sibling chains when pruned by a Process Reward Model. Despite prior work suggesting benefits, the authors find PPFG performs statistically identically to independent parallel-CoT across all tested configurations (3 LMs, 6 benchmarks, 2 PRMs). The failure is attributed to poor targeting: only 14% of injection events actually target struggling chains, with the rest landing on chains that have already succeeded, are near completion, or on flat PRM plateaus where rescue is impossible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG) - a mechanism where when a Process Reward Model (PRM) prunes a chain-of-thought, its high-scoring prefix is extracted and grafted as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling chain. Prior work suggested this technique should improve performance, but the authors test it at a specific operating point where prior work reported gains only with additional compensating ingredients.

Method: Tested PPFG on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds). Conducted a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events to understand targeting accuracy. Tested across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and performed a compatibility-gate sweep. Used random control comparison and hindsight oracle analysis.

Result: PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. Only 14% of injection events targeted genuinely struggling chains; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or on a flat PRM plateau. A random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate. Injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but no population-level compensation exists. Hindsight oracle bounds per-problem gain at +0.13 percentage points.

Conclusion: The equivalence between PPFG and independent parallel-CoT is established as positive equivalence across all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells tested. The failure is due to poor targeting: the mechanism cannot rescue chains that have already succeeded, are near completion, or are on flat PRM plateaus. The paper contributes an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point.

Abstract: Diversity collapse in parallel chain-of-thought has motivated inference-time interventions built on a natural design: when a process reward model (PRM) prunes a chain, its high-PRM prefix is extracted and grafted verbatim as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling. We isolate this mechanism, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), as the most cost-minimal operationalization of cross-trajectory step-level transfer, and test it at the operating point where prior fragment-grafting work reports gains only under additional compensating ingredients. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds), PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. We characterize why: a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events shows only 14% targeted a genuinely struggling chain; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or sat on a flat PRM plateau, states a rescue graft cannot change. No compound-gate refinement jointly achieves well-targeted firing and adequate density, and a random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate, so the inertness is not heuristic-specific. The finding replicates across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep; two-one-sided-tests analysis promotes the parity to positive equivalence on all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells. A per-event spot-check finds injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but a surviving-sibling counterfactual finds no population-level compensation. A hindsight oracle bounds any per-problem gain from choosing PPFG over independent at +0.13 pp. We contribute an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point.

</details>


### [269] [Gradient-Aligned Pair Selection for Personalized Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00061)
*Ruoming Jin,Xinyu Li,Hao Zhou,Jianfeng Zhu,Ruixin Guo,Feodor Dragan,Lei Xu,Haixun Wang,Yang Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), a method that treats preference pair selection as a geometric decision in the optimization landscape rather than a heuristic preprocessing step. By analyzing the interaction between utility gradients and DPO update directions, the authors show that pair selection critically affects whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to personalizing LLMs using DPO rely on heuristic pair selection criteria (e.g., likelihood-based extremes) that decouple optimization from explicit user utility, leading to degraded personalization. There was a need to formalize pair selection as an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry.

Method: The authors formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. They reveal that under off-policy sampling, DPO transitions from error-corrective to reinforcement-like when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. Based on this insight, they propose GAP-DPO, which performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration.

Result: Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants.

Conclusion: Gradient alignment serves as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization. Pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step, which should be considered in future preference learning research.

Abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires aligning generation behavior with user-specific preferences rather than aggregate quality. While Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a stable framework for preference learning, its effectiveness in personalized settings critically depends on how preference pairs are selected. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic criteria, such as likelihood-based extremes, which decouple optimization from explicit user utility and can lead to degraded personalization. We formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Our analysis reveals that, under off-policy sampling, the DPO update transitions from a purely error-corrective signal to a reinforcement-like update when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. This perspective exposes pair selection as a geometric decision that governs whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization. Motivated by this insight, we propose GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), an iterative algorithm that performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration. Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants. Together, our results establish gradient alignment as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization and demonstrate that pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step.

</details>


### [270] [K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00074)
*Aubrey M. Brueckner,Darshil Patel,Yuhuan He,Timothy Kassis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: K-Dense BYOK is an open-source AI research assistant that runs locally on researchers' computers, providing scientific scaffolding, workflow templates, and a living lab notebook. It records agent actions by observation rather than self-report to address model overclaiming, and outperformed two managed platforms on 20 interdisciplinary research prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses a critical problem in AI-assisted research: model overclaiming (where models make unverifiable claims). The authors previously benchmarked nine frontier models and found overclaiming to be the most common failure mode. They designed K-Dense BYOK to make claims checkable rather than preventing them, and to give researchers complete control over their data and environment.

Method: The system was evaluated on 20 interdisciplinary research prompts using a rubric fixed in advance. It was compared against two managed platforms (one running the same frontier model). Evaluation covered both scientific quality and research execution. The system was assessed for deliverables including software environment records and reproducibility (commands to regenerate results).

Result: K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran and the only ones that usually arrived with a command to regenerate results. One managed platform ran the same frontier model but provided neither environmental records nor regeneration commands.

Conclusion: K-Dense BYOK demonstrates that a local, researcher-controlled AI assistant can outperform managed platforms on scientific quality and research execution. The key innovation is recording agent actions through observation rather than self-report, addressing model overclaiming. The system maintains complete records in ordinary folders, ensuring data longevity without requiring the application. The code is available under MIT license.

Abstract: K-Dense BYOK (bring your own keys) is a free, open-source AI research assistant for scientists in any field that runs on the researcher's own computer. The researcher supplies access to a model of their choice, hosted or running locally, and the application supplies everything else: a place for the work to run, a layer of scientific scaffolding, and a complete record. Each project is an ordinary folder, so the data, the code, the results, and the record stay on a machine the researcher administers and can be read years later without the application. Three things separate it from a chat assistant or a general-purpose coding agent. It ships a library of written scientific procedures, guided workflow templates, catalogs of where research data can be found, and reviewer and writer roles the agent can hand work to. It keeps a Living Lab Notebook whose entries link into an argument and are added to but never erased. And it records what happened by watching what the agent does rather than by taking the agent's word for it, in a log the agent has no tool that can write to. That choice targets the most common failure, model overclaiming, in our earlier benchmark of nine frontier models, by making claims checkable rather than preventing them. On twenty interdisciplinary research prompts, scored under a rubric fixed in advance, K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran in, and the only ones that usually arrived with a command that regenerates the results. One of the managed platforms ran the same frontier model and supplied neither. Those environment records were files the agent wrote, not part of the observed log, which does not yet capture the software environment itself. The code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok.

</details>


### [271] [Scientific Agents: Evaluating Profession-Specific System Prompts on Scientific Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00084)
*Timothy Kassis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Detailed profession-specific system prompts (503 profiles) do not improve accuracy over minimal baselines on scientific tasks, while increasing token use 1.5-2.3x and costs 2.2-4.5x. One unexpected benefit: longer prompts provide more resilience against API failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether detailed profession-specific system prompts (Scientific Agents corpus) improve LLM accuracy on scientific tasks, as these prompts are widely used but have not been systematically benchmarked.

Method: Compared matched profession profiles against 4 controls (minimal baseline, opening role sentence, generic scientific rigor guide, unrelated domain profile) across 9 text-based science benchmarks (4,531 questions, 100 profiles) and 60 BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems. Used Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in Pi agent harness with automated rule-based grading.

Result: No accuracy improvement: profile-baseline difference = -0.6 percentage points (95% CI [-1.5, +0.2]). On BioMysteryBench, profile actually performed worse (46.7% vs 56.7%, -10.0 pp). Costs increased 2.2-4.5x. Unexpected benefit: longer prompts had higher first-pass success on API drops (71.6% vs 54.0%).

Conclusion: Loading full profession profiles by default does not improve accuracy and costs significantly more. The API resilience advantage suggests prompt length/formatting, not domain expertise, drives this benefit. Selective retrieval of profile sections or testing on open-ended tasks may yield different results.

Abstract: Detailed profession-specific system prompts raise token use and estimated cost per response without a consistent accuracy gain. We evaluate Scientific Agents, an open-source corpus of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles, with Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in the Pi agent harness. We compare matched profiles with four controls: a minimal baseline ("You are a helpful assistant"), the profile's opening role sentence, a generic scientific rigor guide, and a profile from an unrelated domain. Across nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 sampled questions, 100 matched profiles), 4,488 items completed all five conditions after API-error retries, scored with automated, rule-based grading. The average profile-baseline accuracy difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-1.5, +0.2] across fixed tasks), and no benchmark shows a statistically clear improvement. Matched profiles produced 1.5-2.3 times as many output tokens and cost 2.2-4.5 times more per successful call. On 60 tool-using BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems (three runs each for baseline and profile), mean solve rates were 46.7% with the profile and 56.7% at baseline, a difference of -10.0 percentage points (95% interval [-16.7, -3.3]) driven by more frequent token- and time-limit stops under the profile. Longer prompts had one unexpected operational advantage: on SuperGPQA, frequent provider API drops left the short baseline with a correct first-pass answer on only 54.0% of items, against 71.6% with the profile. Generic and mismatched prompts were about as reliable, so this gain comes from prompt length or formatting rather than domain expertise. For the tested model and tasks, loading full profession profiles by default does not improve accuracy and costs considerably more; whether selective retrieval of profile sections or open-ended scientific tasks would change this remains to be tested.

</details>


### [272] [Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01787)
*Beining Wu,Zihao Ding,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the debate about where self-improving GUI agents should store trajectories (context vs weights) by proposing component routing - splitting experience into locators, procedures, state facts, and lessons, and sending each to its optimal destination based on recurrence and state-conditionality properties. This approach beats all baselines by +3.5 points on average.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature disagrees on whether self-improving GUI agents should store trajectories in the context (prompt) or in the weights (fine-tuning). The authors attribute this disagreement to the "unit of experience" problem: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so conclusions about the bundle depend on its mix.

Method: The authors introduce "component routing" - splitting experience into four components (locators, procedures, state facts, and lessons) and sending each to its optimal destination (context or weights). They test this across three backbone families, two environments, and three seeds. They also develop a predictive rule based on two properties: recurrence and state-conditionality, measured before training.

Result: 1) Locators and lessons perform better in weights, while procedures and state facts perform better in context. 2) The rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality correctly predicts the destination for 24/24 held-out backbone family cells. 3) Two interventions move a component toward the boundary. 4) Routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and outperforms the better single destination by +3.5 points on average.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that component-level routing significantly outperforms whole-trajectory approaches. The key insight is that different types of experience components have optimal destinations based on their properties (recurrence and state-conditionality). The authors also identify how training and producer-consumer differences change destination value: note readout decreases after the same component is written into weights (most for items that recur most), context gains increase with information gap, and weights gains decrease with policy gap.

Abstract: Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing, which splits the experience into locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights, compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. (ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on average, the better single destination of each backbone. (iii) We identify how training and producer-consumer differences change the value of the two destinations: note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most, context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data will be released.

</details>


### [273] [Comedic Fool's Gold: Reward Exploits and Countermeasures in Conversational Humor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00197)
*Sam Larson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates automated reward design for training language models to generate conversational humor, focusing on identifying and countering reward exploits where models find shortcuts that satisfy the reward signal without producing genuine humor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning for language models: automated rewards can be exploited by finding shortcuts that satisfy the reward function without achieving the intended goal (genuine humor), necessitating countermeasures that block exploits while preserving the desired behavior.

Method: The researchers tested two reward approaches: (1) an embedding-based surprise reward using unexpectedness, and (2) an audience model's predicted laughter. They conducted controlled tests to identify exploits, developed a fluency filter to detect word-shuffled replies, and implemented speaker-normalization to block laughter cue exploits. Three sequential RL training runs evaluated successive reward revisions.

Result: The embedding-based surprise reward was exploited by word-shuffled replies (which have surprise but no wit). The fluency filter detected shuffles but rejected some legitimate witty replies. The audience model's laughter predictions were exploited via laughter cues in speaker messages; normalization blocked this attack but left unmatched expressions exploitable. Final RL run improved combined evaluation score by 0.0903 and reduced zero-score sessions by 40%, but humor-specific improvement remained below the preregistered target.

Conclusion: The findings illustrate that automated reward design faces a fundamental trade-off: countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the behavior the reward was intended to encourage. This represents a broader challenge in RL for language models where reward functions can be gamed by unintended strategies.

Abstract: We investigate automated rewards for training language models in conversational humor, focusing on reward exploits and countermeasures. Two approaches aim to capture understandable surprise and predicted audience amusement. Controlled tests show that an embedding-based surprise reward accepts word-shuffled replies as readily as witty ones. A fluency filter detects the shuffles, but the combined reward also rejects some witty replies and fails further validation. An audience model's predicted laughter is instead vulnerable to laughter cues in either speaker's messages. Normalizing these cues across speakers blocks the covered attacks, although unmatched expressions remain exploitable. Three reinforcement-learning runs evaluate training with successive reward revisions. The final run improves the combined evaluation score by 0.0903 and reduces zero-score sessions by 40%, but its humor-specific improvement remains below our preregistered target. These findings illustrate a broader challenge for automated reward design: countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the behavior the reward was intended to encourage.

</details>


### [274] [EviGraph: Proof-Carrying Selective Recommendation over Temporal Public-Service Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00212)
*Yixi Zhou,Sikun Wang,Lei Fan,Fan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EviGraph is a system that distinguishes critical decision requirements from non-essential information in public-service recommendations, using a language agent linked to a temporal knowledge graph and a deterministic checker to reduce unnecessary abstention while maintaining decision quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public-service recommendations require evidence matching service, scope, and date, but treating every missing detail as decisive can withhold useful recommendations from users who need them.

Method: EviGraph uses a language agent to link decision requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, combined with a deterministic checker to verify whether a recommendation is supported. Evaluated on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references.

Result: The distinction between critical and non-critical requirements reduces unnecessary abstention. However, additional verification can paradoxically withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality.

Conclusion: Reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification layers.

Abstract: Public-service recommendations require evidence that matches the requested service, scope, and date. Yet treating every missing detail as decisive can withhold useful recommendations. We introduce EviGraph, which distinguishes critical decision requirements from information that can remain unresolved. A language agent links these requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, while a deterministic checker establishes whether a recommendation is supported. Evaluation on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references shows that this distinction reduces unnecessary abstention. Additional verification, however, can withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality. These findings suggest that reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification.

</details>


### [275] [Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00224)
*Wooyoung Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Build2SPARQL is a large-scale benchmark for text-to-SPARQL queries on building knowledge graphs. It uses a KG-grounded pipeline where SPARQL queries are generated by graph-traversal code (ensuring correctness) while LLMs only generate natural-language questions. The benchmark yields 6,136 SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions across 201 building KGs and six query-pattern families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs using ontologies like Brick and ASHRAE 223P. A promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL queries, enabling building operators to query graphs through language agents. However, progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks.

Method: The benchmark uses a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions. This keeps query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families (linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered) and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P).

Result: The benchmark yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. Human validation of 300 questions (two raters) found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. Retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

Conclusion: The proposed Build2SPARQL benchmark provides a large-scale, high-quality dataset for text-to-SPARQL research on building knowledge graphs. The KG-grounded pipeline ensures query correctness while LMs handle question generation. The significant improvement from zero-shot to three-shot retrieval (0.2-20% → 56-65%) demonstrates the value of retrieval-augmented approaches for this task.

Abstract: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

</details>


### [276] [Robust Is Salient: An Informed Adversary Moves the Optimal Signal onto the Salience Pole](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00233)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how to signal truthfully when an adversary with knowledge of the true state observes the signal and tries to persuade a listener toward the wrong answer. The key finding is a structural coincidence: the adversary-robust optimal signal exactly matches the salience-based heuristic (margin-maximizing signal) on most items, making it impossible to empirically distinguish whether models are being adversary-aware or simply using salience.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand optimal signaling in adversarial settings where an adversary knows the truth, observes the signal, and tries to persuade the listener toward an incorrect answer. The goal is to find what signal best protects the truth against such an adversary.

Method: The authors introduce an adversary into a forced-choice task (abstracted from the game "Deception: Murder in Hong Kong"). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget β. They test across a 200,000-item pool and conduct experiments with 7 language models using two adversary framings.

Result: The adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with salience on 108 confirmatory items. Across 200,000 items, they differ on only 2,748 items—specifically where the salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. As β increases, optimal signal shifts from posterior-maximizing to margin-maximizing. At β=0, the game reproduces the original oracle model with τ=1. 18.2% of the pool has an optimum that shifts under finite budget. Two adversary framings changed 7 language models' choices on 30-77 of 108 items.

Conclusion: This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items. This coincidence structurally limits empirical evaluation—no measurement can determine whether model movement is toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience because the two options are identical.

Abstract: When an informed adversary shares the audience of a constrained signalling channel, the signal that best protects the truth is the signal that best describes it. On 108 confirmatory items, the adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole from prior work. Across a 200,000-item pool, the two differ on only 2,748 items --- lying exactly where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. We show this by introducing an adversary to a forced-choice task (abstracted from Deception: Murder in Hong Kong). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget, $β$. As $β$ grows, the optimal signal shifts from the posterior-maximizing option to the margin-maximizing one; at $β= 0$, the game reproduces the original oracle model with a listener temperature of $τ= 1$. This effect is real: 18.2 percent of the pool has an optimum that shifts under a finite budget, and each item's critical budget is exact. This coincidence structurally limits empirical evaluation. Two adversary framings change the chosen option of seven language models on 30 to 77 of 108 items against an exact no-effect rate. Yet, no measurement can determine whether this movement is toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience, because the two options are identical. This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

</details>


### [277] [Conflicting Supervision Moves Commitment, Not Capability: A 12.29σ arrangement effect that is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic score](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00234)
*Wenhui Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how training data ordering interacts with learning rate (LR) schedules to affect model parameters. The authors argue that LR schedules act as "averaging operators" that determine whether data order matters, and they provide experimental evidence showing that constant vs. decaying schedules produce dramatically different outcomes on the same data, even though conventional accuracy metrics remain constant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question is: when a model is trained on the same problems written under two different but equally valid conventions, what does the ordering of that data write into the parameters? The authors challenge the assumption that "order matters" or "order doesn't matter" is a binary statement—instead, they argue it's controlled by a continuous "knob" (the LR schedule).

Method: The authors:
1. Prove a theoretical bound showing arrangement (data ordering) and LR schedule enter as separate multiplied factors
2. Run controlled experiments with ten orderings of one corpus, one budget, all else fixed
3. Compare two families differing only in lr_scheduler_type: constant rate vs. single cosine
4. Measure both conventional metrics (accuracy) and allocation shares (how models commit to conventions)
5. Test whether marking the convention in the prompt collapses the effect

Result: Key findings:
- Under constant rate: interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is
- Under single cosine: 10 arms occupy only two distinguishable states (vs. ~10 expected)
- Across 12 arms: acc_A+acc_B constant to within 9.7% while allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87
- The 12.29-sigma arrangement switch is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic metric
- Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling

Conclusion: The authors conclude that:
1. The LR schedule is not a background condition—it is the averaging operator that decides whether order matters
2. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are two ends of one knob (the LR schedule)
3. What the training path writes is which convention the model commits to
4. No exact-match benchmark can see this effect (conventional metrics miss it)
5. This explains why ordering effects have been reported in pretraining but the mechanism was unclear
6. Prompt engineering (marking convention) can recover most of the ceiling performance

Abstract: "Train a model on the same problems written under two incompatible conventions, both correct, and ask what the ordering of that data writes into the parameters. The learning-rate schedule is not a background condition for that question. It is the averaging operator, and it decides the answer. We prove a bound in which the arrangement and the schedule enter the ordering effect as separate multiplied factors: the arrangement only as a block period, the schedule only as how much weight the endpoint can place on any one moment of the run. A decaying schedule cannot put a large step size and an uncontracted remainder at the same moment; a constant one does exactly that at the last step. That decay moderates ordering effects has been reported in pretraining; the mechanism, the separation, and a controlled measurement of both halves are ours. Ten orderings of one corpus, one budget, everything but the path held fixed, run twice under families differing in lr_scheduler_type and nothing else: at a constant rate the interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is. Under the single cosine every published arm uses, the same ten arms occupy two distinguishable states where their own resolution would allow about ten. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are the two ends of one knob. What the path writes is which convention the model commits to, and no exact-match benchmark can see it. Across twelve arms acc_A+acc_B is constant to within 9.7% while the allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87, so the 12.29-sigma arrangement switch this paper measures is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic metric. That conservation is quoted from the decayed family throughout, the constant-rate one being a noisier place to read it. Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling."

</details>


### [278] [Knowing When to Yield: Grounded Arbitration of User Corrections in Text-Based Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00282)
*Yezhou Cheng,Runjia Du,Zeming Liu,Hang Lyu,Zehua Yang,Bojun Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAVA (Ground Augmented Verification Agent) arbitrates between accepting, rejecting, inspecting, or asking when receiving potentially wrong human corrections in embodied agents. In ALFWorld experiments, semantic priors reduce interaction costs by 0.490-0.595 and joint costs by 0.420-0.517, achieving 98.8% accuracy without establishing VOI advantage over clarification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When embodied agents receive human corrections, those corrections may be wrong. Agents need a systematic way to decide whether to accept corrections, reject them, inspect the environment, or ask for clarification—rather than blindly trusting or always verifying.

Method: GAVA implements grounded correction arbitration using: (1) observation-bounded evidence, (2) legal probes, and (3) a one-step expected-loss rule. Experiments in text-only ALFWorld use 162 checkpoints producing 972 paired true/false interventions. Exploratory training uses 340 unseen scenarios; testing on 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints covers 308 scenarios.

Result: Complete local inspections achieve 100% correction accuracy. GAVA reduces interaction cost vs. always verify. Training-only object-location prior lowers interaction cost by 0.490 and joint cost by 0.420 on unseen scenarios. On 77 seen checkpoints: 0.595 and 0.517 respectively, with 95% CIs excluding zero. Semantic GAVA makes 4 factual errors per cohort (98.8%/98.7% accuracy). All methods complete every task.

Conclusion: Selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs is supported, but no general advantage of environmental value of information (VOI) over clarification is established. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it does not evaluate human participants, visual input, or physical robots.

Abstract: How should an embodied agent respond when a person's correction may be wrong? We formulate grounded correction arbitration as a choice among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the world, and asking the speaker. GAVA implements this interface with observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. In text-only ALFWorld, 162 checkpoints produce 972 paired true and false interventions. Complete local inspections give GAVA and always verify 100 percent correction accuracy, establishing the evidence contract rather than a comparative advantage. In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost against always verify but ties a cost threshold under a perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowers interaction and declared joint cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420 relative to uniform GAVA. After freezing the policy, costs, baselines, and multiplicity plan, the gains replicate on 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints, covering 308 scenarios: 0.595 and 0.517, with both 95 percent checkpoint-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Joint cost also improves over an identical-prior fixed policy, while the matched calibrated no-VOI comparison remains inconclusive. Semantic GAVA makes four factual errors in each cohort, corresponding to 98.8 percent and 98.7 percent accuracy, and all methods complete every task. Results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it evaluates neither human participants, visual input, nor physical robots.

</details>


### [279] [Rules to Tools: Executable Checks for LLM Agents in Scientific Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00313)
*Jingjie Ning,Guojiang Zhao,Chen Xu,Shanshan Zhong,Xiaochuan Li,Ji Zeng,Guolin Ke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R2T provides executable checks for scientific coding agents. In matched comparisons across multiple cohorts (30-task, 8-ID, 24-task, and PDE tasks), prepared checks generally outperformed text-based requirements (29/30 vs 26/30; 15/16 vs 13/16; 24/24 vs 23/24), though with increased CPU costs and varying task-dependent benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether prepared executable checks (Rules to Tools/R2T) improve scientific coding agent performance compared to text-based requirements, while measuring associated costs.

Method: Matched SciCode repair groups were compared across two task-ID cohorts: one with 30 tasks (26/30 and 29/30 completion rates), an eight-ID cohort (13/16 vs 15/16), and a larger shared-definition cohort (13/24 tie). Additional tests included five development-exposed tasks, a fresh source-through-Python arm, and a matched PDE comparison. Metrics included repair completion rates, model output, agent-side output savings, and public CPU use.

Result: Prepared checks achieved 29/30 vs 26/30 for text in the first cohort, 15/16 vs 13/16 in the eight-ID cohort, and 24/24 vs 23/24 in PDE comparison. Tasks 17, 77, and 11 favored tools; Task 37 favored text. The tool group showed 31.2% lower reported model output, with varying agent-side output savings but increased public CPU use in both task-ID cohorts.

Conclusion: Prepared executable checks improve task-dependent repair outcomes compared to text-based requirements, though benefits vary by task type and incur increased computational costs. The approach shows particular strength in PDE tasks but has mixed results across different task clusters.

Abstract: Scientific coding agents receive equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements in writing, then must assess the programs they revise. Rules to Tools (R2T) supplies prepared executable checks of public scientific requirements. Matched SciCode repair groups share written checks, starting programs, model, and budgets; the tool group receives a callable implementation. Across two task-ID cohorts, complete repair is 26/30 with text and 29/30 with the prepared checks. Three task IDs favor tools, one favors text, and eleven tie. The eight-ID cohort scores 13/16 versus 15/16, with a task-cluster bootstrap 95% interval of [-12.5, 43.75] percentage points for the difference. The larger shared-definition SciCode cohort ties at 13/24 per group. Five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs score 3/10 versus 7/10. The tool group favors tasks 17, 77, and 11; initial checks flag task 17 and report no violation for tasks 77 and 11. Task 37 favors text and has no initial reported violation. A fresh source-through-Python arm also reaches 15/16, matching the dedicated command's aggregate. In a matched PDE comparison, detailed text scores 23/24 and checks score 24/24, with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Agent-side output savings vary by cohort, while public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts. These results measure task-dependent repair outcomes and agent-side costs with prepared checks.

</details>


### [280] [Predictive Credit: Measuring What Scientific Explanations Add to Experimental Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00314)
*Jingjie Ning,Xueqi Li,Yibo Kong,Dongting Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework for measuring "predictive credit" - essentially evaluating whether research agents can explain planned experiments in a way that improves predictive performance. The authors test this across multiple domains (controlled learning, Tox21 biochemical endpoints, and OpenML tasks) using various AI models (DeepSeek V4 Pro/Flash). The main finding is that natural-explanation credit (whether matched explanations improve predictions over simple descriptions) remains unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions, though some specific conditions showed partial improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be establishing a rigorous framework for evaluating whether research agents can meaningfully explain their experimental plans in ways that provide predictive value - essentially testing if "explanations" of planned experiments carry genuine predictive credit beyond just descriptions of what will happen.

Method: The authors used paired forecasts sharing intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying: (1) description, (2) matched explanation, and (3) donor context. They conducted five checks tracking commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Experiments spanned 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks. They tested multiple AI systems including DeepSeek V4 Pro and Flash.

Result: Main results were largely inconclusive: (1) v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive; (2) Tox21's ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet (D-M=-.0026); (3) OpenML's joint formation rules were unmet; (4) matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed. However, some specific findings: DeepSeek V4 Pro reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5% (matched) and 59.1% (donor); OpenML full-card assignment widened intervals by 21% with 49.3% coverage; a positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points.

Conclusion: The protocol can measure predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting, but natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions. The authors note this is a method paper establishing the measurement framework rather than demonstrating that current AI systems possess explanatory predictive credit.

Abstract: Research agents explain planned experiments. We measure predictive credit with paired forecasts sharing an intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five checks track commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Across 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive. Tox21's preregistered ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet ($D-M=-.0026$, 95 percent interval [$-.0174$, .0104]); OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet. Matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed, and Tox21/OpenML seed-donor intervals spanned zero. Under requested DeepSeek V4 Pro, matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5 and 59.1 percent. A DeepSeek V4 Flash replay raised matched point MAE from .01823 to .02020 and missed matched-donor interval-score equivalence. OpenML full-card assignment widened nominal 80 percent intervals by 21 percent, with 49.3 percent coverage versus 51.4 percent for description and content in 66/144 cards. Direct-text Flash delivered all 144 notes without detectable matched point-accuracy gain. A researcher-authored mechanism positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points versus description. The protocol measures predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting; natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions.

</details>


### [281] [ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00328)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Yina Sa,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContractRL is a reinforcement learning-based approach for repairing structured tool calls (JSON) that violate schemas or execution contracts. Instead of regenerating the entire object, it uses a sequential repair protocol that makes localized corrections guided by verifier feedback, achieving higher success rates with fewer generated tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured tool calls frequently fail due to schema or contract violations in only a few fields. Complete object regeneration is inefficient (large action surface) and makes auditing difficult. The authors seek a more targeted, auditable repair method.

Method: ContractRL models JSON repair as a bounded decision process (MDP). At each step, the policy observes: candidate object, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer (location), repair history, and remaining budget. A contract-derived action mask filters invalid RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator. Uses contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch/retry/abstention decisions.

Result: ContractRL achieves 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 tokens, outperforming Patch-SFT (0.9076, 44.9 tokens) and full regeneration (0.9148, 137.2 tokens). Policy optimization improves supervised ContractRL (0.9186) to 0.9375. Paired evaluation shows +0.0396 improvement (95% CI [+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039).

Conclusion: ContractRL successfully performs localized, auditable JSON repair using RL. It achieves higher semantic success with fewer tokens than alternatives. The approach is particularly effective because it leverages verifier feedback and action masking to make precise, contract-compliant corrections. Remaining failure modes are analyzed through adversarial and multi-turn evaluations.

Abstract: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

</details>


### [282] [Mathematical Transfer in LLMs Follows Reasoning Approach More Than Topic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00331)
*Sajad Goudarzi,Samaneh Zamanifard,Seyed Amin Seyed Haeri,Moloud Nasiri,Hamed Rahimian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether topic or reasoning approach is a better organizing principle for selecting mathematical training data for LLMs. Across two experimental designs with multiple mathematical domains and reasoning methods, same-approach (sharing solution method but different topic) consistently outperforms same-topic (sharing topic but different method) by 8-16 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When selecting mathematical training data for LLMs, two organizing principles are possible: matching by topic (e.g., probability examples for probability targets) or by reasoning approach (worked solutions sharing a solution method). This study asks which produces greater transfer after fine-tuning.

Method: Two counterbalanced 2×2 designs were evaluated: (1) probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems); (2) number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). Every cell served as the held-out target in turn: same-approach (SA) sources share the target's method but change the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources share the topic but change the method. Five base models and three training seeds were tested per design.

Result: SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model-target comparisons. Model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3). All ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. Notably, ST sources are more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, so the SA advantage runs opposite to measured statement-level resemblance.

Conclusion: Reasoning approach is a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic-approach combinations. The findings suggest that LLMs benefit more from learning solution methods that transfer across domains than from domain-specific content, even when surface-level similarity favors the latter.

Abstract: When selecting mathematical training data for LLMs, a natural organizing principle is topic: probability examples for probability targets. An alternative is reasoning approach: worked solutions that share a solution method with the target, even when the mathematical domain differs. We ask which relation produces greater transfer after fine-tuning. We evaluate two counterbalanced $2\times2$ designs: probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). In each design, every cell serves as the held-out target in turn: same-approach (SA) sources share the target's method but change the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources share the topic but change the method. Every source appears once in each role, so additive source-quality effects cancel from the equally weighted aggregate contrast. Across five base models and three training seeds per design, SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model--target comparisons. Model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3); all ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. In both designs, ST sources are more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, so the SA advantage runs opposite to the measured ordering of statement-level resemblance. These findings identify reasoning approach as a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic--approach combinations.

</details>


### [283] [Fault-Tolerant Budget Conservation in Distributed Multi-Agent Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00349)
*Genliang Zhu,Chu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses resource allocation failures in distributed multi-agent AI systems under failure conditions like lost replies, timeouts, message duplicates, network partitions, and DAG joins. It proposes a fault-tolerant budget conservation mechanism using exclusive escrow credits that persist through a delegation DAG, with signed dispatch permits and quarantine mechanisms to ensure budgets remain conserved across crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resource allocation mechanisms (parent-child constraints, affine objects, distributed escrow) fail to prevent overspending when replies are lost, effects complete after timeout, messages repeat, branches partition, or DAG joins alias one lineage. Resource limits are becoming authorization boundaries for AI agents delegating work across concurrent and failure-prone workers.

Method: The paper formalizes fault-tolerant budget conservation using: (1) Quantized resource vectors as exclusive escrow credits moving through a delegation DAG; (2) Operation reservations bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key; (3) Signed dispatch permits with quarantine verified by gateway before first acceptance; (4) Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. Validation via bounded TLA+ model checking, independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected two-process SQLite experiments.

Result: Proved ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Experiments detect timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants, preserving issued budget bound across evaluated failure scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed mechanism successfully preserves issued budget bounds across crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules through exclusive preallocation and quarantine-based verification, addressing the fundamental problem of resource conservation in distributed multi-agent delegation under failure conditions.

Abstract: Resource limits are becoming an authorization boundary for AI agents that delegate work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, and distributed escrow do not by themselves prevent overspend when replies are lost, effects complete after timeout, messages repeat, branches partition, or DAG joins alias one lineage. We formalize fault-tolerant budget conservation for distributed multi-agent delegation. Budgets are quantized resource vectors represented by exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG. Before dispatch, a branch converts credit into an operation reservation bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key. It persists a signed dispatch permit with quarantine; the gateway verifies that permit before first acceptance. Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, a fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. We prove ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Bounded TLA+ checking, an independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected two-process SQLite experiments exercise the declared scope and detect timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants. The mechanism preserves the issued budget bound across the evaluated crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.

</details>


### [284] [ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00906)
*Sungho Park,Wonjoong Kim,Jue Zhang,Wook-Shin Han,Pengfei Gao,Chanyoung Park,Yongqiang Yao,Rao Fu,Elsie Nallipogu,Qingwei Lin,Victor Rühle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ActiveSaddler, an automated curriculum learning approach for optimizing LLM agent harnesses. It addresses the overlooked dimension of dynamically selecting training scenarios that provide feedback for harness optimization, modeling this as a non-stationary bandit problem with failure-pattern arms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing harness optimization methods focus on how to update prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic, but treat the training curriculum (which scenarios to use) as fixed. The authors argue that as the harness evolves, the most useful scenarios for further optimization change, requiring the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness.

Method: ActiveSaddler models the curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates potential learning progress from targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new failure discovery.

Result: Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler improves test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points respectively over the same harness optimizer using a fixed scenario ordering. Ablations confirm the importance of dynamic optimization targets, evolving utility estimation, and balancing exploration with exploitation.

Conclusion: Automated curriculum learning is established as a crucial new optimization dimension for harness optimization. The approach enables the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness, leading to consistently stronger harnesses.

Abstract: Automated harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents by iteratively updating their prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback. However, existing methods primarily optimize how the harness is updated while largely fixing which training scenarios generate the feedback that drives those updates. As the harness evolves, the scenarios most useful for further optimization can change, suggesting that the training curriculum itself should adapt alongside the harness. We formulate this missing dimension of harness optimization as an automated curriculum learning problem and introduce ActiveSaddler. ActiveSaddler models the evolving curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates the potential learning progress from further targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new ones. Optimization outcomes continually update both the set of discovered failure patterns and their priorities, allowing the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness. Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points over the same harness optimizer using a scenario order fixed before optimization, respectively. Ablations further show that these gains depend on dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery. Together, these results establish automated curriculum learning as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization.

</details>


### [285] [JusticeAxis: Benchmarking Legal Judgment between Rigid Rule Application and Ungrounded Discretion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00353)
*Zhengkai Tu,Mingda Zhang,Zijia Wang,Xiaoying Tang,Jimmy Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents JusticeAgent, an AI framework for legal judgment that combines fact-establishing agents with law-applying agents under experience-based skills. The authors introduce JusticeAxis, a dataset of 256 real-world criminal cases with multi-modal evidence and multiple judgments per case, and demonstrate that their approach can elevate open-weight models to commercial-level performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing legal judgment AI methods oscillate between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion. Current benchmarks only score labels or rubrics, leaving the experiential balance that skilled judges employ unverified and unformalized.

Method: The authors formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task linking decisions to both statute and circumstances. They propose JusticeAgent with element agents for fact-establishment and a judge agent for law application under skills carrying circumstantial experience. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds. They evaluate on JusticeAxis, a dataset of 256 criminal cases from 18 countries with audio, image, and text evidence, each with three lawyer-written judgments (the recorded one and one for each failure mode).

Result: Experiments reveal that failure modes scale differently: open-weight backbones drift toward unsupported grounds while frontier models default to statutory answers. JusticeAgent, as a simple plugin, successfully carries a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial-level performance.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates a novel formalization of legal judgment as reference-anchored task and provides a practical framework (JusticeAgent) that can improve open-weight models to commercial-level legal judgment capability through skill distillation under Bayesian credible bounds.

Abstract: A sound judgment applies the law to established facts and weighs the circumstances in which they arose. However, existing methods swing between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion, benchmarks score a label or a rubric, and the experience that would supply the balance stays unverified. We formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task, whose object is a single decision that stays tied to the statute and to the circumstances at once. We introduce JusticeAxis, 256 real-world criminal cases from 18 countries with audio, image, and text evidence, and three lawyer-written judgments for every case: the recorded one and one for each failure. We further propose JusticeAgent, a harness whose element agents establish the facts and whose judge agent applies the law under skills carrying experience of the circumstances. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds. Experiments show that failure turns direction with scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds, frontier models to the statutory default. We further verify that JusticeAgent, as a simple yet effective plugin, carries a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial level. Project resources are available at https://github.com/beita6969/JusticeAxis.

</details>


### [286] [AVSD-Scenes: A Dataset for Audio-Visual Description of Urban Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01861)
*Dhanunjaya Varma Devalraju,Arshdeep Singh,Mark D. Plumbley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AVSD-Scenes is a new dataset containing 12,291 paired audio-visual scene descriptions for urban environments, generated by combining modality-specific descriptions from Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B through LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, Gemma-3-27B-it).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing datasets for audio-visual scene understanding are limited; there is a need for datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information with rich semantic representations.

Method: 1) Generate audio descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B; 2) Generate visual descriptions using Qwen2.5-VL-7B; 3) Combine modality-specific descriptions using LLMs to produce multimodal descriptions; 4) Benchmark using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge, and human assessment.

Result: Multimodal descriptions outperform modality-specific ones in semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval. Scene classification achieves 94.5% accuracy, improving to 95.4% when combining audio, visual, and description embeddings. Descriptions remain discriminative even without scene labels in prompts.

Conclusion: The proposed AVSD-Scenes dataset successfully captures complementary information from both audio and visual modalities, providing rich semantic representations that improve various audio-visual understanding tasks while maintaining strong scene-discriminative capabilities.

Abstract: Natural language descriptions can provide rich semantic representations of audio-visual urban scenes, yet datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information remain limited. In this paper, we introduce AVSD-Scenes, a paired audio-visual scene description dataset for urban environments.
