The dataset contains 12,291 audio-visual scene descriptions generated from the TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes dataset. To construct the dataset, we first generate audio- and visual-based descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, respectively. These modality-specific descriptions are then combined using large language models, namely Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, and Gemma-3-27B-it, to produce multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information from both modalities. We benchmark AVSD-Scenes using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human subjective assessment. Results show that multimodal descriptions improve semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval performance compared with modality-specific descriptions while preserving strong scene-discriminative information. The generated descriptions achieve up to 94.5% accuracy in urban scene classification, while combining audio, visual, and description embeddings further improves accuracy to 95.4%. Furthermore, the descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative even when scene labels are removed from the prompting instructions, indicating that they capture semantic information derived from the audio-visual content rather than merely reflecting label information.

</details>


### [287] [Finding the Right Fit: Model-Harness Interactions across Agent Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00917)
*Yixuan Li,Yiyun Zhou,Yao Long Teng,Fuchao Yang,Yanchen Deng,Zhiyi Lyu,Xuyu Dong,Feng Chen,Bo An*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether strong language models and harnesses maintain their performance when paired with different components or evaluated on different benchmarks. Evaluating 66 configurations across 3 benchmarks, the authors find that model rankings reverse across harnesses, and the best harness for a model often changes depending on the task. They argue that model, harness, and task should be evaluated together.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in agent system evaluation: the assumption that a strong model or harness will perform well regardless of its pairing or context. The authors challenge this by demonstrating that performance is highly dependent on the specific model-harness-task combination.

Method: The authors evaluated 66 configurations consisting of four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness/DSH, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models across three benchmarks (TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4), plus two native pairings (Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude). They analyzed matched trajectories to understand why fit varies between configurations.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Model rankings reverse across harnesses - on Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails by 30.16 points in PI; (2) For 4 of 5 models, the best harness changes across benchmarks; (3) Some pairings are consistent - openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks (by 5.61 to 11.11 points); (4) Vendor harnesses are not reliably best; (5) Higher cost does not reliably buy higher scores - GPT scores higher under PI than DSH at less than 1/4 the cost; (6) Trajectory analysis shows models start repairs themselves, so harness failure feedback quality matters significantly; (7) GPT performs best with PI's lean scaffold while Kimi (prone to malformed tool calls) performs best in openJiuwen.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that model, harness, and task should be evaluated together as a system, not in isolation. The harness plays a critical role in translating failures into usable feedback for the model, and optimal pairings are highly dependent on the specific task and model characteristics. The work releases all code, adapters, and 6,204 scored trajectories for reproducibility.

Abstract: Choosing an agent system means choosing both a language model and the harness through which it acts. We ask whether a strong model, harness, or pairing stays strong when the setting changes. We evaluate 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models on TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4, plus the native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails it by 30.16 points in PI. For four of the five models, the best harness changes from one benchmark to another, yet some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points. A model's own vendor harness is not reliably its best, and higher cost does not reliably buy a higher score. On Terminal-Bench 4, GPT scores higher under PI than under DSH at less than a quarter of the cost per task. Matched trajectories suggest why fit varies. Models start almost all repairs themselves, so much depends on whether the harness hands failures back in a form the model can use. GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, does best in openJiuwen. We argue that the model, the harness, and the task should be evaluated together, and we release the harness adapters, evaluation code, and all 6,204 scored trajectories at https://github.com/liyix/finding-the-right-fit and https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuanli97/finding-the-right-fit.

</details>


### [288] [What Should an Agent Remember? Disentangling Retention from Retrieval in Bounded-Memory Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00366)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses a critical methodology issue in evaluating persistent memory agents: previous evaluations confound retention (what information to keep) and selection (what to retrieve when queried) decisions. The authors propose a streaming-recall benchmark that separates these two factors, finding that query-aware selection improves recall by 15.5 percentage points when access is held fixed, while access changes account for 53.2 points of the 68.7-point advantage in mixed comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory evaluations in persistent agents conflate two distinct decisions: what information to retain as it arrives, and what to surface when a query appears. This confounding makes it impossible to isolate the true effect of selection strategies, as methods differ in both retention and access mechanisms simultaneously.

Method: Built a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules, evaluating all conditions on identical 300 seeded episodes. The methodology systematically varies retention policies (what gets stored) and selection policies (what gets retrieved) while controlling for access mechanisms. Two comparison types: (1) holding access fixed to isolate selection effects, and (2) mixed comparison that changes both retention and access.

Result: With access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 pp (95% CI: 12.8-18.2). Mixed comparison shows 68.7-point advantage with 53.2 points attributable to access changes. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection all reach the retention ceiling. All 319 failures in bounded recency condition stem from eviction, not ranking errors. Recall drops to 0% as targets recede beyond retention bounds. SQuAD evaluation preserves retention ceiling while showing dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval on natural text.

Conclusion: Bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately to enable fair comparisons. The study reveals that previously reported performance gains may be largely attributable to access mechanism changes rather than selection improvements. The retention ceiling represents a fundamental limit that selection strategies cannot exceed.

Abstract: A persistent agent must decide both what to retain as information arrives and what to surface once a query appears, yet memory evaluations can confound these decisions by comparing methods that differ in both retention and selection. We build a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules and evaluate every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Holding access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8 to 18.2), whereas a mixed comparison that also changes history access reports a 68.7-point advantage, of which 53.2 points are attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling, and all 319 observed failures in the bounded recency condition are caused by eviction rather than ranking errors. Recall falls to 0% as targets recede sufficiently far into the past. Repeating the evaluation on SQuAD preserves the retention ceiling while showing that dense retrieval can outperform lexical retrieval on natural text. These results show that bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately.

</details>


### [289] [Trustworthy Data- and ML-Ops for Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01282)
*Antonio Emanuele Cinà,Giovanni Scodeller,Cecilia Caterina Pasquale,Silvia Siri,Davide Anguita,Fabio Roli,Simona Sacone,Luca Oneto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy Data and Machine Learning Operations (DataOps and MLOps) in Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS&L), addressing their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision. It explores the complexities of DataOps and MLOps, discusses Trustworthiness in AI applications, and identifies future challenges and prospects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid evolution of ITS&L relies heavily on Data, AI, and ML integration. However, there are gaps in current literature regarding DataOps and MLOps in this domain. This paper aims to fill these gaps by providing a foundational understanding and charting a path for future research in developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

Method: Comprehensive literature review focusing on: (1) Identifying gaps in current literature, (2) Exploring DataOps and MLOps complexities including necessity, key components, tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS&L, (3) Addressing Trustworthiness in AI applications with methods and tools for strengthening confidence in AI systems, particularly in real-world ITS&L scenarios.

Result: The paper establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS&L, discusses persisting challenges, and outlines future prospects in this rapidly advancing field. It serves as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers.

Conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive resource for understanding and implementing DataOps and MLOps in ITS&L. It charts a path for further research and innovation toward developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems. The paper aims to benefit researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers working in this domain.

Abstract: The rapid evolution of Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS\&L) has become a cornerstone of the modern social economy, relying heavily on the integration of Data, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and, more specifically, Machine Learning (ML). This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy Data and Machine Learning Operations (DataOps and MLOps) in the ITS\&L domain, underscoring their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision within transportation and logistics services. We begin by identifying gaps in current literature, offering clear context for our contribution. Subsequently, we explore the complexities of DataOps and MLOps, discussing their necessity, key components, available tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS\&L. Additionally, we address the critical issue of Trustworthiness in AI applications, examining methods and tools designed to strengthen confidence in AI systems - especially in real-world ITS\&L scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of persisting challenges and future prospects in this rapidly advancing field, aiming to serve as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers. Overall, this work not only establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS\&L but also charts a path for further research and innovation in developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

</details>


### [290] [When Harnesses Lose the Signal: Causal Evaluation of Recovery in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00372)
*Shuyao Xiao,Shengling Wang,Xuan Chen,Ke Chao,Ming Cui,Feifei Qian,Chaoyang Mei,Fanlin Meng,Ziming Yu,Junxi Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical limitation in LLM agent recovery mechanisms: traditional evaluation via average task success masks whether recovery operations help or harm trajectories. The authors propose framing recovery as a causal decision problem and introduce Causal Intervention Router (CIR), which selectively applies recovery based on pre-recovery information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core tension is that the same recovery operation can either rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. Current evaluation metrics (average success) fail to capture this duality, leading to suboptimal recovery policies that may cause net harm even when appearing beneficial on average.

Method: The authors frame recovery as a causal decision problem, comparing trajectories with and without recovery from the same execution state. They separate rescue effects (helping failing trajectories) from harm effects (disrupting successful ones). They then introduce CIR, a lightweight policy that uses pre-recovery information to decide when intervention is worthwhile.

Result: On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR improves success from 70.33% to 73.33%, a gain of 3.00 percentage points. The method leaves all trajectories with correct observations untouched. Control experiments demonstrate the benefit cannot be explained solely by new observations from recovery.

Conclusion: CIR provides a practical way to evaluate recovery causally and apply it selectively. The approach successfully identifies when recovery will help versus harm, achieving meaningful performance gains while preserving successful trajectories. This work highlights the importance of causal analysis in agent reliability.

Abstract: Large language model agents rely on external harnesses to pass information between the model and its environment and to recover from execution errors. Yet recovery is usually judged only by average task success. This hides an important tension. The same operation can rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. We frame recovery as a causal decision problem. Starting from the same execution state, we compare what happens with and without recovery, separate rescue from harm, and study how the value of recovery changes over time. We then introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), a lightweight policy that uses information available before recovery to decide when intervention is worthwhile. On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR raises success from 70.33% to 73.33%, a gain of 3.00 percentage points. It leaves all evaluated trajectories with correct observations untouched. Additional controls show that the benefit of recovery cannot be explained solely by the new observation returned by the environment. These results provide a practical way to evaluate recovery and apply it selectively.

</details>


### [291] [MCRI: A Four-Dimensional Framework for Analyzing and Evaluating Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01506)
*Zongrui Yang,Li Xintong,Runchen Xu,Zhongsheng Wang,Zhedong Lin,Haoyuan Li,Jiamou Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of structured frameworks for evaluating skills in modular agent systems by proposing the MCRI Framework (four dimensions based on information gain and behavioral constraint) and its operationalization MCRI-Eval, an LLM-based evaluation method. Testing on 63,812 skills across three benchmarks shows MCRI-Eval improves top-1 skill selection by 17.7-22.8 percentile points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills become important for capability development and distribution. However, the academic community lacks a structured framework for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills, creating a need for systematic skill evaluation before costly execution-based assessment.

Method: The authors propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework based on information gain and behavioral constraint, operationalized as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. They evaluate it using 63,812 public skills from OpenClaw skill Hub with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across three benchmarks (BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web).

Result: MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement among evaluated methods. It improves top-1 skill selection across all three benchmarks: compared with the strongest baseline, MCRI-Eval selected skills advance by 17.7 (BigCodeBench), 22.8 (BFCL-Fundamental), and 19.6 (Mind2Web) percentile points in downstream performance rank.

Conclusion: MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation, offering a practical solution for skill selection in modular agent systems.

Abstract: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills are becoming an important mechanism for capability development and distribution. However, the academic community lacks a structured framework for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills. Drawing on information gain and behavioral constraint, we propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework and operationalize it as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. We evaluate MCRI-Eval using 63,812 public skills from the OpenClaw skill Hub, with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web. MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement among the evaluated methods. MCRI-Eval also improves top-1 skill selection across all three benchmarks: compared with the strongest baseline on each benchmark, the skills selected by MCRI-Eval advance by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web, respectively. These results indicate that MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation.

</details>


### [292] [Benchmarking Prompt Optimization of Large Language Models With Chess](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00416)
*Timothée Lesort,Alejandra López de Aberasturi Gómez,Tristan Karch,Tom Veniat,Philippe Modard,Karl Tuyls,Ludovic Denoyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a chess benchmark (1,118 Lichess puzzles) for studying automatic prompt optimization (APO) in frozen LLMs. The benchmark addresses challenges in LLM evaluation by being challenging (~55% solving rate for best model), discriminative (shows gains/regressions), renewable (fresh puzzles), and affordable (~$800 total). Six APO algorithms are evaluated on eight models, measuring optimization response and transferability to game play.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating large language models is increasingly challenging: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks requires expensive infrastructure. These challenges are amplified in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the prompt search process. Existing benchmarks lack the properties needed to study APO effectively.

Method: The authors built a chess benchmark from 1,118 Lichess puzzles to evaluate APO for frozen LLMs. They evaluated six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring: (1) baseline puzzle-solving strength, (2) response to prompt optimization, (3) transferability across models, and (4) transfer to actual game play. The benchmark uses exact-match scoring and engine-based evaluation of alternative moves.

Result: Key findings: (i) The benchmark is challenging—even the strongest model (Gemini 3.5 Flash as meta-model) solves only ~55% of puzzles; (ii) It is discriminative, revealing performance gains, unchanged results, and regressions across different methods and models; (iii) It is renewable with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination risk; (iv) It is affordable, with the complete study costing around $800.

Conclusion: The chess benchmark is well-suited for APO research because it is challenging, discriminative, renewable, and affordable. It successfully connects puzzle-solving performance to actual game play, and provides a reproducible way to evaluate prompt optimization methods. The authors release all resources (puzzles, code, renewal scripts) to support continued research.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models becomes increasingly challenging as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks can require expensive grading or execution infrastructure. These challenges are amplified in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search for better prompts. Studying APO therefore requires a benchmark that is cheap and deterministic to score, hard enough to leave room for improvement, and renewable as models evolve. We introduce a chess benchmark built from 1,118 Lichess puzzles to study APO for frozen LLMs: we optimize their prompts without updating their model weights. Chess combines inexpensive exact-match scoring, engine-based evaluation of alternative moves, and a renewable supply of problems with adjustable difficulty. Unlike evaluations that report only success on isolated test items, the benchmark also connects puzzle-solving gains to short game-play rollouts within the same domain. We use it to evaluate six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring not only baseline strength but also how much each model responds to optimization and whether optimized prompts transfer across models and to game play. Chess is thus a well-suited benchmark for APO: it is (i) challenging, as even the strongest evaluated model, Gemini 3.5 Flash (used as the meta-model), solves only about 55\% of puzzles; (ii) discriminative, revealing gains, unchanged performance, and regressions across methods and models; (iii) renewable, with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination risk and adjustable difficulty to maintain headroom as models improve; and (iv) affordable, as the complete study runs for around \$800. We release the puzzles, optimization and evaluation code, and dataset-renewal scripts (https://github.com/imec-ailabs/Automatic-Prompt-Optimization-with-Chess).

</details>


### [293] [Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01833)
*Ngoc Phuoc An Vo,Aarya Doshi,Vadim Sheinin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continuous evaluation framework that combines outcome-level and process-level checks to detect behavioral drift in enterprise AI agent skills, even when final numerical outputs appear correct. Applied to 240 trials across business value determination skills, the framework found that over 92% of "passing" runs contained process-level deviations when evaluated with process-level checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, but traditional final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift that occurs during execution, potentially leading to undetected errors in production systems.

Method: The framework combines outcome-level and process-level checks using: (1) independently computed per-run ground truth, (2) reusable template tests resolved at runtime, (3) programmatic checks for tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity, and (4) a narrowly scoped LLM judge. Evaluated on 240 trials across two skills (Revenue and Productivity Business Value Determination), two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models.

Result: Among 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6%, 95% CI: 87.7-95.6%) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1%, 95% CI: 86.9-95.3%) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced mean failed checks from 6.34 to 2.65 root causes per run. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with bootstrap intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons.

Conclusion: Runtime-resolved templates provide reusable regression coverage across evaluated configurations. Process-level checks are essential as final-output evaluations alone miss the majority of behavioral deviations. Longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

Abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

</details>


### [294] [JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437)
*Haoyang Su,Weiran Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JevSpawn is a compositional policy that enables fast probabilistic exploration over finite fields derived from natural language instructions, addressing the computational inefficiency of token-by-token LLM agent generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents generate reasoning and actions token-by-token, making extended interactions slow and computationally expensive. Existing Jev-style models require pre-specified finite fields, limiting autonomous task solving where available actions must be derived from natural language and adapted through interaction.

Method: JevSpawn connects natural language task specifications to finite probabilistic exploration through: (1) parallel action spawning, (2) feedback-driven branch selection, (3) representation revision, and (4) recovery from retained alternatives. Shared action structure and model prefixes reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training.

Result: Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant show improved task performance and faster navigation.

Conclusion: JevSpawn establishes a promising approach to structured agentic inference, combining the fast probabilistic predictions of Jev-style models with the flexibility of natural language task specifications through compositional policy design.

Abstract: LLM agents generate intermediate reasoning and actions token by token, making extended interactions slow and computationally expensive. Jev-style models offer fast probabilistic predictions over finite fields, but require those fields to be specified in advance. This requirement limits autonomous task solving, where the available actions must be derived from natural language instructions and adapted through interaction. We introduce JevSpawn, a compositional policy that connects natural language task specifications to finite probabilistic exploration. Parallel action spawning is coupled with feedback driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery from retained alternatives. Shared action structure and model prefixes reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training. Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant establish JevSpawn as a promising approach to structured agentic inference, with improved task performance and faster navigation.

</details>


### [295] [Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00511)
*Yizhi Liu,Balaji Padmanabhan,Siva Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of "epistemic actions" from cognitive science to LLM-based agent design. It argues that agents should not only make decisions but also actively improve the evidence base for decisions through three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing systems for revealing responses. The authors propose "epistemic scaffolding" as the infrastructure needed to support these actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent design focuses on search and exploration but overlooks a fundamental question: whether evidence is ready for decision-making. Sometimes evidence is missing, in the wrong form, or comparisons don't exist yet. This gap in agent design leads to poor decision-making when agents act without adequate evidence preparation.

Method: Conceptual analysis applying cognitive science theory (epistemic actions) to LLM-based agent architecture. The paper identifies three distinct modes of epistemic actions and defines the infrastructure needed to support them (epistemic scaffolding).

Result: A framework identifying three modes of epistemic actions: (1) acquiring missing evidence, (2) transforming available evidence into decision-ready form, and (3) probing systems to generate revealing responses. Also introduces "epistemic scaffolding" as the interfaces, tools, and environments that enable these actions to be auditable.

Conclusion: Agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced, not just how to make decisions. This requires integrating epistemic scaffolding into agent architectures to ensure agents can prepare evidence before committing to choices.

Abstract: Before a difficult decision, people often act simply to understand the situation better. We turn an object to see another side, place alternatives next to each other, or change one condition and observe what happens. These actions may not complete the task, but they improve the evidence needed for the next choice. LLM-based agents can search and explore, yet agent design gives less attention to an earlier question: is the available evidence ready for the decision? Sometimes necessary evidence is missing. In other cases, the evidence is present but its form hides what matters, or the comparison needed to judge it does not yet exist. Cognitive science calls actions that improve the basis for a later choice epistemic actions. We bring this idea to LLM-based agents and distinguish three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing a system to create a revealing response. We use the term epistemic scaffolding for the interfaces, tools, and environments that make these actions possible and auditable. This paper argues that agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced.

</details>


### [296] [Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluations (OB-CAIE) Methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00529)
*Julie Krugler Hollek,Michael Zargham,Mala Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OB-CAIE (ontology-based contextual AI evaluation) is a methodology that addresses scientific rigor gaps in AI evaluation by providing structured ontologies (DSO for "what" and EPO for "how") to define testing coverage, enable human judgment at irreducible points, and ensure reproducibility and traceability of failure points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The methodology addresses three critical gaps in current AI evaluation: (1) lack of scientific rigor from unclear testing coverage, (2) the need to balance human expertise with automation, and (3) lack of reproducibility in AI testing environments.

Method: OB-CAIE uses two ontologies to represent the problem space: the Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) defines what is being tested, and the Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO) defines how testing is conducted. The methodology incorporates human judgment at specific, scientifically grounded points where human feedback is irreplaceable.

Result: The methodology strengthens AI evaluation by clearly defining the first step of the scientific method (明确界定测试内容), enabling traceable and visualized failure points within a canonical problem space, and supporting both single and multiple AI evaluations within one problem space.

Conclusion: OB-CAIE provides a scientifically grounded framework that balances automation with human expertise, enhances reproducibility, and allows systematic tracing and analysis of failure points in complex AI evaluation scenarios.

Abstract: The ontology-based contextual AI evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology was developed to address a lack of scientific rigor that arises from unclear testing coverage, to balance human expertise and automations, and to address a lack of reproducibility of AI evaluation testing environments. OB-CAIE strengthens the current state of AI evaluations by addressing the first step in the scientific method by clearly defining what will be tested. Two ontologies represent the tractable problem space in the OB-CAIE methodology: the Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) and the Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO). The DSO is the what; the EPO is the how. An OB-CAIE problem space can be used for one or multiple AI evaluations. The OB-CAIE methodology allows for human judgment at specific points, in scientifically grounded ways, and in complex subject areas where human feedback is genuinely irreducible or machine irreplaceable. A key advantage of the OB-CAIE methodology is that failure points can be traced, visualized and analyzed within the canonical OB-CAIE methodology problem space.

</details>


### [297] [Science or Slop?: Benchmarking and Mitigating Scientific Slop in AI-Generated Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00531)
*Yerim Oh,Young-Jun Lee,Jaewoo Ahn,Gunhee Kim,Dongyeop Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces SciSlopBench, a benchmark of 390 AI-generated scientific papers paired with human-written counterparts, to detect "scientific slop" through six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts. The proposed measures achieve 85.9% accuracy in identifying AI papers (vs 68.7% for Binoculars), and higher slop correlates with lower ICLR ratings and paper acceptance rates. The authors also propose SciSlopHarness, a framework that reduces the AI-human gap by 63% through evidence-based revision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing token-based AI detectors fail to identify AI-generated scientific papers because while individual sections appear plausible, the global scientific reasoning connecting them is fundamentally flawed. This "scientific slop" can mislead readers into overestimating the quality of AI-generated research.

Method: The authors constructed SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers (mostly in CS but spanning life, social, and natural sciences), each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. They developed six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts to detect slop. For remediation, they proposed SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where experimental records support changes.

Result: The six measures identify AI papers with 85.9% accuracy (vs 68.7% for Binoculars). Higher scientific slop correlates with lower ICLR ratings and distinguishes rejected from accepted papers above chance across 2017-2025. SciSlopHarness reduces the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets.

Conclusion: AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning. Responsible mitigation requires strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement. The proposed SciSlopHarness framework demonstrates that evidence-based revision can effectively reduce scientific slop.

Abstract: AI-generated content, often called AI slop, is increasingly common everywhere, particularly in academia. Slop in AI-generated scientific papers, however, has more complex patterns that cannot be easily detected by existing token-based AI detectors. Each part of such a paper looks plausible while the scientific reasoning that connects the parts breaks down, which can mislead how readers assess the work. We benchmark these failures as scientific slop through six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts. We construct SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers, mostly in computer science but spanning the life, social, and natural sciences, each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. Our measures identify the AI paper in each pair with 85.9% accuracy, compared with 68.7% for Binoculars. Higher scientific slop accompanies lower ICLR ratings and distinguishes rejected from accepted papers above chance in every year from 2017 to 2025. Reducing these patterns, however, is not as simple as directly optimizing the measures. We therefore propose SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where the experiment records support the change. While standard revisions leave residual slop and direct slop-aware prompting triggers reward hacking, SciSlopHarness reduces the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets. Overall, we demonstrate that AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning, and that responsible mitigation demands strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement.

</details>


### [298] [Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00583)
*Sahan Paliskara,Nattaput Namchittai,Andrew Lampinen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies multi-user, multi-agent coordination where different agents act for different users sharing resources (codebase, calendar, budget). Across 5 frontier models and 77 scenarios in 4 environments, the authors find that teams of agents consistently underperform a single coordinator agent, with coordination failures including stalling, action overriding, and fabrication. The paper identifies environment-specific mitigations and releases three environments as MAMUBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents increasingly interact with each other over shared resources, coordination failures when each agent serves different users with different goals lead to worse group outcomes than if a single agent acted for everyone.

Method: Experimental comparison across 5 frontier models and 77 scenarios in 4 environments: (1) API key environment with shared compute budget, (2) clinic with shared calendar, (3) personal assistant with shared group order/booking, (4) merge queue with shared release cutoff. Each scenario compares a coordinator (single agent serving all users) vs. a team (one agent per user), with and without communication channels.

Result: Teams deliver worse group outcomes than coordinator in every environment. Without communication channel, complete collapse in 2 environments. With communication channel, substantial coordination overhead remains. In personal assistant environment, coordinator fulfills ~2x as many user requests as teams. Identified failure behaviors: stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, fabricating claims.

Conclusion: Multi-user, multi-agent coordination is inherently problematic. Effective but environment-specific mitigations exist: team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and platform check (reading peers' messages before committing). Three environments released as MAMUBench (74 scenarios).

Abstract: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

</details>


### [299] [Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00609)
*Katrina Drozdov,Oliver Chen,Langston Nashold,Rayan Krishnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Legal Research Bench (LRB) is a benchmark of 413 U.S. legal research questions designed to evaluate language model agents on legal research tasks. The study tests 13 frontier models with web search, case-law search, and retrieval tools, finding that the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) achieves only 42.9% fully correct answers, indicating agents remain far from reliable for legal research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal research is a core but time-consuming workflow requiring identification of controlling authority, verification of validity, reconciliation of statutes and cases, and synthesis of grounded answers. Language model agents could automate this process, but reliability is critical—a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an answer unusable. This motivates the creation of a rigorous benchmark to evaluate LLM performance on real legal research tasks.

Method: The authors created LRB, a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. They evaluated 13 frontier models using a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. Responses were scored through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. The LLM judge was validated against expert attorneys.

Result: The strongest model, Claude Opus 4.8, achieved fully correct answers on only 42.9% of questions. Performance varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

Conclusion: Current language model agents remain far from reliable for legal research tasks. Even the best-performing models fail on the majority of questions, and increased computational resources do not necessarily improve accuracy. The benchmark reveals that legal research automation requires significant improvement before practical deployment, particularly for complex tasks involving conflicting authorities.

Abstract: Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

</details>


### [300] [Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00613)
*Gabriel Turinici*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a hybrid architecture that combines geometrical tools with a LLM (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) as a high-level orchestrator to address spatial understanding limitations in LLM-based agents. The approach uses geodesic trajectory collection and vector quantization to create a tool library, which the LLM then selects from based on current state and goal. This two-level approach (unsupervised tool discovery + LLM reasoning) achieves comparable goal-reaching rates to chain-of-thought methods while dramatically reducing computation time from minutes to seconds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are criticized for lacking spatial understanding and primarily exploiting statistical text patterns rather than true spatial reasoning. This limits their effectiveness in environments requiring geometric and spatial comprehension.

Method: The architecture combines: (1) Geodesic trajectory collection in grid-world environments, (2) Vector quantization to extract representative trajectory subsets, (3) LLM associates natural language descriptions with trajectories to create tools, (4) LLM selects appropriate tool conditioned on current state and goal, (5) Low-level primitive actions execute the selected trajectory. The system uses three tools: geometry-derived tool library, agent-centered zoom tool, and collision detection tool.

Result: The fast, non-reasoning configuration paired with geometry-derived tools matches the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while reducing decision time from minutes to seconds.

Conclusion: Separating learning into two levels—tool discovery through unsupervised trajectory quantization and reasoning via LLM—enables efficient spatial reasoning in LLM agents. This approach bridges the gap between statistical pattern matching and genuine spatial understanding, offering a promising direction for agentic AI systems.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset. Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool. Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.

</details>


### [301] [CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00636)
*Chenmu Zhang,Levi Felix,Jun-Jie Zhang,Xingfu Li,Xuelian Jiang,Tao Jiang,Subhendu Mishra,Xixi Qin,Boris Yakobson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

</details>


### [302] [Incident-Arena: Getting agents to the last nine of reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00648)
*Andre Fu,Malik Drabla,Leon Liu,Meji Abidoye,Marek Suppa,Lata Mishra,Adnan El Assadi,Yiyuan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Incident-Arena, a benchmark for evaluating AI coding agents in agentic Site-Reliability Engineering (SRE) tasks. It consists of 20 real-world production incident response tasks deployed on Kubernetes clusters with injected faults and functional verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic SRE benchmarks are limited by unrealistic environments (toy repositories), non-standard framework implementations, and simple static verifiers. There is a need to evaluate AI agents' ability to execute production incident response in real-world settings.

Method: The authors built a benchmark of 20 tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injects a fault from config layer through underlying images, and applies a sustained load profile. They use a novel functional verification method that goes beyond static checks, holding system-level metrics stable while ensuring repairs are done safely.

Result: Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%. Agent trials run an average of 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, demonstrating agentic long-horizon reasoning. Failures extend from diagnosis/localization errors through incomplete repairs to unsafe regressions.

Conclusion: Current frontier models struggle with agentic SRE tasks in production environments. The benchmark reveals significant gaps in diagnosis, repair completeness, and safety, highlighting the need for improved agentic capabilities in real-world incident response scenarios.

Abstract: AI coding agents are ubiquitous in engineering workflows amongst industry and academia. Yet, despite their use in app coding, relatively less attention has been paid to their ability to execute on production incident response. This emerging field, termed agentic site-reliability-engineering (SRE) contains benchmarks limited by (1) unrealistic environments, typically toy repositories (2) non-standard framework implementations and (3) simple static verifiers. We introduce Incident-Arena, a human-built benchmark of 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injecting a fault from the config layer through underlying images, and a sustained load profile given the task requirements. We also present a novel verification method, going beyond static checks to functional verifiers, holding systems level metrics stable, while ensuring repairs are done safely. Agent trials run an average of 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, going beyond existing benchmarks, demonstrating agentic long horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%, with failures extending from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs and unsafe regressions.

</details>


### [303] [Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00651)
*Michael Hardy,Ruhana Azam,Anka Reuel,Mykel Kochenderfer,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates the reliability of agent evaluations for comparing LLMs, developing a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework to separate meaningful signal from noise. Applied to 22 benchmarks, the study reveals that while fixed model-scaffold systems rank reliably (0.935-0.994), underlying model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). Scaffold choice significantly impacts conclusions, and even infinite tasks only marginally improve reliability when scaffold coverage is limited. Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve reliability at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, but rankings may reflect evaluation conditions (scaffolds, tasks) rather than the models themselves. This raises questions about what conclusions these evaluations can reliably support.

Method: The authors develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal (performance differences relevant to the intended claim) from noise (irrelevant variation that can change rankings).

Result: Four key findings: (1) Reliability depends on measurement goal—fixed model-scaffold systems rank reliably (0.935-0.994) while underlying model reliability is much lower (0.148-0.841); (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions as inter-scaffold reliability varies substantially across evaluations; (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty—infinitely many tasks improve model-ranking reliability by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage; (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings from 0.44 to 0.75 reliability at the same task budget, reducing costs by up to 83%.

Conclusion: Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and allocate evaluation budget toward the sources of uncertainty that matter most.

Abstract: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks can reflect not only the model but also the effects of the evaluation conditions such as the scaffolds or tasks. This makes reliability claim-dependent: an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. We ask which conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support and what additional evaluation would improve them. We develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal, performance differences relevant to the intended claim, from noise, irrelevant variation that can still change rankings. We find: (1) Reliability depends on the measurement goal. Fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions. Inter-scaffold reliability measures whether scaffolds preserve model rankings, showing that scaffold effects vary substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty. Even infinitely many similarly constructed tasks improve model-ranking reliability of a benchmark by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings at lower cost. For rankings across diverse agentic tasks, pooling benchmarks raises projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and can reduce projected cost by up to 83\%. Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter.

</details>


### [304] [When More Data Is Not Enough: The Context-Sufficiency Frontier in Generative AI Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00654)
*Merieme Askour,Ayoub Merimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a theory of "context sufficiency" for generative AI personalization, arguing that the relevance of context to customer intent matters more than volume. It identifies four states (insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, interference) and proposes a Context-Sufficiency Frontier to find minimal relevant context sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the new challenge created by generative AI: once context becomes easy to supply, more context is not necessarily better. The authors seek to shift personalization from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires.

Method: Full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender at a large home-furnishing retailer, testing different types and amounts of context.

Result: Relevant context improved appropriateness of recommendations, while irrelevant context reduced appropriateness and destabilized retrieval. The framework identifies four states of context: insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference.

Conclusion: The framework shifts personalization paradigm from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process. The Context-Sufficiency Frontier helps locate the minimal relevant set of context.

Abstract: Personalization has long relied on customer data to infer what an individual is likely to value. We call this customer evidence: the customer's historical behavior and preferences. Generative AI extends personalization by allowing providers to supply changing situational information at the moment a response is produced, without encoding every condition in advance. We define this provider-side context as information about what is possible, permitted, or advisable now. This flexibility creates a new problem: once context becomes easy to supply, more is not necessarily better. We develop a theory of context sufficiency in which the relevance of context to the customer's current intent matters more than its volume. The theory identifies four states, insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference, and introduces the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to locate the minimal relevant set. In a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender at a large home-furnishing retailer, relevant context improved appropriateness, while irrelevant context reduced it and destabilized retrieval. The framework shifts personalization from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process.

</details>


### [305] [Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00663)
*Jianwei Li,Min-Seon Kim,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Quarantined Expert Shutdown (QES), a novel backdoor defense strategy for LLMs that allows backdoor formation during training but routes it into a quarantined expert component that can be disabled at deployment, reducing attack success rate from 100% to 0-10% while preserving model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor defenses either suppress backdoor learning (filtering poisoned data) or learn then purify (repairing weights after backdoor forms). This paper proposes a third strategy: "learn, but channel" - allowing backdoor formation but routing it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment time.

Method: QES augments a Transformer-based LLM with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers. It uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation is achieved by zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight - a single constant-time operation.

Result: Across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, QES reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 100% to 0-10% in most settings, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected.

Conclusion: The "learn, but channel" strategy represents a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs, offering computational efficiency and simple deployment-time mitigation without trigger screening or model weight updates.

Abstract: Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

</details>


### [306] [A Simple Doxastic Deontic Logic for Norm-Guided Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00668)
*Thorsten Engesser,Agata Ciabattoni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a doxastic deontic logic framework for autonomous decision-making under conflicting norms and uncertainty. It combines conditional norms with multi-agent belief systems (KD45) and defines the distinction between subjective optimization (based on agent's beliefs) and objective optimization (based on actual facts), providing conditions for when these coincide and can be efficiently solved via MaxSAT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems face challenges when making decisions with conflicting norms, incomplete information, and unreliable data. Existing deontic logics lack the ability to handle norms that depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and other norms, creating a gap in modeling realistic decision-making scenarios.

Method: The paper proposes a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45 belief logic. This allows norms to depend on agents' beliefs about facts and norms. The Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem is defined to choose decisions minimizing weighted norm violations.

Result: The authors identify conditions under which subjective optimization (relative to agent's beliefs) coincides with objective optimization (relative to actual facts). They also show that optimal decision-making can be reduced to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time under certain conditions.

Conclusion: The framework provides a principled logical approach to norm compliance in uncertain environments. The key insight is that when an agent's beliefs are accurate (or properly bounded), subjective and objective optimization align, enabling efficient decision-making through standard optimization techniques.

Abstract: Making decisions despite conflicting norms and incomplete or unreliable information is a fundamental challenge for autonomous systems. We introduce a simple doxastic deontic logic for this setting: a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45, so that norms can depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. On this logic we define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem, where an agent chooses a decision minimizing weighted norm violations. We distinguish subjective optimization (relative to the agent's beliefs) from objective optimization (relative to the actual facts). We give conditions under which (i) the two coincide and (ii) optimal decision-making can be reduced to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time.

</details>


### [307] [Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00682)
*Nishtha N. Vaidya,Stephan Grimm,Thomas Hubauer,Thomas A. Runkler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin scientific AI applications that reason over structured knowledge, from biomedical question answering to materials informatics. However, their logical reasoning often falls short, producing factual inaccuracies unacceptable in these settings. Reliable evaluation remains challenging: manual dataset construction scales poorly, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws it aims to measure. High-quality benchmarks must ground both correct and incorrect labelled examples in explicit background knowledge, formally verifiable by a standard reasoner. We propose a pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology, with correct answers grounded in the ontology by design. Distractors are generated by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms, and their incorrectness is formally verified by an OWL reasoner via entailment checks. We evaluate the pipeline on three ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively. Distractors span four semantic categories from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures. Items meet natural language quality standards: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 confirm fluency, and correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8 shows that wrong options cannot be dismissed on surface form alone. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative. This work is a step towards more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI.

</details>


### [308] [Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00685)
*Jianwei Li,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel backdoor purification method for LoRA-tuned LLMs that works without prior knowledge of triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining. The method uses null-space projection to extract backdoor directions and project LoRA updates onto orthogonal null spaces, reducing attack success rates from ~100% to <10% while preserving model capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor purification methods rely on strong assumptions (prior trigger knowledge, clean references, aggressive retraining) and lack comprehensive evaluations, limiting practical applicability. There's a need for purification methods that work without these constraints.

Method: The approach involves: (1) Data curation and feature approximation to extract high-fidelity backdoor directions; (2) Constructing orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels for each layer/head; (3) Projecting LoRA updates onto these null spaces. The method scales from single-layer text classification to full-parameter LLM in generative tasks through ablation studies.

Result: The null-space projection method reduces ASR from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving both the base model's general capabilities and the adapter's learned downstream skills.

Conclusion: The proposed null-space projection method successfully purifies LoRA-tuned LLMs without requiring prior trigger knowledge, clean references, or post-hoc retraining. It achieves significant ASR reduction while maintaining model utility, demonstrating practical applicability across different tasks and model scales.

Abstract: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, the risk of backdoor attacks has become more severe. Existing backdoor purification methods typically rely on at least one of the strong assumptions, such as prior knowledge of triggers, access to clean references, or aggressive retraining, and they often lack comprehensive evaluations. These constraints substantially limit their practical applicability. To overcome these challenges, our work proposes purifying LoRA-tuned LLMs without these assumptions and even without post-hoc retraining of the suspect parameters. Our objective is to significantly reduce the attack success rates (ASR) while preserving both (i) the base model's general capabilities and (ii) the new downstream skills learned through the adapter. Through a series of ablation studies, we progressively scale our approach from a single layer in a text classification setting to a full-parameter LLM in the generative task. Through careful data curation and feature approximation, we extract high-fidelity backdoor directions and, for each layer or head, construct orthogonal null spaces in both the input and output channels, onto which the LoRA updates are projected. Empirically, our null-space projection method reduces the ASR from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving the base model's benign performance and the adapter's learned abilities during downstream task adaptation.

</details>


### [309] [R-GroundBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for R-Group Groundingin Markush Molecular Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00700)
*Xin Wang,Zichuan Ying,Xinna Lin,Junqi Zhang,Hanyi Xiong,Tianyu Gao,Hairong Zhang,Qixiang Hua,Botian Shi,Zhenhailong Wang,Kaicheng Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R-GroundBench is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating AI models on grounding Markush structures (variable R-group placeholders in pharmaceutical patents) in molecular, textual, and chemical modalities. The benchmark reveals a significant gap in current AI systems' ability to handle incomplete chemical representations, with performance dropping substantially on harder tasks despite domain-specific pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing molecule-language benchmarks focus on fully specified molecules, leaving R-group grounding (critical for pharmaceutical patents) largely unevaluated. This gap hinders AI-driven scientific discovery in molecular design.

Method: Built from real patent Markush structures, featuring two tracks: (1) Multiple-Choice VQA track with controlled difficulty (Easy/Hard) and modality splits, and (2) Open-ended Generation track. Evaluation includes testing with shortcuts controlled to assess true grounding capability.

Result: Easy VQA achieves >90% accuracy. Hard VQA drops to 56-66%. Chemical-domain VLMs achieve only 25.7-46.2% on Hard VQA despite domain-specific pretraining. Generation Exact Match remains below 20% for most models and below 8% when visual input is required.

Conclusion: Current AI systems lack reliable grounding and execution for Markush editing. The substantial gap between recognition and molecular grounding highlights fundamental challenges for AI-driven scientific discovery in pharmaceutical molecular design.

Abstract: Recent advances in AI for scientific discovery enable molecular understandingand design, yet reasoning over incomplete chemical representations remainsunclear.Markush structures, which encode molecular families through variable R-groupplaceholders (\textit{R\textsubscript{1}}, \textit{R\textsubscript{2}}, \textit{X}, etc.), are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical patents and requiregrounding across molecular, textual, and chemical information.However, existing molecule-language benchmarks focus on fully specifiedmolecules, leaving R-group grounding largely unevaluated.We introduce R-GroundBench:, a diagnostic benchmark built from real patent Markushstructures, featuring a Multiple-Choice (VQA) track with controlled difficultyand modality splits, and an open-ended Generation track.Our results reveal a substantial gap between recognition andmolecular grounding.While models achieve over 90\% accuracy on Easy VQA, performance drops to56--66\% on Hard VQA when shortcuts are controlled.Chemical-domain VLMs also remain unreliable, achieving only 25.7--46.2\% on HardVQA despite domain-specific pretraining.Moreover, Generation Exact Match remains below 20\% for most models and below8\% when visual input is required.These findings reveal that current AI systems lack reliable grounding andexecution for Markush editing, highlighting challenges for AI-drivenscientific discovery.

</details>


### [310] [Meta-Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Fast Adaptation of Interactive Policies with Applications to Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00705)
*Huiwen Yan,Kyriakos G. Vamvoudakis,Mushuang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework that enables fast adaptation of interactive policies across a distribution of Markov games. It extends meta-RL from single-agent to multi-agent settings by modeling MARL problems as Markov games and introducing the concept of meta-NE as the solution concept.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing meta-RL approaches focus on single-agent systems, but extending them to multi-agent systems is challenging because tasks involve both the environment and agents' strategic interactions. There was a need for a framework that enables rapid adaptation of interactive policies in multi-agent systems.
