Method: The paper models MARL problems as Markov games (MGs) and develops a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. It defines a new concept called "meta-NE" to describe the desired solution concept and establishes sufficient conditions for the equivalence between meta-NE and stationary points of gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithms.

Result: The proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, as demonstrated on autonomous driving tasks.

Conclusion: The meta-MARL framework effectively enables fast adaptation of interactive policies in multi-agent systems, with the meta-NE concept providing a valid solution concept for meta-MARL problems.

Abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.

</details>


### [311] [ReLiveGym: Evaluating Long-Lived Agents over Weeks of Replayed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00710)
*Xisen Jin,Jingheng Li,Zhenglun Chen,Junyi Du,Xiang Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReLiveGym is a diagnostic evaluation environment for long-lived LLM agents that need to operate unattended for extended periods (days to weeks), acting at appropriate times and adapting to dynamic environments. It simulates weeks of real-world news, market, and social-media streams with tasks varying in time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-horizon agent work assumes static environments, but real-world deployment requires agents to operate in temporally changing environments over extended periods. Current benchmarks fail to capture challenges like persistent monitoring, recurring actions, and dynamic adaptation.

Method: The researchers developed ReLiveGym to replay real-world data streams chronologically and evaluated eight base language models across diverse long-lived tasks. They investigated how model choice and harness design (particularly action timing mechanisms) affect performance, and evaluated the impact of continuous learning from hindsight feedback.

Result: Action timing mechanism emerged as a critical harness-design axis for long-lived tasks. The optimal design varies across different tasks and sometimes across model choices. Continuous learning from hindsight feedback helps address failure modes observed in these long-lived tasks.

Conclusion: Three key factors are important for designing effective long-lived agents: (1) model choice, (2) action timing mechanism, and (3) use of feedback. The findings suggest that LLM agent deployment for persistent monitoring or recurring tasks requires careful consideration of all three design elements.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents become widely adopted, they are increasingly deployed for tasks that require persistent monitoring or recurring actions (e.g., market analysis). These agents are expected to operate unattended for days or weeks, act at the right timing, and adapt to the dynamic environment over time. These challenges are not fully captured in the existing long-horizon agent work, as they often consider a static environment that is not temporally changing. We introduce ReLiveGym, a diagnostic evaluation environment of long-lived tasks in which agents act sparsely over simulated weeks of chronologically replayed real-world news, market, and social-media streams. The tasks span diverse levels of time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence. Across eight base language models, we investigate how model choice and harness design affect agent performance on such long-lived tasks. Our results show that how agents determine when to act arises as an important harness-design axis for long-lived tasks; and that the optimal design varies across tasks and sometimes model choices as well. We also evaluate how continuous learning from hindsight feedback affects performance and addresses failure modes observed in these long-lived tasks. These findings indicate model choice, action timing mechanism, and use of feedback as important considerations in the design of long-lived agents. Code: https://github.com/SaharaLabsAI/ReLiveGym

</details>


### [312] [Robust Nash Alignment under Preference Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00715)
*Shihab Ahmed,Debamita Ghosh,David Tang,Yudan Wang,Alvaro Velasquez,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for aligning AI systems to uncertain pairwise preferences. It addresses the brittleness of existing preference-based alignment methods that optimize against a single preference model by introducing a robust optimization approach that considers an ambiguity set around nominal preferences. The method involves a four-player primal-dual proxy game and achieves O(1/√T) convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based alignment methods optimize against a single preference model and are brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain (noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment). The authors aim to develop a framework that provides certified lower bounds on worst-case performance when preferences are uncertain.

Method: The authors propose a game-theoretic framework where a major learner seeks a policy with large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel in an ambiguity set around nominal preferences. They introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving: (1) leader policy, (2) follower policy, (3) adversarial kernel, and (4) dual variable. They develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm to solve this.

Result: The proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective. The authors quantify the proxy-to-hard gap and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. They prove O(1/√T) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, implying near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment show improved performance over nominal baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed Robust Nash Alignment framework provides a principled way to handle preference uncertainty in AI alignment, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation. The game-theoretic approach with the four-player proxy game and optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm offers a tractable solution with certified worst-case performance bounds.

Abstract: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, and can therefore be brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain: noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. To address these issues, we propose Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for alignment to uncertain pairwise preferences. Our formulation has a major learner seeking a policy with a large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel lying in an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. When the ambiguity set captures the uncertainty in preferences, the resulting robust objective of the game directly yields a certified lower bound on worst-case performance. However, we note this problem is computationally challenging to optimize, and to address this, we introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving the leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable, and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm for it. We show that the proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, quantify the proxy-to-hard gap, and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. We then prove an \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})\) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, which implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference further validate the convergence theory and show improved performance over nominal baselines.

</details>


### [313] [Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS): Reducing Representational Complexity for Enterprise AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00791)
*Terry Dorsey,Kevin Huggins*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as a framework for reducing unnecessary complexity in enterprise information representations while preserving required information. It also proposes Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model with four dimensions (Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, Supporting Sources) for comparing complexity across different representation states. The paper explores two consequences: 1) an economic model for evaluating lifecycle costs, and 2) evidence that reduced complexity improves AI reasoning accuracy (citing Text-to-SQL research).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise information accumulates complexity over time through applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. This representational complexity creates maintenance burdens and interpretation challenges for both human consumers and AI systems. The authors aim to provide a systematic way to measure, compare, and potentially reduce this complexity.

Method: The authors developed a conceptual framework (ERC) with four dimensions to characterize representational extent. They defined ERC at both representation and task levels to enable comparison between states. They also created an economic model distinguishing recurring global costs, recurring task-level costs, and one-time transformation costs over a defined time horizon.

Result: The paper establishes that: 1) ERC provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives; 2) reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent AI systems must interpret; 3) Text-to-SQL research demonstrates that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.

Conclusion: ERC is not a universal metric but serves as a measurable architectural variable for comparing alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance. The framework enables organizations to make informed decisions about representation simplification investments.

Abstract: Enterprise information is represented through artifacts shaped by applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. These structures accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by the enterprise and interpreted by information consumers and AI systems. This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as reducing unnecessary representational complexity while preserving required information within a defined scope, and Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model for comparing complexity across representation states.
  ERC characterizes representational extent through four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterize representation exposure. ERC is defined at representation and task levels, enabling comparison and distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization.
  The paper develops two consequences of ERS. First, representational structures create lifecycle obligations for maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation. An economic model distinguishes recurring global representation cost, recurring task-level cost, and one-time transformation cost, enabling evaluation over a defined time horizon. Second, reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Text-to-SQL research provides evidence that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.
  ERC is not a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. It provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance.

</details>


### [314] [Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00797)
*Corinn Tiffany,Wen Zhang,Eugene Bagdasarian,Lillian Tsai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sapien is a policy engine for AI agents that enforces stateful contextual policies to prevent rogue actions in multi-step tasks. It uses extended regular expressions with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks to maintain agent utility while blocking 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current contextual security defenses for AI agents are limited because they synthesize a static task-specific policy, but in multi-step tasks, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. There was a need for a policy engine that can enforce stateful contextual policies that adapt to the agent's execution history.

Method: Sapien uses a policy specification that extends regular expressions with three key features: (1) stateful predicates that track the agent's execution history, (2) deferred policy generation that allows policies to be generated during execution based on context, and (3) scoped semantic checks that validate tool calls against the current state.

Result: Sapien maintains high agent utility, staying within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's performance. In security evaluations, Sapien blocks 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% of attacks on Toolathlon. This represents twice the protection of tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks.

Conclusion: Sapien effectively balances security and utility in AI agent systems. By enforcing stateful contextual policies, it can prevent most attacks even when the agent is fully hijacked, while incurring minimal performance overhead compared to unconstrained agents.

Abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

</details>


### [315] [Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00834)
*Wensen Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Kepler is an open-source harness for evaluating agents on ARC-AGI-3, representing hypotheses as executable world models and validating them through transition and prediction checks. Under a frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, it achieved 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with 181 of 183 levels using no more actions than median-human baselines. The system processed 858.0 million tokens at $777.72 cost, with three evaluation failures reported.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments where rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. The motivation is to develop a robust evaluation harness that can properly assess agent performance in these complex, inference-based tasks.

Method: Kepler represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. The evaluation uses a frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns.

Result: Kepler achieved a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games. Of 183 completed levels, 181 used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. Retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions (7,292 in scored levels). The system processed 858.0 million tokens with 97.37% cache reads at $777.72 cost. Across final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100.

Conclusion: Public-set score alone has limited discriminative value. The results motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting. Three evaluation failures were identified: source-code leakage producing an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. Animation frames were found to contain task-relevant information absent from settled text grids.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments whose rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. We present Kepler, an open-source harness that represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. Under one frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, Kepler obtained a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. The retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions, of which 7,292 occurred in scored levels. Retained local provider-session records yield 858.0 million tokens, 97.37% cache reads, and a \$777.72 cost at September 1, 2026 API list-equivalent rates. We also report three evaluation failures: source-code leakage that produced an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness in a control condition, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. A single-game observation case study showed that animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across the final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100. These results indicate that public-set score alone has limited discriminative value and motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting.

</details>


### [316] [Learning Multiple Timescales for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00849)
*Pedro Robles Dutenhefner,Dikshant Shehmar,Wagner Meira,Marlos C. Machado*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GITA addresses long-horizon offline goal-conditioned RL by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple temporal abstraction levels (k values), achieving state-of-the-art results on OGBench with 73% relative improvement over HIQL and 14% relative improvement over the best fixed-k method OTA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing offline GCRL approaches struggle with long-horizon tasks because discounting shrinks value differences between distant states below function approximation error, eliminating the signal for ranking states. While temporal abstraction (treating k steps as one transition) restores this signal, no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances—large k preserves long-range but collapses nearby distinctions, and vice versa.

Method: Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA) conditions a single value function on k and trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values. Larger positive advantages for state-goal pairs contribute more strongly to updates, allowing the method to retain both local resolution and long-range signal without committing to a single k.

Result: On OGBench, GITA raises average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL, and by 7 percentage points (14% relative improvement) over the strongest fixed-k method OTA.

Conclusion: GITA effectively resolves the trade-off between local resolution and long-range signal in temporal abstraction by leveraging multiple k values simultaneously, establishing a new state-of-the-art for offline GCRL on the OGBench benchmark.

Abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).

</details>


### [317] [An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870)
*Sara Riazi,Pedram Rooshenas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-based pedagogical agent that provides scaffolded feedback for conceptual database design (ERD) tasks. The system uses a four-stage workflow with hidden diagnosis to deliver progressively detailed feedback, showing 71.1% of student revisions incorporated the diagnostic targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the challenge of providing effective, personalized feedback in database design education. Traditional feedback methods often lack grounding in student work, assignment requirements, and instructional resources. The motivation is to create a system that can provide scaffolded feedback while maintaining student agency and allowing educators to control feedback disclosure.

Method: The system was deployed across three ERD environments with 383 feedback episodes. It uses a four-stage workflow: (1) concept checks, (2) guided application, (3) low-detail feedback, and (4) localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. The architecture separates hidden diagnostic processes from the workflow controlling feedback form and disclosure. Analysis combined quantitative measurement of target-level changes with qualitative analysis of feedback disclosure patterns and student survey responses.

Result: 71.1% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after early stages (1-2). Qualitative analysis revealed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, and allowed later recovery, though some errors still influenced revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted concerns about indirectness and repetition.

Conclusion: The educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent demonstrates effective scaffolded feedback in database design education. The staged disclosure approach shows promise for maintaining student agency while providing progressive guidance, though challenges remain in managing indirectness and preventing error propagation. The architecture separating diagnosis from disclosure provides a viable model for similar educational AI systems.

Abstract: We present an educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent for scaffolded feedback in conceptual database design. Integrated into an entity--relationship diagram (ERD) editor, the system grounds feedback in the student artifact, assignment requirements, educator-authored rubrics, and instructional resources. Its architecture separates hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis from the workflow that controls the form and disclosure level of student-facing support.
  We instantiate the architecture as a four-stage workflow progressing from concept checks and guided application to low-detail feedback and localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. In a deployment spanning three ERD environments and 383 feedback episodes, 71.1\% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages~1--2. Qualitative analysis showed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, or allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

</details>


### [318] [MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872)
*Mitchell Piehl,Muchao Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemFit is a long-term memory system for conversational LLM agents that reduces memory operation costs by using LLM-free insertion (appending turns verbatim) and LLM-free multi-path retrieval with cross-encoder reranking, achieving state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks while significantly reducing memory construction time and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM memory systems rely on expensive LLM calls for memory organization and consolidation, leading to costly and inefficient write operations. Additionally, compression-based approaches discard surface-level details. There is a need for a scalable, efficient memory system that reduces both cost and latency.

Method: MemFit uses an append-only store that stores each conversation turn verbatim with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. Retrieval combines lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption-augmented episodes, supporting both textual and multimodal settings.

Result: MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance on three widely used benchmarks (LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S) while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold.

Conclusion: MemFit provides a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory, significantly reducing the cost and latency of memory operations through LLM-free insertion and retrieval strategies while maintaining high performance.

Abstract: Long-term memory systems for large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity for extending reasoning capabilities across applications. Current memory systems rely on LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly, inefficient write operations. To address this limitation, we propose MemFit, a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces the cost and latency of memory operations. Unlike existing systems that rely on expensive LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression, MemFit stores each turn verbatim in an append-only store with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. Additionally, MemFit uses an LLM-free, multi-path retrieval strategy that combines lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption- augmented episodes in both textual and multimodal settings. Empirical results on three widely used benchmarks, LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S, show that MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold, providing a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory.

</details>


### [319] [OR for AI That Does OR: Routing LLMs up the Escalator inside the OSCAR Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00912)
*Jinzhi Bu,Haixin Tang,Huanan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OSCAR is an LLM-based framework that uses a certified offline Simulator to verify optimization model formulations, achieving 95-100% accuracy on benchmarks while costing 3-6x less than commercial alternatives like Codex and Claude Code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but the generated code may misrepresent constraints/objectives, leading to optimal solutions for the wrong problem. Existing solutions may also miss better plans even when feasible. Organizations need accurate, low-cost, and preferably local solutions.

Method: OSCAR uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare model candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. The search for certified improvements is modeled as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty, determining which LLMs to call and when to stop.

Result: On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95-100% accuracy using two small open-weight LLMs deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively.

Conclusion: Organizations should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when LLM interpretation conflicts. Its simple operating rules and adjustable settings help adapt to changing LLM capabilities and prices, supporting both local and cloud deployment based on budget and confidentiality requirements.

Abstract: Large language models can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives. A solver can then return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. Even when the solution satisfies the intended operating rules, a better plan may exist. For organizations that repeatedly use optimization modeling, an LLM-based framework should produce accurate formulations at low cost and, ideally, run locally. We study how to verify improvements and allocate attempts across LLMs that differ in price and capability. We develop OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), which uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. We model the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty: which LLMs to call and when to stop. In a simplified known-prior setting, we give conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal. For general menus, we derive a prior-free competitive guarantee. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95% to 100% accuracy at the reported settings using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively. OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud, depending on budget and confidentiality requirements. Firms should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify plain-language operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when an LLM's interpretation conflicts with them. As LLM capabilities and prices change, OSCAR's simple operating rules and adjustable settings help firms adapt their model choices and benefit from these advances.

</details>


### [320] [ABDA-NL: A Natural-Language Scenario Explorer for Argument-Based Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00947)
*Shawn Bowers,Martin Caminada,Haoyang Liu,Bertram Ludäscher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ABDA-NL extends an argument-based discussion system (ABDA) with a natural-language interface powered by large language models. It allows users to understand argument acceptance statuses, explore hypothetical scenarios, query reference documents, and author new knowledge in plain English, while maintaining the deterministic ABDA engine as the authoritative source with user validation for all changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to make argument-based reasoning systems more accessible to non-technical users by providing a natural language interface that allows them to interact with the system without needing to understand the underlying formal representation (ASPIC knowledge bases, grounded semantics).

Method: The system uses a large language model as an intermediary between natural language and formal representation. The LLM performs two key functions: (1) answering questions from reference documents and current scenario state, and (2) translating plain-English edits into formal statements. The deterministic ABDA engine validates all arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every LLM proposal requires user validation before implementation.

Result: Users can now view which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided; explore interactive renderings of grounded discussion games to understand reasoning; suspend assumptions/rules or change preferences for what-if analysis; ask questions answered from scenario documents; and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English.

Conclusion: The paper presents ABDA-NL as a hybrid system that combines the interpretability and formal guarantees of argument-based reasoning with the accessibility of natural language interfaces, while maintaining human oversight through mandatory user validation of all AI-generated proposals.

Abstract: ABDA-NL adds a natural-language interface to ABDA, a system for argument-based discussion using ASPIC- knowledge bases under grounded semantics. Users see which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided, open an interactive rendering of the grounded discussion game to learn why, explore what-if alternatives by suspending assumptions and rules or changing preferences, ask questions that are answered from a scenario's reference documents, and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English. A large language model provides the bridge between language and formalism: it answers questions from the documents and the current state of the scenario, and it translates plain-English edits into candidate formal statements. The deterministic ABDA engine remains the sole source of arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every proposal of the model is validated and confirmed by the user before it takes effect.

</details>


### [321] [PG-SFT: Balancing Capability Acquisition and Retention in Offline Agent Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00949)
*Ronghua Li,Zi Liang,Zhishan Li,Shinan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on agent trajectories improves target tool-using benchmarks but degrades other capabilities. This paper proposes Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT) that uses turn-level information gain to adjust supervision strength, achieving better trade-off between acquiring new skills and preserving existing ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised fine-tuning on offline agent trajectories is the standard approach for training specialized tool-using agents, but this approach harms other capabilities (general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) of the base model. The authors seek to balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT.

Method: The paper proposes Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT), which leverages turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. This approach was compared against several baselines including standard SFT, KL penalty constraints, and limiting update magnitude.

Result: Standard SFT improves the target benchmark while lowering several non-target benchmark scores. Simply constraining distributional drift using KL penalty or limiting update magnitude did not avoid this regression trend. PG-SFT yields a more favorable observed trade-off, substantially reducing distributional drift and broad capability degradation at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance.

Conclusion: Balancing the acquisition-retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior. The turn-level information gain can serve as an effective indicator for adjusting supervision strength during fine-tuning.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline agent trajectories is the standard approach for training specialized tool-using agents, but forcing models to imitate reasoning and actions token by token may harm other capabilities (e.g., general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) of the base model. In this work, we focus on studying \emph{how to better balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT}. By comparing several baselines in our setup, standard SFT improves the target benchmark while lowering several non-target benchmark scores; meanwhile, simply constraining distributional drift using KL penalty or limiting the update magnitude did not avoid this regression trend. Motivated by recent token-wise adaptive learning objectives, this work proposes \textbf{Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT)} to leverage turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. PG-SFT yields a more favorable observed trade-off on the evaluated benchmarks, substantially reducing distributional drift and broad capability degradation at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance. Our findings suggest that balancing the acquisition--retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior.}

</details>


### [322] [Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00961)
*Jérémie Lumbroso*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: As code generation is increasingly delegated to AI systems, the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to supervising the systems that write it --- a shift CS-education researchers have begun to name. This shift exposes a vocabulary gap: the field asks for "human oversight" without a working distinction between the two things language does in a delegation channel --- coordinate action (cybernetic: words succeed when the world comes to match them) and coordinate understanding (epistemic: they succeed when they answer to the world and a hearer can check that they do). The failure this names is not cybernetic language but epistemic-form language doing cybernetic work: explanation-shaped output calibrated for approval rather than truth. Oversight that checks only whether an output was approved is satisfiable by rubber-stamping; oversight that holds an agent accountable requires the reasoning behind its work be retrievable and checkable. We present three delegation episodes --- illustrations, not controlled evidence --- in which epistemic engagement proved practicable while remaining auditable, one public record where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight that requires no reasons for its discretionary choices. We propose a criterion for agentic-system governance, alongside existing technical trust properties: every consequential choice should carry the condition under which it would have gone otherwise, in a form a third party can test. Without such a condition, a third party cannot distinguish a decision from a rubber stamp. We give the criterion an operational form --- a two-part reconstruction test scoring a delegation record by whether a second reader can predict what the agent does under a perturbation --- and a deliberation-recording convention, ORRCF, that makes the condition a required component of every recorded choice.

</details>


### [323] [VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00972)
*Caiqi Zhang,Rujun Han,Zifeng Wang,Zoey CuiZhu,Nigel Collier,Tomas Pfister,Chen-Yu Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriHarness is an agentic verification framework that strengthens LLM output verification in long-horizon tasks by using disagreement resolution and consensus challenging, achieving up to 6.4 points improvement over single rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents handle increasingly complex tasks, verifying their outputs becomes difficult without reference answers. The authors observe that disagreement can reveal correct alternatives while consensus may hide errors, motivating a new verification approach.

Method: VeriHarness transforms the base LLM into an agentic verifier with workspace, evidence tools, and reusable skills. It uses two mechanisms: (1) disagreement resolver that checks competing claims against environmental evidence, and (2) consensus challenger that tests shared claims for omitted requirements. Results guide artifact selection and revision.

Result: Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8), VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among baselines. Evidence-backed revision yields 6.2 and 6.4 point gains over single rollouts respectively. Verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback.

Conclusion: VeriHarness represents a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. The released dataset of ~26,000 rollouts ($100,000+ cost) will support future research in this area.

Abstract: As LLM agents undertake increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes increasingly challenging. We study how verification capability can be strengthened with a fixed base model, without access to reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. Repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts that can contain complementary correct claims, but we need a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust. We first find that disagreement often exposes correct alternatives, while consensus can conceal errors. These observations motivate VeriHarness, which turns the underlying LLM a generator uses into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. A disagreement resolver checks competing claims against environmental evidence, while a consensus challenger tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Their findings guide the selection and revision of the final artifact. Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among the evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, bringing gains over a single rollout to 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. We further show that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, demonstrating VeriHarness as a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. We release the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000, to support future research on agentic verification.

</details>


### [324] [RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00979)
*Jingtan Wang,Sirajul Salekin,Young mok Jung,Javier Movellan,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low,Manjot Bilkhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RISED is a method for training LLM agents across diverse interactive environments using rubric-based feedback. It uses an LLM judge to tag rollouts with predefined rubrics, guiding data selection, policy supervision, and rollout generation to improve overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-environment RL training relies on scalar rewards, which have limitations: 1) They provide no information about cross-environment relationships for prompt-group selection, and 2) When all rollouts succeed or fail in a batch, there's no reward contrast to learn from. This motivates using richer textual feedback (rubrics) instead of just scalar rewards.

Method: RISED uses rubric-based feedback in three ways: 1) An LLM judge tags each rollout with rubrics from a predefined vocabulary shared across environments; 2) These profiles guide online data selection to align with overall behavioral composition while limiting overlap; 3) Positive rubrics provide privileged context for on-policy self-distillation teacher (token-level supervision), while negative rubrics guide subsequent rollout generation away from failure modes.

Result: Across different model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis can further characterize the behavioral changes accompanying these gains.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that rubric-based feedback is more effective than scalar rewards for multi-environment LLM agent training. Rubrics provide richer information about cross-environment relationships and enable within-group reward contrast, leading to improved performance across diverse environments.

Abstract: Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning. Beyond rubrics' usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes. Together, these components form RISED. Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

</details>


### [325] [Evaluating LLM-Generated Preference Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01000)
*Fan Huang,Minsuk Kim,C. Tyler Diggans,Filippo Radicchi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study systematically analyzes whether Large Language Models produce reliable preference distributions when used as probabilistic generators for simulation and synthetic data generation. The authors test 9 open-weight models across 3 domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products) under various conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support where real-world data is unavailable. However, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied.

Method: Systematically analyzed LLM-generated distributions of preferences across 9 open-weight models and 3 choice domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products). Tested robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering.

Result: All models exhibited self-coherence with most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. However, substantial discordance was observed across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns were robust across all conditions tested.

Conclusion: Outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by the wording of the prompt. This challenges the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support in settings where real-world data are unavailable. Yet, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied. Here, we systematically analyze LLM-generated distributions of preferences for air travel, restaurants, and consumer products. Encouragingly, all models considered in our analysis exhibit self-coherence, with the most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. At the same time, we observe substantial discordance across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns hold across nine open-weight models, three choice domains, and show robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering. Our findings indicate that outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by the wording of the prompt, challenging the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents.

</details>


### [326] [Calibration-risk routing for controlled world-model adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01001)
*Yifan Zhang,Liang Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MC-WM addresses the simulator-to-target shift problem in MBRL by separating target data into fit, selection, and calibration partitions, using learned confidence signals and validity predicates to weight policy updates without rewriting physical rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that in MBRL, when there's a shift between simulator and target environments, standard approaches of either correcting the simulator or fitting the target directly can fail when target data is limited. This creates a model-selection problem.

Method: MC-WM separates initial target data into three disjoint partitions: fit, selection, and calibration. It uses a learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates to weight one-step imagined policy updates, choosing the model family with lower standardized calibration risk.

Result: Evaluated across 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled MuJoCo shifts, with one exact-routing cell repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, resulting in 541 completed executions.

Conclusion: The approach provides a systematic way to handle simulator-to-target shifts in MBRL by leveraging partitioned data and confidence-based model selection without modifying physical rewards.

Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can exploit simulated experience, but a simulator-to-target shift creates a model-selection problem: correcting the simulator and fitting the target directly can each fail under limited target data. We introduce the Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM), which separates initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions and deploys the family with lower standardized calibration risk. A learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates weight one-step imagined policy updates without rewriting physical rewards. We evaluate 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts; one exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, giving 541 completed executions.

</details>


### [327] [What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01002)
*Keith J. Holyoak,Martin M. Monti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a causal framework for evaluating consciousness in non-human entities (animals and AI) by distinguishing between similarities in causal factors versus behavioral/cognitive effects. It argues that behavioral similarity alone provides limited evidence for consciousness because the relevant causal mechanisms remain poorly understood.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the question of who or what is conscious, particularly given advances in AI that have raised the possibility of conscious machines. The authors note that subjective experience is only directly accessible in first person, so judgments about consciousness in other entities must rely on analogy, but existing approaches lack a systematic framework for evaluating such evidence.

Method: The authors develop a causal framework that: (1) distinguishes between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness versus similarities in downstream behavioral/cognitive effects; (2) weights source-target similarity by causal relevance; (3) allows for unknown causes, disabling differences, and alternative routes to consciousness.

Result: Applied to biological systems, the framework explains why analogical support for consciousness generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, behavioral similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also identifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

Conclusion: The framework provides a systematic approach for evaluating consciousness claims in non-human entities, distinguishing between causal similarity and behavioral similarity. For AI specifically, behavioral evidence alone is insufficient; stronger evidence would require establishing relevant causal mechanisms that correspond to those thought to generate consciousness in biological systems.

Abstract: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

</details>


### [328] [Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01006)
*Sharath M Shankaranarayana,Davor Runje,Jan Jannink*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether confidence scores in decision models properly indicate missing knowledge versus random uncertainty. The authors audit Jev, a decision model, across 15+ datasets and 6 task families, finding that while confidence is calibrated on familiar tasks, it fails as an indicator of missing knowledge—assigning high confidence (up to 0.80) even with no relevant information, and exceeding accuracy by 0.21-0.33 on out-of-domain news. Targeted yes/no questions ("does the model know the answer?") provide better detection (AUROC 0.91-1.00), but surface cues can undermine these audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address a critical gap in decision model evaluation: standard calibration ensures probabilities are useful on average, but does not establish whether low confidence reflects genuine uncertainty (chance) or missing knowledge. This distinction is crucial for routing, abstention, and automated action in real-world deployments.

Method: The authors audit Jev, a decision model, using over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families. They employ paired interventions that vary information supplied for fixed items to test whether confidence properly indicates knowledge boundaries. They compare standard confidence scoring against targeted yes/no questions about whether the model knows the answer.

Result: Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: (1) with no answer-relevant information, it assigns up to 0.80 confidence to a salient option; (2) on news beyond the observed knowledge boundary, confidence exceeds accuracy by 0.21-0.33; (3) recalibration on earlier months does not close this gap. Targeted yes/no questions perform much better: whether an outcome is settled achieves AUROC 1.00, and whether evidence suffices achieves 0.95 (vs 0.85 for confidence on same items). Asking "whether Jev knows the answer" can flag fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91), but with realistic names or removed dates, it shows no advantage over answer uncertainty.

Conclusion: Black-box knowledge audits require explicit controls for surface cues. Standard calibration alone is insufficient for determining when models operate beyond their knowledge boundaries. Targeted epistemic questions (e.g., "do you know the answer?") provide better signals but can be fooled by surface features, necessitating careful design of audit controls.

Abstract: Decision models return probabilities intended for routing, abstention and automated action. Calibration makes those probabilities useful on average, but does not establish whether low confidence reflects chance or missing knowledge, nor whether confidence falls when a model moves beyond what it knows. We audit this distinction in Jev, a decision model, with over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families, with paired interventions that vary the information supplied for a fixed item. Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary it exceeds accuracy by 0.21--0.33, a gap that recalibration on earlier months does not close. Targeted yes/no questions give sharper readouts of the case: whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) and whether the evidence suffices (0.95, against 0.85 for confidence on the same items). Asking whether Jev knows the answer appears to flag fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91), but with realistic names or with dates removed it shows no advantage over answer uncertainty. Black-box knowledge audits therefore need explicit controls for surface cues. Code: https://github.com/Syntheme/beyond-answer-confidence.

</details>


### [329] [From Discovery to Decision: Finite-Budget Recoverability in LLM Voting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01014)
*Shaoang Li,Jian Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the "discovery-to-decision gap" in LLM ensemble inference—where a correct answer is discovered but may fail to win due to insufficient remaining votes. The authors characterize this gap through realized vote state and remaining call budget, derive recoverability thresholds, and propose an "exact locking" mechanism that saves 28-30% of calls while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When scaling LLM inference with multiple response samples, there exists a fundamental tension: discovering a correct answer early doesn't guarantee it wins the plurality vote if enough calls remain to accumulate votes for other candidates. This creates a "discovery-to-decision gap" that wastes computational resources while potentially failing to select the correct answer.

Method: The authors model the voting process under iid response law, analyzing the realized vote state and remaining call budget. They derive finite-horizon endpoint probabilities, study the effects of merging wrong-answer identities, and introduce "exact locking" certificates based on singleton reachability. Empirical validation uses a controlled Word16 study with input permutation.

Result: Key findings: (1) The observed candidate set can only expand while reachable endpoint winners can only contract during sampling; (2) Merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness but cannot improve plurality accuracy; (3) Singleton reachability yields gold-free exact locking certificates; (4) Empirically, most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery; (5) Input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points; (6) Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at 16-call budget.

Conclusion: The discovery-to-decision gap is a fundamental property of plurality voting in LLM ensembles. The exact locking mechanism provides a theoretically grounded way to terminate early when the outcome is guaranteed, offering significant computational savings without sacrificing accuracy. The framework enables precise reasoning about candidate conversion windows and provides practical tools for optimizing test-time scaling.

Abstract: Voting over multiple LLM responses is a common primitive in test-time scaling and ensemble inference. Collecting more responses can expand the candidate pool and increase the chance that a correct answer is discovered. Under a fixed call budget, a discovered answer still needs to accumulate enough support within the remaining calls to become the final plurality winner, creating a discovery-to-decision gap. In this work, we characterize this gap through the realized vote state and remaining call budget. We derive a sharp recoverability threshold and show that, as sampling proceeds, the observed candidate set can only expand while the set of reachable endpoint winners can only contract, inducing a candidate-level conversion window. Under a specified iid response law, the same state yields exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities. We further show that merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness and cannot improve plurality accuracy, and that the effect of redistributing wrong-answer probability depends on the realized vote state. Singleton reachability yields a gold-free exact locking certificate. For a known answer universe, its first trigger is the earliest prefix at which all admissible continuations yield the same fixed-budget output. Empirically, most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery. In a controlled Word16 study, input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with essentially unchanged single-call correctness. Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at a 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output.

</details>


### [330] [Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01017)
*Xuehang Guo,Haoyu Wang,Shengyu Chen,Zach Chen,Wei Cheng,Qingyun Wang,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InFlowOp is a framework that uses a label-free cost function to determine task decomposition granularity and agent assignment in multi-agent LLM workflows, while also enabling in-execution fault correction. It introduces the Braid benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coordination tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building multi-agent workflows with LLMs is challenging because: 1) It requires upfront decisions on task decomposition granularity, agent assignment, and when to create new specialists; 2) Improving workflows is costly as it requires reference answers, graded outcomes, or trained assessors; 3) Fault correction requires whole workflow re-execution, re-search, or retraining.

Method: InFlowOp prices every decision using a label-free cost that balances agent competence against task demands versus the agent's computational cost. It performs bidirectional determination of task decomposition and agent assignment before execution using this cost. During execution, it corrects faults via the cheapest move using the same cost mechanism. The Braid benchmark is introduced to evaluate multi-agent coordination tasks requiring capabilities beyond single agents.

Result: InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to +11.97%, and achieves +9.64% with in-flow optimization across various domains and backbones.

Conclusion: The cost-based approach enables both workflow construction and runtime fault correction within a unified framework, demonstrating significant improvements over single-agent baselines on the Braid benchmark for multi-agent coordination tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

</details>


### [331] [Beyond Final Accuracy: Auditing Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01042)
*Shixuan Li,Wei Yang,Peiyu Zhang,Anzhe Cheng,Heng Ping,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICR is a controlled framework that evaluates multi-agent communication by measuring answer revision following independent reasoning, separating the effects of communication from architecture and additional reasoning. It reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can hide substantially different revision behaviors, and that communication quality depends on message content and receiver policies rather than being an intrinsic channel property.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent communication evaluation is fundamentally ambiguous because improvements in system performance could derive from effective communication, favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning. Since communication methods are evaluated within their native systems, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Additionally, final accuracy merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication actually changes decisions.

Method: The paper introduces Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. It fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. The framework was tested across four reasoning benchmarks, comparing textual and latent communication, and examining receiver-policy effects on MedQA and GPQA-D.

Result: Across four reasoning benchmarks, similar aggregate accuracy conceals substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks—meaning richer messages amplify both beneficial and harmful influence. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks.

Conclusion: Communication quality should not be treated as an intrinsic property of a channel. Evaluation should focus on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms. ICR recenters evaluation on the process of revision rather than just final accuracy.

Abstract: Multi-agent communication aims to help agents benefit from one another's information. Yet improvements in system performance leave a fundamental ambiguity: do they reflect effective communication, a favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning? Because communication methods are commonly evaluated within the systems they were designed for, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Final accuracy further merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. We introduce Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. ICR fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Across four reasoning benchmarks, our audit of textual and latent communication reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks, so richer messages amplify beneficial and harmful influence alike. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D further show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks. These findings challenge treating communication quality as an intrinsic property of a channel. ICR therefore recenters evaluation on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms.

</details>


### [332] [Empty Commitments: When Agents Promise What Their Runtime Cannot Deliver](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01045)
*Jiaqi Tang,Lan Wei,Bingyu Shen,Boyang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of "empty commitments" in conversational agents—promises of future actions (e.g., "I will remind you tomorrow") that agents cannot fulfill due to their configuration limitations, distinct from broken promises which require observing a later trajectory. The work defines empty commitments on commitment semantics, proposes three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises that tools could realize, and a response-level outcome taxonomy. A measurement protocol is described with five setups adding persistence affordances incrementally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chatbots frequently make promises about future actions they cannot actually perform because they lack persistence—they only respond when users initiate contact. This creates a mismatch between user expectations and agent capabilities, where promises appear meaningful but are structurally impossible to fulfill based on the agent's design alone.

Method: The authors extend commitment semantics to define empty commitments, identify three distinct failure types, establish an anchoring condition to identify promises that tools could potentially fulfill, and develop a response-level outcome taxonomy. They propose a measurement protocol using five experimental setups that incrementally add persistence affordances, with the environment either left implicit or explicitly stated.

Result: The abstract describes the conceptual framework and measurement protocol rather than reporting empirical results.

Conclusion: The paper provides a systematic framework for identifying, categorizing, and measuring empty commitments in conversational agents, offering a foundation for improving agent design and user expectation management.

Abstract: A chatbot that says "I will remind you tomorrow" will not run again until the user writes. We call such a promise an empty commitment: a promise of an action after the current turn that nothing in the agent's tools or runtime can carry out. Unlike a broken promise, its emptiness follows from the agent's configuration alone; no later trajectory is needed. We define empty commitments on top of commitment semantics, with three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises that a tool could make real, and a response-level outcome taxonomy. We then describe a measurement protocol: follow-up requests run in five setups that add one persistence affordance at a time, with the environment either left implicit or stated.

</details>


### [333] [Network World Models as Environments for Algorithm Design on Complex Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01048)
*Rishab Alagharu,Hongji Pu,Zeeshan Memon,Xinyuan Song,Yuntong Hu,Liang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns to predict network diffusion dynamics under interventions, serving as a fast simulator to accelerate algorithm design for network optimization tasks. The method achieves comparable or superior performance to baselines in 138/141 settings while enabling up to 14.5x speedup over Monte Carlo simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex systems like networks have delayed effects from actions - seeding nodes or immunizing against epidemics changes little immediately, but the outcome unfolds over subsequent steps. Current simulation-based evaluation of candidate actions is computationally expensive, becoming a bottleneck when evaluating many candidates across multiple trajectories.

Method: The proposed method consists of: (1) An action-conditioned Network World Model that learns network diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies actions to networks, and predicts outcomes. (2) Integration into an algorithm design loop where a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit assignment, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions.

Result: Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 out of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation.

Conclusion: The action-conditioned Network World Model effectively serves as a fast evaluator for network optimization tasks, enabling efficient algorithm design while achieving strong performance across diverse settings. The significant speedup (up to 14.5x) makes this approach practical for real-world applications requiring extensive candidate evaluation.

Abstract: World models, which simulate an environment and predict how it changes under actions, are increasingly used in real-world applications such as robotics. Complex systems call for the same tool because the effect of an action is not immediate. Seeding nodes for a campaign, or immunizing nodes against an epidemic, changes little on its own; what matters is the outcome that unfolds over the steps that follow. Designing an algorithm that selects such actions to maximize expected performance on a task is inherently iterative, and every candidate must be scored by the outcome it produces. Obtaining that outcome has relied on simulation, whose cost becomes a bottleneck when candidates are evaluated over many sampled trajectories. We propose an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns a network's diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies each action to the network, and predicts the outcome that follows.
