It serves as a fast evaluator inside an algorithm design loop in which a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions. Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [334] [Improving Math Reasoning through Value-guided Informative Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01080)
*Shaohuai Liu,Yuning Wu,Haoran Liu,Enzo Jia,Devin Chen,Kai Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: APIVIS is a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning in RLVR, combining direct and searched responses to produce informative relative rewards and applying selective supervision to preserve learning signals when uniform group rewards fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing search-based RLVR methods increase trajectory diversity but diversity alone does not guarantee that the searched rollout policy improves upon the current policy. There is a need for a method that ensures search-induced improvements actually enhance the policy.

Method: APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens to preserve learning signals when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. The method uses exact value-guided selection that improves expected verifier reward at each searched state.

Result: The theoretical analysis shows that exact value-guided selection improves expected verifier reward at each searched state, with this guarantee extending to the complete rollout policy. An approximate guarantee holds under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods across different model scales.

Conclusion: APIVIS effectively addresses the limitation that trajectory diversity alone does not ensure policy improvement in search-based RLVR. The combination of relative rewards from searched improvements and selective supervision enables meaningful learning signals, validated by strong empirical results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Recent work introduces search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not ensure that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. To address this gap, we propose APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning. APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It further applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving a learning signal when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. We show that exact value-guided selection improves the expected verifier reward at each searched state and that this guarantee extends to the complete rollout policy, with a corresponding approximate guarantee under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods, validating the effectiveness of APIVIS.

</details>


### [335] [YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01097)
*Yoonkyu Woo,Woojin Lee,Jin-Xia Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: YouRA is a stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research architecture that preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across research trajectories. It integrates three components: Verification State Architecture (VSA), Independent Controller, and Stateful Reflection. On MLR-Bench's ten-task subset, YouRA outperforms MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 across all three matched backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, but manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines.

Method: YouRA integrates three core components: (1) Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; (2) Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; (3) Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. Evaluation uses MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset with hallucination taxonomy diagnostics and data-provenance diagnostics.

Result: YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones on MLR-Bench's ten-task subset. The automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablation study confirms separable contributions: removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system.

Conclusion: The three-component architecture (VSA, Independent Controller, Stateful Reflection) effectively addresses the structural gap between manuscript claims and executed experiments. Each component contributes separably, and the full system outperforms prior approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.

Abstract: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.

</details>


### [336] [Beyond State-of-the-Art: Standardising Environmental Impact Metrics for AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01116)
*Lachlan McGinness,Dan Pagendam,Robert Offner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the environmental impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) by conducting an automated literature review of 5,285 NeurIPS 2025 papers, finding that environmental impact reporting is nearly non-existent. The authors propose standardized sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, heuristics for estimating carbon cost of LLM inference, and implement these in a tool called carbonbenchmark. They also formalize the 'Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ) framework to promote computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing capabilities and ubiquity of LLMs have led to increased environmental footprint, yet the machine learning community lacks standardized practices for carbon accounting. Despite calls for responsible AI, there is no consistent way to measure or report the environmental impact of LLM training and inference.

Method: The authors conducted an automated literature review of 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 to assess the current state of environmental impact reporting. They defined standardized sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency and developed heuristics to estimate carbon cost of LLM inference. These metrics were implemented in carbonbenchmark, a software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.

Result: The literature review revealed that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent in the ML community. The authors proposed standardized sustainability metrics and implemented them in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution. They also formalized the SMAJ framework to challenge the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs.

Conclusion: To promote sustainable AI, the field should adopt standardized carbon accounting practices, use tools like carbonbenchmark for emissions tracking, and embrace the SMAJ framework to prioritize computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional state-of-the-art accuracy metrics.

Abstract: As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.
  Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

</details>


### [337] [AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01119)
*Zhicheng Feng,Yubo Zhao,Xuefeng Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AbsorbEvo is an AI agent framework that autonomously designs high-performance microwave absorbers from natural-language specifications, using LLM reasoning combined with physics-based prediction and evolutionary optimization to reduce the need for specialized expertise and lengthy design cycles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing microwave absorbers requires interdisciplinary expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science, and simulation programming, involving time-consuming optimization processes. There is a need for automated systems that can translate natural-language performance objectives into validated designs.

Method: The framework uses a candidate evolution strategy integrating: (1) LLM-based language reasoning for proposing parameter adjustments, (2) a low-cost predictive model as physics prior for ranking candidates, (3) directed increments combined with global sampling, and (4) experience distillation into textual skills. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation, with results passing physical validity checks used to guide subsequent search.

Result: On AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved 79.17% task success rate vs 25.00% for generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Mean best coverage was 0.7816 vs 0.6434 and 0.6448 respectively.

Conclusion: AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers by integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, significantly outperforming generic agents and random search approaches.

Abstract: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. Here, we present AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. Its candidate evolution strategy integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction and historical feedback. A large language model proposes the directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history. The system combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates and uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation. Results passing physical validity checks are used to evaluate performance and guide subsequent search. Experience from training tasks is further distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before use in new tasks. Under identical proposal budgets on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17%, versus 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448, respectively. By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers.

</details>


### [338] [CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01124)
*Jiazhen Hong,Xiaotian Zhou,Zihao Ding,Kailong Wang,Yu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CortexBridge is a lightweight adapter that maps EEG data from arbitrary electrode montages into a shared cortical latent space by combining EEG features with electrode and atlas coordinates, enabling transfer learning across different EEG setups without retraining the foundation model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models are pretrained with fixed channel vocabularies or limited montages, creating transfer difficulties when electrode layouts change across different datasets or recording setups.

Method: CortexBridge combines EEG features with electrode coordinates and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. Evaluated using three frozen foundation models (EEGPT, LaBraM, CBraMod) on five BCI datasets from MOABB.

Result: CortexBridge improved performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. Average gains in balanced accuracy: 0.80% (EEGPT), 0.70% (LaBraM), 3.26% (CBraMod). Maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class SSVEP classification. Visualizations showed task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing more concentrated representation in Yeo Visual network than auditory P300.

Conclusion: Cortical alignment is a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism that enables transfer from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models, addressing the challenge of variable electrode layouts in EEG-based BCI systems.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are often pretrained with a fixed channel vocabulary or a limited set of montages, making transfer difficult when electrode layouts change. We propose CortexBridge, a lightweight adapter that combines EEG features with electrode and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. Evaluated with three frozen foundation models on five brain-computer interface (BCI) datasets from the Mother of All BCI Benchmarks (MOABB), CortexBridge improves performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. The gains in balanced accuracy average 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) classification. Visualizations of the learned atlas representations reveal task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing a more concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network than auditory P300. These results establish cortical alignment as a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models.

</details>


### [339] [Grounding Large Language Models in DSGE Simulators for Policy Generation and Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01128)
*Aditya Dubey,Namah Gupta,Vinti Agarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper tests whether large language models can produce economically consistent policy responses by placing an LLM inside six DSGE simulators. The study addresses the long-horizon credit assignment problem where policy effects may appear quarters after actions, comparing PPO (with learned value function) against GRPO (critic-free baseline) as training methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to move beyond evaluating LLMs by their linguistic plausibility and instead test whether their policy actions are actually consistent with economic dynamics. The authors note that LLMs can produce reasonable-sounding economic policy responses, but this doesn't guarantee their actions align with real economic principles.

Method: The researchers implemented a common Python interface for six DSGE simulators, allowing the LLM to observe economic states and discourse, select bounded policy actions, and receive rewards. They tested PPO (with learned value function for delayed reward propagation via generalized advantage estimation) against GRPO (no learned value function, uses group-relative advantage). Experiments included directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks.

Result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results. It focuses on the experimental methodology and framework design rather than reporting findings. The key contribution appears to be the novel experimental setup for evaluating LLM policy agents in economic simulations.

Conclusion: The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone. The framework enables systematic evaluation of whether LLM policy decisions align with established economic dynamics through DSGE model feedback.

Abstract: Large language models can produce economic policy responses that sound reasonable, but this does not show that their actions are consistent with economic dynamics. We test this by placing an instruction-tuned language model inside six Snowdrop-backed dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) simulators. At each turn, the model observes the economy and a change in economic discourse, selects a bounded policy action, and receives the next simulated state and an economic reward. We implement a common Python interface for repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation.
  This setting creates a long-horizon credit-assignment problem. Policy effects may appear several quarters after an action is taken. PPO has a learned value function that can propagate delayed reward to earlier tokens through generalized advantage estimation. GRPO has no learned value function and instead assigns a group-relative advantage from complete rollout returns. It therefore cannot distinguish which earlier turn caused the outcome; if every rollout receives the same return, the normalized advantage is zero. We use PPO as the primary method and GRPO as a matched critic-free baseline. The experiments also test directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks. The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone.

</details>


### [340] [Auditing Action Settlement in LLM Agent Environments: Order, Progress, and Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01138)
*Haotian Chen,Bowen Ye,Yuning Zhang,Jingkun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses arbitration of concurrent actions in LLM agent environments through a typed snapshot-settlement contract. It tests five settlement policies across 28,800 permutation trials and 2,160 scripted episodes, evaluating order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency. Key finding: conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents vs 90.28% for random tickets in a six-agent doorway task. A full-state journal audit successfully replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 corruptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Concurrent actions in LLM agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. The authors aim to implement and audit a settlement mechanism for handling such conflicts.

Method: Implemented a typed snapshot-settlement contract; tested five settlement policies in 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes; audited full-state journal for replay consistency with 156 checkpoints and 1,332 constructed corruptions.

Result: Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities. Conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents versus 90.28% for random tickets (59.03 percentage point improvement, 95% CI: 50.00-68.06). All policies preserve spatial constraints. Priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum. Full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects all 1,332 corruptions.

Conclusion: The evidence concerns execution semantics in LLM agent concurrent action settlement, not human realism or long-run fairness. The study demonstrates that random ticket policies significantly outperform priority-based arbitration for useful progress, while all policies preserve spatial constraints.

Abstract: Concurrent actions in large language model (LLM) agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. We implement a typed snapshot-settlement contract and audit three distinct properties: order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency. Five settlement policies are tested in 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes. Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities, yet conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets; the paired improvement is 59.03 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval: 50.00-68.06). All policies preserve the tested spatial constraints, and priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum. A separate full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 constructed corruptions with a retained terminal anchor. The evidence concerns execution semantics, not human realism or long-run fairness.

</details>


### [341] [ReSolve: Reusing Candidate Reasoning through Selective Generative Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01140)
*Bangji Yang,Jiajun Fan,Hongba Ma,Xi Zhu,Weizhi Zhang,Minghao Guo,Ye Li,Hamid Palangi,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReSolve is a training-free inference procedure that reuses candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation. It examines existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack parseable answers, then incorporates generated solutions into a bounded loop. On 130 competition-math problems, ReSolve achieves 100/99 correct answers vs 91/92 for voting, using 46-47% fewer tokens than 8-sample self-consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. The paper aims to reuse this candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation rather than discarding it.

Method: ReSolve uses an answer-distribution controller that invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Hybrid scoring is used for evaluation.

Result: On 130 competition-mathematics problems with two independently sampled candidate pools, ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers, compared with 91 and 92 for voting over the same four candidates. Eight-sample self-consistency obtains 94 and 96 correct answers while consuming substantially more tokens; ReSolve uses 46.3% and 47.2% fewer tokens. Ablation removing visible derivations reduces accuracy from 100 to 93. Selective moderation solves 97 problems while reducing moderation tokens by ~54% and total pipeline tokens by 6.2%.

Conclusion: Results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. However, the method does not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions.

Abstract: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. We introduce ReSolve, a training-free inference procedure that reuses this candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation. An answer-distribution controller invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Under Hybrid scoring on 130 competition-mathematics problems evaluated with two independently sampled candidate pools, ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers, compared with 91 and 92 for voting over the same four candidates, with no correct-to-incorrect changes relative to that vote in either pool. Eight-sample self-consistency obtains 94 and 96 correct answers while consuming substantially more tokens; ReSolve uses 46.3% and 47.2% fewer tokens in the two evaluations. A controlled ablation removes visible derivations while retaining answer keys, vote counts, and the per-state output-cap rule, reducing accuracy from 100 to 93 correct despite increasing computation. Selective and always-on Uniform moderation both solve 97 problems, while selectivity reduces moderation tokens by approximately 54% and total pipeline tokens by 6.2%. These results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. They do not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions.

</details>


### [342] [When Does Exercise-Specific Joint Selection Help? An Audit of Evaluation and Control Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01188)
*Haotian Chen,Jingkun Yu,Yuning Zhang,Bowen Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits a previous study claiming that exercise-specific joint selection improves skeleton-based exercise correctness classification. Through rigorous analysis examining evaluation aggregation methods, subset structures, and temporal representations across 1,057 repetitions from 10 subjects, the authors find that the reported gains are highly sensitive to the choice of estimand. They demonstrate that when appropriate controls and estimands are used, the gains diminish or disappear, concluding that such claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be methodological scrutiny—auditing previous claims about exercise-specific joint selection benefits to determine whether these gains are robust or artifacts of particular evaluation choices. The authors seek to establish what the "gain" actually represents and whether it generalizes across different analytical approaches.

Method: The authors conducted an exploratory audit using: (1) different evaluation aggregation methods (pooled out-of-fold vs. equal-weight within-person AUROC); (2) random map controls (1,000 dimension-matched random maps, with additional controls matching bilateral structure and trunk inclusion); (3) multiple classifiers (RBF-SVM, logistic regression, random-convolution); (4) sequence-order and paired-seed controls. They analyzed 1,057 repetitions from ten REHAB24-6 subjects.

Result: The manual-subset kNN gain dropped from 0.055 (pooled out-of-fold AUROC) to 0.020 (equal-weight within-person AUROC), with both confidence intervals including zero. Among 1,000 random maps, 14 matched or exceeded the manual pooled result, but 145 matched when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion were also matched. RBF-SVM retained a positive within-person gain, while logistic regression and random-convolution showed negative point gains under that estimand.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls. This exploratory audit does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit—it merely questions the robustness of previous claims and emphasizes the importance of rigorous evaluation methodology in skeleton-based motion analysis.

Abstract: Exercise-specific joint selection can improve skeleton-based correctness classification, but what does that gain establish? We audit 1,057 repetitions from ten REHAB24-6 subjects, separating evaluation aggregation, subset structure, and temporal representation. The manual-subset kNN gain changes from 0.055 for pooled out-of-fold AUROC to 0.020 for equal-weight within-person AUROC; both paired intervals include zero. Among 1,000 dimension-matched random maps, 14 match or exceed the manual pooled result, versus 145 when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are also matched. RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, whereas logistic regression and a random-convolution comparator have negative point gains under that estimand. Sequence-order and paired-seed controls further qualify the interpretation. This exploratory audit shows why joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls; it does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit.

</details>


### [343] [Federated Agent Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01195)
*Qiang Yang,Zhiqiang Kou,Xueyi Zhang,Dong-Dong Wu,Hanlin Gu,Jing Guo,Yang Liu,Di Jiang,Qian Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Federated Agent Optimization (FAO), a new framework for enabling distributed LLM agents to collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while preserving privacy and keeping raw data, trajectories, and private knowledge local.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience (task execution, tool use, feedback, local knowledge), but this experience cannot be directly shared due to privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient because agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to include memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge.

Method: The paper formulates FAO as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost. It organizes the optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge/skills. It characterizes how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities.

Result: The paper provides a unified view of how distributed agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing, defines the key challenges of FAO, and outlines promising research directions for trustworthy federated agent systems.

Conclusion: FAO represents a novel paradigm for collaborative agent improvement that addresses the limitations of conventional federated learning for modern LLM agents operating in private environments.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate \textbf{Federated Agent Optimization (FAO)}, which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

</details>


### [344] [Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207)
*Ziyi Chen,Yan Zhang,Jianhui Wei,Daoan Zhang,Zuozhu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DARS addresses the credit assignment problem in RL training of LLMs by using a dependency graph of predicates to assign step-level rewards based on prerequisite relations, verifying/invalidating/repairing predicates, and discounting based on graph distance from broken prerequisites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal rewards in RL training of LLMs provide insufficient guidance about which steps matter. Steps in failed episodes all receive zero credit, even when they made progress. Common step credit assignment methods overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid.

Method: Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS) represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite, while independent predicates remain unaffected. Repairs update weights based on remaining errors; invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts annotations into signed per-step rewards.

Result: Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B: up to 10 points improvement over GiGPO on ALFWorld; improved WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy; complements AEPO on AIME24/25 with Python interpreter; exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations confirm step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. A distilled 8B annotator matches API annotator on ALFWorld.

Conclusion: DARS provides a general reward and annotation interface that integrates with various reasoning and agentic training methods (GiGPO, ARPO/AEPO) without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. It effectively addresses credit assignment in LLM RL training by modeling task progress as a dependency graph and assigning step-level credit based on predicate relationships.

Abstract: When training large language models with reinforcement learning, terminal rewards provide little guidance about which steps matter. Common methods for assigning step credit overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. With only a final success/failure reward, every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward, even when it made progress. We propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), which represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations and assigns step-level credit over the dependency graph. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite, while independent predicates are unaffected. Repairs update these weights based on any errors that remain; invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts these annotations into signed per-step rewards. A common reward and annotation interface allows DARS to integrate with a range of reasoning and agentic training methods, such as GiGPO and ARPO/AEPO, without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B, DARS improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO trained with the same budget and harness (ALFWorld), raises the WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy, complements AEPO's entropy-based training on AIME24/25 with a Python interpreter, and exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning comparisons at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show that step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. On ALFWorld, a distilled 8B annotator matches the API annotator, enabling DARS to run efficiently without a frontier judge. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/DARS.

</details>


### [345] [Reputation, Strategy, and Emotion Effects on Generative AI Cooperation: A Comparison Across Reasoning and Non-Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01222)
*Celso de Melo,Zishan Feng,James Hale,Kazunori Terada,Giorgio Coricelli,Jonathan Gratch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates cooperative behavior in frontier generative AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma framework, examining how reputation, strategy, and emotional signaling influence cooperation. Two studies compared non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o) with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2), finding that reasoning models show more sophisticated but heterogeneous social behavior, with implications for responsible AI deployment in interactive settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Gen AI systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in consequential interactions, understanding their propensity to cooperate and the signals that shape this propensity has become essential for responsible deployment.

Method: The researchers used the iterated prisoner's dilemma paradigm, manipulating three factors: (1) counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), (2) strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and (3) non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals). Two studies were conducted: Study 1 with non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o) and Study 2 with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2).

Result: Study 1 found cooperation was systematically shaped by all three factors, paralleling human behavioral patterns, though models varied substantially in weighting each factor. Study 2 revealed reasoning models had more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, eliminated the Potemkin effect (shown in diagnostic harmony game), and showed more conditional role for emotion consistent with hierarchical cue-weighting. Reasoning models also exhibited heterogeneous end-game behavior ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles.

Conclusion: Gen AI models are increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors. The findings underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings like negotiations and multi-round interactions.

Abstract: As generative AI (Gen AI) systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in economically and socially consequential interactions, understanding their propensity to cooperate -- and the signals that shape this propensity -- has become essential. We examine cooperative behavior in frontier Gen AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma, manipulating counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals). In a first study with non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o), cooperation was systematically shaped by all three factors, paralleling patterns long documented in human behavioral research, though models varied substantially in how heavily each factor was weighted. A second study with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2) revealed a more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, a near-elimination of the Potemkin effect observed in non-reasoning models (evidenced by near-uniform cooperation in a diagnostic harmony game), and a more conditional role for emotion consistent with a hierarchical cue-weighting strategy rather than a simple loss of social sensitivity. Reasoning models also showed heterogeneous end-game behavior, ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection effect, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles with direct practical relevance for deployment in negotiation and other multi-round interactions. Together, these findings characterize Gen AI models as increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors, and underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform the responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings.

</details>


### [346] [HHR: Hierarchical Hash Retrieval for Efficient LLM Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01230)
*Lianjun Liu,Tiantian Zheng,You Huang,Weiqi Yan,Mingte Qiu,Huazhong Liu,Xiaofeng Zhu,Yunshan Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HHR (Hierarchical Hash Retrieval) is a coarse-to-fine framework that improves hash-based sparse attention for long-context LLM inference by addressing the mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance through Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hash-based retrieval for efficient long-context inference suffers from a critical mismatch: query-key logits depend on directional similarity and feature magnitudes, but hash binarization discards magnitude information, causing false positives (low-logit keys retrieved) and false negatives (high-logit keys omitted).

Method: HHR combines two components: (1) GKR learns head-wise orthogonal transformations to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive discriminative page-level logit bounds for pruning low-logit keys while preserving important candidates; (2) LHP learns head-wise projection spaces that align Hamming distance with true query-key relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval.

Result: On LongBench, HHR improves average score by 1.10 points. At 128K context length, it achieves 3.30x decoding speedup and 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Demonstrated across diverse LLMs and benchmarks.

Conclusion: HHR effectively suppresses false positives and recovers false negatives in hash-based sparse attention, substantially improving retrieval fidelity while maintaining significant computational efficiency gains for long-context LLM inference.

Abstract: Efficient long-context inference is essential for large language models (LLMs), yet it poses a severe computational bottleneck. Hash-based retrieval offers an efficient alternative by encoding queries and keys into binary codes and using Hamming distance for key selection. However, this leads to a critical mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance. Query-Key logits depend jointly on directional similarity and feature magnitudes, whereas hash binarization discards magnitude information, causing both false-positive retrieval of low-logit keys and false-negative omission of high-logit keys. To address these failures, we propose Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine framework that progressively improves retrieval accuracy through Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP). GKR learns a head-wise orthogonal transformation to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive more discriminative page-level logit bounds, enabling effective pruning of low-logit keys while preserving important candidates. LHP then learns a head-wise projection space that aligns Hamming distance with the true Query-Key relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval. By combining GKR and LHP, HHR suppresses false positives and recovers false negatives, substantially improving the fidelity of hash-based sparse attention. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that HHR achieves superior performance over existing methods. For example, on LongBench, HHR improves the average score by 1.10 points and, at a context length of 128K, achieves up to a 3.30x decoding speedup and a 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/HHR.

</details>


### [347] [Learning to Ask: Information Acquisition for SLM-LLM Collaboration, under a budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01236)
*Yongjun Kim,Xiaoxiao Li,Jaeho Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel SLM-LLM collaboration framework that treats the interaction as an information acquisition problem rather than computation allocation. A small language model acts as the primary reasoner and selectively queries a black-box LLM advisor only when needed, using a three-stage RLVR framework to learn when to call the advisor, how to formulate useful queries, and how to integrate the acquired information into reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SLM-LLM collaboration approaches frame the problem as computation allocation, determining which model handles each portion of reasoning. However, in black-box API-based settings, this paradigm is inefficient due to coarse-grained delegation or repeated context transmission across model switches. The authors propose reformulating collaboration as an information acquisition problem under API budget constraints.

Method: The authors develop a three-stage RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Value-based Rewards) framework with three components: (1) learning whether to call the advisor, (2) learning how to formulate useful queries, and (3) learning how to integrate collaboration into the reasoning process by jointly refining advisor invocation and information use. The SLM remains the primary reasoner and issues targeted queries to the black-box LLM advisor only when needed.

Result: Across mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, the approach improves the performance-cost tradeoff over existing collaboration baselines. In some settings, it matches or exceeds oracle problem-level routing. The strategy also transfers to other advisor model families without further training.

Conclusion: The information acquisition paradigm is more effective than computation allocation for SLM-LLM collaboration in black-box API settings. The three-stage RLVR framework successfully enables selective, targeted querying that balances performance and cost, demonstrating transferability across different advisor model families.

Abstract: Collaboration between a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM) offers an opportunity to combine the efficiency of smaller models with the strong reasoning capabilities of larger ones. Existing approaches primarily frame such collaboration as a computation allocation problem, determining which model should handle each portion of the reasoning process. In black-box API-based settings, however, this paradigm can be inefficient due to coarse-grained delegation or repeated transmission of context across model switches. In this work, we instead formulate SLM-LLM collaboration as an information acquisition problem, under an API budget constraint. The SLM remains the primary reasoner and selectively queries a black-box LLM advisor only when needed, issuing targeted queries rather than delegating the reasoning process itself. To realize this strategy, we develop a three-stage RLVR framework that learns whether to call the advisor, how to formulate useful queries, and how to integrate the collaboration into the reasoning process by jointly refining advisor invocation and information use. Across mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, our approach improves the performance--cost tradeoff over existing collaboration baselines and, in some settings, matches or exceeds oracle problem-level routing. Finally, we show that our strategy can transfer to other advisor model families, without further training.

</details>


### [348] [Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graphs for Dynamic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01249)
*Yan Luo,Selim-Antoine Lali,Jeremy Moebel,Iliass Khoutaibi,Ahmadou Aidara,Mengyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces dynamic task routing, a new problem where event streams revise task bindings and systems must select the valid document version at query time before solving tasks. They propose RIAG, a bounded multi-agent policy that achieves 54.24% accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, significantly outperforming comparison methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional reasoning protocols use fixed, preselected tasks and cannot test whether an agent propagates relevant updates, preserves unaffected work, or reconstructs historical task bindings. This limitation motivates the study of dynamic task routing.

Method: The authors repurpose six benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, HumanEval) into 31,119 dynamic episodes with 373,428 temporally categorized queries. They introduce RIAG (Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph), which: 1) separates deterministic temporal resolution from task reasoning, 2) caches solutions by immutable document identity, 3) starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and 4) conditionally invokes audit and repair using at most four calls per document version.

Result: Homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, compared with 32.22% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest comparison method. Heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78% at 0.63 calls/query.

Conclusion: RIAG effectively addresses the dynamic task routing problem by balancing the trade-off between recomputing after every event (wasting work) and unguarded reuse (returning stale conclusions). The method achieves high accuracy with significantly fewer calls per query than comparison methods.

Abstract: Conventional reasoning protocols present a fixed, preselected task, so they cannot test whether an agent propagates relevant updates, preserves unaffected work, or reconstructs a historical task binding. We therefore study \emph{dynamic task routing}, in which an event stream revises task bindings and a system must select the document version valid at each query time before solving it. To study this problem, we repurpose six widely used benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, and HumanEval into 31{,}119 dynamic episodes comprising 373{,}428 temporally categorized queries. This setting exposes a central trade-off: recomputing after every event wastes work, whereas unguarded reuse returns stale conclusions. We introduce the Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph (RIAG), a bounded multi-agent policy that separates deterministic temporal resolution from task reasoning. RIAG caches solutions by immutable document identity, starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and conditionally invokes audit and repair, using at most four calls per document version. On this collection, homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24\% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, compared with 32.22\% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest comparison method; heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78\% at 0.63 calls/query.

</details>


### [349] [DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01256)
*Bo Deng,Xinlei Zheng,Yi Wei,Kang Zhou,Chongyang Tao,Renzhao Liang,Xuanren Chen,Lifan Guo,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeFA is a dependency-guided framework for localizing decisive errors in LLM agent executions by combining protocol and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph, then tracing failure propagation to identify the responsible agent, error step, and error category. It uses segmentation to handle long trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Errors in LLM agent executions are separated from their visible consequences by many steps, making decisive-error localization challenging as it requires understanding both step content and step dependencies.

Method: DeFA combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and effects to construct a failure propagation graph. It then uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment's detailed content with summaries of other segments.

Result: DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy across Who and When and Who and When Pro text subset with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. It also works on image and video trajectories (multimodal). Ablations support the contributions of segmentation, event dependency graph, and failure propagation graph. Using DeFA's diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points over the native pipeline.

Conclusion: DeFA provides effective failure attribution for LLM agents across text and multimodal trajectories. The diagnostic feedback can support agent improvement on subsequent tasks through skill evolution, demonstrating both diagnostic capability and practical utility for agent development.

Abstract: Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally, DeFA uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment's detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis access to global execution context. Across Who and When and the Who and When Pro text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video trajectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. Using DeFA's diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points over the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improvement on subsequent tasks.

</details>


### [350] [Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01262)
*Lili Chen,Gavin Buskes,Yuxin Ren,Chin Tong Leong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, specific feedback in large electrical engineering classes by designing a Generative AI (GenAI) practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice, resolving the tension between immediacy and human oversight by relocating human verification from real-time grading to upfront solution verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the well-established importance of timely feedback on student learning, but the practical difficulty of sustaining it in large classes where students may wait days for feedback. While GenAI offers a solution for scaling conversational feedback, using it for grading raises trust and accountability concerns, and keeping humans in the loop reintroduces delays that undermine feedback's value.

Method: The researchers designed and piloted a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. This approach relocates human oversight from real-time grading to the upfront verification of solutions, rather than using GenAI for actual grading of assessed work.

Result: The abstract does not present specific results, as it appears to be describing the research design and pilot implementation rather than reporting outcomes. The study aimed to understand how students engaged with the tool, their perception of its feedback value and reliability, and lessons transferable to other engineering subjects.

Conclusion: The abstract concludes by identifying the key research questions: understanding student engagement patterns, perceptions of feedback value and reliability, and identifying transferable lessons for other engineering subjects. No conclusions are drawn yet as this describes the research aims rather than outcomes.

Abstract: Timely and specific feedback is one of the strongest influences on student learning, yet it is difficult to sustain in large electrical engineering classes where the ratio of students to demonstrators is high and a learner who is stuck may wait days to find out why an approach was wrong. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers a way to scale conversational feedback, but using it to grade assessed work raises trust and accountability concerns, and keeping a human in the loop to assure its judgements reintroduces the very delay that erodes the value of feedback. The result is a tension between the immediacy that makes feedback so impactful and the human oversight that makes it trustworthy. In this work, we set out to resolve that tension in practice by designing and piloting a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. This relocates human oversight from real-time grading to the upfront verification of solutions. Our goal was to understand how students engaged with the tool, how they perceived the value and reliability of its feedback, and what lessons transfer to other engineering subjects.

</details>


### [351] [SCOPE-AD: Sequential cost-aware ordinal-belief planning with energy-based models for diagnostic agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01278)
*Ziwen Yu,Ivan Koychev,Elizabeth Coulthard,Ting Zhou,Bolin Chen,Dian Hong,Zinuo You,Yujiao Wang,Anthony Mulholland,Qiang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE-AD is a reinforcement learning-based framework for cost-effective Alzheimer's disease diagnosis that sequentially decides which diagnostic tests to acquire and when to stop, balancing diagnostic accuracy with patient burden and financial costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Alzheimer's disease diagnosis uses fixed-modality predictors that acquire all tests upfront without jointly deciding which tests to acquire or when sufficient evidence is available. This leads to unnecessary costs and patient burden. The goal is to develop a cost-aware diagnostic agent that selectively acquires tests only when needed.

Method: The framework uses a mask-aware ordinal model to represent uncertainty along the CN-MCI-AD continuum. An energy-based teacher provides training signals using sampled Bellman targets from retrospective data, and a Qwen policy distills the teacher's action distributions. At deployment, the agent selects acquisition or diagnosis actions under budget and availability constraints, updating evidence and ordinal belief after each acquisition.

Result: SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of $50.46, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34 percentage points. Full-modality evaluation only improves Macro-F1 by 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times.

Conclusion: Selective acquisition is highly cost-effective for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis. The proposed approach significantly reduces diagnostic costs while maintaining competitive accuracy, supporting the value of sequential, cost-aware decision-making in clinical diagnostics.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis requires sequential evidence acquisition under heterogeneous test costs and patient burden. Fixed-modality predictors do not jointly decide which test to acquire or when the available evidence is sufficient for diagnosis. We propose SCOPE-AD (Sequential Cost-Aware Ordinal-Belief Planning with Energy-Based Models for Diagnostic Agents) for cost-aware classification of cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD cases. A mask-aware ordinal model represents uncertainty along the ordered CN--MCI--AD continuum. Retrospective training records provide sampled Bellman targets for an energy-based teacher, whose action distributions are distilled into a Qwen policy. At deployment, the agent selects acquisition or diagnosis actions under availability and budget constraints without access to unacquired values. After each acquisition, the evidence and ordinal belief are updated before the next decision. On ADNI, SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70\% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of \$50.46, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.34 percentage points. Full-modality evaluation raises Macro-F1 by only 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times. These results support selective acquisition for cost-effective diagnosis.

</details>


### [352] [ITC-MoE: Importance-guided Token-aware Compression for MoE Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01296)
*Lianjun Liu,Shipeng Li,You Huang,Weiqi Yan,Mingte Qiu,Huazhong Liu,Xiaofeng Zhu,Yunshan Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ITC-MoE is a compression framework for Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models that addresses computation and storage costs through adaptive Tucker decomposition and token-aware routing optimization, achieving 96.33% accuracy retention with 7.22x speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE DLMs offer flexible parallel decoding and increased model capacity but suffer from substantial computation and storage costs due to large expert parameters. Existing low-rank MoE compression methods use static factorization and fixed rank allocation, which fail to capture the distinctive properties of MoE DLMs: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy and token-wise utilization variation.

Method: ITC-MoE consists of two complementary components: (1) Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) incorporates activation and gradient importance into expert weight transformation, jointly factorizes expert weights across input, output, and expert modes, and adaptively allocates ranks under fixed parameter budget; (2) Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts candidate expert set for cold tokens with concentrated routing patterns.

Result: On SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, ITC-MoE maintains 96.33% accuracy on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget while achieving up to 7.22x end-to-end speedup.

Conclusion: ITC-MoE effectively reduces computation and storage costs of MoE DLMs while preserving generation quality by jointly adapting compression capacity and inference execution to parameter redundancy and token-wise variation. The framework demonstrates significant speedup while maintaining high accuracy.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer flexible parallel decoding and increased model capacity, but their large number of expert parameters incurs substantial computation and storage costs. Existing low-rank MoE compression methods largely rely on static factorization and fixed rank allocation, which overlook the distinctive properties of MoE DLMs. Specifically, we identify two properties: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy, where parameter redundancy and sensitivity to rank truncation vary across the input, output, and expert modes, and token-wise utilization variation, where hot and cold tokens exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and expert activation patterns. To address these challenges, we propose ITC-MoE, an Importance-guided Token-aware Compression framework for MoE DLMs. ITC-MoE consists of two complementary components. First, Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) incorporates activation and gradient importance into expert weight transformation, jointly factorizes expert weights across multiple modes, and adaptively allocates ranks under a fixed parameter budget. Second, Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts the candidate expert set for cold tokens with concentrated routing patterns. By jointly adapting compression capacity and inference execution to both parameter redundancy and token-wise variation, ITC-MoE substantially reduces the computation and storage costs of MoE DLMs while preserving their generation quality. For example, on SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, ITC-MoE maintains an accuracy of 96.33% on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget, while achieving up to a 7.22x end-to-end speedup. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/ITC-MoE.

</details>


### [353] [Questionnaire-Guided Disaggregation of Energy Appliance Use for Domestic Smart Meter Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01297)
*Achal Nanjundamurthy,Rupam Misra,Suzanne Little,Alan F. Smeaton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a label-free energy disaggregation system for Ireland's smart metering data that combines event detection for high-power loads with questionnaire-guided estimation to break electricity usage into 9 appliance categories. The hybrid method outperforms two existing disaggregation systems across multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ireland's smart meters record electricity at 30-minute resolution, which is too coarse to capture individual appliance usage. This limits the usefulness of smart metering data for understanding domestic energy consumption patterns and providing actionable advice to consumers.

Method: The researchers developed a hybrid disaggregation method combining: 1) event detection for high-power loads, and 2) questionnaire-guided estimation. They evaluated against two independently developed disaggregation systems using four datasets: a calibration household with commercial comparator, two public benchmarks (UK-DALE and REFIT) with per-appliance sub-metering, and a large Irish smart meter dataset (4,800+ years from 2,968 consumers).

Result: The hybrid method achieved the lowest whole-decomposition error across all buildings in all datasets. It showed significantly better month-level performance over 54 paired months (p<0.001, Holm-corrected) compared to the two other disaggregation systems.

Conclusion: The proposed method provides useful advice on household energy consumption patterns and recommendations for reducing or shifting usage to lower costs. This approach enables better understanding of domestic energy use from coarse smart meter data.

Abstract: Ireland's smart metering programme records electricity use at 30-minute resolution, with smart meters installed in over 80\% of households as of late 2025. While this is useful for billing of smart, time-of-use tariffs, it is too coarse to capture use of domestic appliances. We present a label-free disaggregation system that breaks usage data into 9 appliance categories by combining event detection for high-power loads with questionnaire-guided estimation. Our evaluation draws on four datasets: a calibration household with a commercial comparator, two public benchmarks (UK-DALE and REFIT) with per-appliance sub-metering, and a smart meter dataset of more than 4,800 years of use from 2,968 Irish consumers. Compared against two independently developed disaggregation systems our hybrid method combining analysis of usage data with questionnaire results, achieves the lowest whole-decomposition error on all buildings across the datasets, with better month-level performance over 54 paired months ($p<0.001$, Holm-corrected). Our method provides useful advice on a household's energy consumption patterns and advice on how to reduce or shift usage on some appliances in order to reduce costs.

</details>


### [354] [DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01306)
*Stephanie Finley,Liudas Panavas,Thomas Mikkelson,Cam Hinton,Stacey Ganss,Bradley Monton,Emily Kendall,Michelle Spradlin,Lydia Bye,Michael O'Brien,Lauren Ylvisaker,Derek Ray,Suhaas Garre,Sushant Mehta,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DAYJOB is a benchmark of 130 professional tasks in healthcare (50) and finance (80), with estimated completion times of 13.6 and 16.6 hours respectively. The benchmark uses containerized environments with expert rubrics of binary criteria evaluated by an agentic judge. The best model (Claude Opus 5.5) achieves only 24.7% pass rate in healthcare and 23.9% in finance, revealing that agents often accept contradictory premises and carry errors through analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional work often begins with brief requests that require professionals to determine what is needed, which documents matter, and whether the request's premise is valid. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this realistic complexity of professional work.

Method: The benchmark consists of 130 containerized Harbor environments with expert rubrics of binary criteria (median 47.5 per healthcare task, 57.5 per finance task). An agentic judge evaluates attempts, which only pass if every criterion is met. Evaluation spans 30 model configurations from 13 developers.

Result: Claude Opus 5.5 (strongest model) passes 24.7% of healthcare and 23.9% of finance attempts. Median configuration passes only 0.6% and 2.5% respectively. Case studies reveal agents accept premises contradicting the record and carry wrong inputs through otherwise consistent analyses.

Conclusion: Current AI agents struggle significantly with professional tasks requiring premise validation and error detection. The benchmark reveals fundamental limitations in AI's ability to handle realistic professional work. All healthcare tasks, 50 finance tasks, evaluation harness, and leaderboard are released.

Abstract: Professional work often starts with a brief request that leaves the professional to work out what is needed, which documents matter, and whether the request's premise holds. We introduce DAYJOB, a benchmark of 130 tasks built by professionals in healthcare (50) and finance (80). The tasks are estimated to take a professional 13.6 hours on average in healthcare and 16.6 in finance. Each task is a containerized Harbor environment with an expert rubric of binary criteria (median 47.5 and 57.5 per task) that an agentic judge applies to the delivered files, and an attempt passes only if it meets every criterion. Across 30 model configurations from 13 developers, the strongest, Claude Opus 5.5, passes 24.7% of healthcare and 23.9% of finance attempts, and the median configuration passes 0.6% and 2.5%. In case studies, agents accept premises that the record contradicts and carry wrong inputs through otherwise consistent analyses. We release all healthcare tasks, 50 of the 80 finance tasks, the evaluation harness, and the leaderboard.

</details>


### [355] [ProtoFlow: Prototype-Guided Flow Matching for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01320)
*Shibo Feng,Wanjin Feng,Yang Qiu,Deheng Ye,Peilin Zhao,Chunyan Miao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProtoFlow proposes a novel multivariate time series forecasting framework that combines vector-quantized autoencoding with prototype-prior flow matching. Instead of using generic Gaussian noise as prior for flow matching, it leverages the learned VQ codebook as an informative prior, avoiding autoregressive token generation issues like exposure bias and training-inference mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VQ-based forecasting methods rely on autoregressive token generation, which suffers from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch. Flow matching provides non-autoregressive alternatives but typically initializes from generic Gaussian prior. The authors observe that the trained VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes that can serve as a more informative prior.

Method: ProtoFlow has three main components: (1) Vector-quantized autoencoding that maps multivariate sequences into discrete latent space; (2) Construction of a structured prior from the learned codebook; (3) DiT-based rectified flow that transports samples from the prototype prior to future latent representations conditioned on historical observations.

Result: ProtoFlow consistently achieves superior forecasting performance on benchmark datasets with efficient inference, while also promoting faster training convergence by replacing generic noise initialization with a learned prototype prior.

Conclusion: By combining VQ autoencoding with prototype-prior flow matching, ProtoFlow successfully addresses the limitations of autoregressive token generation and generic Gaussian priors, offering an efficient and accurate solution for high-dimensional multivariate time series forecasting.

Abstract: Generative modeling has shown strong promise for multivariate time mseries (MTS) forecasting, especially scale to high-dimensional settings. Diffusion-based methods achieve competitive performance but typically require many sampling steps at inference. VAE-based non-iterative forecasting frameworks have therefore emerged as an efficient alternative. Within this line of work, vector quantization (VQ) enables controllable latent space modeling by mapping multivariate series into compact discrete representations. Existing VQ-based forecasting methods, however, typically rely on autoregressive (AR) token generation, which suffers from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch. Flow matching provides an efficient non-autoregressive alternative for latent forecasting, but existing formulations usually initialize transport from a generic Gaussian prior. We instead observe that the trained VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes and can thus serve as a more informative prior for flow matching. Based on this insight, we propose ProtoFlow, a forecasting framework that combines vector-quantized autoencoding with Prototype-prior Flow matching. Our method first maps multivariate sequences into a discrete latent space, then constructs a structured prior from the learned codebook, and finally learns a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prior to future latent representations conditioned on historical observations. By replacing generic noise initialization with a learned prototype prior, ProtoFlow avoids the rollout mismatch of AR token prediction and promotes faster training convergence. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that it consistently achieves superior forecasting performance with efficient inference.

</details>


### [356] [TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01323)
*Fengpeng Li,Kemou Li,Qizhou Wang,Haiwei Wu,Jiantao Zhou,Di Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a token-level training objective for safety-aligned LLMs that addresses multi-turn jailbreak attacks where harmful goals are spread across conversations. It uses refusal-attributable advantage weighting and contrastive erasure to bound multi-turn trajectory risk while maintaining model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs often refuse harmful requests in single turns but comply when the same goal is spread across multiple turns (multi-turn jailbreak attacks). Existing preference objectives only score whole responses to single prompts and cannot control risk on unseen conversation histories, creating a critical security gap.

Method: TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure) works by: (1) weighting each token on safe responses by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage comparing a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy, allowing earlier tokens to receive credit from later refusal evidence; (2) at high-gap positions on rejected responses, combining observed tokens with policy-selected alternatives in erasure targets; (3) replacing retain sets with gradient-norm penalties.

Result: Across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, TRACE achieved the lowest attack success rate (ASR) in all 35 model-attack pairs. Model utility on MMLU and HellaSwag dropped by at most 1.23 percentage points.

Conclusion: Theoretical sufficient conditions can bound multi-turn trajectory risk from single-turn supervised learning. TRACE successfully minimizes multi-turn jailbreak vulnerability while preserving model utility, offering a principled approach to LLM safety that accounts for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage in risk evaluation.

Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse a harmful request but comply once the same goal is spread over several turns. Preference objectives score whole responses to single prompts, so their training loss alone cannot control risk on unseen histories. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions under which suppression at supervised single-turn contexts yields a bound on multi-turn trajectory risk.
