The bound accounts for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and characterizes contraction relative to a base-policy risk budget evaluated on the trained policy's contexts. TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure) turns this principle into a token-level objective. On the safe response, each token is weighted by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. The advantage compares a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy, allowing earlier response tokens to receive credit from later refusal-related evidence. At high-gap positions on rejected responses, TRACE combines the observed token with policy-selected alternatives in the erasure target. A gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set. Across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, TRACE gives the lowest attack success rate (ASR) in all 35 model and attack pairs, while the model utility evaluated on MMLU and HellaSwag drop by at most 1\.23 points. Source code can be found in the supplemental material.

</details>


### [357] [PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01325)
*Duong Hien Chi Kien,Thanh Trung Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PPO-HRAP is a hybrid regime-aware reinforcement learning trading policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization with an interpretable volatility-aware regime prior to balance upside participation with drawdown control. It blends learned PPO actions with regime-derived target exposures and uses a reward function incorporating log returns, VIX-conditioned drawdown penalties, exposure deviation, and turnover costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning trading policies struggle to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies tend to collapse toward passive long exposure, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards become too defensive during volatile periods. There is a need for a method that can adapt to different market regimes while maintaining risk-adjusted returns.

Method: PPO-HRAP combines PPO with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a composite reward (portfolio log return + VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty + target-exposure deviation + turnover cost), and executes blended actions between PPO actor output and regime-derived target exposure. The regime prior is volatility-aware using VIX conditioning.

Result: On held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window: 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe, 0.8588 Sortino, 0.4592 Calmar. Maximum drawdown reduced from 34.10% (Buy and Hold) to 18.47%. Five-seed stability: mean total return 0.2725 ± 0.0109, mean Sharpe 0.6219 ± 0.0565. Cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA rank first on total return and Sharpe ratio.

Conclusion: Blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior improves risk-adjusted trading behavior. PPO-HRAP effectively reduces maximum drawdown while maintaining competitive returns. Limitations include high turnover and limited cross-asset robustness beyond SPY (currently only single-run evidence for QQQ and DIA).

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for trading often struggles to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies can collapse toward passive long exposure on upward-drifting assets, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards can become too defensive during volatile periods. This paper proposes PPO-HRAP, a hybrid regime-aware policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes both market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a reward combining portfolio log return, VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty, target-exposure deviation, and turnover cost, and executes a blended action between the PPO actor output and a regime-derived target exposure. On the held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window, PPO-HRAP achieves 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe ratio, 0.8588 Sortino ratio, and 0.4592 Calmar ratio, while reducing maximum drawdown from 34.10% for Buy and Hold to 18.47%. Across five SPY seeds, PPO-HRAP remains stable with mean total return $0.2725 \pm 0.0109$ and mean Sharpe ratio $0.6219 \pm 0.0565$. Single-run cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA further show that the proposed method ranks first on total return and Sharpe ratio for all three reported assets. These results suggest that blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior is a practical way to improve risk-adjusted trading behavior, although the current policy still incurs high turnover and cross-asset robustness beyond SPY remains limited to single-run evidence.

</details>


### [358] [An ontology for cross-sectoral crisis management: core and public health modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01326)
*Aldo Gangemi,Rita T. Sousa,Luigi Asprino,Giorgia Lodi,Andrea G. Nuzzolese,Valentina Presutti,Johannes Gysen,Diana F. Sousa,Luigi Spagnolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECMO is a modular OWL-based ontology for cross-sectoral disaster risk reduction and response, featuring a CORE module with fundamental crisis concepts and domain-specific modules (e.g., public health aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11). It successfully populates knowledge graphs from unstructured epidemiological data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for a unified, cross-sectoral reference ontology for disaster risk reduction and response, addressing inconsistencies in knowledge representation across different crisis domains.

Method: Designed as a network of ontological modules using OWL2 punning and ontology design patterns. The public health module was aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. Demonstrated through the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system to generate an end-to-end pipeline for ECMO-compliant knowledge graph population.

Result: Initial results demonstrate that ECMO provides formal guardrails for consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration. The ontology is publicly available via Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 license.

Conclusion: ECMO effectively enables standardized crisis management knowledge representation and integration across sectors, with proven utility in epidemiological data processing.

Abstract: This paper presents the European Crisis Management Ontology (ECMO), a modular OWL-based ontology intended as a cross-sectoral reference for disaster risk reduction and response. ECMO is designed to be organised as a network of ontological modules. Among the modules, ECMO-CORE captures fundamental crisis management concepts such as hazard, event, exposure, impact, and response measure and uses ontology design patterns and the OWL2 punning technique to resolve ambiguities between hazard types and event manifestations. In addition, domain-specific modules are defined as in the case of the public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. To demonstrate the resource's utility, we used ECMO to represent the data of the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system of the Joint Research Centre to generate an end-to-end pipeline that populates an ECMO-compliant knowledge graph from unstructured epidemiological news. Initial results demonstrate that ECMO provides the formal guardrails necessary for consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration. The ontology is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20070268 and is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

</details>


### [359] [Verify Claims, Not Scores: Evidence-Based Verification of Modular Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01348)
*Ali Atiah Alzahrani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a verification audit framework for modular agents that replaces aggregate scoring with evidence-based evaluation. The framework uses three tools (oracle policies, component replacement, and verifier testing) to trace performance to specific components. Applied to a portfolio-allocation agent, the audit reveals that perfect information value is action-set dependent, scenario generators may discard critical signals, and runtime verifiers can be bypassed without detectable effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent development practices evaluate changes using aggregate task scores, which fail to provide actionable insights about: (1) whether improvement was actually attainable, (2) which specific component lost value or contributed to performance, and (3) what the agent's own verification checks actually certify. This lack of diagnostic granularity impedes systematic agent improvement and verification.

Method: The authors introduce a claim-specific verification audit framework with three evidence-gathering tools: (1) Oracle policies that measure attainable improvement under explicit action sets to distinguish evaluation limitations from environment constraints, (2) Component replacement analysis that substitutes individual components with perfect counterparts to locate value loss, with null results interpreted as unresolved when downstream components could mask them, and (3) A separate verifier test that validates whether the verifier's score accurately bounds the quantity it claims to measure. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent operating in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes.

Result: The empirical application revealed three significant findings: (1) The value of perfect regime information is dependent on the action set used to measure it, demonstrating that oracle valuations are not intrinsic but rather evaluation-method dependent; (2) The scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while improved local fidelity fails to improve decisions, indicating that fidelity improvements do not necessarily translate to better outcomes; (3) The runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes, exposing a fundamental weakness in current verification approaches.

Conclusion: The audit protocol provides a systematic framework for evaluating modular agents by shifting focus from aggregate scores to evidence-based evaluation. The key contribution is the introduction of three auditing tools (oracle policies, component replacement analysis, and verifier testing) that can trace performance limitations to specific components. The empirical findings on a portfolio-allocation agent reveal that: (1) perfect information value is action-set dependent, (2) scenario generators may discard critical signals, and (3) runtime verifiers can be circumvented without detectable outcome changes. These findings suggest that current verification practices may be insufficient for ensuring agent reliability.

Abstract: When developers change one component of an agent, such as its controller, a learned model or its verifier, they usually judge the change by an aggregate task score. That score cannot tell whether improvement was attainable, which component lost value, or what the agent's own checks certify. We introduce a claim-specific verification audit for modular agents that plan, act, check and refine. Instead of scoring the agent, the audit scores the evidence: each conclusion is recorded with the evidence behind it, one of four verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved or not evaluated) and the boundary within which it holds. Three tools supply that evidence. Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under an explicitly stated action set, so that a low value can be traced to the evaluation rather than to the environment. Replacing one component at a time with a perfect counterpart locates lost value, with null results read as unresolved whenever a downstream component could mask them. A separate test asks whether the verifier's score identifies the quantity it is read as bounding. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes, the audit shows that the value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it, that the scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while better local fidelity does not improve decisions, and that the runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes. The contribution is the protocol and the evidential distinctions it enforces; the empirical findings are specific to the agent and environment studied.

</details>


### [360] [Generation Provenance Before Behavior Attribution: Auditing Synthetic Speech Research Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01378)
*Sidi Chang,Peiying Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Attributing model behavior to synthetic training data requires knowing what produced each training item before estimating what that item caused. A waveform-label pair does not preserve this knowledge. We propose a generation-provenance substrate in which a synthetic research object binds source specification, generated content, waveform, target, fact requirements, quality signals, review lineage, and immutable manifest identity. Producer and selection mechanism determine evidentiary meaning; storage location and variable name do not. We audit this substrate in a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline. A 113-asset review population contains 1.552 hours of synthetic speech across six scenario families; all items have linked audio, transcripts, candidate notes, and fact checklists, but human evidence is selective and source-specific. Two faithful-only manifests are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned, while exact upstream attribution remains blocked by floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS and code stamps, and an unversioned checking prompt. We argue that generation provenance is necessary but not sufficient for behavior attribution: it defines the candidate causal graph and audit units, whereas contributive attribution still requires frozen training runs and intervention or influence evidence. The paper contributes a compact provenance contract, an audit protocol, and a bounded case study for synthetic-data attribution; controlled research access may be offered, but we do not claim causal training-data attribution, clinical validity, or unrestricted public release.

</details>


### [361] [Gacha Decoding: Eliciting Diverse Generations Through Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01382)
*Scott Geng,Yufei Zhang,Joseph Lee,Jerry Li,Marjan Ghazvininejad,Pang Wei Koh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Gacha Decoding is an inference-time method that elicits diverse language model generations by treating diversity as an instruction-following problem, combining the model's instruction-following capability with external RNG randomness rather than relying on token entropy. It outperforms prior approaches across multiple domains and paradoxically improves as underlying models become better instruction followers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The long-observed tension between diversity and model capability - as models improve, their token entropy and diversity under prior approaches actually decline. The authors seek to invert this relationship by leveraging instruction-following rather than entropy-based methods.

Method: Combine the LM's instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG tool to identify and realize distinct modes of the response space. This "planning with dice" approach treats diversity as an instruction-following problem rather than relying on token entropy.

Result: Up to 2.4x Vendi score improvement over prior approaches at equal quality, discovers novel modes that other approaches don't surface, and achieves the same number of high-quality modes with over 11x fewer samples.

Conclusion: Instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity. As underlying LMs become better instruction followers, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves - inverting the traditional diversity-capability relationship.

Abstract: We introduce Gacha Decoding, an inference-time method for eliciting diverse language model generations that scales with model capability. Across open-ended domains (in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning for image generation, and protein design), Gacha Decoding significantly outperforms existing generation diversity approaches at equal quality (up to 2.4x Vendi over the next-best prior approach), reaching the same number of high-quality modes with over an order of magnitude fewer samples (11.0x) and discovering novel modes that no other approach surfaces. Our key insight is to treat diversity as an instruction-following problem: rather than relying on the LM's token entropy, we combine its instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG tool to scalably identify and realize distinct modes of the response space. This approach of "planning with dice" enables Gacha to invert the long-observed tension between diversity and model capability. As the underlying LM becomes a better instruction follower, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves--even as its token entropy and diversity under prior approaches decline. Together, our results highlight that instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity.

</details>


### [362] [PRISM: A Category-Theoretic Framework for Measuring and Refining Multimodal Analogies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01383)
*Mirella Zeisler,Ojas Shirekar,Mircea Licǎ,Chirag Raman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PRISM is a modality-agnostic framework that uses category theory to measure and improve relational alignment in multimodal analogies, evaluated on visual metaphor generation. It employs a pullback score to quantify relational alignment and an iterative refinement loop to improve generated outputs based on this score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI approaches to multimodal analogy generation lack an interpretable measure of whether relational structure is understood and maintained in generated outputs. This gap limits the ability to assess and improve the quality of analogies across modalities.

Method: PRISM represents analogies as explicit relational mappings grounded in category theory and uses Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to instantiate these structures across modalities. It has two components: (1) the pullback score, which quantifies relational alignment from graph representations, and (2) an iterative refinement loop that uses the pullback score as in-context feedback to revise generated images toward greater relational depth.

Result: On AnaloBench benchmark, selecting the correct analogy purely by pullback score achieves 82.5% accuracy. VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations show PRISM consistently improves metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness over zero-shot generation. Human participants prefer refined outputs in 57.65% of pairwise comparisons. However, qualitative analysis reveals refinement can favor visually crowded compositions over genuine deeper relational correspondences.

Conclusion: The pullback score captures meaningful relational information, demonstrating that category-theoretic approaches can provide interpretable measures of analogy quality. While PRISM shows consistent improvement in analogy generation, limitations include the tendency toward visually crowded compositions rather than deeper relational alignment. Future work may address this refinement bias.

Abstract: Analogical reasoning involves identifying and preserving relational structures across domains. However, existing approaches to AI-driven multimodal analogy generation lack an interpretable measure of whether this structure is understood and maintained in the generated output. We address this gap with Pullback Refinement via Interpretable Structural Mapping (PRISM), a modality-agnostic framework for measuring and improving relational alignment in multimodal analogies, evaluated on visual metaphor generation. PRISM represents analogies as explicit relational mappings grounded in category theory and uses VLMs to instantiate these structures across modalities. Its first component, the pullback score, quantifies relational alignment from the resulting graph representation. On the AnaloBench benchmark, selecting the correct analogy purely by pullback score achieves 82.5% accuracy, demonstrating that the score captures meaningful relational information. PRISM's second component is an iterative refinement loop that uses the pullback score as an in-context feedback signal to iteratively revise the generated image towards greater relational depth. VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations show that PRISM consistently improves metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness over zero- shot generation, with human participants preferring the refined output in 57.65% of pairwise comparisons. However, a qualitative analysis reveals that refinement can favour visually crowded compositions rather than genuinely deeper relational correspondences.

</details>


### [363] [AiSearch: Interactive Multi-Modal Search with VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01389)
*Ali Koksal,Mei Chee Leong,Vicky Sintunata,Ching Ling Chin,Wee Teck Fong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AiSearch is a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages zero-shot Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos, featuring interactive search refinement through user feedback and visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern retrieval systems need to be both automated and interactive, allowing users to search and refine results in real time. The goal is to enable natural language search over visual content and help users select the most suitable VLM for their specific tasks.

Method: AiSearch leverages the zero-shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) to enable natural language search over images and videos. It supports interactive search refinement through user feedback and provides visual benchmarking capabilities across multiple VLMs.

Result: A flexible multimodal retrieval framework (AiSearch) that enables natural language search over visual content, supports real-time search refinement via user feedback, and allows comparative visual benchmarking across different VLMs.

Conclusion: AiSearch provides a comprehensive solution for multimodal retrieval that balances automation with interactivity, enabling users to effectively search visual content using natural language and select the optimal VLM for their specific use cases.

Abstract: Modern retrieval systems must both be automated and interactive, allowing users to search and refine results in real time. We present AiSearch, a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages the zero shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos. AiSearch supports interactive search refinement through user feedback to tailor results to the user's intent, and allows visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs, enabling users to select the most suitable model for their task.

</details>


### [364] [Contrastive Attention Mitigates Spectral Bias in Spiking Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01403)
*Xiaoli Liu,Malu Zhang,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA), a novel paradigm to address the performance gap between Spiking Transformers and ANN counterparts by enhancing high-frequency information retention through contrastive aggregation and differential refinement, inspired by biological visual systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The performance gap between Spiking Transformers (energy-efficient SNN-based architectures) and ANN counterparts persists. Unlike prior works blaming binary activations, this paper identifies that both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) act as low-pass filters, causing dissipation of high-frequency components.

Method: The proposed Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) draws inspiration from edge-detection and differential sensing in biological visual systems. It extracts contrast prototypes via global contrastive aggregation and applies local differential refinement to enhance high-frequency information.

Result: SCA is a general module that consistently boosts Spiking Transformers across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking tasks. It achieves lower complexity and superior efficiency compared to original SSA.

Conclusion: SCA establishes itself as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers, offering a biologically-inspired solution that effectively addresses the spectral filtering limitation while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Spiking Transformers merge the energy-efficiency of spiking neural networks (SNNs) with the representational power of self-attention, creating a promising architecture for high-performance, energy-efficient computation. However, a performance gap persists versus its counterparts in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Unlike prior works attributing this to binary activations, we reveal that both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) act as low-pass filters through multiscale spectral analysis. This characteristic leads to the dissipation of high-frequency components. To address this issue, we propose the Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) paradigm, which draw inspiration from the edge-detection and differential sensing properties of biological visual system. By extracting contrast prototypes via global contrastive aggregation and applying local differential refinement, SCA effectively enhances high-frequency information. Extensive experiments show that SCA is a general module that consistently boosts Spiking Transformers across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. Furthermore, it achieves lower complexity, offering superior efficiency over original SSA. These results establish its potential as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers.

</details>


### [365] [Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415)
*Yu Luo,Jiamin Jiang,Yimin Zuo,Xidao Wen,Rongchen Gao,Yongqian Sun,Shenglin Zhang,Guiyang Liu,Cheng Zhang,Fang Situ,Qi Zhou,Dan Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PoS is an inference-time framework that constructs and maintains explicit belief states for LLM agents, combining world state estimates with unresolved task requirements. It detects "Belief Trapping" where agents stall progress and provides tailored recovery mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents lack coherent understanding of current world state because existing memory systems only retain/compress history without maintaining explicit beliefs about what is known, unknown, and still needs to be accomplished.

Method: 1) Belief state construction combining world state estimates + unresolved requirements
2) Consistency validation to keep beliefs reliable
3) Task progress monitoring to detect Belief Trapping
4) Tailored recovery mechanisms based on trapping pattern and task requirement type

Result: Achieved highest overall performance on all four benchmarks with three LLM backbones. Ablations confirmed importance of consistency validation and recovery. Showed resilience to context growth.

Conclusion: Belief construction and continual maintenance is a foundational approach for long-horizon context management, surpassing methods based solely on history retention and compression.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world. We introduce PoS, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent's decision context. Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish. To keep this belief reliable and actionable, PoS validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth. Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

</details>


### [366] [SpikeMoE: Brain-Inspired Competitive Routing for Flexible Spiking Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01418)
*Xiaoli Liu,Yujie Liang,Jialin Li,Malu Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpikeMoE integrates Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) through a biologically inspired spike-based k-WTA Router that uses lateral inhibition and refractory period mechanisms for expert selection. The framework also includes a two-stage missing-modality modeling module for multimodal tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Combine the energy-efficient event-driven computation of SNNs with the conditional computation capability of MoE, while addressing the challenge of designing spike-based expert selection and handling missing-modality scenarios in multimodal learning.

Method: 1) Spike-based k-WTA Router: inspired by hippocampal CA1 region competition-inhibition, incorporates lateral inhibition and refractory period to select Top-K experts based on discrete spike counts.
2) Two-stage missing-modality modeling: combines empirical prototypes from observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to reconstruct missing-modality representations.

Result: SpikeMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance among SNN baselines, matches or exceeds ANN counterparts, maintains robustness across diverse missing-modality conditions, and demonstrates favorable trade-off between performance and energy efficiency.

Conclusion: The integration of neuronal-scale spiking dynamics with model-scale expert selection is a promising approach for energy-efficient brain-inspired computing, validating the synergy between SNNs and MoE architectures.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) enable event-driven computation through biologically inspired dynamics at the neuronal scale, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) perform conditional computation through expert selection at the model scale. Integrating their strengths offers potential for flexible neural architectures. A key challenge, however, lies in designing an expert selection mechanism based on spiking activity. To address this, we introduce a spike-based k-WTA Router inspired by competition-inhibition observed in the hippocampal CA1 region. The router incorporates lateral inhibition and refractory period to select Top-K experts according to discrete spike counts. Building on this, we present SpikeMoE, a framework that integrates neuronal-scale spiking dynamics with model-scale expert selection. To address incomplete multisensory inputs in multimodal tasks, we further equip SpikeMoE with a two-stage missing-modality modeling module that combines empirical prototypes from an observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to construct missing-modality representations. Experiments on vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that SpikeMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance among the SNN baselines, matches or exceeds the performance of ANN counterparts, and maintains robustness across diverse missing-modality conditions. These results demonstrate a favorable trade-off between performance and energy efficiency, validating the integration of spiking dynamics with sparse expert computation and highlighting SpikeMoE as a promising approach to energy-efficient brain-inspired computing.

</details>


### [367] [A Deterministic and Auditable AI Security Risk Assessment Framework with ATLAS Aligned Executable Rules and Formal Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01436)
*Yixuan Huang,Basel Halak,Boojoong Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An evidence-driven AI security assessment framework that operationalizes assessment as a deterministic decision function using MITRE ATLAS technique mappings, Control ID taxonomy, and formal verification to enable reproducible, machine-evaluable security audits of AI systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI security assessment is difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches rely on narrative checklists or assessor-driven scoring, lacking explicit machine-evaluable mappings from observable engineering artifacts to stable technique-level outcomes.

Method: The framework normalizes heterogeneous artifacts into a project-independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four-level ordinal scale. It compiles technique-level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation-to-control mapping, and outputs technique-indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links to evidence. All normative choices are packaged as a versioned assessment policy object. Formal verification is performed on boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator.

Result: Evaluation on five public open-source AI projects showed consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls. Worst-case residual feasibility persists when technique-specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope.

Conclusion: The proposed evidence-driven framework enables deterministic, reproducible AI security assessment with traceable evidence links. It successfully quantifies security improvements through unified hardening interventions and responds to real engineering changes via SBOM generation and CI security scanning gates.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high impact and safety critical settings, yet security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches often rely on narrative checklists or assessor driven scoring, and they lack an explicit, machine evaluable mapping from observable engineering artefacts to stable technique level outcomes. We present an evidence driven AI security assessment framework that operationalises assessment as a deterministic decision function. The framework normalises heterogeneous artefacts into a project independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four level ordinal scale, compiles technique level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation to control mapping, and outputs technique indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to the triggering evidence. We package all normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object to support repeatable reassessment across snapshots. To ensure semantic correctness, we formally verify boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain. We evaluate the framework on five public open source AI projects pinned to explicit repository snapshots, quantify before and after changes under a unified hardening intervention, and validate responsiveness to real engineering changes through fork based implementations of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and Continuous integration (CI) security scanning gates. Results show consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls, while worst case residual feasibility persists when technique specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope.

</details>


### [368] [DRelay: Global Draft Context for Prefix-Aware Parallel Speculative Decoding Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01439)
*Zhuoyu Wang,Junnan Huang,Xinyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DRelay is a prefix-aware selective repair mechanism for speculative decoding in LLMs that uses global information from entire draft blocks to correct early selection errors, thereby extending the accepted prefix length and improving end-to-end decoding speedup by 8.1%-16.8% over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parallel drafting in speculative decoding suffers from limited gains due to early selection errors. Even when the correct token exists in the candidate pool, a single early error prevents subsequent predictions from being used, constraining the accepted prefix length.

Method: DRelay uses two key components: (1) a global reader that extracts predictive information across positions for each candidate based on candidate correlations and selected path, and (2) a causal selector that combines candidate-level information with tokens selected at preceding positions to determine whether the native choice is consistent with global evidence and selected prefix. The method jointly trains the draft backbone and selector, combining candidate-support learning with a repair objective weighted according to each block position's potential contribution to consecutive accepted prefix.

Result: Across eight diverse benchmarks on H800 GPU, DRelay consistently improves both average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding performance over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. Under SGLang serving, DRelay achieves 14.7%-16.8%, 8.7%-9.3%, and 8.1%-9.3% average end-to-end speedup improvements over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark respectively.

Conclusion: DRelay successfully addresses the early selection error problem in speculative decoding by introducing prefix-aware selective repair using global information. The approach demonstrates consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks, making it a promising technique for accelerating LLM inference through speculative decoding.

Abstract: Parallel drafting reduces the drafting overhead of speculative decoding for large language models (LLMs), but its gains remain limited by the accepted prefix length. Even when the correct token is present in the candidate pool, a single early selection error prevents subsequent predictions from being used. We propose DRelay, which uses global information from the entire draft block to perform prefix-aware selective repair of candidate selections before target-model verification. DRelay bases its decisions on candidate correlations and the selected path: a global reader extracts predictive information across positions for each candidate. While a causal selector combines candidate-level information extracted by the global read with the tokens selected at preceding positions to determine whether the native choice at the current position is consistent with the global evidence and the selected prefix. It then decides whether to retain or replace the token, thereby repairing early errors and extending the accepted prefix. We further jointly train the draft backbone and the selector, combining candidate-support learning with a repair objective, while weighting the repair loss according to each block position's potential contribution to the consecutive accepted prefix. Across eight diverse benchmarks on an H800 GPU, DRelay consistently improves both average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding performance over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. Under SGLang serving, DRelay improves average end-to-end speedup over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark by 14.7%-16.8%, 8.7%-9.3%, and 8.1%-9.3%, respectively.

</details>


### [369] [A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Personalized Health Checkup Interpretation and Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01451)
*HyungJun Kim,Taehan Lee,Soojin Cheon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a multi-agent LLM system for personalized health checkup result interpretation that identifies multiple intents, maps them to task-specific agents, executes in parallel, and synthesizes outputs. The multi-agent approach significantly outperforms single-agent baseline across multiple evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized interpretation of health checkup results requires reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance, and healthcare navigation - tasks too complex for single-agent LLM systems.

Method: Multi-agent LLM system with intent identification, task-specific agent mapping, parallel execution, and output synthesis. Compared Single Agent vs Multi Agent on 120 Korean compound queries (2-4 requirements) using synthetic health checkup records. Evaluated using 4 LLM judges and 2 human evaluators.

Result: Multi Agent improved weighted LLM-judge score from 1.695 to 1.797 (p=0.027). Three additional LLM judges showed consistent improvements (Δ = +0.111 to +0.186, all p<0.05). Improvements seen in usefulness, consistency, and handling of compound queries. Numerical accuracy and grounding improved under only one judge. Medical safety unchanged; critical failures similar (15.0% vs 13.3%). Human evaluators preferred Multi Agent in 66.7% and 68.3% of comparisons. Latency increased 1.31×, cost increased 2.02×. Improvement concentrated in queries involving personal-record lookup.

Conclusion: Multi-agent LLM architecture significantly improves health checkup result interpretation for compound queries, particularly for personal-record lookup tasks, with acceptable trade-offs in latency and cost. Medical safety remains comparable to single-agent approach.

Abstract: Personalized interpretation of health checkup results requires reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance, and healthcare navigation. We present a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system that identifies multiple intents, maps each to a task-specific agent, executes them in parallel, and synthesizes their outputs. We compared answers generated in Single Agent and Multi Agent settings on 120 Korean compound queries combining two to four requirements, using synthetic health checkup records. The Multi Agent improved the weighted LLM-judge score from 1.695 to 1.797 (p = 0.027), and three additional LLM judges showed consistent improvements ($Δ$ = +0.111 to +0.186, all p < 0.05). The gains came from usefulness, consistency, and the handling of every requirement in compound queries, whereas numerical accuracy and grounding improved significantly under only one of the four judges and medical safety did not differ, and critical failures occurred at similar rates (Single Agent 15.0% vs. Multi Agent 13.3%). Two human evaluators preferred Multi Agent in 66.7% and 68.3% of pairwise comparisons. Multi Agent execution increased latency and cost by 1.31$\times$ and 2.02$\times$, respectively. In exploratory subgroup analyses, the improvement was concentrated in queries involving personal-record lookup.

</details>


### [370] [Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458)
*Shiu-Hong Kao,Yubo Zhao,Zhenyu Tian,Pengzhan Sun,Yicong Li,Angela Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies a failure mode in verifier-free RL for LLMs called the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP), where probability rewards become indistinguishable in long reasoning traces. The authors propose RLCPR, a framework with uncertainty-aware sampling and concentration-aware regularization to address this issue, achieving up to 4.0% improvement on six of seven benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifier-free RL with probability-based rewards lacks external verifiers for general reasoning tasks, and the reliability of these rewards in long-horizon reasoning remains underexplored. The researchers discovered that as reasoning traces become lengthy, the probability of reference answers collapses to a low-variance interval, causing nearly indistinguishable rewards that destabilize GRPO-based optimization.

Method: The authors proposed RLCPR with two components: (1) Uncertainty-aware data sampling to reduce concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and (2) Concentration-aware regularization to penalize unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse.

Result: RLCPR outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks, including general-domain and mathematical reasoning challenges, while achieving higher token efficiency.

Conclusion: The Posterior Concentration Phenomenon is a significant failure mode in probability-based verifier-free RL for LLMs. RLCPR effectively addresses this issue through uncertainty-aware sampling and concentration-aware regularization, providing more stable optimization and better token efficiency across diverse reasoning benchmarks.

Abstract: Verifier-free reinforcement learning with probability-based rewards offers a promising way to train LLMs on general reasoning tasks where external verifiers are unavailable. Yet the reliability of these rewards, especially in long-horizon reasoning, remains underexplored. This work identifies a length-dependent failure mode of probability rewards, which we call the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP). We show that the probability of a reference answer conditioned on a reasoning trace often collapses to a low-variance interval as the trace becomes lengthy. This phenomenon results in nearly indistinguishable rewards, which, under GRPO-based settings, makes probability-based policy optimization unstable and inefficient. Motivated by this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Concentration-aware Posterior Rewards (RLCPR), a verifier-free RL framework to explicitly account for PCP for better optimization stability and token efficiency. It has two components: uncertainty-aware data sampling, which reduces concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and concentration-aware regularization, which penalizes unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse. Extensive experiments show that, alongside higher token efficiency, RLCPR outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks, including general-domain and mathematical reasoning challenges.

</details>


### [371] [NextMe-800: Anticipating Personal Behavior from Months of Egocentric Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01461)
*Zhaoxu Meng,Yiming Sun,Mingyuan Gao,Jiachang Zhang,Zhuhan Dai,Yipeng Du,Zheng Lian,Jian-Qiao Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces NextMe-800, an ~800-hour first-person dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with 1 Hz images, gaze, and audio, annotated at five hierarchical abstraction levels. Combined with EgoLife dataset, they create NextAct, a 1,500-point benchmark for evaluating personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People often plan ambitiously but act habitually, and wish they could have foreseen their actual behavior when making decisions. The goal is to help people formulate more realistic plans by generating plausible trajectories from one's personal history, enabling better-informed decisions.

Method: Collected ~800 hours of egocentric data (1 Hz images, gaze, audio) from one volunteer over 126 days, annotated at 5 hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. Formulated personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction. Created NextAct benchmark combining NextMe-800 with multi-person EgoLife dataset. Used embedding-based soft edit distance as evaluation metric.

Result: The paper presents the dataset and benchmark framework for studying personal behavior anticipation across abstraction levels and prediction horizons. Specific prediction accuracy results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: NextMe-800 and NextAct provide a months-long resource and evaluation framework for studying how far ahead personal behavior can be anticipated from egocentric observation, enabling research on personalized action anticipation at various abstraction levels and prediction horizons.

Abstract: We often plan ambitiously yet act habitually and wonder, in retrospect, whether we would have planned differently had we known what we would actually do. Hindsight offers a valuable perspective on past decisions, although we often wish we could have simulated hindsight at the moment of choosing. If a system could generate plausible trajectories from one's personal history, such previews might help people formulate more realistic plans and make better informed decisions. We introduce NextMe-800, an approximately 800-hour first-person dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with 1 Hz images, gaze, and audio, captioned at five hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. We formulate personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction and construct NextAct, a 1,500-point benchmark combining NextMe-800 with the multi-person EgoLife dataset. Using an embedding-based soft edit distance as the metric, we evaluate how well different models can anticipate personal behavior across abstraction levels and prediction horizons. NextMe-800 and NextAct provide a months-long resource and evaluation framework for studying how far ahead personal behavior can be anticipated from egocentric observation.

</details>


### [372] [Auditing Routing Entropy as an Uncertainty Signal in Attention-Residual Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01495)
*Wenhao Liang,Lin Yue,Wei Emma Zhang,Mingyu Guo,Olaf Maennel,Weitong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether routing entropy in dynamic neural network architectures (Attention-Residual variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small) provides additional information about prediction correctness beyond the model's own confidence scores. The authors conduct multiple tests including fixed-confidence checks, cross-seed replication, and held-out predictor experiments, along with a sensitivity audit with injected effects. The results show that routing signals do not survive multiplicity correction, fail to replicate across seeds, and provide no improvement over confidence-only predictors, though the authors note this establishes "control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery" rather than proving absence of conditional routing information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to audit whether the routing trace (a per-example routing pattern left by dynamic architectures) carries information about prediction reliability that goes beyond what the model's own confidence already reveals. The authors question whether "diffuse routing" can be reliably read as a sign of unreliable predictions.

Method: The authors trained Attention-Residual (AR) variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small from scratch on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss. They performed three main checks: (1) whether routing signals appear at fixed confidence levels, (2) whether results replicate across different training seeds, and (3) whether a held-out predictor can exploit routing information against output-only and shuffled-trace controls. A sensitivity audit was also conducted by injecting effects of known size and measuring recovery rates.

Result: The main findings are: (1) No test in the fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, (2) Neither nominal hits nor borderline results recur across sibling seeds, (3) Across 24 paired runs, a scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration, (4) An entropy-profile probe predicts correctness better than shuffled profiles but worse than confidence-only predictors in both binary log-loss and Brier score, (5) Sensitivity audit: at 0.010 nats injected effect, profile probe recovers 24-59% of oracle gain, and reference-preserving correction probe recovers 8% and 23% in CIFAR-100 settings.

Conclusion: The results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, rather than proving the absence of conditional routing information. The authors acknowledge that their non-detections have bounds—the audit shows partial recovery of injected effects, suggesting routing information may exist but is not reliably detectable with their methods.

Abstract: Dynamic architectures leave a per-example routing trace beside each prediction, and diffuse routing is easy to read as a sign that the prediction is unreliable. We audit that reading for routing entropy in Attention-Residual (AR) variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small, trained from scratch on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss, asking whether the trace carries information about correctness beyond what the model's own confidence already reveals. Three checks probe this increment: does a routing signal appear at fixed confidence, does it replicate across training seeds, and can a held-out predictor exploit it against output-only and shuffled-trace controls? A sensitivity audit then injects effects of known size and measures the fraction of each that the probes recover. No test in the fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, and neither the nominal hit nor a borderline result recurs in its sibling seeds. Across 24 paired runs a scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration, and an entropy-profile probe predicts correctness better than the same probe given shuffled profiles yet worse than a confidence-only predictor in both binary log-loss and Brier score: a gain over shuffled traces does not become a gain over the output. Conditioning on the complete logit vector leaves the corresponding comparison unresolved. The audit bounds how far these non-detections can be read: at an injected effect of 0.010 nats the profile probe recovers 24-59% of the oracle gain, and a reference-preserving correction probe recovers 8% and 23% in the two CIFAR-100 settings, below the threshold we fixed for applying it to real labels. The results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, not the absence of conditional routing information.

</details>
